en: First Chapter: The Procedure for Examining the Ground. First, the procedure for examining the ground is stated.

The patron (yajamāna)—whether a Brāhmaṇa, Kṣatriya, Vaiśya, Śūdra, or even one born of a natural order (anuloma)—should be endowed with all the aforementioned qualities: possessed of faith, orthodox, devoted, increased in wealth and grain, highly energetic, pure, skillful, grateful, and free from greed; and he should seek out a priest who is a knower of the Pāñcarātra, tranquil, one who has exerted himself in the Siddhāntas, born of the lineage of the Lord, pure, free from greed and hypocrisy, sinless, upright, healthy, and one whose supreme faith is not seen [by others].

First, one should select an Ācārya who possesses the characteristics described in such passages as these. Then, on an auspicious day, the Ācārya and the patron (yajamāna), together with an astrologer, should first examine the omens for the establishment of the village and other sites. When the omens are auspicious, one should begin the construction of the village and so forth. For that purpose, the Ācārya, along with a chariot-maker (rathakāra), should inspect the ground. Now, the characteristics of the ground are stated: the ground is of four kinds—Supadmā, Bhadrakā, Pūrṇā, and Dhūmrā.

It is filled with *supadma*, *caṃpaka*, *agaru*, *kharjūra*, *kadaṃba*, *tilaka*, *arjuna*, *kramuka*, *nārikela*, *kuśa*, *kāśa*, *kamala*, and *kuvalaya* plants; it slopes toward the east and north, is surrounded by auspicious waters, and is situated near the Bhadrakā river and the ocean. It is adjacent to sacred fords (*tīrtha*) and shrines (*āyatana*), abounding in milky trees (*kṣīravṛkṣa*), fruit-bearing trees, gardens, groves, creepers, shrubs, sacrificial trees, and fields of *kuśa*, *kāśa*, rice, and water at its base.

A land filled with *pūrṇā*, *kuluttha*, *kaṅku*, *niṣpāva*, *kodrava*, and *śyāmāka* grains; situated on the slopes of a mountain or a mountain peak where water is abundant; crowded with *dhūmra*, barley, bamboo, *snuhī*, *śleṣmātaka*, *vibhītaka*, and *arka* trees; hard and stony; teeming with crows, hawks, vultures, jackals, and wolves; and saline—such ground is known as *supadmā*, which bestows peace; *bhadrakā*, which bestows happiness; *pūrṇā*, which bestows nourishment; and *dhūmrā*, which causes decay. Having recognized the earth as being of such a nature [one should avoid it].

Having dug a pit equal in width and depth to a staff (daṇḍa) and reaching down to the knees, one should fill it again with that very same earth. If it becomes level or even more than full, it is the best; if level, it is middling; if less, it is known as the lowest. Having set aside the lowest, one should examine the other two by sowing seeds of rice, mung beans, barley, and so forth. If sprouts emerge within three nights, it is the best; if within five nights, it is middling; if within seven nights, it is the lowest.

Even when the sprouts have not yet emerged, it is considered inferior; one should avoid the inferior [site] and take another. Where *kuśa*, *palāśa*, and *hariṇa* grasses are found, even that which is inferior becomes superior. That which is endowed with a sweet taste is superior; that which is pungent is middling; those with other tastes, such as sour and so forth, are inferior. That which is white is superior; yellow or red is middling; black is inferior.

Having reflected thus correctly, the preceptor who is learned in the *Pāñcarātra*, together with the patron and the chariot-maker, should circumambulate the boundary of the site clockwise, accompanied by dance, song, instrumental music, auspicious recitations, full water-pots (*pūrṇakumbha*), lamps, banners, and parasols, along with the study of the Vedas and the chanting of benedictions (*svastivācana*). Then, in all the cardinal and intermediate directions, beginning from the east, he should perform the ritual offering of oblations (*balikarma*) with milk-rice (*pāyasa*) for the Piśācas and other spirits, extending as far as the station of Brahmā.

"May the bhūtas, piśācas, nāgas, asuras, rākṣasas, and grahas—all of them—depart as they please, satisfied by this offering. I duly prepare the place for the gods and the twice-born, and for the divine Vāsudeva, who is the soul of all beings. Reciting this mantra, he scattered white mustard seeds consecrated with the Astra-mantra on all sides. Having offered the bali according to the prescribed rule, he laid down the lines there, and fixed stakes at the intersections of the lines.

Then, one should perform the ritual worship of Vāstupati according to the rules. Having drawn the figure of Vāstupuruṣa with his face downward, his head toward the east, and his hands and feet extended toward the corners, and having invoked and worshipped him; one should kindle the fire, duly consecrated in either a fire-pit or a sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila), to the south of Vāstupuruṣa.

Having invoked him [the deity] into that [fire], one should offer a thousand or a hundred oblations of ghee with the five Upaniṣads, and likewise offer as many oblations with fuel-sticks (*samidh*) of *apāmārga*, *śamī*, and *khadira*. Then, having personally offered oblations into the fire with the aforementioned fuel-sticks for the *yakṣas*, *rakṣasas*, and *piśācas* in the previously mentioned number, one should then offer one hundred and eight oblations separately with the two root mantras (*mūlamantra*), and one hundred oblations of sacrificial porridge (*caru*) with the mantra of the Lord of the Site (*vāstunātha*). Finally, having offered the final oblation (*pūrṇāhuti*) and dismissed the deity residing in the fire.

One should offer oblations (bali) to Indra and the other deities in the eight directions with their respective mantras. Thus ends the first chapter, titled "The Procedure for Examining the Ground," in the *Kriyākairavacandrikā* composed by the venerable Varāhaguru. Between giving and protecting [a gift], protecting is superior to giving. Through giving, one attains heaven; through protecting, the imperishable state (*acyuta-pada*). He who seizes land given by himself or given by another shall be born as a worm in excrement for sixty thousand years.

The merit of protecting what has been given by another is twice that of what one has given oneself. By seizing what has been given by another, one’s own gift becomes fruitless. In this world, there is but one sister for all kings: the earth given by Viṣṇu, which must never be enjoyed nor ever seized.
The Second Chapter:
Ploughing.
Now the procedure for plowing is described.

Having thus prepared the village and so forth, one should approach the previously mentioned ground intended for the construction of a temple in its center, preceded by an offering (bali). After circumambulating it clockwise, one should scatter white mustard seeds consecrated with the Astra-mantra in all directions, reciting the mantra: "O Yakṣas, Piśācas, and Nāgas who always dwell here, may you all depart elsewhere; I am preparing a place for Viṣṇu. Then, as before, one should perform the Vāstupūjā and the Homa, ending with the bali offering.

Immediately thereafter, the preceptor should plow the ground with a plough according to the procedure to be described. If the patron is a Brāhmaṇa, there should be two oxen that are not castrated and are white in color; if he is a Kṣatriya, they should be red; if a Vaiśya, yellow; and if a Śūdra, dark blue. In the event that oxen of the specified colors are unavailable, they may be tawny, white, or red. Having washed those two large and powerful bulls, [one should proceed].

One should decorate the hooves, horns, and other parts with golden ornaments. If the sacrificer is a Brāhmaṇa, the yoke and the plough should be made of *pālāśa* wood; if a Kṣatriya, of *naiyagrodha* (fig) wood; if a Vaiśya, of *plākṣa* (fig) wood. For all castes, however, they may be of *naiyagrodha* or *paippala* wood. For all, the thong (*yoktra*) should be made of *kauśika* grass, gold, silver, or copper. The rope should be made of *kuśa*, *dhanus-jyā* (bowstring), *vīraṇa* grass, or *kāśa* grass, respectively, according to the caste.

Having performed all this for those who have become like bulls and share a single womb, the preceptor—having bathed, put on new garments, and adorned himself with all ornaments—should wash his feet, perform the ritual sipping of water (ācamana), practice breath control (prāṇāyāma), and perform the purification of the elements (bhūtaśuddhi). Then, permitted by the Brahmins and accompanied by Vaiṣṇavas who are knowers of the mantras, he should cause the declaration of an auspicious day (puṇyāha-vācana) to be made. Having sprinkled all the materials and himself with that water, he should fasten the yoke to the shoulder of the bull using the root mantra (mūlamantra).

Having yoked the plow to the pole with that very mantra at an auspicious moment, preceded by the sounding of drums, kettledrums, conchs, and other instruments, and accompanied by the chanting of Vedic hymns such as the *Śākuna-sūkta*, the Guru—facing east and meditating on Nārāyaṇa within the lotus of his heart—should make a palāśa or similar staff serve as a vehicle. Then, taking the goad and pressing it with the syllables *huṃ phaṭ* and so forth, he should first draw [the plow] while facing east, using the root-mantra (*mūla-vidyā*).

The second furrow is made with the *Pauruṣa Sūkta*, the third with the *Viṣṇu Sūkta*, the fourth with the *Viṣṇu Gāyatrī*, the fifth with the *Nārāyaṇa Anuvāka*, the sixth with the mantras of the five Upaniṣads, and the seventh furrow with the *Bhū Sūkta*. All are performed in a clockwise direction; one should thus plow from south to north. At that time, one should examine the omens: the satisfaction of the preceptor’s mind and the well-being of the temple and the patron [are signs of success].

And the opposite of that leads to unhappiness. If the two oxen lie down, if the yoke or other equipment breaks, if there is confusion or wandering about, or if any other cause arises, one should offer one hundred oblations of ghee with the five Upaniṣads for the sake of pacifying all defects. Then, the preceptor and the patron, having satisfied the Brāhmaṇas, should level that ground with great effort, have separate basins provided along with water channels, and having sprinkled it with water, they should sow seeds such as rice, mung beans, barley, and so forth.

For the sake of its growth, one should water it daily with a large amount of water and protect it until the stage of full ripening. Then, having harvested the ripe fruits and brought the cows to graze upon the field cleared of fruit, that abode will yield abundant crops for a long time; however, if the yield is small, it will last for a shorter period. The presence of Hari remains as before. But when the field is devoid of fruit, one's wealth and grain will be exhausted; in that case, one should feed a thousand or a hundred Brahmins.

Having bestowed upon them sacrificial fees such as cows and wealth, and having sprinkled that site with the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*) while reciting the five Upaniṣads, one should dig the ground with spades or shovels to whatever extent is required.

To the extent of the width of the first enclosure, one should dig into the ground—either to the depth of a staff, in accordance with the defects of the site, or in proportion to the height of the temple. Upon seeing ash, charcoal, husks, impure substances, living beings, insects, or the like, one should perform a propitiatory *homa* with clarified butter and other offerings, and give gold or other gifts as a sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) to the Brahmins according to one’s capacity. Upon seeing gems and such, the abode shall always be prosperous. Outside the excavation, on a square altar (*sthaṇḍila*), [one should establish] the fire.

Having performed the installation, one should perform the *khātahoma* (pit-offering) with clarified butter using the *mūlamantra*, with the *nṛsūkta*, and with *caru* made of guggulu, sesame, and wild rice (*nīvāra*), while reciting the *mūlamantra*; then, having caused the proclamation of an auspicious day (*puṇyāha*) and having sprinkled [the site] with water.

Having cast rice grains into [the pits] and placed upon them nine jars—either made of metal or clay—wrapped with cloth, thread, and so forth; having placed a golden *ādhāra-śakti* in the central jar; and having placed seeds in the east, all metals in the southeast, all minerals in the south, earth from sacred bathing places (*puṇyatīrtha*) in the southwest, honey in the west, clarified butter (*sarpiḥ*) in the northwest, gems in the northern direction, and mountain soil in the northeast; and furthermore, having placed earth from a rice field in the center.

Having dried the mud produced from a lake and the mud from an anthill, as well as lotus bulbs, he stands facing the east and casts them [into the central jar]. Having placed therein metals, gems, and a bundle of *darbha* grass, and having covered it with a shallow bowl (*śarāva*), he places another jar upon the middle jar; in that [upper jar], he places a golden tortoise and the Fire of Time (*kālāgni*). Upon that, he places another jar; in that, he places a golden image of Ananta.

Upon that, one should place another pitcher; upon that, a golden earth; and upon that, another pitcher; and upon that, having placed a golden lotus, one should fill all [the vessels] with scented water. Having filled [the pit] with sacred earth from a sacrificial site and with pure sand, and having filled the excavated ground with water and made it firm with the feet of elephants, one should fill it again with water.
Thus ends the second chapter, titled "The Procedure for Ploughing," in the *Kriyākairavacandrikā* composed by the venerable Varāhaguru.
The Third Chapter.
The Ritual for the Consecration of the Child-Abode (Bālālaya-pratiṣṭhā-vidhi). Now, the ritual for the consecration of the child-abode is described.

One should construct the child-abode in a location of one’s own preference within the temple currently under construction, situated between Indra and Īśāna, or Soma and Indra, or Yama and Nairṛta, or Nairṛta and Varuṇa, or Varuṇa and Vāyu, or Vāyu and Soma.

There, one should construct the Bālālaya (the nursery temple) with seven, five, or three cubits [in size]. One should place the Bālālaya in the very same direction as the *valaja* (the surrounding wall or enclosure) of the main temple. The image of the Child (Bālabimba) should be made of metal, stone, or wood, possessing four arms and holding the conch, discus, mace, and lotus. Depending on the decrease in height, it should be five *aṅgulas*, or upon increase, twenty-three *aṅgulas*; or it may be made according to a measurement that brings comfort to the patron (*yajamāna*). This applies to the incarnations such as Matsya and others who are to be installed in the main temple.

Alternatively, having caused a child-form (*bālabimba*) of such a kind to be made—specifically four-armed for the Viśvarūpa form—and likewise a child-form for the standing, sitting, and reclining postures; having performed the preliminary rite of offering the sprouts (*aṅkurārpaṇa*), the consecration in water (*adhivāsa*), the installation of the pitcher (*kumbhasthāpana*), the consecration, the fire-oblation (*homa*), and so forth; and having prepared an altar (*vedikā*) in the center or the divine portion of the child’s house, three cubits in height and provided with three girdles (*mekhalā*);

At dawn, during an auspicious moment, having installed the deity according to the prescribed rites—excluding the fourth bath of the *śaktinyāsa*—and having sprinkled [the deity] and applied the mantras, one should worship him. Then, from the commencement of the foundation until its completion: "O Lord Hari, O All-pervading One! O Blessed One, accept this worship in this temple for the child. Subduing the obstacles caused by the demons associated with the original sanctuary."

Having thus prayed with this mantra, made the request, and prostrated, one should worship Caṇḍa and Pracaṇḍa at the door, the Kṣetrapālas and the lords of birds (khageśas), the world-protectors such as Indra and others in their respective directions, Seneśa in the northeast (īśāna) quarter, and Gaṇeśa in the southwest (naiṛta). Having worshipped all these bodiless deities on altars (vedikās) or similar sacrificial mounds (sthaṇḍilas)—which are either circular or square and provided with three girdles (mekhalās) at a distance of one cubit (hastamātra) all around the child’s temple—one should then honor all the hosts of Kumuda and the other attendants upon the great pedestal (mahāpīṭha).

The Guru, having thus consecrated the temple for the child-form (bāla), should at the conclusion perform a festival beginning with the hoisting of the flag and ending with the flower-sacrifice (puṣpayāga), or else a single-day festival. If the image of the child is made of metal, one should perform all the daily and other rites with that very image. If it is not for the purpose of a festival, one should fashion the image from the child-form itself. If the child-image is made of stone or wood, one should first procure the timber or the stone and then consecrate the child-image. Regarding the procedure for constructing the temple: subsequently, the chariot-maker (rathakāra), together with the architects (sthapati), shall begin the construction of the temple.

In that regard, having thoroughly understood the distinctions between the primary, middle, and inferior types, as well as those that are accumulated, unaccumulated, or partially accumulated—such as stones, bricks, wood, and so forth—and having correctly identified defects such as flaws in the foundation, and other defects such as the site being occupied by another deity's temple, one should construct the main temple. Having observed the levelness of the excavated ground with water and having established the *prakṛti* (the foundational principle) upon the earth, one should take up the first plank with the eye of the scriptures and strengthen it with lime, observing its levelness with water.

Above that is the *upapīṭha*, and above that is the *adhiṣṭhāna*; one may conceive of the *adhiṣṭhāna* even without the *upapīṭha*. Alternatively, having established the *adhiṣṭhāna*, or whatever was previously the *adhiṣṭhāna*, one should construct the *upānaha* above it, the *pāda* above that, then the *prastara*, followed by the *grīvā*, and then the *śikhara*; thus, in the construction of a single story (*ekatala*), one should proceed according to this sequence as far as the *stūpikā*.

In the conception of two stories (*dvitala*), however, there are the base (*adhiṣṭhāna*), the plinth (*caraṇa*), the stone course (*prastara*), the pinnacle chamber (*kūṭaśālā*), the framework (*pañjara*), the stone course, the altar-platform (*vedikā*), the neck (*grīvā*), and the spire (*śikhara*). In this same sequence, from three stories up to twelve stories, it is exactly the same. Beyond that, for those [temples] with more stories, there are the pedestal (*upānaha*), the plinth (*jagatī*), the *kumuda* band, the neck-band (*kaṇṭhapaṭṭikā*), the great band (*mahatīpaṭṭikā*), the cornice (*vājana*), the altar-platform, the floor of the plinth (*caraṇatala*), the upper [moulding], the row of swans (*haṃsamālā*), the pigeon-niches (*kapota*), the individual altar-frames (*prativedikā*), the neck, and the spire (*śikhara*). Thus, this is the arrangement up to eighteen stories, ending with the finial (*stūpī*).

Or one may act according to the suitability of the patron (*yajamāna*). Having first constructed everything, such as the cloth [mandala] and so forth, according to the rules, one should thereafter construct the temple. Thus ends the third chapter, titled "The Ritual for the Installation of the Child-Abode" (*bālālayapratiṣṭhāvidhi*), in the *Kriyākairavacandrikā* composed by the venerable Varāhaguru.
The Fourth Chapter:
The Ritual for the First Brick (*prathameṣṭakāvidhi*).
Now, the procedure for the first brick is described.

First, the preceptor, having examined the east according to the path prescribed in the scriptures and having determined the orientation of the doors according to the divisions of the east and so forth, should bring a beautiful, straight peg made from a milky tree (kṣīravṛkṣa), twenty-four or twelve finger-breadths in length and one thumb-breadth in circumference. Having established it in the central part of the site of the temple with the root mantra, he should observe the shadows at the eastern and western ends of the circle surrounding the peg at a distance twice its length.

Having drawn two dots, one in the east and one in the west, at the edge of the inner circle within the shadow; having laid a string from the eastern dot to the western dot through the middle of those two; and having arranged the space between them so that it resembles the mouth and tail of a tortoise; then, having done exactly the same in the north and the south.

In this manner, having laid out threads in the four directions measuring three, five, seven, or more cubits as desired, one should draw the outline so that it becomes perfectly square by rotating the directional threads. One should then properly fix stakes at the eight cardinal points. At the time of fixing the stakes, one should examine the omens; if they are auspicious, the result will be auspicious, but if they are contrary, one should perform a propitiatory rite (*śānti*). Having understood the distinctions between the square, circular, oval, and rectangular shapes in accordance with the various forms of the deity—whether standing, seated, reclining, or moving—one should proceed accordingly.

If the patron desires worldly enjoyment (*bhukti*), he should measure with even numbers of cubits; if he seeks liberation (*mokṣa*), with odd numbers. Having measured the temple (*prāsāda*) from one cubit up to ten cubits, or up to twelve finger-breadths (*aṅgula*) according to his means, and having constructed the *vimāna* therein, he should begin with the first brick (*iṣṭakā*).

The [image] is of three kinds, distinguished as being made of brick, stone, or wood. In a temple made of stone, [the image] should be made of stone; in one made of wood, of wood; in one made of baked bricks, of well-baked bricks; in one made of unbaked bricks, of unbaked bricks; and in one made of both stone and wood, or of both stone and wood, it should be made of stone; while in a shrine made of bricks and wood, it should be made of brick, using the first brick for the foundation. Having collected stones for the sake of the image according to the ritual procedure for collecting stones, one should perform an examination of their gender and other characteristics.

One should fashion the image from the base up to the pinnacle using a male stone (*pulliṅgaśilā*), the first brick (*prathameṣṭakā*) using a female stone (*strīśilā*), and the topmost brick (*mūrdheṣṭakā*) using a neuter stone (*napuṃsakaśilā*). Wooden bricks (*dārviṣṭakā*) should also be selected according to the same procedure as the collection of wood for an image. If these are made in reverse, there is great fault, resulting in the ruin of the king and his kingdom. Regarding the sound when struck: that stone which produces the sound of a bronze bell (*kāṃsya-ghaṇṭā*) at the top, the sound of bronze in the middle, and the sound of a palm-clap (*tāla*) at the base is a male stone (*puṃśilā*). Therefore, one with slightly less sound is a female stone (*strīśilā*).

A stone that lacks resonance becomes a neuter stone. Now, regarding the procedure for bricks made of clay: first, the teacher, having reached the site designated by the chariot-maker, should establish the sacred fire there, preceded by the *puṇyāha* (auspicious day) ceremony.

When this [fire] has been kindled, one should offer one hundred and eight oblations of clarified butter with the root mantra; sixteen oblations of sacrificial porridge (*caru*) with the *Puruṣasūkta*; and one hundred and eight oblations of fuel sticks (*samidh*). Having offered again with the root mantra, one should offer oblations of clarified butter ending with the word "svāhā," accompanied by the seven vyāhṛtis beginning with *bhūr*, dedicated to Viṣṇu’s attendants, to the guardian of the field (*kṣetrapāla*), to the spirits (*bhūta*), to the Lord of the Site (*vāstunātha*), to the gods, to the sages (*ṛṣi*), and to the host of deities. Finally, having offered the full oblation (*pūrṇāhuti*), [the rite is complete].

Having offered an oblation of *caru* with these mantras ending in *namaḥ*—"To Viṣṇu, to the attendants, to all beings, to the Lord of the Site (*Vāstunātha*), and to the Guardian of the Field (*Kṣetrapāla*)"—in the four directions beginning with the east, and having extinguished the fire, one should have bricks made by a potter. Among those, first is the *puruṣeṣṭakā*, which has straight, even lines; second is the *strīṣṭakā*, which has transverse, uneven lines; and third is the *napuṃsakeṣṭakā*, which has no lines or has curved lines on its sides.

The first [measurement] is for the construction of palaces and the like; the second is for the construction of seats (pīṭha) and the like; the third is for the construction of the consecration of the womb-chamber (garbhādhāna) and so forth of a palace. If its length is one cubit, it is excellent; if its length is eighteen finger-breadths (aṅgula), it is middling; if its length is sixteen finger-breadths, it is inferior. The width is half the length, and the thickness is half the width. The roof-tiles (iṣṭakā) should have a width equal to the length. This is the "great measurement" (mahāmāna), where the width is equal to the palace [itself]. The "small measurement" (alpamāna) has a width that is double that [of the palace] and a length that is double that [of the small measurement].

Having thus caused the bricks to be made, one should prepare them so that they are baked, auspicious, and firm. In a temple, there should be four primary bricks; in a human dwelling, five. It should be understood that in a structure made of baked bricks, the primary bricks are likewise baked, and so forth. Then, having prepared either a pavilion (maṇḍapa) or a water-shed (prapā), and having adorned it with canopies and other ornaments, one should construct an altar in its center measuring seven palm-trees in length and one cubit in height. This should be done following the collection of clay and the offering of the auspicious sprouts (aṅkurārpaṇa).

Then, having prepared a sacrificial mound (*sthaṇḍila*) in the center of the altar with four *bhāras* of rice, half that amount of unhusked grain (*taṇḍula*) on top of that, and half that amount of sesame seeds on top of that; having covered it with new, unwashed cloths arranged in alternating layers; and having placed upon it nine jars—each possessing the proper marks, wrapped in thread and cloth, containing gems, golden *kūrca*-grass, and *pippala* leaves—one should arrange them there. On the northern side of that altar, having prepared a pedestal of grain as before and having strewn *darbha* grass for the consecration of the bricks (*iṣṭakādhivāsa*).

Having had the *puṇyāha* (declaration of an auspicious day) recited, and having placed nine jars endowed with the previously mentioned characteristics upon a pedestal of grain for the purpose of the ceremonial bath (*snāna*), one should fill them from Brahmā to Īśāna with clarified butter, milk, curd, molasses, the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*), fruit juice, perfumes, metals, and honey; then, having wrapped them with cloth, one should invoke and worship, in sequence, Paravāsudeva, Puruṣa, Satya, Acyuta, Ananta, Keśava, Nārāyaṇa, Mādhava, and Govinda. Then, taking four bricks in the feminine form...

Having preceded the rite with the declaration of an auspicious day (*puṇyāha*), having invoked and worshipped Vāsudeva and the other deities, and having established them upon the pedestal, he should bathe them with milk while reciting the *payovrata-sāman*; with jaggery while reciting "madhu vātā"; with water infused with fruit while reciting "yāḥ phalinīḥ"; with water infused with metal while reciting the "hiraṇyagarbha" mantra; with curd while reciting "dadhi krāvṇaḥ"; with the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*) while reciting "pañcavāruṇikā"; with scented water while reciting "gandhadvārām"; with honey while reciting "madhu vātā"; and with ghee while reciting the "ghṛtasnāti" *sāman*.

Having wrapped each brick individually with a pair of cloths and *darbha* grass, having caused the proclamation of an auspicious day (*puṇyāha*), and having sprinkled them with water, one should consecrate the bricks upon the bed. Then, having installed the archways and water-pots at the eastern and other doors, and having invoked and worshipped their respective deities, one should invoke the Supreme Self into the central pot previously established and Viṣṇu and the others into the eight subsidiary pots, and worship them. Having offered milk-rice and rice mixed with jaggery as oblations, one should bring fire to the sacrificial pits or altars situated to the east or north of that [bed].

Having again offered oblations according to the rules with fuel-sticks (*samidh*), clarified butter (*ājya*), and cooked rice (*caru*), and separately offering one hundred and eight oblations each with fuel-sticks, clarified butter, sesame seeds, and flowers, as well as oblations of cooked rice accompanied by the *Nṛsūkta*, he should collect the residual clarified butter (*saṃpātājya*) in another vessel. With that, he should touch the bricks while reciting the *sparśamantra*. Then, having made the formal resolve (*saṃkalpa*)—"I shall perform the rite of binding the *pratisara* (protective cord)"—he should sprinkle the *pratisara* with water from the *puṇyāha* ceremony and bind it with *pratisaras* made of gold or cotton while reciting the *astramantra*.

Having offered one hundred and eight oblations of clarified butter with the mantra, “Oṃ hrīṃ svaṃ svapnādhipataye svāhā,” the preceptor shall then lie down upon a bed of *darbha* grass together with the patron for the purpose of seeing dreams. If the dream is auspicious, the result will be auspicious; if inauspicious, he shall perform a propitiatory fire-oblation (*śānti-homa*). When the night has dawned, at an auspicious moment, he shall take the bricks along with the officiating priests, circumambulate the sacred site (*dhāma*), and enter within.

To the south of the prepared entrance, at the base of the foot [of the image], one should place [the materials] accompanied by the chanting of the Vedas and the sounding of musical instruments. Moving clockwise from Indra to Soma, one should lay down the bricks in the Temple of Śrī with the Root Mantra and the Śrīsūkta. One should ensure that the base is toward the southwest and the tip is toward the northeast. One should place it so that the shoes do not become uneven. All rites should be performed preceded by the declaration of an auspicious day (apuṇyāha).

Then the patron (yajamāna) shall give to the preceptor (guru) a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) consisting of garments and ornaments, amounting to one hundred niṣkas; half of that to the officiating priests (ṛtvij), and half of that to the attendants. Thus ends the fourth chapter, named "The Rule for the First Brick.
Chapter Five: The Deposition of the Embryo (garbhanyāsa).
Now, the procedure for the deposition of the embryo (garbhanyāsa) is described.

Having prepared the central altar as before, one should smear the central altar with cow dung. Upon it, having constructed a sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila) covered with cloth, using four measures of rice, half that amount of husked grain (taṇḍula) on top of that, and half that amount of sesame seeds on top of that, arranged in successive layers; and having placed in the center a great jar (mahākumbha) covered with cloth, jewels, metal, a brush (kūrca), and a leaf of the holy fig tree (pippala), and having set around it eight jars made of copper.

Having filled [the jars] with scented water, and having placed golden conch, discus, mace, sword, Śārṅga bow, and pestle in the central jar, one should invoke Vasudhā into it with "Oṃ hrīṃ, obeisance to Vasudhā; come, come! and worship her with perfumes and other offerings. Then, having invoked Indra and the other deities into the eight jars and worshipped them, [one proceeds].

One should take earth from a mountain, a lake, a sacred bathing place (puṇyatīrtha), an anthill, the dwelling of a crab, a river, the tip of a bull's horn, the tusk of an elephant, the ocean, and where a plough has been turned; as well as the five tubers—kumuda, aravinda, kaśeru, utpala, and nīlotpala; the seven minerals—realgar, yellow orpiment, collyrium, black lead, red arsenic, yellow ochre, and mercury; and the gems known as diamond, cat’s-eye, pearl, crystal, topaz, moonstone, sapphire, ruby, and conch-shell.

One should collect the nine gems; the nine seeds—rice, wild rice, *kaṅgu*, *priyaṅgu*, sesame, black gram, green gram, barley, and bamboo seed; and these nine items—gold, silver, copper, iron, tin, lead, gold (again), a tortoise, and a conch-shell marked with a discus.

The womb-vessel (*garbhapātra*) should be made of gold, silver, copper, or iron; in their absence, it may be made of wood. It should be sixteen *aṅgulas* in length, with a width of either twelve, eight, or four *aṅgulas*, and a height of half that [width]. It should be provided with four feet or three, be circular or square, and have a lid. Having caused sixteen or nine pits to be made in its center, one should cause the day of merit (*puṇyāha*) to be proclaimed, sprinkle [the vessel] with water, and wash it with the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*).

Having consecrated [the disciple] with water from the nine jars situated on the altar while reciting the Vedas and other mantras, one should prepare a sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila) on that very same altar as before. Having wrapped that vessel with a cloth containing *darbha* grass, one should place it in the center of the altar. Into its sixteen pits, one should deposit substances beginning with gold and ending with earth from the ocean; or, in their absence, one may simply deposit gold alone. However, according to the procedure for nine pits, one should first pour earth from the ocean into those nine excellent pits.

In the eastern pit: mountain earth, soft lotus-root, realgar, diamond, rice, and gold; in the southern: sacred bathing-place earth, tuber, yellow orpiment, lapis lazuli, wild rice, and silver; in the western: river earth, emerald, blue lotus-root, collyrium, *kaṅgu* grain, and copper; in the northern: lake earth, *kaśeru* root, topaz, millet, and woolen cloth; in the south-eastern: earth from a crab’s lair, sulphate of iron, crystal, black gram, and *trapuṣa* fruit; in the south-western: anthill earth, *saurāṣṭra* clay, pearl, sesame, and bell-metal; in the north-western: ploughshare earth.

Having placed—by means of the root mantra (mūlamantra)—images of a tortoise made of yellow pigment (rocanā), moonstone (candrakānta), mung bean (mudga), and gold; and [images of] an elephant’s tusk, earth from the northeast, sapphire (mahānīla), red ochre (gairika), bamboo, grain, conch, and gold; and at the station of Brahmā (brahmapada), images of the tip of a bull’s horn, earth, lotus-root (padmakanda), ruby (padmarāga), mercury (pārada), barley (yava), and a golden discus; and having worshipped that lotus with the Viṣṇu-gāyatrī; one should duly kindle the fire in either a sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) or on a sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila).

Having offered one hundred and eight oblations with fuel sticks and clarified butter while reciting the six-syllabled mantra of Viṣṇu, and having collected the remaining clarified butter (saṃpātājya) into another vessel, he should offer sixteen oblations of the sacrificial porridge (caru) while reciting the Puruṣasūkta.

Immediately thereafter, having offered oblations of *caru* mixed with sesame and clarified butter, beginning with the syllable *Oṃ* and ending with *svāhā*, to Indra and the other world-protectors (*lokapālas*), to the worlds (*bhuvanās*), to the mountains (*parvatās*), to the oceans (*samudrās*), to the Ādityas, to the Vasus, to the Maruts, to the Ṛṣis, to the Vedas, to all the Śāstras, to the Purāṇas, to the netherworlds (*pātālās*), to the directions (*diśas*), to the Nāgas, to the Gaṇas, to all beings (*sarvabhūtās*), to the lords of men (*narendrās*), to the lunar mansions (*nakṣatras*), and to all the planets (*grahas*).

Having sprinkled the womb-vessel with the *sampāta* clarified butter previously collected, reciting: "Oṃ Dhīṃ, salutation to the Supreme, the red-colored one, whose essence is the subtle element of touch," and having offered the final oblation (*pūrṇāhuti*), he should take that vessel at an auspicious hour during the night amidst the sound of Vedic chanting and musical instruments. Having circumambulated the temple of the deity and entered the inner sanctum, he should divide the right side of the door into three parts while facing inward; then, leaving aside two parts, [he should place it in the remaining third].

On one side near the door, at the foot of a tree on a panel for the deities, the Brāhmaṇa should perform the placement of the embryo (*garbhanyāsa*); if he is the patron (*yajamāna*), he should place it there; if he is a king, upon a lily (*kumuda*); if a Vaiśya, below the lily; and if a Śūdra, within the enclosure of the ground. If the placement is done contrary to what has been stated, a great fault arises. Therefore, one must not cause a displacement from the proper location. Then the Preceptor, having meditated upon the orb of the earth together with its mountains, islands, oceans, and directional elephants, situated upon the circle of the hoods of the lord of serpents, Śeṣa;

Having meditated upon himself as Keśava—two-armed, dark-complexioned, adorned with all ornaments—and upon the Earth, who has bathed after her menses, likewise adorned with every ornament; and having smeared the pit serving as the receptacle for the embryo with cow’s urine, he should place the vessel containing the embryo into that pit while reciting this mantra: “O beloved upholder of all beings, adorned with mountains for breasts and clothed by the ocean, O Goddess, take refuge in this womb! Having thus placed the vessel for the embryo in that pit, he should cover it according to the prescribed rite and make it firm with mortar.

One should provide protection on all sides. Then, in the event of the miscarriage of the embryo or any ill omen, one should perform the expiation (*prāyaścitta*) as previously described. If one should construct a village or a palace without having performed the rite of depositing the embryo (*garbhanyāsa*), then both shall soon go to ruin. At that time, the patron (*yajamāna*) should give the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) to the preceptor (*guru*) in the number previously mentioned. Thus ends the fifth chapter, titled "The Rule for Depositing the Embryo.
The sixth chapter: The rule for the *mūrdheṣṭakā* (the "head-brick") is now stated.

Having first prepared a pavilion or a water-shed in the east, together with two altars in the center; having, on the central altar, prepared a sacrificial mound (*sthaṇḍila*) as before using rice, *śāli* rice, husked rice, and sesame seeds, covered with cloth; and having placed upon it nine jars possessing the previously mentioned characteristics, following the rite for an auspicious day (*puṇyāha*); and having likewise prepared a sacrificial mound on the second altar for the consecration of the bricks (*iṣṭakādhivāsa*), having spread *darbha* grass; [one declares: "I shall perform the ritual bathing for the purification of the head-bricks."

Having thus made the resolve and caused the declaration of an auspicious day (*puṇyāha*) to be recited; having established nine jars there, endowed with the proper characteristics; and having prepared them according to the specific distinctions mentioned previously; having filled them from Brahmā to Īśāna with substances such as clarified butter as before; and having invoked and worshipped their presiding deities therein as before; one should take four neuter bricks (*napuṃsakeṣṭakā*), cause the declaration of an auspicious day to be recited, sprinkle them with water, invoke Vāsudeva and the others into them, worship them, and place them upon the pedestal.

Having consecrated those [images] individually and in sequence with the nine pitchers using their respective mantras; having wrapped them individually with fresh garments along with *darbha* grass; having caused the proclamation of an auspicious day (*puṇyāha*) and having sprinkled [them]; having laid them down upon the sacrificial mound (*sthaṇḍila*) on the previously constructed second altar; having installed the door-arches and the pitchers as before; having invoked and worshipped the respective deities; and having invoked the Supreme Self (*paramātman*) in the central pitcher of the middle altar and Viṣṇu and the others in the eight subsidiary pitchers and worshipped them; [one should offer] milk-rice (*pāyasānna*).

Having offered oblations on the altar in the four cardinal directions, having performed the *adhivāsa-homa* for the temple and the *śānti-homa* in the eight directions, and having collected the residual clarified butter (*saṃpātājya*), he should touch those [threads] with the *sparśa-mantra*. Then, as before, he should bind the *pratisara* (protective cord) following the previous sūtras beginning with the formal resolve (*saṃkalpa*). Thereafter, having made the resolve, "I shall perform the rite of ablution with twenty-five pitchers," and having caused the declaration of an auspicious day (*puṇyāha-vācana*) to be recited, and having sprinkled [the area], he should lay down ten threads extending eastward and as many extending northward. When that has been done:

There are eighty-one squares in total. Among them, having leveled two rows on each side surrounding the central nine-square area for the sake of the pitchers (*kumbha*), one should place three pitchers each in the cardinal directions from the east to the north-west, and one pitcher each in the intermediate directions from the south-east to the north-east, upon a sacrificial mound (*sthaṇḍila*) made of rice, husked grain, and sesame seeds.

Having filled the nine central jars in sequence from Brahmā to Īśāna with ghee, warm water, the nine gems, fruits, the seven metals, cleansing agents, perfumes, unbroken rice, and barley; having filled the four jars situated in the cardinal directions starting from the East in order with water for the feet (pādya), water for the honor-offering (arghya), water for sipping (ācamana), and the five products of the cow (pañcagavya); having filled the four jars situated in the corners starting from the Southeast with curd, milk, honey, and decoctions; and having filled the eight jars situated at the sides with pure water; and having placed the specific substances therein according to the previously mentioned particulars—in these jars containing the ritual materials:

Having invoked the deities beginning with Paravāsudeva and ending with Dāmodara, as well as Nārāyaṇa, into the jars of pure water and having worshipped them, the patron and the preceptor then bathe; adorned with garments, rings, and other ornaments, and having fasted, they spread *darbha* grass there.

Meditating upon the Supreme Person (Paramapuruṣa), he should lie down. At dawn, at an auspicious moment, having fulfilled his duties, the preceptor (Guru) shall bathe the bricks with water from twenty-five jars and the great pitcher (Mahākumbha) using the root mantra (Mūlamantra); having worshipped them and enveloped them with water and cloths by means of the root mantra; and having placed them upon the heads of all the officiating priests (Ṛtviks) who are fully adorned; then, accompanied by the sound of Vedic recitations and musical instruments, having circumambulated the temple (Dhāma), he shall place the bricks on the upper surface of the pavilion (Vimāna).

Having caused the proclamation of an auspicious day (*puṇyāha-vācana*), the preceptor (*ācārya*), facing east and meditating on Nārāyaṇa within his heart-lotus, should place the bricks with the *praṇava* (Om) according to the sequence of the directions starting from the east. At that time, he should expel those afflicted by sin or disease, as well as those born of inverse unions (*pratiloma*), from outside. Thereafter, the patron (*yajamāna*), having bowed his head to the Guru, should give great sacrificial fees (*mahādakṣiṇā*) consisting of cows, land, gold, ornaments, female and male slaves, vehicles, umbrellas, chowries, sandals, and so forth; and likewise, he should honor the chariot-maker (*rathakāra*) with garments, food, wealth, grain, and other gifts.

One should satisfy [the deities]. Herein, the procedure for the finial pin (*sthūpikākīla*) is described: the finial pin may be made of gold, silver, copper, or wood, free from bends and knots; its width and length should correspond to the measurement of the height of the head and the base [of the stupa]. Its tip should be one finger-breadth in measure, and it should be fashioned as circular, square, or five-sided, with a size equal to the neck of the temple (*vimāna*), or one and a half times that measure, or twice that measure.

In circular and square vimānas, the finial-pins (sthūpikākīla) should be in pairs; in other vimānas, they should be single. Up to twenty, they may be in pairs; up to nineteen, they may be single. In the circular, hexagonal, and octagonal sanctuaries, the finial-pins should be arranged in this same manner. Having thus prepared the pins—

The preceptor, having performed for it all the rites according to rule—beginning with the consecration (*adhivāsa*) and bathing (*snāna*), and ending with the installation (*āropaṇa*) of the pinnacle brick (*iṣṭakā*)—and having brought the ritual stake (*kīla*) to the top of the temple (*vimāna*), the preceptor then causes the proclamation of an auspicious day (*puṇyāha*) to be made there. Having deposited the nine gems, minerals, metals, and seeds into the pit of the pinnacle according to the rules, he, wearing a new upper garment and the five-fold ornaments, facing east, establishes the pinnacle-stake in the pit with the root mantra, and secures it firmly with lime mortar (*sudhā*).

Thereafter, one should perform the visualization of the deities of the directions of the celestial chariot (vimāna). Following that, the patron (yajamāna), according to his wealth, should give the sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) to the preceptor (ācārya) and the guardians of the forms (mūrtipās). Then, having placed the crest-pitcher (śikhākumbha)—which may be made of gold, silver, copper, brass, or clay—either circular, square, or polygonal in shape, upon its base; |||

Having filled it with various jewels and metals, one should fashion its top in the shape of a bud or a lamp; thereafter, one should make it in the shape of a full-blown lotus. Now follows the procedure for the visualization of the deities of the directions of the temple (vimāna): in the eastern direction of the temple, [one should visualize] dark-blue Indra, or red Kumāra; in the south, red Umāpati or Dakṣiṇāmūrti; in the west, white Nṛhari or Śrīdhara; in the north, golden-colored Brahmā or Dhanapati; or alternatively—

Whether as the infallible and infinite Puruṣasatyas, or as Vāsudeva, Saṃkarṣaṇa, Pradyumna, and Aniruddha of dark, red, golden, and deep-blue complexions; or as Nara, Nārāyaṇa, Hari, and Kṛṣṇa; or indeed as Varāha, Narasiṃha, Śrīdhara, and Hayavaktra—whether these four-armed forms bearing the conch and discus, or Brahmā and the others bearing their respective weapons; whether they are standing while he stands, sitting while he sits, or lying down while they stand or sit; or whether they are mounted on vehicles while he is mounted on a vehicle, or standing while they are so mounted.

One should fashion Indra and the other deities—whether they are of manifold forms, or possess universal forms, or have four arms—as seated upon their respective vehicles within all the enclosures; and upon the mountain-made vimāna, one should fashion the mountain-born goddesses. Having performed for them the rites beginning with the ritual immersion in water (*jalādhivāsa*) and ending with the ritual installation on the bed (*śayanādhivāsa*) according to the prescribed rules, and having established them in their respective places at an auspicious moment (*sumuhūrta*), one should apply the coloring. However, in a temple made of bricks, having performed for the *śūlas* the rites beginning with the ritual immersion in water and ending with the ritual installation on the bed, [one should establish them] in their respective places.

Having established [the deities] and fashioned them from the three substances (clay, wood, or stone), one should color each according to its prescribed hue. All of these, situated upon the wall-path, should be fashioned as either half-painted (*ardhacitra*) or with painted outlines (*ābhāsa-citra*), along with lotus seats. In a temple that has only a single entrance, there shall be only a single directional image (*diṅmūrti*).

In the case of a temple lacking a *nāsikā* (central spire), however, the *diṅmūrti* (directional deities) are not desired. In a temple that is square, oblong, circular, or oval, one should install Vīrasena, Suṣeṇa, Bhadra, and Subhadra respectively in the intermediate directions starting from the southeast (*āgneyī*), each holding the temple with four arms. In an oblong temple provided with two *nāsikās* on the south and north, one should conceive of Pūrṇa and Puṣphara, who hold a conch and a discus, with their hands touching the curtain. On every floor of the temple, one should depict gods and *vidyādharas* dancing.

One should depict Kinnaras and Uragas holding lutes and drums, as well as manifestations of the Blessed One everywhere. Above the pedestal and below the neck, in the four corners, one should fashion a golden-colored Garuḍa or a lion, rising either to the height of the neck, the height of a foot, one and a half times that, or the height of three feet. Below the base of the pedestal, in the southeast, one should place the elephant-faced [Gaṇeśa]; in the south, the red Lord (Īśa) attended by sages, or Dakṣiṇāmūrti; and in the west, Viśvarūpa.

In the north is Kamalāsana, golden-hued; in the northeast is Mahiṣāsuramardinī, or otherwise, all the directional forms as before. Below that, on the pedestal, one should likewise fashion the manifestations accompanied by their respective makers. With stone, gravel, and curdled milk—or with the three kinds of nectar—using the waters of the three myrobalans (triphalā), ground either three times, twice, or once, with the decoctions of the milky sap from the wood-apple, arjuna, silk-cotton, and milk-exuding trees, and having prepared it thus, [one should place it] again in the jar.

One should plaster [the structure] with a mixture of flour, black gram, and bark-decoction, combined with jaggery, cooked juices, and sand; this should be thoroughly pounded and applied in three stages known as *sthūla* (gross), *sūkṣma* (fine), and *para* (ultimate). When done in this manner, the structure becomes long-lasting. One should prepare a paste by grinding stone-grit, buttermilk, and fragrant powder together with double the amount of sand. That which is ground once is *sthūla*; that which is ground twice is *sūkṣma*; and that which is ground thrice is *para*. Thus, in this sequence—

The Procedure for Plastering: Having adorned that temple with five colors according to the prescribed rule, one should decorate everything from the sandals up to the pinnacle (stūpikā) with gold and other precious materials. Now, the procedure for installing the door-panels is described: Having brought the two door-panels and the two door-posts, one should wash them while reciting: “Oṃ lāṃ, salutation to the Supreme Self, the Soul of All. Then, having caused the declaration of an auspicious day (puṇyāha-vācana) to be made, one should sprinkle the four door-panels and door-posts with water while reciting the five Upaniṣadic mantras. Finally, one should cover them with unwashed (new) cloths.

As before, having prepared a heap of grain and placed the door-panels and door-posts there, and having prepared a sacrificial mound (*sthaṇḍila*) as before for the purpose of placing the water-jars (*kumbha*), one should place in the center a great jar (*mahākumbha*) together with its small jar (*karaka*), covered with an ashvattha sprout and containing gems, metals, and a brush (*kūrca*); and around it, one should sequentially arrange eight jars (*kalaśa*) similarly endowed with those specific attributes. Having invoked the respective deities into the door-arches (*toraṇa*) and the jars and worshipped them, one should perform the preliminary consecration fire-sacrifice (*adhivāsahoma*) preceded by the recitation of the *puṇyāha* formula.

Having performed [the preliminary rites], at dawn the preceptor, having deposited the jewels as before in the foundations for the door-panels and the foundation-stone, and having placed the foundation-stones for the door-panels upon them, shall cause the proclamation of an auspicious day (*puṇyāha*). Having washed the foundation-stones with the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*), he shall fix the door-panels at a favorable moment (*sulagna*) and, using the *tūrya* from the great water-pot (*mahākumbha*), perform the ritual placement (*vinyāsa*) of the deities upon the two door-panels.

The sequence for that is as follows: one should worship Śānti on the lower branch, Vāgdevī on the southern branch, Śrī on the upper branch, and Rati on the northern branch; on the southern door-panel, Viśvadṛk and Bhūtanātha; and on the northern [panel], Viśvavakra and Pratāpavat.

Stationed there, having consecrated the ten forms beginning with Matsya with their respective Vidyās, one should install the Vedas and Śāstras in the bamboo poles (*vetra*), the thirty-three deities in the iron arrows (*nārāca*), the Sages (*ṛṣi*) in the stakes (*kīla*), Bhūtanātha on the door-panels (*kavāṭa-paṭṭikā*), and Viśvabhāvana on the door-sill (*kavāṭa-kanda-paṭṭa*), using their respective mantras beginning with *praṇava* and ending with *namaḥ*, along with the waters from the great pitcher (*mahākumbha*). Then, one should give sacrificial fees (*dakṣiṇā*) to the preceptor (*ācārya*) and others according to one's means. Thus ends the sixth chapter, titled "The Rite for the Head-Brick.
The Seventh Chapter:
The Rite for the Collection of Stone and Wood.
The procedure for the collection of stone and wood is now described.

Images are of six kinds, distinguished by their material: gems, metals, stone, clay, and wood. The first type, made of precious gems (*māṇikya-ratna*), possesses limbs such as hands and feet; it may be entirely painted (*citra-rūpa*) or partially painted (*ardha-citra-rūpa*). Free from defects such as cracks or flaws, when properly worshipped, it bestows the fruit of all desires.

Metallic [images] are of three kinds, distinguished by their material substance as gold, silver, copper, or iron. The first [gold] bestows all prosperity; the second [silver] brings wealth, fame, victory, and wisdom; the third [copper] grants prosperity, peace, and good fortune. Stone [images] are of four kinds, distinguished by their color as white, pale-red, yellow, or black. The first is for the Brāhmaṇa, the second for the Kṣatriya, the third for the Vaiśya, and the fourth for the Śūdra. These are declared to be the primary [materials] in their respective order.

Alternatively, these four types [of stones] belong to the Brāhmaṇa; those that are pale-red, yellow, and black belong to the King (Kṣatriya); those that are yellow and black belong to the Vaiśya; and for the fourth (the Śūdra), there is only the black one—this is the secondary rule. Those stones upon which the conch, discus, mace, lotus, spear, rosary, lion, elephant, deer, boar, goad, water-pot, śrīvatsa, chowrie, umbrella, banner, fish, bird, sesame seeds, rice grains, or sand are seen are auspicious. Among those, stones containing embryos (fossils) are not to be accepted.

The fetus remains inside due to the humors (*doṣas*). One should grind buffalo butter with powdered sheep horn and powdered *kuruvinda* on a stone slab, mix it with cow's milk, and smear it upon wood; then the fetus becomes visible. Those [wooden structures] which have altar-like circular patterns and produce a faint sound or heat when touched should be considered pregnant. Having carefully examined them, one should extract [the fetus].

When that *maṇḍala* appears as pale-red (*pāṭala*), there are pale-red dust particles; when it is white like a lotus (*śvetapaṅkaja*), there are white dust particles; when it is smooth and brownish-yellow (*kapila*), there is a tortoise; when it is dove-colored (*kapotavarṇa*), there is a *gaulī*; when it is madder-colored (*mañjiṣṭhavarṇa*), there is a red frog (*lohita-dardura*); when it is pale-white (*pāṇḍaravarṇa*), there is a white frog (*śukla-dardura*); when it is reddish-yellow, there is a turtle (*kacchapa*); when it is saffron-yellow (*kusumbhapītavarṇa*), there is a yellow rain-frog (*varṣābhū*); when it is white-golden (*śuklahemavarṇa*), there is a small bird; when it is the color of black cloth, there is a monitor lizard (*godhā*); when it is the color of molasses (*guḍavarga*), there is a stone; and when it is honey-colored (*madhuvarga*), there is a firefly (*khadyota*).

A scorpion appears on a [stone] the color of a deer; water resembling a sword-blade on a blue one; a locust on a dark-red one; foam on a tawny one; a mouse on a black one; and a fish resembling young grass on a [stone] like that—such signs as these are seen. Having thus determined the presence of an embryo, the chariot-maker should extract it. If, out of delusion or greed, images are made from stone or wood containing an embryo, then the destruction of the kingdom, the realm, and the patron occurs.

Once the extraction of the image from the womb has been performed, the consecrator (sthāpaka), in order to remedy that defect, shall perform a propitiatory rite (śānti) according to the rules, feed the Brāhmaṇas, cause them to pronounce benedictions, and give them sacrificial fees (dakṣiṇā). If the making of the image is done with a cool stone, then the presence (sānnidhya) of the Deity in it will occur very soon. Regarding the cutting of the stone, however, that which produces the sound of a bronze bell at the head-region and the sound of a cymbal at the base is a male stone (puṃśilā).

If it has a slightly diminished resonance, it is a female stone (strī-śilā); if it lacks resonance, it is a neuter stone (napuṃsaka-śilā). One should fashion the image (bimba) from a male stone and the pedestal (pīṭha) from a female stone. One should perform the ritual placement of gems (ratnanyāsa) upon the neuter stone. For the installation of goddesses such as Śrī and others, one should fashion the pedestal from a female stone and the image from a male stone; the placement of gems should be performed upon the neuter stone. A stone that is gentle and cool is Vaiṣṇavī and bestows great fruit. A black stone is Āgneyī and Raudrī, and brings disease. A stone that is both gentle and fiery is of a fearful nature.

The *brāhmī* stone brings rain; it is cool during the summer season and warm during the rainy season. A stone that is uniform in color and pure should be selected for the making of an image. A stone that is mottled and multicolored causes suffering. For the purpose of making an image, stone should be taken from mountains; even there, one should avoid stone found underground. That ground which is interspersed with various flowers and surrounded by reservoirs of water is *vāruṇī*; stone from such a place grants all desires.

That land where there is water to the north, fertile fields to the south, and a milky tree to the west is Māhendrī; it bestows nourishment and yields many fruits. That land where there are trees such as the Khadira and Kāśmarya to the east and south, where there are crickets, lapwings, vultures, wild boars, and Āpadas, and where water is scarce within its interior, is Āgneyī; it bestows little wealth upon those residing there.

Stones should not be taken from places such as those inhabited by Vibhītaka trees, or those frequented by bipeds, waterless regions, deer, lions, grass, thorns, or Khadira trees; nor from areas covered by Sāla or Vānīra trees, or from the stones found there; nor from empty temples, rivers, lakes, riverbanks, or ground consisting of ashes; nor from quadruped-infested villages, cremation grounds, anthills, salty water, or impure ground; nor from places occupied by Śabaras or Caṇḍālas, or from rocky terrains, crowded marshes, grassless tracts, waterless spots, or near temples; nor from regions scorched by wind and heat. [However, stones may be taken] from a holy field, an auspicious location, or from beneath a Brāhma tree.

In a place that is continuous [without gaps], endowed with *kuśa* grass, *kāśa* grass, and water, frequented by black antelopes, strewn with *padma* and *utpala* lotuses, dense with fields of rice, surrounded by *hintāla*, *pūga*, *punnāga*, and coconut trees, and inhabited by ascetics—a stone should be taken. Having thus understood the qualities and defects of what is to be accepted and what is to be rejected, one should know [the site] through the distinctions of region, soil, signs, and color. Then, on an auspicious day favorable to the patron (*yajamāna*), the preceptor (*ācārya*), having fed the Brahmins together with him, [proceeds].

Having distributed sacrificial fees (dakṣiṇā) to them, and having reached the site for collecting stones with chariot-makers and master builders, he should have a water-shed (prapā) constructed there. Having performed the ritual sowing of sprouts (aṅkurārpaṇa) there according to the rules, and having prepared an altar (vedikā) in its center, he should fashion a sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila) upon it with rice, grain, and sesame seeds. In the middle of that, he should place a large jar (mahākumbha), to its south a small water-pot (karaka), and around it eight smaller jars (kalaśa), all wrapped with threads and cloth.

Having prepared the vessel with its lid covered by a bundle of *kuśa* grass together with jewels, iron, and *aśvattha* shoots—reciting: “Oṃ ṣauṃ, salutation to the Supreme Self, the Parameṣṭhin; salutation!”—and having scattered white mustard seeds while reciting “Sahasrāra huṃ phaṭ,” caused the declaration of an auspicious day (*puṇyāha*) to be made, sprinkled [the area], displayed the discus-mudrā (*cakramudrā*), and prostrated with joined palms, he invoked the Lord into the great jar (*mahākumbha*) with the root mantra, Sudarśana into the small jar (*karaka*), and the forms of Viṣṇu and the others into the subsidiary jars. Then, he offered supreme rice-pudding (*paramānna*).

In the four directions, having offered one hundred and eight oblations separately with the root mantra using the five substances—palāśa wood, flowers, fruits, clarified butter, and *caru*—and having offered sixteen oblations with the *Nṛsūkta* upon the sacrificial pits or altars;

In the eastern pit, with clarified butter: *Oṃ* to the forest deities, *svāhā*; *Oṃ* to the mountains, *svāhā*; *Oṃ* to the Garuḍa-mountains, *svāhā*; *Oṃ* to the riverbanks, *svāhā*; *Oṃ* to the peaks, *svāhā*; *Oṃ* to the waterfalls, *svāhā*; *Oṃ* to the oceans, *svāhā*; *Oṃ* to the trees, *svāhā*; *Oṃ* to the medicinal herbs, *svāhā*; *Oṃ* to the lords of the forest, *svāhā*; *Oṃ* to the womb-born, *svāhā*; *Oṃ* to the egg-born, *svāhā*; *Oṃ* to the sweat-born, *svāhā*; *Oṃ* to the sprout-born, *svāhā*; *Oṃ*.

Having offered oblations with "Svāhā to all beings" and "Oṃ bhūr bhuvaḥ svaḥ svāhā," and having collected the residual ghee (saṃpātājya), he should offer the full oblation (pūrṇāhuti). Then, having poured the residual ghee onto the stone while reciting the touching-mantra (sparśamantra), he should mix it with powdered sesame paste (palala), turmeric powder, parched grain (lāja), fried cakes (apūpa), groats (karambha), bark, and fragrant substances. Having given the offering to the spirits (bhūtabali) with "Oṃ, obeisance to all beings," and having offered one hundred and eight oblations of ghee while reciting the mantra of the Lord of Dreams (svapnādhipati), he should extinguish the fire.

At night, amidst the sounding of all musical instruments, the preceptor, having fasted and recited the mantra of the Lord of Dreams one hundred and eight times, should go to sleep upon a bed of *darbha* grass. Then, if he sees a mountain ablaze in his dream, the preceptor should rise immediately at dawn and perform the ritual collection of the stone there according to the rules. In the event that no dream is seen, or if an inauspicious dream is seen, he should perform a rite of pacification (*śānti*).

Thereafter, at an auspicious moment, having inspected the stone and consecrated white mustard seeds (*siddhārtha*) with the Astra-mantra, he scatters them there with the mantra: "May all the Yakṣas, Piśācas, and Nāgas who always dwell here depart; may Hari be ever present. Having again offered the oblation (*bali*) in each direction with the mantra: "Oṃ Lāṃ! Salutation to the Supreme, the Self of All; I give this oblation to all beings," and then having caused the declaration of an auspicious day (*puṇyāha-vācana*) to be recited and having sprinkled [the site] with water.

Reciting "Oṃ yāṃ namo parāya puruṣātmane namaḥ," one should touch the stone. Having offered *arghya* with the root mantra (*mūlamantra*), one should recite the root mantra one hundred and eight times. Having laid down a measuring line according to the proportions of the temple and the image, the master builders should cut the stones with the permission of the chariot-maker (*rathakāra*). Whichever direction the head of that stone falls toward—east, south, west, or north—in that direction it shall bestow victory, peace, prosperity, and nourishment.

If it [the stone] should be in a corner, one should avoid it; or else, if it is in the direction facing the front of the temple, it may be accepted. Having thus examined it, having lifted the stone, and having consecrated it with the waters from the altar-pitchers while reciting the *Puruṣasūkta*, and having sprinkled it with water from the ritual vessel (*karaka*), one should likewise separately consecrate the jars for the sake of accomplishing the images of the goddesses as before. In the central jar, one should [invoke] Śrī, the Mother of the Three Worlds.

In the eight small jars (*upakumbha*), one should invoke the eight Śaktis—Vāgīśvarī, Kriyā, Kīrti, Lakṣmī, Sṛṣṭi, Prahvī, Satyā, and the one named Brāhmī—and Sudarśana in the *vardhanī* jar. Having performed the invocation as before, one should offer oblations of fuel-sticks (*samidh*), clarified butter (*ājya*), and sacrificial porridge (*caru*) with the mantra: "Oṃ Śrīṃ, svāhā to Śrī. Then, having taken up the female stone (*strīliṅgaśilā*), one should sprinkle it with water from the main jar while reciting the *Śrīsūkta*, and sprinkle it with water from the *vardhanī* jar while reciting: "Oṃ Sahasrāra Huṃ Phaṭ."

For the purpose of conceiving the retinue deities, one should likewise collect the stones with their respective mantras, load them onto carts and the like, and lead them to the site. Thereafter, by the permission of the chariot-makers, the master-builders (sthapati) should fashion the image according to the prescribed rules. Now, the procedure for collecting wood is stated: one should collect wood during eight months, from the month of Vṛścika (Scorpio) to the end of Mithuna (Gemini).

The collection of stones, however, should always be performed. Trees suitable for collection are: sandalwood (*candana*), eaglewood (*agaru*), *kāśmarya*, yellow sandalwood (*haricandana*), saffron tree (*kesara*), *khadira*, *kuravaka*, *āsana*, *madhuka*, deodar (*devadāru*), jasmine (*jāti*), *bilva*, *śamī*, *śāka*, *kadamba*, *tilaka*, *meru*, *phalinī*, *surabhi*, *campaka*, *śiṃśupā*, *akṣīrikā*, *sālabījaka*, *kuruvinda*, *tiniśa*, *syandana*, mango (*cūta*), *tamāla*, *sarala*, *arjuna*, *kuṭaja*, *kaṅkolī*, *saptaparṇa*, *madhuṣṭhīla*, *uraṇa*, *nicula*, *punnāga*, and *khadira*.

The *rājavṛk�saprabhṛti* (royal-tree and other) species are recommended. One should have the image fashioned from timber that is substantial, free from all defects, and possessed of density. One must avoid trees that are self-dried, burnt, broken, struck down, stripped of bark, crooked, decayed at the core, inhabited by birds, constantly frequented by *caṇḍālas* and other low-castes, inhabited by those born of inverse unions (*pratiloma*), serving as dwellings for spirits, located near a *caitya*, presided over by deities, standing in a cremation ground, on a path, near a temple, a well, or a pond; as well as trees that are deformed or otherwise unsuitable. This concludes the section on the collection of timber.

Furthermore, having first performed all the preliminary rites—such as the gathering of stones, the feeding of Brahmins, the bestowing of blessings and favors, the distribution of sacrificial fees (*dakṣiṇā*), the collection of earth, and the planting of sprouts—the Preceptor (*ācārya*) proceeds to the site where the timber is gathered. There, he causes a pavilion (*prapā*) to be constructed, complete with a central altar and sixteen supporting pillars. Upon the central altar, on a heap of grain, he places a great jar (*mahākumbha*) endowed with the auspicious marks, accompanied by a water-pot (*karaka*) and the eight auspicious vessels (*kalaśa*), filled with scented water, and wrapped in thread, cloth, and other ornaments.

Having prepared a covering of *kūrca* grass consisting of the sprouts of *parameṣṭhi-manu*, *nāgaramotha*, gems, iron, and *aśvattha* wood; having scattered white mustard seeds with the *astra-mantra* as before; having caused the declaration of an auspicious day (*puṇyāha*) to be recited; having sprinkled [the area]; having displayed the *cakra-mudrā*; having bowed with joined palms (*añjali*); and having mentally constructed the pedestal (*pīṭha*)—beginning with the *ādhāra-śakti* and ending with the lotus—in the large jar (*kumbha*), the small vessel (*karaka*), and the water-pot (*kalaśa*); having invoked and worshipped the deities within them as before; having offered the supreme food (*paramānna*); and having kindled fire in the four quadrants.

Having invoked and worshipped Vāsudeva and the others, one should offer one hundred and eight oblations with the root mantra using palāśa fuel-sticks, flowers, fruits, clarified butter, and sprouts; then, having offered sixteen oblations of caru with the Nṛsūkta.

As before, in the eastern pit (*prācīnakuṇḍa*), [one offers] with clarified butter: *Oṃ vanadevatābhyaḥ svāhā*, *Oṃ garuḍaśailebhyaḥ svāhā*, *Oṃ śilādevatābhyaḥ svāhā*, *Oṃ taṭadevatābhyaḥ svāhā*, *Oṃ śrṛṅgadevatābhyaḥ svāhā*, *Oṃ samudrebhyaḥ svāhā*, *Oṃ vṛkṣebhyaḥ svāhā*, *Oṃ oṣadhibhyaḥ svāhā*, *Oṃ vanaspatībhyaḥ svāhā*, *Oṃ jarāyujebhyaḥ svāhā*, *Oṃ aṇḍajebhyaḥ svāhā*, *Oṃ svedajebhyaḥ svāhā*, *Oṃ udbhijjebhyaḥ svāhā*, *Oṃ sarvebhyaḥ*...

Having offered the oblation with the mantra, "Svāhā to the beings," he rises, washes the base of the tree, wraps it with a new cloth while reciting the root-mantra (*mūlamantra*), and covers it with *darbha* grass using that same mantra. Thereafter, he offers oblations with the respective mantras—beginning with Keśava and ending with Dāmodara, as well as beginning with Matsya and ending with Kalki—each preceded by the *praṇava* (Oṃ) and ending with *svāhā*. Finally, he collects the residual clarified butter (*saṃpātājya*).

Having offered oblations with the words: "Oṃ bhūḥ svāhā, oṃ bhuvaḥ svāhā, oṃ suvaḥ svāhā, oṃ bhūrbhuvaḥsuvaḥ svāhā," and having offered the full oblation (*pūrṇāhuti*) with the mantra: "Oṃ, seven are your fuel-sticks, O Agni, seven your tongues, seven your seers, seven your hotṛ-priests, and seven your beloved abodes; they worship you in seven ways; choose the seven wombs with clarified butter, svāhā!"—and having touched the tree with the *sampāta* [remnants] while reciting the touching-mantra, [one should know that] by this rite, she has taken refuge in the form of a stationary being within the previous tree.

"O tree, for the sake of Viṣṇu’s ritual, you who bring about all prosperity, depart from this state of being stationary and assume an unsurpassed, divine form. By the grace of Vāsudeva, enjoy abundant pleasures. O tree, I do not harm you, but I release you from birth. Having thus addressed the tree, he should wrap it with a protective thread while reciting the root mantra. Then, having offered a *bhūtabali* (oblation to the spirits) consisting of minced meat, turmeric powder, *karambha*, parched rice, sacrificial porridge, and products of the cow, while reciting: "Om, salutation to all beings (*sarvebhyo bhūtebhyo namaḥ*)."

Having offered oblations as before with the Svapnādhipati mantra and having extinguished the fire, the preceptor should recite the mantra for the sake of auspicious dreams—*oṃ hrīṃ namaḥ svapnādhipataye susvapnaṃ mama kuru svāhā*—one hundred and eight times while making the sound of the Vedas. Then, the preceptor should lie down upon a bed of *darbha* grass. If wood is seen burning in a dream, the preceptor should bathe at dawn and collect the wood according to the prescribed rite. In the event that nothing is seen, or if a bad dream is seen, he should perform a propitiatory oblation (*śānti-homa*).

Then, at an auspicious moment, the preceptor, looking at the tree, should recite the verse beginning with "The Yakṣas and Piśācas," scatter white mustard seeds while reciting the Astra-mantra, offer a bali-oblation to the spirits, have the declaration of a "meritorious day" (puṇyāha) made, sprinkle the tree, touch it while reciting the Puruṣa-mantra, present the Arghya water while reciting the Mūla-mantra, and having muttered that same mantra one hundred and eight times, the preceptor, facing east, should himself cut the tree with an axe. Thereafter, by the preceptor's command, the chariot-makers should perform the cutting.

If it has fallen toward the east or the north, then it brings prosperity. Thereupon, the preceptor, meditating upon the severed tree as having the form of Hari, sprinkles it with water from the pitcher situated on the altar while reciting the root mantra; he then sprinkles it with water from the *vardhanī* vessel and leads it to the temple.

Therefore, one should have an image or the like fashioned from clay and other materials. Thereafter, the patron (yajamāna) should give five ornaments and one hundred gold coins to the preceptor (guru), and half of that amount as a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) to the officiating priests (ṛtvij). If, out of delusion, one should have an image made by an uninitiated youth according to the prescribed rite, it will lead to misfortune. O Brahmin, one should perform [the rite] according to the prescribed rule to bring about prosperity. Thus ends the seventh chapter, titled "The Procedure for Collecting Stone and Wood.
The Eighth Chapter: The Procedure for Consecration (Pratiṣṭhā-vidhi). The procedure for consecration is now declared.

For the successful accomplishment of the rite of new consecration (*nūtana-pratiṣṭhā-karma*), one should plant sprouts (*aṅkura*) in earthen mounds (*pālikā*), pots (*ghaṭikā*), and bowls (*śarāva*) according to the prescribed ritual, either twelve days, nine days, seven days, five days, or three days prior to the day of commencing that rite. The characteristics of these [vessels], beginning with the *pālikā*, will be described in order. First, the *pālikās* should have a height of one cubit (*hasta*) including the fingers.

The *ghaṭikās* (small jars) have mouths sixteen *aṅgulas* in width, with openings seven *aṅgulas* deep and bases eight *aṅgulas* in width; they resemble the *dhuttūra* flower and have faces like lotuses. They are twenty-two *aṅgulas* in height and possess five faces: the central face is shaped like a jar, while the four faces on the four sides are each four *aṅgulas* wide, and the central portion features a face six *aṅgulas* in width. The *śarāvas* (shallow bowls), however, are twenty *aṅgulas* in height and twelve *aṅgulas* in width.

According to one's means and the extent of the elaboration, vessels made of gold or other metals, or those made of clay—such as shallow bowls (*śarāva*), jars (*ghaṭa*), or small offering-cups (*pālikā*)—should be prepared. In the case of the primary arrangement, if there are thirty-six for each [deity], then there are one hundred and eight; in the case of the lowest arrangement, if there are sixteen for each, then there are forty-eight. Alternatively, twelve each, eight each, or four each may be taken. Or else, even for all purposes, only the *pālikās* should be taken, numbering sixteen, eight, or four.

Furthermore, in all matters pertaining to the gods (*daiva*), they should be even in number; however, in matters pertaining to humans (*mānuṣa*), they should be odd. The procedure for collecting the clay: Following that, for the purpose of casting the image, one should construct a pavilion (*maṇḍapa*) in an auspicious, secluded, and pleasing location, provided with sixteen pillars and four doors on the four sides. Having smeared it with cow dung, one should decorate it with garlands of *vandana* flowers, garlands of *darbha* grass, strings of pearls, silken canopies, rows of lamps, unbroken rice (*akṣata*), fragrant powders, and so forth.

Then, for the purpose of collecting the clay, the preceptor—having bathed, adorned himself, applied the *udvapuṇḍra* mark, washed his hands and feet, and performed the ritual sipping of water (*ācamana*) three times—brings a spade, washes it with water, covers it with a new cloth, and adorns it with flowers. Having summoned a bathed and adorned officiating priest (*ṛtvij*), he places [the spade] upon the priest’s head and mounts him upon the back of an elephant, a chariot, or a horse.

Accompanied by the sounds of auspicious banners, umbrellas, flags, musical instruments, and the Vedas, and by those reciting the *Śākuna-sūkta*, together with devotees and Vaiṣṇavas carrying vessels of sprouts and many lamps, one should go toward the east or the north—a distant and pleasing direction. Having established a water-shed (*prapā*) there and decorated it, one should sit upon a seat facing east. Having made the resolve, "I shall perform the rite of collecting earth for the sake of accomplishing the ritual of installation," and having performed breath control (*prāṇāyāma*), one should carry out the purification of the self and the mental sacrifice (*mānasayāga*) up to its conclusion.
