Having invoked [the deity] into the water-pitcher with the mantra: *Oṃ namo bhagavate sudarśanāya cakrarājāya jvālāmāline huṃ phaṭ svāhā āgaccha āgaccha*, and having worshipped it and caused the declaration of an auspicious day (*puṇyāha*) to be recited; then, having sprinkled the earth and the spade—which has been washed with that water using the mantra *sahasrāra huṃ phaṭ* while chanting the Viṣṇugāyatrī; there, one should draw the ground to the measure of nine *tālas*, with its face upward, its head placed in the northeast (*aiśāna*), and its feet placed in the southwest (*nairṛta*).

Having strewn *darbha* grass around [the site], touching the ground with the *kūrca* while meditating upon the Boar (*varāha*) and reciting the hymn *oṃ bhūmir bhūmnā*, he consecrates it. There, having invoked her with "Oṃ Bhūṃ, obeisance to the Earth; come, come," and having performed the six-limbed ritual placement (*ṣaḍaṅga-nyāsa*) with "Oṃ Bhāṃ, obeisance to the heart for knowledge," and having displayed the *kalāra-mudrā*, he worships her with the *arghya* and other offerings using the very mantra of the Earth. Then, having strewn *darbha* grass around the digging tool (*khanitra*), [he proceeds].

In that [spot], having invoked [the deity] with "Oṃ, obeisance to the Blessed One, Huṃ, to Varāha! Come, come!", and having performed the six-limbed assignment (*ṣaḍaṅganyāsa*) with "Oṃ Hrāṃ Hrīṃ" and so forth; having displayed the Varāha-mudrā and worshipped with water for the guest-offering (*arghya*) and other offerings; having invoked and worshipped Indra and the others in the directions starting from the east; and having offered [food] to all; one should dig up earth from the ground at the face, arms, thighs, breasts, belly, middle, hips, and feet, while sounding all musical instruments and reciting the Varāha-mantra.

Having collected [the materials] in either a metal or an earthen vessel with the Root Mantra (mūlamantra), and having covered them with a new cloth using the Weapon Mantra (astramantra), the Guru himself should then collect sand from a river or a cow-pen and cow-dung, placing each separately into two vessels and covering them with cloths. Carrying all three vessels, he should mount either an elephant or a chariot and, accompanied by the sound of Vedic recitations and musical instruments, circumambulate the village and enter the pavilion for the offering of sprouts (aṅkurārpaṇamaṇḍapa).
Thus ends the eighth chapter, titled "The Procedure for Collecting Clay," in the *Kriyākairavacandrikā* composed by the venerable teacher Varāha.
The Ninth Chapter:
The Procedure for the Planting of Sprouts (*Aṅkurārpaṇavidhi*).
Now, the procedure for the offering of the sprouts (*aṅkurārpaṇa*) is described.

The preceptor (*ācārya*), having bathed, wearing new linen garments as lower and upper robes, and adorned with special ornaments such as a turban, perfumes, garlands, purificatory threads (*pavitra*), earrings, necklaces, bracelets, and so forth, together with the image-bearers (*mūrtipāḥ*) similarly adorned, first washes his hands up to the knees and down to the wrists; having sipped water (*ācamya*), he sprinkles the *aṅkurārpaṇa* pavilion with water consecrated by the *puṇyāha* rite. Therein, he lays out twelve threads extending eastward and fifteen extending northward, using fragrant sandalwood threads.
Therein, among the one hundred and fifty-four squares, twelve squares each—extending from Brahmā to Īśāna—are set aside for the purpose of placing the *pālikās*, *ghaṭikās*, and *śarāvas*.

Having swept the remaining forty-six squares, one should place *ghaṭikās* in those [squares] belonging to Brahmā, Indra, and Varuṇa; *pālikās* in the places of Agni, Yama, and Nirṛti; and *śarāvas* separately in the places of Vāyu, Soma, and Rudra. Thus, one should establish them in the number of one hundred and eight. If, however, the procedure for sixteen vessels is followed for each, one should lay down nine lines extending eastward and twelve lines extending northward. In those eighty-eight squares, four [vessels] should be placed in the positions from east to west.

In this manner, there are four squares each in the four locations from the southeast (Āgneya) to the southwest (Nairṛta), totaling sixteen; likewise, there are four squares each in the four locations from the northeast (Raudra) to the northwest (Vāyavya), also totaling sixteen. Thus, having set aside forty-eight squares for the purpose of placing the vessels, one should sweep the remaining forty squares and place the vessels according to the previously mentioned procedure.

Regarding the procedure for taking each of the three types of vessels, one should first lay down nine threads extending eastward and nine threads extending northward. Within those sixty-four squares, having divided two rows at the outer edge and having omitted one row between each pair, one should place four vessels in each of the northeast, east, southeast, southwest, west, and northwest sections.

Regarding the procedure for placing the twelve vessels (*pātra*): having laid out four lines extending eastward and five lines extending northward, one should place four *pālikās*, four *ghaṭikās*, and four *śarāvas* in the twelve resulting squares. Alternatively, sixteen, eight, or four *pālikās* may be placed around the *soma* jar.

Having done this, one should wash the vessels, such as the *pālikā* and others, with the *Viṣṇugāyatrī*. Having tied *sahadevī*, *dūrvā*, and *aśvattha* sprouts to their necks, and having secured the roots of the *bilva* tree with *kuśa*, *kāśa*, and other grasses, one should fill them first with earth, then with sand, and thereafter with powdered cow-dung. Then, having placed a tuft of grass (*kūrca*) inside each of them—

In places such as the *pālikā* vessels, having prepared a seat (*pīṭha*) on each successive day with rice, husked rice, and sesame seeds—measured respectively by one *āḍhaka*, half an *āḍhaka*, and one *prastha*—either circular or square, while reciting "Oṃ Rāṃ, obeisance to the Supreme Self, the Soul of the Universe," and having drawn a lotus upon it;

Facing either east or north, having established the *ghaṭikās* starting from the west (Vāruṇī) and ending at the east (Aindra) with the mantra "Oṃ ṣauṃ, obeisance to the Supreme Being, obeisance to the Self of Parameṣṭhin"; the *pālikās* starting from the southwest (Nairṛti) and ending at the southeast (Āgneya) with the mantra "Oṃ yāṃ, obeisance to the Supreme Being, obeisance to the Puruṣa Self"; and the *śarāvas* starting from the northwest (Vāyavya) and ending at the northeast (Aiśāna) with the mantra "Oṃ rāṃ, obeisance to the Supreme Being, obeisance to the Viśva Self"—and then having strewn them around with *darbha* grass.

Having lifted the Soma-vessel and bowed to Indra with the mantra, "O Indra, [grant] me vigor," one should wrap the threads with a thick cord so that there is a space between them equal to the width of a barley grain or half a finger-breadth. Then, having prepared a pedestal of grain—consisting of rice, husked rice, and sesame seeds—in the western part of the *pālikā* vessels and the like, and having drawn a lotus upon it, one should place the Soma-vessel therein.

Having wrapped the *pālikā* vessels and so forth with fresh cloths—or, if unable, having wrapped each individual arrangement (*prativyuha*) and the Soma-pitcher with two new cloths using the mantra "yuvā suvāsāḥ"—and having filled them with scented water; having placed a covering of *aśvattha* sprouts along with gems and *kūrca* grass; having strewn them around with *darbha* grass; and having placed various sacrificial grains such as wild rice, *śāli* rice, *mudga*, *māṣa*, *priyaṅgu*, barley, sesame, wheat, and so on, into a new vessel; he should place that [vessel] upon the head of his attendant.

Having circumambulated the abode resounding with the music of instruments and having entered the sacrificial pavilion (*yāgamaṇḍapa*), he places the *pālikā* vessels and other items upon a seat prepared with *droṇa* measures of rice and other grains at the eastern side. Having washed those seeds with cow’s milk while reciting the *Viṣṇugāyatrī*, and having strewn them around with *darbha* grass, he offers salutations: "Oṃ, obeisance to Brahmā, the presiding deity of barley; Oṃ, obeisance to Rudra, the presiding deity of mustard seeds; Oṃ, obeisance to Subrahmaṇya, the presiding deity of *priyaṅgu* seeds."

Oṃ, salutation to Vāyu, the presiding deity of *niṣpāva* (flat beans). Oṃ, salutation to Viṣṇu, the presiding deity of *mudga* (mung beans). Oṃ, salutation to Śrī, the presiding deity of *śāli* (rice). Oṃ, salutation to Yama, the presiding deity of *godhūma* (wheat). Oṃ, salutation to the Yakṣa, the presiding deity of *māṣa* (black gram). Oṃ, salutation to the protector of water and other elements, the presiding deity of *tila* (sesame seeds). Oṃ, salutation to Vināyaka, the presiding deity of bamboo grain (*veṇudhānya*).

Thus, having invoked and worshipped the presiding deities of each respective seed-syllable (*bīja*), and having covered [the vessel] with a new cloth; and having fashioned a pedestal (*pīṭha*) in the Soma-pitcher, beginning with the support (*ādhāra*) and ending with the lotus (*padma*), and having worshipped it therein; one should invoke Soma with the mantra: "Soṃ, obeisance to Soma! Come, come! (soṃ somāya namaḥ āgaccha āgaccha).

Having performed the six-limbed ritual placement (*ṣaḍaṅganyāsa*) beginning with *oṃ sā*, having worshipped [the deity] with water for offerings (*arghya*) and other substances, having again caused the declaration of an auspicious day (*puṇyāha*) to be recited, having sprinkled [the area], and having sounded external musical instruments such as conchs and kettledrums; then, having invoked Brahmā into the water-jars (*ghaṭikā*) with "Oṃ Kaṃ, obeisance to Brahmā! Come, come! and Viṣṇu into the small bowls (*pālikā*) with "Oṃ Aṃ, obeisance to Viṣṇu! Come, come!", and having invoked and worshipped Īśāna into the shallow dishes (*śarāva*) with "Oṃ, obeisance to Īśāna! Come, come!", [one should worship] the deities of the door-surroundings, the banners, and the pitchers.

Having made the formal resolve (*saṃkalpa*), "I shall perform the worship," one should prepare a pedestal of grain at each of the four gates starting from the east. Having established the respective arches (*toraṇa*) and banners, and having also placed the water-pots (*kumbha*) with the mantra "idaṃ viṣṇu," one should proceed as follows: At the eastern gate, which is of the nature of the *Ṛgveda* and named Suśobhana, in the Aśvattha arch, one should offer salutations to Indra with "Oṃ Laṃ Indrāya Namaḥ. In the two red banners situated at its sides, one should place coral and ruby respectively in the two pots located there, offering salutations to Kumudākṣa.

Having invoked [the deities] into those two with "Oṃ, obeisance to Pūrṇa" and "Oṃ, obeisance to Puṣkara," and having worshipped them with perfumes and other offerings; then, on the southern *audumbara* archway named Subhadra, which is the form of the Yajurveda, one invokes "Oṃ, obeisance to Yama. On the yellow banners situated at its sides, one invokes "Oṃ, obeisance to Puṇḍarīka" and "Oṃ, obeisance to Vāmana. There, upon the *vajra* and *vaiḍūrya* [stones] on the two jars respectively, one invokes "Oṃ, obeisance to Ānanda" and "Oṃ, obeisance to Nanda," and worships them. On the western [archway], which is the form of the Sāmaveda and named Subandhu...

At the Nyagrodha archway: *Oṃ vaṃ varuṇāya namaḥ*. At the two blue banners situated at its sides: *Oṃ śaṅkukarṇāya namaḥ*, *Oṃ sarvanetrāya namaḥ*. There, upon the two water-pots (*kumbha*) containing, respectively, a topaz (*puṣparāga*) and a sapphire (*nīla*), one should invoke and worship them with: *Oṃ vīrasenāya namaḥ*, *Oṃ suṣeṇāya namaḥ*. In the north, at the Plakṣa archway in the form of Atharvan named Suhotra: *Oṃ saṃ somāya namaḥ*. At the two white banners situated at its sides: *Oṃ sumukhāya namaḥ*, *Oṃ*...

Homage to Supratiṣṭha; there, having invoked and worshipped [the deities] in the two jars, respectively those made of pearl and crystal, with "Oṃ, homage to Sambhava" and "Oṃ, homage to Prabhava," and having covered them all, one should clothe each of the door-archway jars with new cloths. Having again fully worshipped the presiding deities of the *pālikās* and the Soma jar, one should offer milk-rice (*pāyasānna*) or pure rice (*śuddhānna*).

Then, having performed the rites from the formal installation of the fire (*agni-pratiṣṭhā*) up to the "mouth of the fire" (*agni-mukha*) according to the rules—whether in a sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*) or on a sacrificial mound (*sthaṇḍila*)—and having mentally fashioned the pedestal (*pīṭha*) within the fire, beginning with the *ādhāra* and ending with the lotus (*padma*), one should invoke Soma there as before, meditate upon him, and worship him.

Having offered everything from the *arghya* to the *naivedya* with ghee, one should perform one hundred and eight oblations (*āhuti*) of clarified butter (*sarpiṣā*) with their respective mantras; one hundred and eight oblations of fuel-sticks (*samidh*) of *palāśa*, *khādira*, *aśvattha*, and *bilva* with the root mantra (*mūlamantra*); sixteen oblations of sacrificial porridge (*caru*) with the *Nṛsūkta*; and again, having offered one hundred and eight oblations of clarified butter with the *Soma-mantra*, one should collect the remaining clarified butter for the *saṃpātājya*.

Having poured the remainder [of the seeds] from the palms with the *sparśa* mantra into the *pālikā* vessels and other receptacles, as well as into the seed-vessel (*bījapātra*), and having performed the final oblation (*pūrṇāhuti*), he should remove the Soma from the fire. Having recited the Soma mantra one hundred times and caused the declaration of an auspicious day (*puṇyāha*) to be made, and having sprinkled [the area], the Preceptor, with a composed mind at an auspicious moment, being authorized by the members of the assembly and the Vaiṣṇavas, shall perform the sowing of seeds into the *pālikā* vessels and other receptacles using the twelve-syllable mantra.

Having covered [the vessel] with earth while reciting the mantra "mūrddhānaṃ divo aratim," and having sprinkled it with water from the Soma-pitcher while reciting the portion beginning with "imaṃ me" and ending with "pramoṣīḥ," and having covered it with lids, one should offer an oblation (bali) to the guardians, Kumuda and the others. In this manner, until the conclusion of the rite, day and night, one should be devoted to the worship of the Soma-pitcher and the offering of supreme food (paramānna).

While performing the lighting of lamps and the offering of oblations, one should sprinkle water mixed with turmeric for the sake of promoting the growth of the sprouts, place them in a well-protected spot, and guard them. The patron (*yajamāna*), the preceptors (*guru*), and the officiating priests (*ṛtvij*) should satisfy one another with wealth, betel leaves, fruits, and other offerings. Thus ends the ninth chapter, titled "The Procedure for Depositing Sprouts," in the *Kriyākairavacandrikā*. The Tenth Chapter: The Procedure for the Preparatory Rites of Consecration (*Pratiṣṭhopakaraṇavidhi*).
Now, the procedure for the installation of the ritual implements is described.

Regarding that, as for the characteristics of the sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*): in the front part of the temple, within the first, second, or third enclosures, in suitable spaces, in these eight directions, at a desired location, one should construct a pavilion measuring ten cubits in width and length, with four doors on the four sides.

In the middle of that, having constructed a square altar (vedi) measuring five cubits in length and breadth and one cubit in height according to the measurement of the *mānāntarāṅgula* using bricks; and having excavated from the outside of its three tiers, in the eastern direction, a square ground-level area measuring twenty-four finger-breadths in length and breadth according to the *muṣṭyaṅgula*—which serves as the base for the twenty-finger-breadth primary measure—and having left a space of two finger-breadths outside the excavated ground-level.

Then, one should construct the three girdles (mekhalās) according to the dimensions of the pit (kuṇḍa) using bricks alone, in due order and according to the rules: first, the *sāttvikī* girdle, measuring one *tāla* in height and four *aṅgulas* in width; surrounding that, the second *rājasī* girdle, measuring eight *aṅgulas* in height and four *aṅgulas* in width; and surrounding that, the third *tāmasī* girdle, four *aṅgulas* in height and of the same width. Furthermore, on the southeast side of the altar (*vedikā*), as before, one should [draw] a cord measuring twenty-four *aṅgulas* in length and width.

Having laid out a square, leave five finger-breadths on each side from the southwest and northwest corners at the western edge. Then, starting from the peg at the western edge, rotate the cord toward the south and north. Next, having laid the cord from the eastern edge back to the peg, form the shape of a yoni. Having swept away the remainder, dig a pit twenty finger-breadths deep according to the standard measurement.

Therefore, having set aside two finger-breadths [from the previous measurement], one should construct three girdles (mekhalā) according to the dimensions of the pit (kuṇḍa) as before. Having fixed a peg (śaṅku) on the outside, one should likewise lay down an eighteen-finger-breadth cord from the east to the west of the peg. Then, starting from the east and ending at the west, one should rotate the eighteen-finger-breadth cord [to mark the circumference].

Then it takes the shape of a bow. Having dug the ground to its natural state to a depth of twenty finger-breadths (aṅgulas), and having set aside two finger-breadths from that, one should fashion the three girdles (mekhalās) in accordance with the pit as before. Having fixed a wooden pin (śaṅku) to the southwest of that [pit], and having drawn a thread according to the measurement of nineteen finger-breadths (the number of worlds, *bhuvana*), one should make a circle. Having divided the circle into six parts according to the measurement of twenty-four finger-breadths, and having placed the pin, one should drop the thread from the eastern and western pins.

In this very manner, when the *sūtra* arrangement is completed, there arises a hexagonal (*ṣaḍaśra*) sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*) with sides eight finger-breadths (*aṅgula*) apart. Likewise, having dug a base of twenty finger-breadths, and leaving two finger-breadths from the excavated ground-level, one should fashion three girdles (*mekhalā*) according to the dimensions of the pit. Then, having fixed a peg (*śaṅku*) three palm-lengths (*tāla*) outside from that western side, and having drawn a circle like a wheel along the path of the thread according to the measurement of the wings (*pakṣāṅgula*), [the pit is formed].

As before, one should fashion the natural form and the three girdles according to the suitability of the pit (*kuṇḍa*). If twelve or eight petals are fashioned in place of its girdles, it becomes a lotus-shaped pit (*padmakuṇḍa*). If spokes are fashioned in place of the girdles, it becomes a wheel-shaped pit (*cakrakuṇḍa*). Having fixed a peg (*śaṅku*) at the northwest corner of that [pit], one should draw a circle by dropping a cord measuring twenty-seven finger-breadths (*aṅgula*).

Having divided the sūtra-lineage into five parts and fixed a peg, one should lay down the lines according to the five-cornered shape and construct the base and the three girdles in accordance with the dimensions of the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa). To the north of that, at a distance of ninety-six finger-breadths beyond three palm-lengths, one should divide it into nine parts according to the proportions of the altar (veda). Having laid down the lines for a triangle of those measurements as prescribed, and having dug a pit twenty finger-breadths deep, one should construct the three girdles as before in accordance with the dimensions of the pit. Then, one should fix a peg in the northeast corner of that [pit].

Having drawn a circle by means of a cord according to the measurement of one, three, or four finger-breadths (aṅgulas), and having divided the cord-measurement into eight parts according to the measurement of the pitcher (kalaśa), one should plant a gnomon (śaṅku). Then, having laid down eight cords so that the center of each corner is six finger-breadths [from the center], one should construct the three tiers of the altar-rim (mekhalā) in accordance with the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) as previously described.

In the center of the sacrificial pits (kuṇḍas), one should fashion an eight-petalled lotus. To the west of the pits, upon the raised base (tala) above the girdle (mekhalā), one should construct the *yoni* starting from the root; it should extend for five finger-breadths (pañcāṅgula) and be gradually widened and deepened by ten, six, two, or one finger-breadth respectively. At the edge of the girdle, it should be four finger-breadths long, with a three-finger-breadth neck and a six-finger-breadth opening. It should be shaped like a tube, resembling a trumpet (kāhala) or the leaf of an *aśvattha* tree.

One should avoid placing a lotus in a lotus-shaped pit (*padmakuṇḍa*) and a vulva (*yoni*) in a vulva-shaped pit (*yonikuṇḍa*). If the officiant (*hotṛ*) faces north or toward the direction of Yama (south), he may fashion the vulva [within the pit]. If one seeks liberation (*mokṣa*), one should construct the pit without a vulva. As long as the cord (*rajju*) may be, so long shall the measurement (*āgama*) be; the peg (*śaṅku*) shall be half that measurement, and the space between them shall be free of any stain. The pericarp (*karṇikā*) of every pit shall be ninety-six finger-breadths (*aṅgula*) in length. Thus, the characteristics of the injunctions are to be correctly understood.

In the rite of the single form (*ekamūrti*), one should indeed employ an odd number [of pits], or otherwise have odd-numbered sacrificial pits (*kuṇḍa*) constructed. On the eastern or southern side of the central altar (*madhyavedikā*), one should construct an altar with the proper characteristics for the preliminary consecration of the bed (*śayanādhivāsa*), as previously described. Now, the procedure for the *sruk* and *sruva* ladles is stated: one should have the *sruk* and *sruva* fashioned from metals such as gold, or from sacrificial trees such as the *pālāśa*. Having made the handle of the *sruk* as long as a forearm, or two spans (*tāla*) plus two finger-breadths (*aṅgula*) in length, and six finger-breadths wide on all sides;

Having divided that [length] by the number of qualities (nine), and having divided the upper portion into two parts, and having made the upper portion the elemental part (*bhūtāṃśa*), one should set aside the first part there. Then, using the Vedic parts situated above, one should fashion the tip like the face of a boar with a width of one finger. When this is joined with the single part projected below and with the half-portion remaining from the third part of the *sahasvat* (the whole), it becomes a square measuring six fingers, equal in both width and length. Having thus fashioned the neck (*gala*).

Below that, the stalk (*nāla*) is two finger-breadths (*aṅgula*) in width; having made it on both sides with a depression (*nimna*) measuring half a finger-breadth in length and width, one should discard the remainder situated outside the layout of the lines (*sūtrapāta*). Having fashioned the remaining portion below the neck (*gala*) as either circular or square, one should make a pit (*garta*) in the middle of the neck, equal in width and length to one-third [of the neck], and equal in depth; this pit may also be circular. Having divided the exterior of the pit into three parts, one should fashion eight petals in the first circle.

Having divided the middle portion into four parts, one should combine the first part—the navel-circle (nābhimaṇḍala)—with the two circles within the rim-circle (nemimaṇḍala). Having fashioned six or ten spokes in that [combined area], like the petals of a blue lotus, and having constructed the rim-circle with the remaining single part, one should fashion conch-shells in its four corners. Having made a border (mekhalā) outside [the navel] one barley-corn high, one should begin a hollow of the measure of four barley-corns and create an opening for the clarified butter (sarpiḥ) extending to the tip.

Having made the back portion of that [ladle] square, resembling the back of a tortoise or like the shell of a tortoise; and having made the base—without a supporting stand—circular, marked with three rings, or otherwise octagonal; one should fashion its tip into the shape of a lotus as before. As for the handle of the *sruva* ladle, having made it one cubit in length, one should fashion two circular depressions at its tip, each two finger-breadths in width, with a circular opening in their middle measuring half a finger-breadth in width and length, like the nostrils of a nose.

Below that, between the two pits, one should fashion a line raised by one barley-corn (*yava*) at its ends, and with the remaining one finger-breadth (*aṅgula*), form the neck (*gala*). With what remains, having fashioned the globular shape (*golākṛti*), one should cause the base to be two finger-breadths wide. At each of the four doors of the pavilion, in the order starting from the east, one should construct arches (*toraṇas*) using the *aśvattha*, *udumbara*, *plakṣa*, and *vaṭa* trees; or, if one of these is unavailable, one may make them from sandalwood (*candana*).

Having made those bases seven, five, or four cubits in length, twenty-two finger-breadths in thickness, and either circular or square; having fashioned above them pattikās (strips) of half that length, of similar [thickness], and likewise [shaped]; and having placed upon each pattikā three pegs measuring two tālas and joined by a span of eight finger-breadths.

At the bases of the archways (toraṇas), one should paint full jars, conch shells coiling to the right, wheels, banners, drums, bows, and serpents. Now follows the procedure for the eight auspicious signs (aṣṭamaṅgalavidhi): according to one's means, having fashioned planks together with their pedestals—made of gold or other metals, or from sacrificial wood—with lengths, breadths, and thicknesses respectively of twenty-two aṅgulas, eleven aṅgulas, and two aṅgulas; upon these [one should place] the Śrīvatsa, the full jar, the kettle-drum (bherī), the circular mirror, the pair of fish, and the conch and wheel.
Having fashioned Garuḍa seated in the lotus posture with a measurement of twenty-two finger-breadths, one should mark chowries, lamps, and an umbrella on his two sides and upon his head.

Having first prepared all the necessary materials—such as a bathing pedestal made of udumbara wood proportionate to the size of the image; the pedestal for the opening of the eyes, the water-vessel for the preliminary consecration (adhivāsana), and the seats for the preceptor and the attendants; the sandals for the preceptor and the image-attendants; the secondary jars, the main pitchers, the water-pots, the crystal vases, the lamp-stands, clarified butter and other substances for the bath, sandalwood and various fragrant items, sacrificial fuel, flowers, kusha grass, various grains, gold and other metals, gems, a cow with its calf, and other such requisites.

Thereafter, the preceptor should commence the consecration according to the prescribed rules. Thus ends the tenth chapter, titled "The Procedure for the Preparatory Rites of Consecration," in the *Kriyākairavacandrikā*.
The Eleventh Chapter:
The Procedure for the Consecration of the Shadow and the Consecration of the Water.

Once the image has been fashioned by artisans according to the path prescribed in the scriptures—endowed with the characteristics known as *māna*, *unmāna*, *pramāṇa*, *parimāṇa*, *upamāna*, and *lambamāna*—and once the gross and subtle limbs have been well-executed, the preceptor, together with the patron, should perform the placement of jewels and other substances upon the pedestal of the ritual image (*karmārcā*). Then, when the eyes have been opened by the artisan himself, the preceptor should satisfy the chariot-maker and the artisans with gifts such as ornaments, garments, and other articles.

When they have departed, having purified the interior and exterior of the residence by sweeping, smearing with cow-dung, and other means, and having performed the rite of circumambulation by fire (*paryagnikaraṇa*) using bundles of kindled *darbha* grass; and having purified the walls, gate-towers, and pavilions by sweeping, smearing, and so forth; and having sprinkled them with the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*) while reciting the *Pavamāna* hymns and other mantras; and having lit many lamps everywhere with cow-ghee; and having perfumed everything on all sides with incense substances such as black aloe-wood (*kālagaru*).

Having adorned the temple with *dūrvā* grass, unbroken rice (*akṣata*), and powdered lime (*sudhācūrṇa*), one should then, at the time of the afternoon worship, make the formal resolve (*saṃkalpa*): "I shall perform the *śānti-homa* for the sake of pacifying any deficiency or excess in the measurements and other attributes of the Guru’s image. Having caused the proclamation of the *puṇyāha* (day of merit), one should consecrate the fire according to the prescribed rules.

With unbroken grains and *śamī* leaves, one should offer one hundred oblations for each of the following: “*oṃ bhūḥ svāhā*,” “*oṃ bhuvaḥ svāhā*,” “*oṃ suvaḥ svāhā*,” “*oṃ mahaḥ svāhā*,” “*oṃ janaḥ svāhā*,” “*oṃ tapaḥ svāhā*,” and “*oṃ satyaṃ svāhā*. Then, with the *caru* offering and the *Nṛsūkta*, one should offer sixteen oblations. Furthermore: “*oṃ ṣauṃ namaḥ parāya parameṣṭhyātmane svāhā*,” “*oṃ yāṃ namaḥ parāya puruṣātmane svāhā*,” “*oṃ rāṃ namaḥ parāya viśvātmane svāhā*,” “*oṃ vāṃ namaḥ*...”

Having offered oblations into the presence of the image with the mantras: “*Oṃ svāhā to the Supreme Self who is the nature of cessation,*” and “*Oṃ lāṃ namaḥ svāhā to the Supreme Self who is the universal soul,*” one should thereafter worship the Lord Adhokṣaja, who resides within the fire, with palms joined in reverence, reciting this mantra: “Salutations to You, O Blessed One, whose form is Jātavedas (Fire). To Nārāyaṇa, the true consumer of both *havya* (offerings to gods) and *kavya* (offerings to ancestors), the enjoyer, the deity to be worshipped, the Self, the Supreme Self—O God, remain present for a long time in this image for our welfare.”

Having prostrated before the fire, one should cover the image with a new cloth together with *darbha* grass while reciting the root mantra; having likewise spread out an upper garment (*uttarīya*) with that same mantra, one should worship with offerings such as water for the guest (*arghya*), water for the feet (*pādya*), water for sipping (*ācamanīya*), perfume, flowers, incense, and lamps, while reciting the *Viṣṇugāyatrī*. Then, for Śrī and Bhūmi, one should worship with their respective mantras—namely, "Oṃ Śrīṃ, obeisance to Śrī" and "Oṃ Hrīṃ, obeisance to Bhūmi"—performing the rites from the covering of the garments up to the lamps. One should likewise perform these acts for the retinue beginning with Brahmā using their own individual mantras.

Having made the formal resolve (saṅkalpa): "I shall perform the rite of binding for protection in order to achieve success in the preliminary consecration (adhivāsa)," one should place in a vessel of gold or other precious metal—filled with rice measuring a khārī or a droṇa, along with sixty betel nuts (*kramuka*) and four times that amount of *nāgavallī* leaves, and half as many plantains and other fruits—the threads of a golden cord of the prescribed measure, or else threads made of linen or cotton spun from seven or five strands. Having covered [the vessel] with a new, unwashed cloth (*ahata-vāsas*), [one proceeds].

Having placed that [image] upon the head of an attendant, and having circumambulated the temple enclosures or the village together with whisks, fans, a parasol, dance, song, and large lamps; having smeared a square area of ground before the image with cow dung; having fashioned a pedestal there from a heap of grain; having placed that vessel upon it; and having caused the proclamation of an auspicious day (*puṇyāha*); having sprinkled [the vessel]; and having consecrated the threads seven times with the mantra *sahasrāra hūṃ phaṭ*, one should worship them.

Having worshipped the image and taken those [flowers] with the thumb and ring finger of both hands, one should smear them with powdered sandalwood while reciting the mantra: "We worship Tryambaka, the fragrant, the increaser of prosperity; may I be liberated from death, like a cucumber from its stem, yet not from immortality."

Having tied [the thread] to the right hand of the deity and the left hand of the goddess with the mantra "All these deeds of yours are to be proclaimed at the Soma-pressings, O Maghavan Indra, what you have done for the presser; when you opened the cave for Śarabha, the kinsman of the seer," or with the root-mantra (*mūlamantra*); having recited the *astra-mantra* one hundred times; having consecrated it with the *ghṛtasūkta* beginning with "He who extracted the Brahman from the Brahman"; and having performed protection with ashes on the incense vessel with the verse "The Bṛhat-sāman, the bearer of power" (*bṛhatsāmakṣatrabhṛt*).

Having worshipped the God and the Goddess with *arghya* and other offerings, and having presented the great cake (*mahāpūpa*), the preceptor should tie the protective thread (*kautuka*) on his own right hand. Having prostrated before the God with the sixteen-syllable mantra and having offered praise, he should place before the God upon a pedestal of grain a water-vessel made of gold or other metal, or one made of clay, or likewise a large pan, for the purpose of the preliminary consecration (*adhivāsa*). Having filled it with filtered scented water, strewn it around with *darbha* grass, and caused the proclamation of an auspicious day (*puṇyāha*) to be made;

Having sprinkled [the area] and worshipped the door-arches and the water-pots as before, one should purify the water in the large water-vat (*jaladroṇī*) and other vessels with the mantra: *Oṃ yāṃ, obeisance to the Supreme One, obeisance to the Self of Puruṣa*. Having incinerated [impurities] with the mantra: *Oṃ rāṃ, obeisance to the Supreme One, obeisance to the Universal Self*, one should meditate upon the Nivṛtti-mantra—possessing a radiance equal to ten thousand moons—with the mantra: *Oṃ vāṃ, obeisance to the Supreme One, obeisance to the Self of Nivṛtti*. Then, one should visualize the large water-vat as being filled with the nectar flowing forth from that [mantra].

Having mentally conceived the *yogapīṭha* (the seat of yoga) within that [space], beginning from the support (*ādhāra*) and ending with the lotus (*padma*), and recollecting the process of dissolution (*saṃhārakrama*), one should invoke Hari with the root mantra upon a cushion (*kūrca*) made of twenty-eight blades of *darbha* grass. Having worshipped Him, one should lay the cushion down within the water-vessel (*jaladroṇī*) with its head toward the east, following the sequence of dissolution. Then, displaying the *cakramudrā* while reciting the mantra: “To the one with arrows, to the arrow, to the iron shaft, *huṃ phaṭ*, to the Sudarśana, *svāhā*.”

Having laid down a *kūrca* made of twenty-three blades of *darbha* grass for Śrī and Bhūmi, one made of twenty-five blades for Rudra and Vedhas, and a *kūrca* made of two blades for the other deities, according to the previous procedure and their respective mantras in the order of withdrawal (*saṃhārakrama*), one should prepare a pedestal to the south of that with rice grains. Upon it, one should place a great jar (*mahākumbha*) made of gold or other metals along with its lid, and eight smaller jars (*upakumbha*) made of clay, all wrapped with thread.

Having covered [the image] with a cloth containing jewels and a tuft of *aśvattha* sprouts, and having strewn it around with *darbha* grass; having invoked Brahmā into the central jar, Sudarśana into the *karaka* vessel, and Indra and the other deities into the eight subsidiary jars; having worshipped them; and having properly veiled the image with a new cloth made of all [nine types of] fibers; having scattered white mustard seeds in all directions with the mantra "rakṣohaṇa"; and having placed an unextinguished lamp there.

There, while non-Brahmins are reciting the Vedas, Itihāsas, Purāṇas, and so forth, the Guru, having worshipped at the doors of the temples with the mantra "Oṃ, obeisance to Sudarśana," and having circumambulated the temple together with the image-keepers (mūrtipās), shall go outside. For whichever image it is not appropriate to perform the formal ritual immersion in water (jalādhivāsa) directly, for that one, immersion by means of its shadow (chāyādhivāsa) is prescribed; however, for images made of wood, metal, or stone, the direct jalādhivāsa is indeed performed.

Among those [materials], after joining the pedestal of the metal image, one should perform the preliminary consecration (*jalādhivāsa*). Then the Guru, having made the formal resolve (*saṃkalpa*), should arrange a load of *śāli* rice in a circular shape for the purpose of joining the pedestal; upon that, he should place half as much rice, and upon that, half as much sesame, covering each layer with cloth at intervals. Upon that, having drawn an eight-petalled lotus and spread *darbha* grass over it.

Having covered [the area] with a fresh cloth having its fringe facing east, and having placed upon it a pedestal—either one with a lotus design or a plain one—and having strewn it with *darbha* grass; having cast jewels and metals upon it while reciting the *Viṣṇugāyatrī*; having duly kindled the fire; and having offered one hundred and eight oblations of clarified butter with the *Viṣṇugāyatrī*, as well as sixteen oblations of *caru* with the *Nṛsūkta*; then, having caused the declaration of an auspicious day (*puṇyāha*) to be recited and having sprinkled [the materials]; with a composed mind, meditating on the Supreme Vāsudeva, [he should place the deity] upon the pedestal with the root mantra.

Having mounted the deity [upon the pedestal], and having established it while reciting the mantra, “*Pratiṣṭhāsi*,” and having likewise performed the opening of the eyes, and having gratified him with great wealth; then, having performed as before the *śānti-homa* for the pacification of defects such as deficiencies in measurement and other characteristics, and having uttered the *gāthā*, “*Namastubhyam*”: “Salutations to you, O Blessed One, whose nature is Jātavedas (Fire), to Nārāyaṇa, who is the recipient of both the offerings to the gods (*havya*) and the offerings to the ancestors (*kavya*), according to the rule.”

"O God, who art the enjoyer of the deities to be worshipped, the Self, and the Supreme Self; remain present for a long time within this image for our welfare. Welcome, O Lord of the gods of gods, O Universal Form! Salutations unto You! Although You are pure, we perform purification upon Your abode; please forgive that. Having caused the declaration of an auspicious day (*puṇyāha-vācana*) to be recited, and having placed a water-pot filled with cow's ghee—covered with sprouts and provided with a cord and a tuft of grass (*kūrca*)—upon a pedestal of grain for the sake of purifying the image, one should invoke the Deity into it by means of the sixteen-syllable mantra and worship Him.

Having bathed the image with the root mantra (*mūlamantra*), then having rubbed it with powders of turmeric, *āmalaka*, and so forth, and having bathed it with warm water while reciting the *Puruṣasūkta*; having wrapped the image in a new cloth along with *darbha* grass while reciting the root mantra, and having likewise given it an upper garment; having worshipped it with the *arghya* offering and other rites, one should make the formal resolve (*saṃkalpa*): “I shall perform the rite of binding the protective thread for the purpose of the preliminary consecration in the water (*jalādhivāsa*). Then, as before, one should perform the binding of the *pratisara* thread.

Having raised the deity with the mantra, "Arise, O Brahmaṇaspati," and having placed him upon a vehicle such as a chariot with the verse, "May we hear what is auspicious with our ears," he should proceed to the village together with other Veda-knowers reciting the Bṛhat, Rathantara, Puruṣasūkta, Nārāyaṇānuvāka, Śākuna, and Rakṣoghna hymns, accompanied by various services such as a white parasol, white chowries, silken canopies, banners made of peacock feathers, auspicious fans, diverse kinds of offerings, and specific varieties of dance, song, and instrumental music.

Having circumambulated the temple and other sacred sites, and having reached the location for the preliminary consecration (*jalādhivāsa*), one should construct a water-shed (*prapā*) near the water. There, having placed the image upon a seat facing either east or north, and having constructed a multi-pillared water-shed in the midst of the water, one should arrange it with four gates, four garlands for salutation, canopies, banners, *darbha* grass wreaths, strings of pearls, flower garlands, lamps, and various fruits as ornaments. Then, making the formal resolve (*saṃkalpa*): "I shall perform the rite of the preliminary consecration in the water."

As before, having dried that water with the *puruṣamantra*, burnt it with the *viśvamantra*, and meditated upon it as being like nectar with the *nivṛttimantra*; having caused the proclamation of an auspicious day (*puṇyāha*) and sprinkled [the site], one should place there a new, great square pedestal (*mahāpīṭha*) provided with a coverlet and a pillow; having mentally constructed upon it the *yogapīṭha* beginning with the *ādhāra* and ending with the lotus, and having worshipped it, one should install the doors, arches, and ritual jars (*kuṃbha*) therein.

Having performed the worship according to the rules, the preceptor, together with the Brahmins who recite the Śākuna Sūkta and the image-keepers (mūrtipās), should lift the image with the mantra “Uttiṣṭha. Having placed it upon a pedestal situated in water with the mantra “Bhadraṃ karṇebhiḥ,” and remembering the process of reabsorption (saṃhārakrama), he should lay the image down facing north and turned eastward for a long time. As before, he should establish the jars, the small pitchers, and the large vases, complete with their characteristic marks, upon a pedestal of grain for the sake of protection.

In those [vessels], as before, having invoked Brahmā, Sudarśana, Indra, and the others, and having worshipped them, one should place them too in the water to the right of the image in due order. Having displayed the Cakra-mudrā with the mantra: “Oṃ sa-śarāya śārṅgāya nārācāya huṃ phaṭ sudarśanāya svāhā,” and the Agni-prākāra-mudrā with the mantra: “Oṃ namo bhagavate raṃ pralaya-kālānalāya huṃ phaṭ.”

While Brāhmaṇas recite the four Vedas, beginning with the Ṛgveda, in the cardinal directions such as the east, and the Itihāsas and Purāṇas in the intermediate corners, one should light lamps that do not go out and cause various musical instruments to resound on the bank. In this manner, one should perform the preliminary consecration (adhivāsa) in the water for three nights, one night, or even half a watch. From that point until the final raising of the image (biṃbotthāpana), no ritual action whatsoever—such as bathing or drinking—should be performed in that water. However, in the case of installing a household deity (gṛhārcā), one should perform the installation immediately.

No specific time is prescribed for the ritual consecration of the water (jalādhivāsa), the opening of the eyes (nayanonmīlana), or the ritual consecration of the bed (śayanādhivāsa). However, in the case of a Great Consecration (mahāpratiṣṭhā), one should perform the consecration of the water at dusk, the laying of the bed at midnight, and the actual installation during the day. One should perform the consecration of the water in a river, a long pond, a lake, or even a mountain spring, provided the water is clear. One should not do so in water that is scanty, located at the edge of a cremation ground, polluted by salt water, or tainted by being astringent, pungent, bitter, or frothy.

Furthermore, one should not perform the preliminary consecration (*adhivāsana*) of an image near a sacred tree (*caityavṛkṣa*), nor in places that are low-lying, saline, covered with moss, or inhabited by creatures of a different species. In such defective locations, one should not install the image. In the absence of a river or similar body of water, the ritual bathing of the image in water may take place in a wooden trough or a large cauldron filled with abundant water; alternatively, it is prescribed for other vessels made of clay or similar materials as circumstances permit. Or, the immersion in water may be performed immediately prior to the main consecration.
Thus concludes the eleventh chapter, titled "The Ritual of Immersion in Water and the Procedure for the Shadow-Consecration," in the *Kriyākairavacandrikā*.
The Twelfth Chapter: The Ritual for the Vāstuyāga and the Opening of the Eyes.

In this regard, having consecrated the image according to the rules, the Guru—having performed his morning duties—enters the pavilion together with the patron. On its right side, he draws the figure of Vāstunātha in a relaxed posture, spreads the sacrificial grass (paristīrya), and makes the formal resolve (saṃkalpa): “I shall perform the Vāstu-homa. Having caused the declaration of an auspicious day (puṇyāha) to be recited, having sprinkled [the area] with water, and having placed a tuft of seven blades of Darbha grass (kūrca), he invokes [the deity] with: “Oṃ vaṃ, obeisance to Vāstupuruṣa; come, come! Thus he performs the invocation.

Having worshipped Vāstunātha with perfumes and other offerings, one should worship as follows: on the head of Vāstunātha, "Oṃ aṃśumāline namaḥ"; on the right side at the base of the arm, "Oṃ jhaṣadhvajāya namaḥ"; at the elbow, "Oṃ kumārāya namaḥ"; at the hand, "Oṃ vināyakāya namaḥ"; at the feet, "Oṃ aśvinīdevatābhyāṃ namaḥ"; in the middle, "Oṃ candramase namaḥ"; on the left side at the hand, "Oṃ durgāyai namaḥ"; at the elbow, "Oṃ saptamātṛbhyaḥ namaḥ"; and at the base of the arm, "Oṃ sthāṇave".

"Oṃ, salutation to Viṣṇu" at the heart; "Oṃ, salutation to Brahmā" at the navel; and surrounding that, in order, in the eight directions: "Oṃ Laṃ, salutation to Indra"; "Oṃ Raṃ, salutation to Agni"; "Oṃ Haṃ, salutation to Yama"; "Oṃ Ṣaṃ, salutation to Nairṛta"; "Oṃ Vaṃ, salutation to Varuṇa"; "Oṃ Yaṃ, salutation to Vāyu"; "Oṃ Saṃ, salutation to Soma"; "Oṃ Śaṃ, salutation to Śaṅkara"; and to the north of the Lord of the Site (Vāstunātha), "Oṃ Kṣaṃ, salutation to Kṣetrapāla. Having thus invoked and worshipped them, [one should proceed].

Having formally kindled the fire in the western region of the Lord of the Site (Vāstunātha) and having invoked Him therein, one should offer a thousand or a hundred oblations of clarified butter with the five Upaniṣadic mantras. Then, saying “Oṃ Vāstunāthāya Svāhā,” one should offer a thousand oblations each with fuel-sticks (*samidh*) of *śamī*, *apāmārga*, and *khadira* wood, as well as with clarified butter and with the *caru* offering while reciting the *Nṛsūkta*, making sixteen oblations. Following that, one should offer: “Oṃ Aṃśumāline Svāhā,” “Oṃ Jhaṣadhvajāya Svāhā,” “Oṃ Kumārāya Svāhā,” and “Oṃ Vināyakāya Svāhā.”

Having offered oblations once each with the *caru* and clarified butter (*ājya*) while reciting: "Svāhā! Oṃ, to the Aśvinī deities, Svāhā! Oṃ, to the Moon, Svāhā! Oṃ, to Durgā, Svāhā! Oṃ, to the Seven Mothers, Svāhā! Oṃ, to Sthāṇu, Svāhā! Oṃ, to Viṣṇu, Svāhā! Oṃ, to Brahmā, Svāhā!"—and having presented the sacrificial offering (*bali*) to Indra and the other gods as well as to Kṣetrapāla with their respective mantras ending in "namaḥ," one should dismiss the Lord of the Site (*Vāstunātha*). If the deity of the site is not honored, the performed rite becomes demonic (*āsura*).

Therefore, with every effort, one should worship the Lord of the Site (Vāstunātha). Having purified the pavilion by opening its eyes and through sweeping, smearing, sprinkling, and so forth; having adorned that ground with lime powder and other materials; and having scattered white mustard seeds consecrated with the Astra-mantra in all directions.

Then, having banished from the outskirts those ignorant mortals who are atheists, violators of social boundaries, revilers of the gods and Brahmins, afflicted by sinful diseases, censurable, backbiters, heretics, those of base livelihood, those born in the inverse order, envious, greedy, foolish, and so forth; and having decorated the pavilion with pillars, canopies, strings of pearls, arches, garlands of *darbha* grass, fruits, flowers, unbroken rice grains (*akṣata*), and other such items; and having dug a pit two *tālas* deep in each of the four directions for the purpose of installing the arches there.

Having erected an *aśvattha* archway in the east, an *audumbara* one in the south, a *nyagrodha* one in the west, and a *plākṣa* one in the north; having caused a pavilion to be constructed, adorned on all sides with various lamps, sprouted shoots in vessels, and incense of sandalwood, agallochum, and camphor, and made resonant by other Brahmins learned in the Vedas and by experts in the four kinds of musical instruments—namely those called *ānaddha*, *tatas*, *suṣira*, and *ghana*; then, in the afternoon, the Guru himself shall raise the image from the water.

Having placed [the image] facing east upon a seat by the bank, having lifted the water-pots from the water, having dismissed the respective deities, and having washed the image with water; if it is made of metal, having cleansed it with the juice of *tintriṇī* fruit and washed it; having adorned it with garments, ornaments, perfumes, and so forth; having mounted the image upon a vehicle as before; and having brought it to the sacrificial pavilion with the sounding of musical instruments and auspicious chants, one should settle it there upon a seat in the northern part.

Thereafter, the preceptor, having entered the inner sanctum (garbhagṛha) together with the image-keepers (mūrtipas), removes the grass mat (kūrca) and the vessel (kaṭāha) and other items from the water that were previously consecrated (adhivāsita). Having performed the ritual dismissal (udvāsana) of the deities residing in the pitcher (kumbha), he visualizes the form (bimba) situated upon the grass mat. Then, having removed the garments, ornaments, and garlands from it, and having made the formal resolve (saṅkalpa): "I shall perform the opening of the eyes," he causes the proclamation of an auspicious day (puṇyāha-vācana) and sprinkles the implements required for the opening of the eyes.

Having performed the separate "leading forth" (*nayanonmīlana*) of the permanent image (*dhruvabera*) and the bed (*śayyā*) and so forth according to the procedure to be described; having displayed the eight grains, cows, and maidens; and having established seventeen jars filled with substances such as clarified butter according to the procedure to be described for the occasion when the actual bathing is to be performed—having invoked and worshipped the respective deities, and having invoked the deity into a mirror provided with a tuft of grass (*sakūrca*), one should bathe [the image] with those [jars].

Having performed the ceremonial bathing (snapana) of the bed and other items with nine separate jars, seven for Brahmā and Īśa, five for the Ṛṣis, and three—or even just one—for the Devas; having meditated upon the image reflected in the mirror; having worshipped it with offerings beginning with garments and ending with the waving of lights (nīrājana); having contemplated and installed the twelve-syllable mantra, brilliant and jewel-like in radiance, within the heart of the permanent image (dhruvabera); and having likewise prepared the bed and other articles; one should cover the permanent image, the bed and so forth, and the goddesses with woolen blankets (kambala).

In front of him, having placed two vessels—one of gold and one of silver—each filled with an *āḍhaka* measure of grain upon a pedestal of grain, arranged east and west; having filled them respectively with honey and clarified butter (*ājya*); having inserted into them two such rods (*śalākikā*) eight finger-breadths long; having covered them with new cloths; having offered oblations (*saṃkalpya*); having caused the declaration of an auspicious day (*puṇyāha*) to be recited; and having sprinkled all that [with water], he should invoke [the deities] into the honey-vessel with "Oṃ haṃ, obeisance to Sūrya," and into the clarified butter vessel with "Oṃ saṃ, obeisance to Candramas."

Having performed worship, and having consecrated the honey and the clarified butter with the mantra “madhuvātā,” or “madhu savitā prasavet,” or “madhu dyaurastu naḥ pitā,” or “śukramasi,” he should place around it—each in separate vessels—the grains of nīvāra, śāli, mudga, śyāmāka, priyaṅgu, yava, tila, and godhūma, as well as betel leaves, coconut, and plantain fruits. Having stationed cows and young girls in front, amidst the sounding of musical instruments and Vedic chants, he should, with a golden probe whose tip is smeared with honey, [apply it] to the right [eye] with the mantra “citraṃ devānām.”

Having opened the left eye with a silver probe smeared with clarified butter while reciting, “*Taccakṣur*,” and having removed the covering cloth, he should give to the Guru a pair of vessels, the probe, the eight grains, and cows, saying, “May Govinda be pleased. He should further satisfy [the Guru] with wealth that sustains life. Thus ends the twelfth chapter, titled “The Ritual for the Vāstuyāga and the Opening of the Eyes.
The Thirteenth Chapter:
The Ritual for the Consecratory Bath as an Auxiliary to the Rite.

Then, having made the formal resolve (saṅkalpa), "I shall perform the rite of bathing for the sake of purifying the image," and having caused the declaration of an auspicious day (puṇyāha) to be recited, and having performed the rite of the protective cord (pratisara) as before, one should first procure the bathing materials—beginning with ghee and ending with decoctions—which are used for the lowest of the low types of bathing.

Having smeared a square area in front of the image with cow dung, one should lay down six lines of sandalwood paste there—extending eastward and pointing northward—and having set aside twenty-five squares for the purpose of placing the ritual jars, specifically nine squares in the center and eight squares in the eight directions surrounding them, one should sweep away the remainder.

In seventeen compartments containing eight jars, one should place in each compartment one *āḍhaka*, half of that, or one *prastha* of rice; then, in order from top to bottom, one-fourth as much of rice-grains and one-fourth as much of sesame seeds. Having drawn lotuses upon them and having placed two tips of *darbha* grass in each, one should wash the jars—made of gold, silver, copper, or clay according to one's means—with the *Viṣṇugāyatrī* mantra, using jars sufficient to hold a *droṇa*.

Having wrapped the earthen vessels with the mantra "indrannatvā" using a thread, one should prepare a pedestal of grain on the western side of the ground for the purpose of consecrating the jars (*kalaśādhivāsa*). Upon that, having spread *kuśa* grass—either with its tips pointing eastward or northward—with the *viśva* mantra, one should place the jars facing downward with the syllable "oṃ," while facing either east or north. Within those jars, having spread three *darbha* blades each with the *parameṣṭhi* mantra, one should sprinkle them with water from the *arghya* vessel with the *puruṣa* mantra.

Having scattered unbroken rice grains (*akṣata*) with the *viśvamantra*, and having raised them up with the *nivṛttimantra*, one should make the formal resolve (*saṃkalpa*): “I shall offer oblations for the purpose of the ritual bath. Having duly prepared the fire, one should offer one hundred and eight oblations of clarified butter (*ājya*) into it while reciting the *Viṣṇugāyatrī*. Then, having sprinkled the materials for the bath with the remaining clarified butter, and having performed the ritual placement of the jars (*kalaśasthāpana*), one should fill the central jar among the jars situated in the middle compartments of the diagram with clarified butter. Finally, one should install [the deity] in that jar while reciting the *Viṣṇugāyatrī*.

To the east of that [central] pot, there should be a pot filled with hot water; then, to the southeast, a pot filled with gems such as māṇikya, ruby, blue diamond, coral, pearl, emerald, and lapis lazuli; and likewise to the south of the ghee-pot, a pot filled with various fruits such as pomegranate, mango, āmalaka, bilva, coconut, jackfruit, and citron.

In the southwest direction (Nairṛti) of the ghee, a jar filled with gold, silver, copper, lead, tin, bell-metal, and iron filings—one *niṣka* of each—should be placed; in the western direction of the ghee, a jar joined with one handful each of the cleansing substances *rajanī*, *sūryavartinī*, *sahadevī*, *śirīṣa*, *sadābhadrā*, and the tips of *kuśa* grass; and in the northwest direction (Māruta) of the ghee, [a jar] with the fragrant substances *candana*, *kuṣṭha*, *kuṅkuma*, *agaru*, *uśīra*, *hrībhera*, *girisaṃbhava*, *māṃsī*, and the substance known as *murā*.

Having placed a jar filled with ghee in each case, one should place a jar of ghee in the north joined with individual handfuls of *nīvāra*, bamboo-seed rice (*veṇu*), *śāli* rice, *priyaṅgu*, barley (*yava*), *kaṅgu*, *ṣāṣṭika* rice, and wheat (*godhūma*) grains; and in the northeast direction, a jar of ghee joined with separate *kuḍuba* measures of barley and *vrīhi* rice.

In the eastern direction from the central pitcher situated at the Brahma-position, one should place the Pādya-pitcher, joined with Tulasi, lotus, Dūrvā grass, unbroken rice (akṣata), Śyāmāka grain, Viṣṇuparṇī, and Bilva leaves—one handful of each—along with sandalwood paste measuring one fruit. To its south, one should place the Arghya-pitcher, joined with white mustard, unbroken rice, tips of Kuśa grass, fruits, sesame seeds, and flowers—one handful of each—along with three Niṣphas of sandalwood paste.

To the west of that, one should place the *upasparśana* pitcher, filled with *taṅkola*, *caṃpaka* buds, camphor, nutmeg, cardamom, cinnamon, sandalwood, and flowers, each measuring half a *pala*. To the north of that, having established a pitcher filled with the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*).

In the southeast of the central group, a pitcher of curd; in the southwest, a pitcher of milk; in the northwest, a pitcher of honey; and in the northeast, having established a pitcher of astringent decoction (*kaṣāya*) filled with the barks of *śamī*, *palāśa*, *khadira*, *bilva*, *aśvattha*, *vitata*, and *nyagrodha*, each measuring half a *pala*.

Having placed a bundle (*kūrca*) made of twenty-seven *darbha* grasses into the central jar of clarified butter, and having placed bundles made of seven, five, or three *darbha* blades into the subsidiary jars with their tips pointing downward to the extent of the necks; having covered them with shallow bowls (*śarāva*) while reciting the mantra, “Oṃ namaścakrarājāya”; and having wrapped their necks with unwashed cloth (*ahatavastra*) while reciting the mantra, “yuvā suvāsāḥ,” one should surround them with *darbha* grass.

In those jars containing ghee, warm water, fruit, cleansing materials, unbroken rice, gems, metals, perfumes, water for the feet, water for the guest-offering, water for sipping, and decoctions, one should invoke—each with their respective mantra—the Supreme Vāsudeva, Puruṣa, Satya, Acyuta, Ananta, Keśava, Nārāyaṇa, Mādhava, Govinda, Viṣṇu, Madhusūdana, Trivikrama, Vāmana, Śrīdhara, Hṛṣīkeśa, Padmanābha, and Dāmodara; and having invoked them, worship them.

Into the fire previously prepared, one should offer oblations of clarified butter with the root mantra according to the number of the jars; sixteen oblations of *caru* with the *Nṛsūkta*; and again, with clarified butter, one thousand, one hundred, twenty-eight, or eight oblations separately with the mantras of the deities of the jars. Having poured the remaining clarified butter into the jars while reciting the *sparśa-mantra*, one should extinguish that fire.

The preceptor, having approached the vicinity of the image together with the guardians of the images and Brahmins well-versed in the Vedas, should raise the image with the mantra “uttiṣṭha brahmaṇaspate” and, with the mantra “bhadraṃ karṇebhiḥ,” seat it facing eastward upon the bathing throne.

Thereafter, having collected nineteen types of clay from a sacred field, a riverbank, a mountain, a sandbank, a lake, a spring, a confluence, a dried-up altar-ground, a fertile plot, a rice field, a Vedic sacrificial pit, a place trampled by a bull, an elephant’s tusk, a boar’s snout, an anthill, a mole’s burrow, a lotus pond, and a long pond—each in a separate vessel—and having had the *puṇyāha* (declaration of an auspicious day) proclaimed and sprinkled [the materials], one should worship the image with the *arghya* and other ritual offerings.

Having smeared the image from head to foot with nineteen types of clay produced from sacred fields while reciting the mantra "mūrdhānaṃ divaḥ," and having washed it with pure water while reciting the mantra "imaṃ me varuṇa," one should thereafter honor the image with offerings such as *arghya* and the rest.

With the mantra “idaṃ viṣṇuḥ,” [he offers] water for the feet with the *pādya* pitcher; with “āpo hi ṣṭhā,” water for the face with the *arghya* pitcher; with “imaṃ me varuṇa,” for the sipping (*upasparśana*); with “pavitraṃ te,” with the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*); with “dadhikrāvṇo,” with curds; with the *sāman* “payovrata,” with milk; with “madhuvātā,” with honey; with “yajñāyajña,” with astringent water (*kaṣāyāmbu*); with “mānastoke,” with warm water; with “vaṣaṭ te viṣṇoḥ,” with water from a gem (*maṇivāri*); and with “yāḥ phalinīḥ,” with water from fruit.

With these mantras and these pitchers—beginning with the water for the feet (*pādya*) and ending with the clarified butter (*ghṛta*)—one performs the immersion in the vessels for each substance: with the mantra "hiraṇyagarbhaḥ samavartata" using molten metal water; with "śanno devīḥ" using purificatory water (*mārjanāmbhas*); with "gandhadvārām" using scented water; with "trātāram indram" using water with unbroken rice grains (*akṣata*); with "idaṃ viṣṇoḥ" using barley water; and with "ghṛtasnāta" using clarified butter. [The ritual continues with] the bathing cloth (*upasnāna*), the *plota* garment, the upper robe (*uttarīya*), the *arghya*, the water for the feet (*pādya*), the water for sipping (*ācamana*), perfume (*gandha*), flowers (*puṣpa*), incense (*dhūpa*), and lamps (*dīpa*).

Having performed the consecration accompanied by the offering of gifts, and immediately thereafter having consecrated [the deity] with a thousand streams of pure water while reciting the *Puruṣasūkta*; having adorned [the deity] with garments and other ornaments; having worshipped with the *arghya* and other offerings; and having presented fruits and the like, one should also offer betel-leaf (*tāmbūla*). The preliminary bath (*upasnāna*) for the clarified butter is with warm water. Thus ends the thirteenth chapter in the *Kriyākairavacandrikā*. The Fourteenth Chapter:
The Ritual for the Bed, the Sacred Incense, and the Installation of the Vessel.

Then, having drawn the *cakrābja* mandala upon the altar in the center of the pavilion, and having prepared a bed-altar to its east, south, and north, the teacher sprinkles it with scented water while reciting the twelve-syllable mantra. Having spread darbha grass upon that altar with its tips pointing either eastward or northward, he distributes five *bhāras* of rice grains, half as much of husked rice, and half as much of sesame seeds, interspersed at intervals and covered with fresh foliage. Then, he draws a lotus upon the sesame seeds.

Upon that, having spread *darbha* grass as before, and upon that, having placed in sequence a tiger skin, a soft mattress, a cotton-down quilt, a jeweled blanket, a linen cloth, a variegated garment, and white clothing; and having placed upon those the bedding items—pillows and bolster-cases for the feet—and having strewn *darbha* grass around it, one should make that [bed] perfumed with substances such as musk, adorned with fragrant flower garlands and various ornaments.

The preceptor, having had the image raised from that [bed] with the mantra "Arise" (*uttiṣṭha*) by Brahmins and officiating priests who recite the *Puruṣasūkta* and other hymns preceded by the sound of musical instruments, should slowly circumambulate it to the right outside toward the ground of the bed-altar (*śayyāvedī*). There, having mentally conceived the pedestal (*pīṭha*) beginning with the *ādhāra-śakti* and ending with the lotus (*padma*), he should worship it.

Reciting the mantra “yadvaiṣṇavam” and the mantra “viśvataścakṣuḥ,” he should lay the image upon the bed with its head toward the east, its face facing south, or with its head toward the southern direction. Then, with the mantra “yuvāsuvāsāḥ,” he should cover the image on all sides with blankets or cloths.

Thereafter, having resolved, "I shall perform the worship of the door-arches (toraṇa)," and having invoked and worshipped the respective deities upon the doors, arches, banners, and water-pots according to the rules as before; while the Vedas, beginning with the Ṛgveda, and other texts are being recited by Brahmins in the eastern and other directions, and while the sound of musical instruments resounds everywhere, the preceptor, with a concentrated mind, meditating on the Blessed Lord within the lotus of his heart, causes the declaration of the auspicious day (puṇyāha) to be recited.

Having worshipped Vāsudeva, together with his limbs and his retinue, according to the prescribed rite within the mandala of the wheel and lotus; and having divided the bed-altar into three parts; when the two images have been consecrated in the middle and southern sections, one should prepare a seat in the northern section—on the north-western side of the deity—with rice, grains, and sesame seeds, and cover it with a cloth. Upon that, one should draw a lotus.

In that place, one should establish a large vessel—either made of iron or clay—measuring one *droṇa* and filled with fragrant water, covered with a cloth, a bundle of *kūrca* grass, and *aśvattha* sprouts as well as jewels; nearby to the right, a similar water-pot (*karaka*); and around the two vessels containing the reclining image, eight *mūrti*-vessels endowed with the same characteristics, placed upon eight pedestals of grain. Having thus arranged them, one should perform the ritual strewing (*paristaraṇa*).

Having placed within them conch-shells, discs, maces, lotuses, banners, *śrīvatsas*, Garuḍas, and tortoises—each made of pure gold from the Jāmbūnada river—and having fixed eight planks made of gold or other metals, or of sacrificial wood, in the middle of the image-pots according to the previously mentioned characteristics; and having set around them earthen vessels (*pālikās*) containing sprouts; one should perform the ritual resolve (*saṅkalpa*), saying, "I shall perform the worship of the pots," and then separately dry the waters of the pots and so forth.

In that water, having consecrated and worshipped the pedestal (*pīṭha*) beginning with the support (*ādhāra*) and ending with the lotus (*padma*), and having done so likewise for all eight [vessels], one should then invoke and worship the deities beginning with Viṣṇu and ending with Dāmodara in the pitchers starting from the east, each with their respective mantra. At that time, having fed more than twelve Brahmins who are embodiments of the Lord with milk-rice (*pāyasa*), one should give them cows, sesame seeds, clothing, and gold.
Thus ends the fourteenth chapter, titled "The Procedure for the Installation of the Pitchers during the Bed-Consecration," in the *Kriyākairavacandrikā* composed by the venerable Varāhaguru.
The Fifteenth Chapter:
The Procedure for Milking the Cow, the Deposition of the Principles (*tattvanyāsa*), the Fire Offering (*homa*), and the Procedure for the Installation of Vitality (*prāṇapratiṣṭhā*).

Now, first of all, the procedure for milking the cow is stated. In that regard, the mantra for summoning the cow is as follows: "You are Pūṣan; announce her to me when she has been approached. He issues the command: "I approach [her]. Thus he addresses her: "May you be free from disease; I unite you with progeny and with the abundance of wealth; may you become prolific."

"Having approached the cow," "May you roam for a month within the monastery. "I approach [you]: O bringer of freedom from disease, may I be united with progeny; becoming abundant through the increase of wealth, swelling with strength, milk, and ghee—living and making others live, may I sit down near you. "May Heaven and Earth together yield this sacrifice; may Dhātṛ, along with Soma and Vāyu, bestow wealth upon the sacrificer. "They draw forth the four-holed vessel, the goddess Iḍā, who is honey-sweet and finds the light of heaven."

O Indra and Agni, quicken this [milk] which is full of truth; may it establish the sacrificer in immortality. [This is] the milking with these two [mantras]. "Om, obeisance to the Blessed Lord Vāsudeva, to Gaṅgā, in whom the milk of the gods and of men is deposited; she is the life of the universe. "By the impulse of the god Savitṛ, may I purify you with the filter of Vasu, with a hundred streams, for the sake of good purification. "The drop has been offered, the spark has been offered to Agni, to the great firmament, Svāhā! "To Agni, to the great firmament, this is my offering. To Heaven and Earth."

"svāhā! To Heaven and Earth, this is my salutation. Having thus caused the second cow to be milked with the formula "Sarasvatī," the third with "Godā," and the fourth with "Yamunā," he releases his speech with the words, "May she be fit for milking again for the calves and for men. Then, while holding [the udders], he silently causes the other four cows to be milked. He pours the rinsings from the two jars [into the pot] with the mantra, "Be united, O you who possess nectar; you who have waves, most rich in honey, pleasant for the winning of wealth," and makes them well-mixed without spilling.

"Behold the cows, behold the lord of the cows; may the master of the sacrifice not harm you. Having made them turn toward the east, he causes them to be driven out. He milks the evening milk. In the same manner as the evening milking, he milks the morning milk. Having taken the milk from the morning milking, [he says]: "I anoint you with Soma. "O Waters, be watchful over the oblation; as you are watchful among the gods, so be watchful for the sacrificer at this sacrifice."

Having poured water into either an iron vessel or a wooden vessel, the teacher mutters: "Thou art Adas; for Viṣṇu, thee I place for the sacrifice, with waters, by means of a non-clay vessel, those which lie purified. With this he places [the vessel]. "The divine vessel, not made of clay, let it be employed for the life of the sacrifice; the waters, led across the strainer, have passed through while being held. If he should place it in an earthen vessel, he should throw a blade of grass or a piece of wood into the lid.

With the mantra, “O Viṣṇu, protect the oblation,” he places it in the designated spot. In this manner, he should perform the rites involving the milking vessel and so forth according to the rules. Now, the fire-offering (homa): Then the image-keepers (mūrtipās), by the command of the Guru, should commence the fire-offering according to the procedure to be described.

Having prepared the fire-drill (*araṇī*) from the heartwood of the *aśvattha* and *śamī* trees, and having churned it with the twelve-syllable mantra, one should then produce the fire. Alternatively, having taken fire produced from a sun-crystal (*sūryakāntāśman*) or ordinary worldly fire, and having sprinkled it with water while meditating upon the divine fire, one should spread three blades of *darbha* grass to the west or south of the sacrificial pit (*praṇīta*). Having offered the "tortoise-seat" (*kūrmāsana*) upon them and sat down there, one should perform the rites beginning with the purification of the elements (*bhūtaśuddhi*) and ending with the mental sacrifice (*mānasayāga*). Then, one should perform the circumambulation with fire (*paryagnikaraṇa*) inside the pit using handfuls of *darbha* grass.

Having performed [the rites] in this very manner for all the *kuṇḍas*, and having performed the consecration of the fire (*agni-saṃskāra*) and the transformation into the Vaiṣṇava state (*vaiṣṇavīkaraṇa*) in each individual *kuṇḍa*, one should draw the fire from that [central one] into the others. Having offered oblations of clarified butter (*ājya*) with the respective mantras, beginning with the *ādhāra* and ending with the *padma*, in the centers of all the square and other *kuṇḍa*-fires, and having worshipped them;

In the center of the lotus situated within the fire of the square sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*), [one should recite]: "Oṃ, obeisance to the Blessed One Vāsudeva! Come, come! I invoke Vāsudeva, who is the color of cow’s milk, wears yellow garments, has four arms, holds a lotus, a discus, a conch, and a mace in sequence, and is accompanied by Śrī, Puṣṭi, and Tuṣṭi. Having thus invoked and worshipped him:

In the Cāpakuṇḍa: "Oṃ, obeisance to the Blessed One Saṅkarṣaṇa; come, come! I invoke Saṅkarṣaṇa, who resembles the rising sun, wears yellow garments, has four arms, and holds in sequence a mace, a discus, a conch, and a lotus, and is accompanied by Śrī and Puṣṭi. Having thus invoked and worshipped him:

In the circular *kuṇḍa*: "Oṃ, obeisance to the Blessed One Pradyumna! Come, come! I invoke Pradyumna, who is emerald-colored, wears yellow garments, has four arms, and holds in sequence the Kaumodakī mace, the lotus, the conch, and the discus. Having thus invoked and worshipped him; In the triangular *kuṇḍa*: "Oṃ, obeisance to the Blessed One Aniruddha! Come, come! I invoke Aniruddha, who resembles a dark blue cloud, wears yellow garments, has four arms, and holds in sequence the gesture of fearlessness (*abhaya*), the discus, the conch, and the mace. Having thus invoked and worshipped him.

One should offer oblations of clarified butter (*ājya*) to those [deities] beginning with Śrīvatsa and ending with Garuḍa, each once, using their respective mantras, from the *arghya* offering up to the lamp. Beyond this, one should worship Vāsudeva and the others in pairs or singly within the sacrificial pits (*kuṇḍas*).

In the sacrificial pits (kuṇḍas) starting from the east, the oblation (homa) should be performed in sequence with fuel-sticks (samidh) of *pālāśa*, *khādira*, *bilva*, and *udumbara* in the four [pits] beginning with the southeast (āgneya), and with fuel-sticks of *pippala*, *plakṣa*, *nyagrodha*, and *kāśmarya*. Even if more [fuel-sticks] are envisioned, or if the aforementioned types are unavailable, it should be done with those made of *pālāśa* alone. For the purpose of cooking the sacrificial porridge (caru), four cows should be stationed facing north at the southern gate: Gaṅgā, Sarasvatī, Godāvarī, and Yamunā in embodied form.

The cooking of the sacrificial porridges (carus) and the offering of oblations should likewise be performed with their respective milks. Having performed the mantra-empowered milking at the very time of evening, one should cook one āḍhaka measure of rice grains with milk in the eastern fire. In the southern fire, one should cook kṛsara; in the western fire, food mixed with jaggery; in the northern fire, turmeric-rice; and in the other fires, milk-rice.

Having thus prepared the square sacrificial pits (kuṇḍas) at the cardinal points, the preceptor himself should perform the oblations in sequence with the Vāsudeva and other mantras, using sacrificial fuel-sticks (samidh) and clarified butter (ājya) separately one hundred and eight times for each; then, with the Caru offering and the Puruṣasūkta, sixteen oblations; and again with clarified butter using the previously mentioned mantras. Likewise, in the other pits, he should offer sesame seeds everywhere. Thereafter, he should cause the Mūrtipas, dressed in upper garments and ornaments, to perform the Homa according to the prescribed rules.

While the image-keepers (*mūrtipe*) are thus offering oblations, the Preceptor (*ācārya*), adorned with all ornaments, shall sit properly upon a seat facing east to the west of the great water-pot (*mahākumbha*). Having performed the drying and other rites of the water in the great pot, he should mentally construct the pedestal (*pīṭha*) therein, beginning with the *ādhāra* and ending with the lotus (*padma*), and worship it. Then, having invoked and worshipped the deities from Brahmā to Nārada around it according to the rules, and having meditated upon the Gurus with the mantra "Salutation to our Gurus," [he should proceed].

Meditating upon Vāsudeva—who is that supreme light, a mass of consciousness, imperishable, and all-pervading—and having invoked Him with the twelve-syllable mantra and meditated upon Him; having offered the *arghya* and other offerings with the *praṇava*; and thereafter, having worshipped the deities of the three enclosures—beginning with Śrīvatsa and others on the petals of the lotus of the yoga-posture, and including Vyāpti and others ending with Garuḍa within the three enclosures.

Having prepared the yoga-pīṭha as before, he should invoke [the discus] upon it with the mantra: “O thousand-spoked one, *huṃ phaṭ*, come, come! I invoke the Sudarśana, which shines like a thousand suns, possesses a thousand spokes, and is encircled by a thousand flames. Having invoked it, he should worship it with water for the guest-offering (*arghya*) and other offerings using its specific mantra and present it. Therein, the preceptor, having sat down after binding the *svastika* posture near the image, should meditate on the image as consisting of the five elements and perform the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) of the dissolution of the principles (*tattva-saṃhāra*) according to the procedure to be described.

Oṃ ṅaṃ, salutation to the Supreme One who is square, yellow in color, endowed with the sense of smell and the organ of generation, possessed of the qualities of sound, touch, form, taste, and smell, the essence of the earth element; salutation from the feet to the knees. Oṃ ghaṃ, salutation to the Supreme One who is crystal-colored, shaped like a half-moon, endowed with the sense of taste and the organ of excretion, possessed of the qualities of sound, touch, form, and taste, the essence of the water element; salutation from the knees to the private parts.
