Oṃ gaṃ, salutation to the Supreme One who is red in color, triangular, [endowed with] sight...

Salutation to the Self of the fire element (*agni-tattva*), who is endowed with the organ of feet and endowed with the qualities of sound, touch, and form; [from the private parts] up to the navel: *oṃ khaṃ*, salutation to the Supreme, who is smoke-colored, circular, endowed with the organ of touch, endowed with the qualities of sound and touch, the Self of the air element (*vāyu-tattva*); [from the navel] up to the nose: *oṃ kaṃ*, salutation to the Supreme, who is the color of a water-cloud, formless, endowed with the organs of speech and hearing, endowed with the quality of sound, the Self of the ether element (*ākāśa-tattva*); [from the nose] up to the head: *oṃ paṃ*.

*Oṃ phaṃ*, salutation to the Supreme One of white and black complexion, the essence of the *manas*-tattva; salutation to the heart. *Oṃ baṃ*, salutation to the Supreme One with the color of a trumpet-flower (*pāṭala*), the essence of the *ahaṃkāra*-tattva; salutation to the heart. *Oṃ bhaṃ*, salutation to the Supreme One with the luster of crystal, the essence of the *buddhi*-tattva; salutation to the heart. *Oṃ maṃ*, salutation to the Supreme One of white complexion, the essence of *prakṛti*; salutation to the heart. *Oṃ yaṃ*, salutation to the Supreme One with the luster of crystal, the essence of the *jīva*-tattva; salutation to the heart. Having thus performed the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) of dissolution for the image (*biṃba*).

Thereafter, having gone near the square sacrificial pit (*caturaśrakuṇḍa*) and sat down properly on a seat, one should make the formal resolve (*saṃkalpa*): "I shall perform the *tattvahoma*. Then, having sprinkled water around the fire with the mantras beginning with "O Aditi, grant permission" (*aditenumanyasva*) and ending with "O God Savitṛ, impel [me]" (*devasavitaḥ prasuva*), and having offered oblations with the mantras to be mentioned hereafter, one should collect the residual clarified butter (*saṃpātājya*) from each oblation into another vessel. With that, one should place [the butter] upon the respective limbs of the Deity using the ritual grass-bundle (*kūrca*), employing those very same mantras ending in "namas" (*namaḥ*).

The Nyāsa of the Principles (Tattva-nyāsa): Oṃ Maṃ, salutation to the Supreme One, who has the luster of crystal, the self of the principle of the individual soul (jīva-tattva); Svāhā! Oṃ Bhaṃ, salutation to the Supreme One, who is white in color, the self of primordial nature (prakṛti-tattva); Svāhā! Oṃ Baṃ, salutation to the Supreme One, who has the luster of crystal, the self of the principle of intellect (buddhi-tattva); Svāhā! Oṃ Phaṃ, salutation to the Supreme One, who is pale-red in color, the self of the ego-sense (ahaṃkāra-tattva); Svāhā! Oṃ Paṃ, salutation to the Supreme One, who is white and black in color, the self of the principle of mind (manas-tattva); Svāhā! [To be placed] in the heart. Oṃ Naṃ, salutation to the Supreme One, who is parrot-colored, the self of the subtle element of sound (śabda-tanmātra-tattva).

Svāhā to the two ears; Oṃ Dhaṃ, salutation to the Supreme, to the one of red color, whose self is the subtle element of touch, svāhā to the skin on the image; Oṃ Daṃ, salutation to the Supreme, to the one of light-colored brilliance, whose self is the subtle element of form, svāhā to the two eyes; Oṃ Thaṃ, salutation to the Supreme, to the one of pale-white color, whose self is the subtle element of taste, svāhā to the palate; Oṃ Taṃ, salutation to the Supreme, to the one of white color, whose self is the subtle element of smell, svāhā to the nose; Oṃ Ṇaṃ, salutation to the Supreme, to the one of pale-red (pāṭala) color, whose self is the sense-organ of hearing.

Svāhā to the two ears; Oṃ Ḍhaṃ, salutation to the supreme one of golden color, to the self of the sense of touch, svāhā to the skin; Oṃ Ḍaṃ, salutation to the supreme one of black color, to the self of the sense of sight, svāhā to the two eyes; Oṃ Ṭhaṃ, salutation to the supreme one of fair color, to the self of the sense of taste, svāhā to the tongue; Oṃ Ṭaṃ, salutation to the supreme one of white color, to the self of the sense of smell, svāhā to the nose; Oṃ Ñaṃ, salutation to the supreme one of white color, to the self of the organ of speech, svāhā to the voice; Oṃ Jhaṃ...

*Oṃ namas* to the Supreme, of red color, the essence of the organ of the hands; *svāhā* to the two hands. *Oṃ jaṃ namas* to the Supreme, of red color, the essence of the organ of the feet; *svāhā* to the two feet. *Oṃ chaṃ namas* to the Supreme, of red color, the essence of the organ of excretion; *svāhā* to the anus (*apāna*). *Oṃ caṃ namas* to the Supreme, of golden color, the essence of the organ of generation; *svāhā* to the organ of generation (*mehana*). *Oṃ kaṃ namas* to the Supreme, of the color of a water-cloud, formless, endowed with the organs of speech and hearing, endowed with the quality of sound, the essence of the element of space (*ākāśa-tattva*); *svāhā*.

From the crown of the head to the nose: *Oṃ khaṃ, obeisance to the Supreme, who is smoke-colored, circular, endowed with the organ of touch, possessed of the qualities of sound and touch, and whose self-nature is the element of air; svāhā!* From the navel to the nose: *Oṃ gaṃ, obeisance to the Supreme, who is red-colored, triangular, endowed with the organs of sight and feet, possessed of the qualities of sound, touch, and form, and whose self-nature is the element of fire; svāhā!*

From the navel to the secret place: *oṃ ghaṃ namaḥ parāya sphaṭikavarṇāya ardhacandrākārāya rasanāpāyvindriyayutāya śabdasparśarūparasaguṇayutāya aptattvātmane svāhā*. From the secret place to the knees: *oṃ ṅaṃ namaḥ parāya caturaśrāya pītavarṇāya ghrāṇopasthendriyayutāya śabdasparśarūparasagandhaguṇayutāya pṛthivītattvātmane svāhā*.

From the knees down to the feet, having offered one hundred and eight, twenty-eight, or eight oblations of clarified butter (ājya) with each of these mantras, one should apply the residual drops (saṃpāta-ājya) to the limbs of the image. Then follows the placement of the ten vital airs (prāṇādi-daśavāyu-nyāsa): Oṃ, svāhā to Prāṇa, who resides in the Suṣumnā channel situated from the root of the navel up to the aperture of Brahmā (brahmarandhra). Oṃ, svāhā to Apāna, who resides in the Iḍā channel from the root [of the navel] up to the left nostril.

Oṃ, to Vyāna, who resides in Piṅgalā from the root [kanda] up to the right nostril, svāhā! Oṃ, to Udāna, who resides in Gāndhārī rising from the root up to the left corner of the eye, svāhā! Oṃ, to Samāna, who resides in Hastijihvā rising from the root up to the right corner of the eye, svāhā! Oṃ, to Nāga, who resides in Pūṣā rising from the root up to the left ear, svāhā!

Oṃ, svāhā to the Tortoise (Kūrma) residing in Yaśasvinī, which has arisen from the root-tuber (kanda) and extends to the right ear. Oṃ, svāhā to Kṛkara residing in Alambuṣā, which is situated from the root-tuber down to the base of the anus. Oṃ, svāhā to Devadatta residing in Kuhū, which extends downward from the root-tuber to the penis. Oṃ, svāhā to Dhanañjaya residing in Kauśikī, which extends downward from the root-tuber to the big toes of the feet. Thus, as before, the fire-oblation (homa) and the ritual placement (nyāsa) are performed.

Now, the Prāṇapratiṣṭhā [mantra]: For this great mantra of the venerable Prāṇapratiṣṭhā, Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Maheśvara are the sages (ṛṣis); the Ṛg, Yajur, Sāma, and Atharva Vedas are the meters (chandāṃsi); the supreme vital energy (prāṇa-śakti), the cause of the creation, maintenance, and dissolution of the entire universe, is the deity (devatā); ĀṂ HRĪṂ KROṂ is the seed-syllable (bīja); SVĀHĀ is the power (śakti); OṂ is the peg (kīlaka); and the application (viniyoga) is for the purpose of establishing the life-force in the image.

1. *Āṃ hrīṃ kroṃ yaralavaśaṣaha oṃ haṃsaḥ, aṃ ṅaṃ ghaṃ gaṃ khaṃ kaṃ pṛthivy-aptējo-vāyv-ākāśa-prāṇātmane kroṃ hrīṃ āṃ āṃ hṛdayāya namaḥ svāhā.* 2. *Āṃ hrīṃ kroṃ yaralavaśaṣasa ha oṃ haṃsaḥ, iṃ ñaṃ dhaṃ daṃ thaṃ taṃ śabda-sparśa-rūpa-rasa-gandhā-pānātmane kroṃ hrīṃ āṃ iṃ śirase svāhā svāhā.*

3. *Āṃ hrīṃ kroṃ ya ra la va śa ṣa sa ha oṃ haṃsaḥ, uṃ ñaṃ jhaṃ jaṃ chaṃ caṃ* [to] the self of speech, hands, feet, anus, and genitals, and the vyāna breath: *kroṃ hrīṃ āṃ ūṃ śikhāyai vaṣaṭ svāhā*. 4. *Āṃ hrīṃ kroṃ ya ra la va śa ṣa sa ha oṃ haṃsaḥ, eṃ ṇaṃ daṃ ḍaṃ ṭhaṃ ṭaṃ* [to] the self of hearing, touch, sight, taste, and smell, and the udāna breath: *kro hrīṃ āṃ aiṃ kavacāya huṃ svāhā*.

5 Āṃ Hrīṃ Kroṃ Ya Ra La Va Śa Ṣa Sa Ha Oṃ Haṃsaḥ; Oṃ Paṃ Phaṃ Baṃ Bhaṃ Maṃ, to the Self who is the mind, ego, intellect, primordial nature, and the individual soul, along with the vital breaths—Kroṃ Hrīṃ Āṃ Auṃ, to the two eyes, Vauṣaṭ Svāhā!

6. *Āṃ hrīṃ kroṃ ya ra lava śa ṣa ha oṃ haṃsaḥ, aṃ yaṃ raṃ laṃ vaṃ śaṃ ṣaṃ saṃ haṃ laṃ kṣaṃ, to the self consisting of speech, movement, pleasure, recreation, and excretion—[namely] Nāga, Kūrma, Kṛkara, Devadatta, and Dhanañjaya—*kroṃ hrīṃ āṃ aḥ astrāya phaṭ svāhā*. The Meditation (*Dhyāna*): Seated upon a blossoming, crimson lotus rising from a red ocean, she holds in her lotus-like hands a noose, a bow made of sugarcane, a bowstring of bees, a goad, and five arrows.

May the supreme *prāṇa-śakti*, bearing a serpent-noose, accompanied by the Three-eyed Lord, adorned with full breasts, and possessing the color of the rising sun, grant us happiness. The root mantra: *Oṃ āṃ hrīṃ kroṃ ya ra la va śa ṣa sa ha oṃ haṃsaḥ*. *Amuṣya prāṇa iha prāṇaḥ* (The breath of this person is here as breath). *Āṃ hrīṃ kroṃ ya ra la va śa ṣa sa ha oṃ haṃsaḥ*. *Amuṣya jīva iha sthitaḥ* (The life-force of this person is established here). *Āṃ hrīṃ kroṃ ya ra la va śa ṣa sa ha oṃ haṃsaḥ*. *Amuṣya sarvendriyāṇi mana-ahaṃkāra-buddhi-pradhānam* (The all-senses, mind, ego, intellect, and primordial matter of this person [are here]).

"May earth, water, fire, air, ether, ear, skin, eye, tongue, nose, speech, hands, feet, anus, genitals, skin, hide, flesh, blood, marrow, bone, semen, prāṇa, apāna, vyāna, udāna, and samāna come here; may they remain happily for a long time, svāhā! Oṃ! As before, perform the *homa* and the ritual placement (*nyāsa*). One should perform the same for the goddesses beginning with Śrī and their retinues beginning with Brahmā.

Now follows the assignment of the weapons (*āyudha-nyāsa*): *Oṃ cakrāya svāhā*, *Oṃ śaṅkhāya svāhā*, *Oṃ gadine svāhā*, *Oṃ padmāya svāhā*, *Oṃ śārṅgāya svāhā*. Thus [are performed] the fire-oblation (*homa*) and the assignment (*nyāsa*). Now follows the assignment of the ornaments (*bhūṣaṇa-nyāsa*): *Oṃ kirīṭāya svāhā*, *Oṃ śrīvatsāya svāhā*, *Oṃ kaustubhāya svāhā*, *Oṃ vanamālāyai svāhā*, *Oṃ vainateyāya darpaṇarūpāya svāhā*. Thus [are performed] the fire-oblation and the assignment. This concludes the fifteenth chapter, titled "The Assignment and Fire-Oblation of the Principles" (*tattva-nyāsa-homa*). Sixteenth Chapter: The Procedure for the Sixteen Assignments (*ṣoḍaśa-nyāsa-vidhi*).

Now, the Nyāsa of the Praṇava: Oṃ Aṃ, salutation to the Supreme Viṣṇu, Svāhā to the heart. Oṃ Uṃ, salutation to the Supreme Brahmā, Svāhā to the right breast. Oṃ Maṃ, salutation to the Supreme Śaṅkara-ātman, Svāhā to the left breast. Oṃ, salutation to the Supreme Trimūrti-ātman Vāsudeva, Svāhā to the heart. Thus ends the Homa and the Nyāsa. Now, the Nyāsa of the Vyāhṛtis: Oṃ, salutation to the Supreme Bhūrloka, Svāhā to the feet. Oṃ, salutation to the Supreme Bhuvarloka, Svāhā to the heart.

"Oṃ namaḥ parāya suvarlokāya svāhā" on the head; thus is the oblation (*homa*) and the ritual placement (*nyāsa*). Now follows the placement of the syllables (*akṣara-nyāsa*): "Oṃ aṃ namaḥ parāya rasanātmane svāhā" on the tongue. Likewise for the subsequent ones: "Oṃ āṃ namaḥ parāya mukhātmane svāhā"; "Oṃ iṃ namaḥ parāya dakṣiṇalocanātmane svāhā"; "Oṃ īṃ namaḥ parāya vāmalocanātmane svāhā"; "Oṃ uṃ namaḥ parāya dakṣiṇakarṇātmane svāhā"; "Oṃ ūṃ namaḥ parāya vāmakarṇātmane svāhā."

Oṃ ṛṃ, salutation to the Supreme One, the self of the right nostril, svāhā! Oṃ ṝṃ, salutation to the Supreme One, the self of the left nostril, svāhā! Oṃ lṛṃ, salutation to the Supreme One, the self of the right cheek, svāhā! Oṃ lṝṃ, salutation to the Supreme One, the self of the left cheek, svāhā! Oṃ eṃ, salutation to the Supreme One, the self of the upper row of teeth, svāhā! Oṃ aiṃ, salutation to the Supreme One, the self of the lower row of teeth, svāhā! Oṃ oṃ, salutation to the Supreme One, the self of the upper lip, svāhā!

Oṃ auṃ, obeisance to the Supreme One, the self of the lower lip; svāhā! Oṃ aṃ, obeisance to the Supreme One, the self of the forehead; svāhā! Oṃ aḥ, obeisance to the Supreme One, the self of the palate; svāhā! Oṃ yaṃ, obeisance to the Supreme One, the self of the skin; svāhā! Oṃ raṃ, obeisance to the Supreme One, the self of the eyes; svāhā! Oṃ laṃ, obeisance to the Supreme One, the self of the nose; svāhā! Oṃ vaṃ, obeisance to the Supreme One, the self of the teeth; svāhā! Oṃ śaṃ, obeisance to the Supreme One, the self of the ears; svāhā! Oṃ ṣaṃ, obeisance to the Supreme One, the self of the belly; svāhā!

Oṃ saṃ, salutation to the supreme one, the self of the hips; svāhā! Oṃ haṃ, salutation to the supreme one, the self of the heart; svāhā! Oṃ laṃ, salutation to the supreme one, the self of the navel; svāhā! Oṃ kṣaṃ, salutation to the supreme one, the self of the genitals; svāhā! Oṃ kaṃ, salutation to the supreme one, to both thumbs; svāhā! Oṃ khaṃ, salutation to the supreme one, to both index fingers; svāhā! Oṃ gaṃ, salutation to the supreme one, to both middle fingers; svāhā! Oṃ ghaṃ, salutation to the supreme one, to both ring fingers; svāhā!

Oṃ ṅaṃ, salutation to the Supreme One, svāhā to the two little fingers. Oṃ caṃ, salutation to the Supreme One, svāhā to the self of the root of the right thigh. Oṃ chaṃ, salutation to the Supreme One, svāhā to the self of the middle of the right thigh. Oṃ jaṃ, salutation to the Supreme One, svāhā to the self of the right knee. Oṃ jhaṃ, salutation to the Supreme One, svāhā to the self of the right shank. Oṃ ñaṃ, salutation to the Supreme One, svāhā to the self of the right foot. Oṃ ṭaṃ, salutation to the Supreme One, svāhā to the self of the root of the left thigh.

Oṃ ṭhaṃ, salutation to the Supreme One, the Self of the middle of the left thigh; svāhā! Oṃ ḍaṃ, salutation to the Supreme One, the Self of the left knee; svāhā! Oṃ ḍhaṃ, salutation to the Supreme One, the Self of the left knee; svāhā! Oṃ ṇaṃ, salutation to the Supreme One, the Self of the left foot; svāhā! Oṃ taṃ, salutation to the Supreme One, the Self of the base of the right arm; svāhā! Oṃ thaṃ, salutation to the Supreme One, the Self of the middle of the right arm; svāhā! Oṃ daṃ, salutation to the Supreme One, the Self of the joint of the right arm; svāhā!

Oṃ dhaṃ, obeisance to the supreme self of the right elbow, svāhā! Oṃ naṃ, obeisance to the supreme self of the palm of the right hand, svāhā! Oṃ paṃ, obeisance to the supreme self of the root of the left arm, svāhā! Oṃ phaṃ, obeisance to the supreme self of the middle of the left arm, svāhā! Oṃ baṃ, obeisance to the supreme self of the joint of the left arm, svāhā! Oṃ bhaṃ, obeisance to the supreme self of the elbow of the left arm, svāhā! Oṃ maṃ, obeisance to the supreme self of the palm of the left hand, svāhā!

Thus concludes the fire offering (*homa*) and the ritual placement (*nyāsa*). Now follows the ritual placement of the lunar mansions (*nakṣatra-nyāsa*): Oṃ, salutation to the Supreme, the essence of Rohiṇī; to the heart, svāhā! Oṃ, salutation to the Supreme, the essence of Mṛgaśiras; to the head, svāhā! Oṃ, salutation to the Supreme, the essence of Ārdrā; to the hair, svāhā! Oṃ, salutation to the Supreme, the essence of Punarvasu; to the forehead, svāhā! Oṃ, salutation to the Supreme, the essence of Puṣya; to the mouth, svāhā! Oṃ, salutation to the Supreme, the essence of Āśleṣā; to the nose, svāhā! Oṃ, salutation to the Supreme, the essence of Maghā; to the teeth, svāhā!

Oṃ, salutation to the Supreme One; to the two Pūrvaphalgunī-selves, to the two ears—svāhā! Oṃ, salutation to the Supreme One; to the Uttaraphalgunī-self, to the right arm—svāhā! Oṃ, salutation to the Supreme One; to the Hasta-self, to the left arm—svāhā! Oṃ, salutation to the Supreme One; to the Citrā-self, to the right hand—svāhā! Oṃ, salutation to the Supreme One; to the Svāti-self, to the left hand—svāhā! Oṃ, salutation to the Supreme One; to the Viśākhā-self, to the right breast—svāhā!

Oṃ, salutation to the Supreme, whose self is Anurādhā; to the left breast, svāhā! Oṃ, salutation to the Supreme, whose self is Jyeṣṭhā; to the belly, svāhā! Oṃ, salutation to the Supreme, whose self is Mūla; to the hips, svāhā! Oṃ, salutation to the Supreme, whose self is Pūrvāṣāḍhā; to the genitals, svāhā! Oṃ, salutation to the Supreme, whose self is Uttarāṣāḍhā; to the testicles, svāhā! Oṃ, salutation to the Supreme, whose self is Śravaṇā; to the anus, svāhā! Oṃ, salutation to the Supreme, whose self is Dhaniṣṭhā; to the right thigh, svāhā!

Oṃ, obeisance to the Supreme One, the essence of Śatabhiṣaj; to Vāmoru, svāhā! Oṃ, obeisance to the Supreme One, the essence of Pūrvabhādrapadā; to the right shank, svāhā! Oṃ, obeisance to the Supreme One, the essence of Uttarabhādrapadā; to the left shank, svāhā! Oṃ, obeisance to the Supreme One, the essence of Revatī; to the right foot, svāhā! Oṃ, obeisance to the Supreme One, the essence of Aśvinī; to the left foot, svāhā! Oṃ, obeisance to the Supreme One, the essence of Bharaṇī; to the right side of the body, svāhā!

*Oṃ, salutation to the Supreme, whose essence is the Kṛttikās; to the left side, svāhā!* Thus is the fire-oblation (*homa*) and the ritual placement (*nyāsa*). Now, the placement of the planets (*grahanyāsa*): *Oṃ, salutation to the Supreme, whose essence is the Sun; to the right eye, svāhā.* *Oṃ, salutation to the Supreme, whose essence is the Moon; to the left eye, svāhā.* *Oṃ, salutation to the Supreme, whose essence is the Ego (*ahaṃkāra*); to the belly, svāhā.* *Oṃ, salutation to the Supreme, whose essence is Mercury (*budha*); to the intellect (*buddhi*), svāhā.* *Oṃ, salutation to the Supreme, whose essence is Jupiter (*bṛhaspati*); to the organ of speech, svāhā.*

Oṃ, obeisance to the Supreme, to the senses whose nature is Śukra; svāhā! Oṃ, obeisance to the Supreme, to the forehead whose nature is Śanaiścara; svāhā! Oṃ, obeisance to the Supreme, to the feet whose nature is Rāhu; svāhā! Oṃ, obeisance to the Supreme, to the hair whose nature is Ketu; svāhā! Oṃ, obeisance to the Supreme, to the navel whose nature is Dhruva; svāhā! Oṃ, obeisance to the Supreme, to all the limbs from the feet upward whose nature is the Seven Sages; svāhā! Thus is the fire-oblation (homa) and the ritual placement (nyāsa).

The ritual placement of the seasons (*kālanyāsa*): Oṃ, salutation to the Supreme One, the Self of the body; to the body, Svāhā! Oṃ, salutation to the Supreme One, the Self of Caitra; to the head, Svāhā! Oṃ, salutation to the Supreme One, the Self of Vaiśākha; to the mouth, Svāhā! Oṃ, salutation to the Supreme One, the Self of Jyeṣṭha; to the heart, Svāhā! Oṃ, salutation to the Supreme One, the Self of Āṣāḍha; to the right breast, Svāhā! Oṃ, salutation to the Supreme One, the Self of Śrāvaṇa; to the left breast, Svāhā!

Oṃ, salutation to the Supreme One, the self of Bhādrapada; to the belly, svāhā! Oṃ, salutation to the Supreme One, the self of Āśvayuja; to the waist, svāhā! Oṃ, salutation to the Supreme One, the self of Kārttika; to the right thigh, svāhā! Oṃ, salutation to the Supreme One, the self of Mārgaśīrṣa; to the left thigh, svāhā! Oṃ, salutation to the Supreme One, the self of Pauṣa; to the right shank, svāhā! Oṃ, salutation to the Supreme One, the self of Māgha; to the left shank, svāhā! Oṃ, salutation to the Supreme One, the selves of Phālguna; to the two feet, svāhā!

Oṃ, salutation to the Supreme One whose self is the year, to the left arm; svāhā! Oṃ, salutation to the Supreme One whose selves are the joints, to all the joints; svāhā! Oṃ, salutation to the Supreme One whose forms are all the limbs, to the seasons; svāhā! Oṃ, salutation to the Supreme One whose selves are the sixty [units] exceeding the nights, to all the articulations; svāhā! Oṃ, salutation to the Supreme One whose selves are the moments—*truṭi*, *lava*, *kalā*, *kāṣṭhā*, *kṣaṇa*, and *nimeṣa*—to the body hairs; svāhā! Oṃ, salutation to the Supreme One whose self is the Kṛta Yuga, to the face; svāhā!

Oṃ, obeisance to the Supreme One, the soul of the Tretā Yuga; to the Heart, Svāhā! Oṃ, obeisance to the Supreme One, the soul of the Dvāpara Yuga; to the Waist, Svāhā! Oṃ, obeisance to the Supreme One, the souls of the Kali Yuga; to the Two Feet, Svāhā! Oṃ, obeisance to the Supreme One, the soul of the Svāyaṃbhuva Manvantara; Svāhā! Oṃ, obeisance to the Supreme One, the soul of the Svarocīṣa Manvantara; Svāhā! Oṃ, obeisance to the Supreme One, the soul of the Uttama Manvantara; Svāhā! Oṃ, obeisance to the Supreme One, the soul of the Tāmasa Manvantara; Svāhā!

Oṃ, salutation to the Supreme One, the soul of the Raivata Manvantara; Svāhā! Oṃ, salutation to the Supreme One, the soul of the Cākṣuṣa Manvantara; Svāhā! Oṃ, salutation to the Supreme One, the soul of the Vaivasvata Manvantara; Svāhā! (On the right arm) Oṃ, salutation to the Supreme One, the soul of the Sūrya Manvantara; Svāhā! Oṃ, salutation to the Supreme One, the soul of the Dakṣa Manvantara; Svāhā! Oṃ, salutation to the Supreme One, the soul of the Brahma Manvantara; Svāhā! Oṃ, salutation to the Supreme One, the soul of the Dharma Manvantara; Svāhā!

Oṃ, salutation to the Supreme One, the soul of the Rudra-manvantara; Svāhā! Oṃ, salutation to the Supreme One, the soul of the Sāvarṇi-manvantara; Svāhā! Oṃ, salutation to the Supreme One, the soul of the Raudrabhūti-manvantara; Svāhā! (To the left arm. Oṃ, salutation to the Supreme One, the soul of the first *parārdha*; Svāhā to the right shank! Oṃ, salutation to the Supreme One, the soul of the second *parārdha*; Svāhā to the left shank! Oṃ, salutation to the Supreme One, the soul of the Great Kalpa; Svāhā to the head!

*Oṃ namas* to the Supreme One, whose nature is the northern solstice, to the right foot, *svāhā*. *Oṃ namas* to the Supreme One, whose nature is the southern solstice, to the left foot, *svāhā*. [Recite] at those respective places. Thus is the fire-oblation (*homa*) and the ritual placement (*nyāsa*). Now follows the ritual placement of the social classes (*varṇa*), beginning with the Brāhmaṇas: *Oṃ namas* to the Supreme One, whose nature is the Brāhmaṇa, to the mouth, *svāhā*. *Oṃ namas* to the Supreme One, whose nature is the Kṣatriyas, to the two arms, *svāhā*. *Oṃ namas* to the Supreme One, whose nature is the Vaiśyas, to the two thighs, *svāhā*.

Oṃ, obeisance to the Supreme One, to the Śūdra-selves, to the two feet, svāhā! Oṃ, obeisance to the Supreme One, to the Saṃkara-selves, to the toes of the feet, svāhā! Oṃ, obeisance to the Supreme One, to the Cow-self, to the mouth, svāhā! Oṃ, obeisance to the Supreme One, to the Goat-and-Sheep-selves, to the two arms, svāhā! Oṃ, obeisance to the Supreme One, to the Goat-and-Sheep-selves, to the two thighs, svāhā! Oṃ, obeisance to the Supreme One, to the village-and-forest-animal-selves, to the two feet, svāhā! In this manner, the fire-oblation (homa) and the ritual placement (nyāsa) are performed.

Now follows the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) of water: *Oṃ namaḥ parāya meghātmane keśebhyaḥ svāhā* (Oṃ, salutation to the Supreme for the clouds, to the hairs of the head, svāhā). *Oṃ namaḥ parāya kūpātmane romakūpāya svāhā* (Oṃ, salutation to the Supreme for the well, to the pores of the skin, svāhā). *Oṃ namaḥ parāya vāpyātmane pādābhyāṃ svāhā* (Oṃ, salutation to the Supreme for the ponds, to the two feet, svāhā). *Oṃ namaḥ parāya nirjharātmane jaṅghābhyāṃ svāhā* (Oṃ, salutation to the Supreme for the mountain torrents, to the two shanks, svāhā). *Oṃ namaḥ parāya nadyātmane sarvāvayavebhyaḥ svāhā* (Oṃ, salutation to the Supreme for the rivers, to all the limbs, svāhā). *Oṃ namaḥ parāya samudrātmanai kukṣyai svāhā* (Oṃ, salutation to the Supreme for the ocean, to the belly, svāhā). Thus ends the oblation (*homa*) and the ritual placement (*nyāsa*).

Now, the assignment of the limbs (*nigaman nyāsa*): Oṃ, salutation to the Supreme, the essence of the Ṛgveda; to the head, Svāhā! Oṃ, salutation to the Supreme, the essence of the Yajurveda; to the right arm, Svāhā! Oṃ, salutation to the Supreme, the essence of the Sāmaveda; to the left arm, Svāhā! Oṃ, salutation to the Supreme, the essence of all the Upaniṣads; to the heart, Svāhā! Oṃ, salutation to the Supreme, the essence of the Itihāsas; to the right shank, Svāhā! Oṃ, salutation to the Supreme, the essence of the Purāṇas; to the left shank, Svāhā!

Oṃ, salutation to the Supreme One; to the Atharva-veda, whose essence is the enemy-subduer, svāhā! Oṃ, salutation to the Supreme One; to the two feet, whose essence is the Kalpa-sūtras, svāhā! Oṃ, salutation to the Supreme One; to the face, whose essence is grammar (Vyākaraṇa), svāhā! Oṃ, salutation to the Supreme One; to the throat, whose essence is the science of logic (Tarka-śāstra), svāhā! Oṃ, salutation to the Supreme One; to the heart, whose essence is Mīmāṃsā and Nirukta, svāhā! Oṃ, salutation to the Supreme One; to the right eye, whose essence is prosody (Chandas), svāhā! Oṃ, salutation to the Supreme One; to the left eye, whose essence is astronomy/astrology (Jyotiṣa), svāhā!

Oṃ, salutation to the Supreme One, whose self is the science of training; to the belly, svāhā! Oṃ, salutation to the Supreme One, whose self is the Gāruḍa Tantra; to the self of the right ear, svāhā! Oṃ, salutation to the Supreme One, whose self is the Bhūta Tantra; to the self of the left ear, svāhā! Oṃ, salutation to the Supreme One, whose self is the science of archery (Dhanurveda); to the right hand, svāhā! Oṃ, salutation to the Supreme One, whose self is the science of medicine (Āyurveda); to the left hand, svāhā! Oṃ, salutation to the Supreme One, whose self is the Yoga Śāstra; to the heart, svāhā!

*Oṃ namaḥ parāya nītiśāstrātmane pādābhyāṃ svāhā.* Thus is the *homa* and the *nyāsa*. Now, the *devatā-nyāsa*: *Oṃ namaḥ parāya brahmaṇe śirase svāhā.* *Oṃ namaḥ parāya sarasvatyātmikāyai jihvāyai svāhā.* *Oṃ namaḥ parāya indrātmane dakṣiṇabhujāya svāhā.* *Oṃ namaḥ parāya mahābalātmane vāmabhujāya svāhā.* *Oṃ namaḥ parāya viśvakarmātmane dakṣiṇastanāya svāhā.*

Oṃ, salutation to the Supreme, whose self is Prahlāda; to the left breast, svāhā! Oṃ, salutation to the Supreme, whose self is Nārada; to the right side of the abdomen, svāhā! Oṃ, salutation to the Supreme, whose self is Ananta and others; to the left side of the abdomen, svāhā! Oṃ, salutation to the Supreme, whose selves are Varuṇa and the rest; to the bones, svāhā! Oṃ, salutation to the Supreme, whose selves are the Pitṛs; to the two feet, svāhā! Oṃ, salutation to the Supreme, whose selves are the Viśvedevas; to the two thighs, svāhā! Oṃ, salutation to the Supreme, whose selves are the Ṛṣis; to the two knees, svāhā!

Oṃ, salutation to the Supreme One; to the two knees, whose nature is that of Yakṣas, Svāhā! Oṃ, salutation to the Supreme One; to the two ankles, whose nature is that of Rākṣasas, Svāhā! Oṃ, salutation to the Supreme One; to the two heels, whose nature is that of Vidyādharas, Svāhā! Oṃ, salutation to the Supreme One; to the soles of the feet, whose nature is that of the nine Planets, Svāhā! Oṃ, salutation to the Supreme One; to the nails, whose nature is that of Pūtanās and Jṛmbhakas, Svāhā! Oṃ, salutation to the Supreme One; to the right side of the hip, whose nature is that of Subrahmaṇya, Svāhā!

*Oṃ namaḥ parāya gandharvātmane oṣṭhāya svāhā.* Thus is the *homa* and the *nyāsa*. Now follows the *Vairājanyāsa*: *Oṃ namaḥ parāya svarlokātmane mastakāya svāhā.* *Oṃ namaḥ parāya sūryātmane dakṣiṇanetrāya svāhā.* *Oṃ namaḥ parāya candrātmane vāmanetrāya svāhā.* *Oṃ namaḥ parāya vāyvātmane nāsikāyai svāhā.* *Oṃ namaḥ parāya digātmabhyāṃ bāhubhyāṃ svāhā.*

Oṃ, salutation to the Supreme One who is the Self of the Ṛṣis; to the heart, svāhā! Oṃ, salutation to the Supreme One who is the Self of the ether; to the body, svāhā! Oṃ, salutation to the Supreme One who is the Self of the gods and the inner self; svāhā! Oṃ, salutation to the Supreme One who is the selves of the clouds; to the hair, svāhā! Oṃ, salutation to the Supreme One who is the essence of the stars; to the ornaments, svāhā! Oṃ, salutation to the Supreme One who is the Self of fire; to the mouth, svāhā! Oṃ, salutation to the Supreme One who is the Self of Sarasvatī; to speech, svāhā! Thus is the oblation and the ritual placement (nyāsa).

Now, the ritual placement of the sacrifices (*kratunyāsa*): Oṃ, salutation to the Supreme, whose essence is the Horse Sacrifice (*aśvamedha*); svāhā to the head. Oṃ, salutation to the Supreme, whose essence is the Human Sacrifice (*naramedha*); svāhā to the forehead. Oṃ, salutation to the Supreme, whose essence is the Rājasūya sacrifice; svāhā to the mouth. Oṃ, salutation to the Supreme, whose essence is the Gosava sacrifice; svāhā to the throat. Oṃ, salutation to the Supreme, whose essence is the Ekādaśinī; svāhā to the navel. Oṃ, salutation to the Supreme, whose essence is the Agniṣṭoma sacrifice; svāhā to the generative organ. Oṃ, salutation to the Supreme, whose essence is the Atirātra sacrifice; svāhā to the testicles.

Oṃ, salutation to the Supreme One; to the two thighs, whose nature is the Āptoryāma sacrifice, svāhā! Oṃ, salutation to the Supreme One; to the two knees, whose nature is the Ṣoḍaśī sacrifice, svāhā! Oṃ, salutation to the Supreme One; to the right calf, whose form is the Ukthya sacrifice, svāhā! Oṃ, salutation to the Supreme One; to the left calf, whose form is the Vājapeya sacrifice, svāhā! Oṃ, salutation to the Supreme One; to the arms, whose nature is the Cāturmāsya sacrifices, svāhā! Oṃ, salutation to the Supreme One; to the hands, whose nature is the Sautrāmaṇī sacrifice, svāhā!

Oṃ, salutation to the Supreme One; to the fingers, whose essence is the Paśu-iṣṭi sacrifice, svāhā! Oṃ, salutation to the Supreme One; to the right eye, whose essence is the Darśa sacrifice, svāhā! Oṃ, salutation to the Supreme One; to the left eye, whose essence is the Paurṇamāsa sacrifice, svāhā! Oṃ, salutation to the Supreme One; to the two breasts, whose essences are the iṣṭi, the sacrificial grass (darbha), the sacrificial post (yūpa), the utterance of svāhā, and the utterance of vaṣaṭ, svāhā! Oṃ, salutation to the Supreme One; to the fingers, whose essence consists of the five great sacrifices (pañcamahāyajña), svāhā! Oṃ, salutation to the Supreme One; to the heart, whose essence is the Dakṣiṇā, svāhā!

Oṃ, obeisance to the Supreme, to the hairs consisting of the *stoma* chants; svāhā! Oṃ, obeisance to the Supreme, to the mouth which is the nature of the *āhavanīya* fire; svāhā! Oṃ, obeisance to the Supreme, to the mouth which is the nature of the *gārhapatya* fire; svāhā! Oṃ, obeisance to the Supreme, to the navel which is the nature of the *dakṣiṇāgni* fire; svāhā! Oṃ, obeisance to the Supreme, to the two feet which are the nature of the *āvasathya* fire; svāhā! Oṃ, obeisance to the Supreme, to the heart which is the nature of the *sabhyāgni* fire; svāhā! Oṃ, obeisance to the Supreme, to the ornaments consisting of the *pravargya* rite; svāhā!

Thus is the *homa* and the *nyāsa*. Now, the *guṇanyāsa*: *oṃ namaḥ parāya sattvaguṇātmane śirase svāhā*; *oṃ namaḥ parāya rajoguṇātmane hṛdayāya svāhā*; *oṃ namaḥ parāya tamoguṇātmabhyāṃ pādābhyāṃ svāhā*. Thus is the *homa* and the *nyāsa*. Now, the *mūrtinyāsa*: *oṃ namaḥ parāya matsyamūrtyātmane śirase svāhā*; *oṃ namaḥ parāya kūrmamūrtyātmabhyāṃ pādābhyāṃ svāhā*.

Oṃ, salutation to the Supreme One; to the two shanks, whose essence is the form of Varāha, svāhā! Oṃ, salutation to the Supreme One; to the forehead, whose essence is the form of Nṛsiṃha, svāhā! Oṃ, salutation to the Supreme One; to the face, whose essence is the form of Vāmana, svāhā! Oṃ, salutation to the Supreme One; to the heart, whose essence is Paraśurāma, svāhā! Oṃ, salutation to the Supreme One; to the two hands, whose essence is Kārtavīrya, svāhā! Oṃ, salutation to the Supreme One; to the heart, whose essence is Rāma of the Lineage of Daśaratha, svāhā!

*Oṃ*, salutation to the Supreme One, whose self is Balarāma; to the heart, *svāhā*. *Oṃ*, salutation to the Supreme One, whose self is Kṛṣṇa; to the heart, *svāhā*. *Oṃ*, salutation to the Supreme One, whose self is Buddha; to the secret place, *svāhā*. *Oṃ*, salutation to the Supreme One, whose selves are the two Kalkis; to the knees, *svāhā*. Thus is the fire-oblation (*homa*) and the ritual placement (*nyāsa*). Now follows the placement of the Śaktis: *Oṃ*, salutation to the Supreme One, whose self is Lakṣmī; to the forehead, *svāhā*. *Oṃ*, salutation to the Supreme One, whose self is Sarasvatī; to the mouth, *svāhā*. *Oṃ*, salutation to the Supreme One, whose self is Rati; *svāhā*.

*Oṃ*, salutation to the Supreme, whose essence is love, to the ears, *svāhā*. *Oṃ*, salutation to the Supreme, whose essence is fame, to the eyes, *svāhā*. *Oṃ*, salutation to the Supreme, whose essence is peace, to the heart, *svāhā*. *Oṃ*, salutation to the Supreme, whose essence is contentment, to the belly, *svāhā*. *Oṃ*, salutation to the Supreme, whose essence is nourishment, to all the limbs, *svāhā*. Thus is the fire-offering (*homa*) and the ritual placement (*nyāsa*). Now follows the sixfold attribute-placement (*ṣaḍguṇanyāsa*): *Oṃ*, salutation to the Supreme, who is knowledge, to the heart, *namaḥ svāhā*.

Oṃ, salutation to the Supreme, to Sovereignty; to the head, svāhā, svāhā. Oṃ, salutation to the Supreme, to Power; to the crest-lock, vaṣaṭ, svāhā. Oṃ, salutation to the Supreme, to Strength; to the armor, huṃ, svāhā. Oṃ, salutation to the Supreme, to Radiance; to the two eyes, vauṣaṭ, svāhā. Oṃ, salutation to the Supreme, to Heroism; to the weapon, phaṭ, svāhā. Thus is the fire-oblation (homa) and the ritual placement (nyāsa). Now, the placement of the worlds (lokanyāsa): Oṃ, salutation to the Supreme, to those whose nature is Atala; to the soles of the feet, svāhā.

Oṃ, salutation to the Supreme One; to the two feet, which are the essence of Vitala, svāhā! Oṃ, salutation to the Supreme One; to the two ankles, which are the essence of Sutala, svāhā! Oṃ, salutation to the Supreme One; to the two shanks, which are the essence of Nitala, svāhā! Oṃ, salutation to the Supreme One; to the two knees, which are the essence of Mahātala, svāhā! Oṃ, salutation to the Supreme One; to the two thighs, which are the essence of Rasātala, svāhā! Oṃ, salutation to the Supreme One; to the waist, which is the essence of Talātala, svāhā! Oṃ, salutation to the Supreme One; to the two feet, which are the essence of Bhūrloka, svāhā!

Oṃ, salutation to the Supreme, the self of the Bhuvarloka; to the genitals, svāhā! Oṃ, salutation to the Supreme, the self of the Svarloka; to the abdomen, svāhā! Oṃ, salutation to the Supreme, the self of the Maharloka; to the heart, svāhā! Oṃ, salutation to the Supreme, the self of the Janoloka; to the throat, svāhā! Oṃ, salutation to the Supreme, the self of the Tapoloka; to the mouth, svāhā! Oṃ, salutation to the Supreme, the self of the Satyaloka; to the head, svāhā! Thus is the fire-oblation (homa) and the ritual placement (nyāsa). One should not perform the sixteen-fold placement (ṣoḍaśanyāsa) upon images that lack shanks.
Thus ends the sixteenth chapter, titled "The Procedure for the Sixteen Installations," in the *Kriyākairavacandrikā*.
Chapter Seventeen: The Peace-Offering Sacrifice (*Śāntihoma*).

Having thus performed the sixteen-fold ritual placement (*nyāsa*), one should then perform the propitiatory oblation (*śāntihoma*). In the eastern fire-pit (*kuṇḍa*), having offered one hundred and eight oblations of honey with the mantra “*oṃ bhūḥ svāhā*,” one should touch the feet of the deity with the residual drops (*sampāta*). In the southern fire, having likewise offered oblations of milk with “*oṃ bhuvaḥ svāhā*,” one should touch the belly of the deity with the residual drops. In the western fire, having likewise offered oblations of curd with “*oṃ suvaḥ svāhā*,” and in the northern fire, having likewise offered oblations of clarified butter (*ājya*) with “*oṃ bhūr bhuvaḥ suvaḥ svāhā*.”

One should touch the head of the deity with the residue (saṃpāta) and all its limbs with all the residues. Having likewise offered oblations at that very spot with molasses, clarified butter, and honey, each time reciting the Viṣṇu-gāyatrī, one should touch the face and all the limbs of the deity with the residue. This procedure applies to images made of metal, stone, or wood.

Having entered the interior of the temple, one should perform the rites beginning with the withdrawal (*saṃhāra*) and creation (*utpādana*), concluding with the peace-offering (*śānti-homa*). Within the bedchamber and other areas, as well as among the attendants and the Brahmans and others, the deposition of the principles (*tattva-nyāsa*) and the fire-oblation (*homa*) should be performed according to the previously mentioned method. At the time of the *prāṇapratiṣṭhā* (consecration of the vital breath), having honored all [the deities] with offerings such as the *arghya*, one should present the four kinds of food with the *praṇava* (Om). Whether the Lord Ananta is seated or reclining upon his serpent-couch, one should perform the rite for him in exactly this same manner.

Then, for the sake of accomplishing the rite of installation (*pratiṣṭhā-karma*), having made the formal resolve (*saṃkalpa*) saying, "I shall perform the rite of binding the protective thread (*rakṣābandhana-karma*)," and having bound the protective thread upon the primary image according to the rules; having covered the image with new blankets and cloths while reciting the mantra "yuvā suvāsāḥ"; and having invoked and worshipped Sudarśana at the entrance with the mantra "Oṃ namaḥ sudarśanāya cakrarājāya jvālāmāline huṃ phaṭ svāhā," and having displayed the Cakra-mudrā, one should offer an oblation (*bali*) there.

In the ritual procedure for the Great Consecration (*mahāpratiṣṭhā*), when the retinue beginning with Indra is to be installed in their respective places, one should perform the rites of water-consecration (*jalādhivāsa*), shadow-consecration (*chāyādhivāsa*), opening of the eyes, bathing, and so forth, as appropriate together with the deity; then, having prepared heaps of grain (*dhānyapīṭha*) on the ground before each respective location as previously described.

Having performed the preliminary consecration (*adhivāsa*) for Caṇḍa and the other gatekeepers, Garuḍa, Viṣvaksena, and the deities of the enclosures within those [shrines] complete with their bedding materials, as well as for the fivefold enclosures beginning with the Great Seat (*mahāpīṭha*) and the offering altars (*balipīṭha*), one should perform the subsidiary fire-oblation (*parivāra-homa*) before each of those respective locations, either in sacrificial pits (*kuṇḍa*) or on sacrificial mounds (*sthaṇḍila*). For each enclosure, in the sacrificial pits of the eight directions, there should be fuel-sticks (*samidh*) of *palāśa*, *khadira*, *aśvattha*, *plakṣa*, *nyagrodha*, *bilva*, *udumbara*, and *kāśmarya* respectively.

With these fuel-sticks (samidh), clarified butter (ājya), and cooked rice (caru), one should cause the Brahmins—who have been previously selected individually—to perform the fire-oblation (homa) for each deity with one hundred and eight oblations (āhuti) using the mantras to be mentioned hereafter; specifically, for Garuḍa, Viṣvaksena, Caṇḍa, and the others, the oblation should be performed separately with the aforementioned number of Palāśa wood sticks, clarified butter, and cooked rice, using the mantras to be mentioned.

At the door of the inner sanctum (garbhagṛha): “Oṃ croṃ Caṇḍāya svāhā,” “Oṃ proṃ Pracaṇḍāya svāhā. At the door of the half-maṇḍapa: “Oṃ śaṃ Śaṅkhine svāhā,” “Oṃ caṃ Cakriṇe svāhā. In the foundational area (adhiṣṭhāna) are Gajānana and others, or Vāsudeva and others, or Puruṣa and others. In the southeast (āgneyī), “Oṃ Gajānanāya svāhā”; in the northeast (aiśānī), “Oṃ Ambikāyai svāhā. In the northern enclosure of the main gate (gopura), [offerings] to Sūrya and Gāyatrī; in the south, to Īśa or Dakṣiṇāmūrti; in the west, in the northern enclosure, to Sūrya.

On the southern pillar: *oṃ candramase*. At the door of the inner pavilion: *oṃ jayāya*, *vijayāya*—these are the deities of the enclosure (*āvaraṇadevatāḥ*). In the southeast: *oṃ kāmāya*. In the south: *oṃ brahmaṇe*. In the southwest: *oṃ gajānanāya*. In the west: *oṃ ṣaṇmukhāya*. In the northwest: *oṃ durgāyai*. In the north: *oṃ dhanādhipataye*. In the northeast: *oṃ śarāya svāhā*. In that same place: *oṃ kṣetrapālāya*. To the north of Brahmā: *oṃ mahiṣāsuramardini*. In front of the dance pavilion (*nṛttārdhamaṇḍapa*): [as above].

Facing the main image: *Oṃ vakratuṇḍāya vidmahe suvarṇapakṣāya dhīmahi | tanno garuḍaḥ pracodayāt svāhā*. There, in the courtyard, in the southwest (*nairṛta*): *Oṃ śrīṃ śriyai*. In the courtyard, in their respective places, [are] Indra and the others. For Indra: *Oṃ trātāramindramavitāramindram have have suhavaṃ śūramindram | huvema śakraṃ puruhūtamindraṃ svasti no maghavā dhātvindraḥ svāhā*. For Agni: *ayāścāgne 'sy anabhiśastīśca*.

"Thou art indeed *ayās*, held by an iron mind; with iron thou carriest the oblation. With *ayās* bestow the remedy, Svāhā! "That which the owl [does], or that which the dove makes as its footprint, O Agni—if this be in vain, or if it be sent as his messenger—to that Yama, to Death, let there be homage, Svāhā! O Nirṛti, seek him who does not press the Soma, who does not sacrifice; follow the path of the thief and the robber. Seek someone other than us for thy satisfaction; O Goddess Nirṛti, let there be homage to thee, Svāhā! Of Varuṇa... these mine..."

Beginning with "O Varuṇa" and ending with "Do not steal our life, Svāhā," [the offering is made]. "O Vāyu, come to the sacrifice with your teams of horses—by the hundreds and by the thousands—to this oblation; O Vāyu, rejoice in this offering. May you all protect us with blessings always; Svāhā! "Of Soma": "May thy courses meet together, may thy strengths meet together, and may thy virile powers meet together, O thou who art the protector against the enemy. Swell for immortality, O Soma; bestow upon us the highest glories in heaven; Svāhā! "Of the Lord": "Him, the Lord of the moving and the stationary world, the Master..."

"We invoke Pūṣan to quicken our intellect for protection, so that he may be the increaser of our wealth and the guardian who stands as a protector for our well-being—svāhā! This [mantra] pertains solely to the single enclosure (ekāvaraṇa).

In the inner chamber of the sanctuary named Antarmaṇḍala, in the first enclosure (prathamāvaraṇa), [one should worship] in the northern gate-pavilion (gopurottarasāla) with "Oṃ puruṣāya svāhā"; in the southern pavilion, Satya; in the southeast (āgneye), Hayagrīva; in the south, Saṃkarṣaṇa; in the southwest (naiṛte), Varāha; in the west (vāruṇyāṃ), Pradyumna; in the northwest (vāyavye), Ananta; in the north, Aniruddha; in the northeast (aiśānyāṃ), Nṛsiṃha; and in the courtyard (aṅgaṇe), at the locations of the pedestals for Indra and the others, with "Oṃ cakriṇe svāhā," "Oṃ musaline svāhā," and "Oṃ śaṅkhiṇe svāhā."

Svāhā! Oṃ, svāhā to Khaḍgin; oṃ, svāhā to Halin; oṃ, svāhā to Gadin; oṃ, svāhā to Pāśin; oṃ, svāhā to Vajrin. In the inner courtyard (antarhāra-dhāman), in the second enclosure (dvitīyāvaraṇa), at the northern gate-tower (gopura): to Sūrya in the east, to Candramas in the south; in that enclosure: to Kāma in the southeast (āgneyī), to Brahmā in the south (yāmyā), to Gajānana in the southwest (naiṛtī), to Ṣaṇmukha in the west (vāruṇī), to Durgā in the northwest (vāyavī), to Dhanādhipati in the north (saumyā), and to Śara in the northeast (aiśānī). Then, the gatekeepers of the four gate-towers of that enclosure.

At the eastern gate, to the bearer of the lotus; at the south, to the bearer of the mace, and to the bearer of the sword; at the west, to the bearer of the thunderbolt, and to the bearer of the club; at the north, to the bearer of the noose, and to the bearer of the goad. In the courtyards, at the locations of the pedestals, [are] Indra and the others. In the third enclosure, named the inner gateway, at the four gates of the towers, [are] Dhātṛ, Aryaman, Vidhātṛ, Mitra-Varuṇa, Bhaga, Vivasvat, Pūṣan, Tvaṣṭṛ, and between Agni and Yama, Oṃ.

To Dhara, Dhruva, Soma, Apas, Anala, Pratyūṣa, and Prabhāsa; between Yama and Nirṛti, to Kavyavāha, Anala, Soma, Agniṣvātta, Somapa, and Barhiṣada; between Nirṛti and Varuṇa, to Rudra, Agni, and Viṣṇu; between Varuṇa and Vāyu, to Āvaha, Vivaha, Udvaha, Saṃvaha, Nivaha, Anuvaha, Vyavaha, and [the others] between Vāyu and Kubera.

To Vasiṣṭha, Vāmadeva, Jābāli, Kāśyapa, Bhṛgu, and Jamadagni. Between Kubera and Īśāna, [offerings are made] to Mṛga, Vyādha, Śarva, Nirṛti, Dhvaja, Ekapada, Ahirbudhnya, Pinākin, Yavada, Sthāṇu, Bhaga, and Kapālin; and right there to Kṣetrapāla. In the courtyard, at the locations of the pedestals for Indra and the others, [are placed] Kumuda and the rest. In the middle [of the enclosure], starting from the east, are the gatekeepers of the *sāla* and *gopura* gates: to Durjaya in the east;

To the powerful one in the east; to Viśvabhāvana in the south; to Puṣkara in the west; to Saṃbhava and Prabhava in the north; and to Suśobhana and Subhadra. As for the deities of the enclosure: in the east, to Anala, Ravi, Purandara, Agni, Āpaḥ, and Āgneya; to the nine planets beginning with Āditya; in the south, to Agni, Vāyu, Prajāpati, Śakti, and Nirṛti; to the two Aśvins; in the west, to Lakṣmī, Sarasvatī, and Vighna; in the northwest, Indra and the others; and in the north, to the Vāsudevas.

Oṃ, to Brahmā, to Marīci, to Atri, to Vivasvat, to Pṛthivīśvara, to Citra, to Apavatsa, to Saṃdhātṛ, to Savitṛ, to Rudra, to Rudrarāja, to Indra, to Indrajaya, to Īśāna, to Parjanya, to Jayanta, to Mahendra, to Bhānu, to Satya, to Bhṛṣa, to Antarikṣa, to Agni, to Pūṣan, to Kuśa, to Bhānu, to Gṛhakṣata, to Vama, to Gandharva, to Bhṛṅgarāja, to Mṛga, to Sugraha, to Puṣpadantaka, and to Varuṇa.

To Bhṛgu, Śyāva, Yakṣman, Manojava, Roga, Nāga, Mṛtyanta, Phallāṭa, Soma, Aditi, and Vāstunātha; in the northeast (aiśāna), to the twenty-seven lunar mansions (nakṣatras); on the pedestals (pīṭhikās) starting with Indra, to Upendra, Prākṛta, Puṇya, Puṣpara, Viśvabhāvana, Asuraghna, Kṛtānta, and Bhūtanātha; to Mahāmaryāda; to the gatekeepers of the city gates (gopura-dvārapālas), Kumuda and the others; in the enclosure (āvaraṇa), in the directions starting from the east, to the Siddhas and the Ṛṣis.

To the Nāgas, Asuras, Rākṣasas, Yakṣas, Vidyādharas, Saurabheyīs, Guhyakas, Gandharvas, Apsarases, and Prajāpatis; in the courtyard (aṅgaṇe) and upon the pedestals (pīṭhikāsu) of Indra and the others, [offerings] to Viśveśvara, Viśvakṛt, Viśva, Viśvātman, Viśvalocana, Viśvapāda, Viśvabhuja, and Viśvakarmakṛt: “Oṃ, on the great pedestal (mahāpīṭhe), svāhā to all the attendants of Viṣṇu.”

This [rite] extends from the first enclosure (prathamāvaraṇa) up to the fifth enclosure. Thus, having caused the Brahmins to perform the subsidiary fire-offering (parivāra-homa)—beginning with the syllable Om and ending with Svāhā—using their respective mantras, and in the worship [of the deities], using mantras ending in "Namaḥ"; and having given sacrificial fees (dakṣiṇā) to them; then, having prepared a pedestal (pīṭha) of rice and other grains, and having spread Darbha grass upon it and performed the ritual encircling (paristaraṇa); and having consecrated (adhivāsya) the pedestal (piṇḍikā) as the form of Lakṣmī and the foundation stone (ādhāra-śilā) as the form of the Support-Energy (Ādhāra-śakti), and having covered each separately with a new cloth.

Having prepared a sacrificial mound (*sthaṇḍila*) as before, one should place many seeds, grains, metals, and gems into a vessel, wrap it with that same cloth, and set it down. Then, having raised the image of Śayana from the bed-altar previously established, and having worshipped it with the *arghya* offering and other rites, one should present the four kinds of food beginning with milk-rice (*pāyasa*). Having likewise fully honored the great water-jar (*mahākuṃbha*), one should then prepare the sacrificial oblation (*balya-anna*) by mixing powdered meat, parched grain (*lāja*), curd, and roasted barley flour (*saktu*).

May those beings who are primordial and those born of karma, who reside in the eastern direction—serene and well-pleased—accept this offering, for they desire it. May those who dwell in trees, on mountain peaks, and in the intermediate directions; and those who abide upon the earth and in the sky—they too shall accept this offering. May the Vināyakas, the Kṣetrapālas, and others who desire offerings, as well as Pūṣan and the other attendants, accept this bali. And may Caṇḍa and the others, Kumuda and the others, and all those beings who stand everywhere [accept it].

"May they all come to my feet; may they accept this bali-offering. Having offered the bali in all directions with this verse, he then offers one hundred and eight oblations of clarified butter with the mantra: "Oṃ, obeisance to the Blessed One, the Lord of Dreams; make my dreams auspicious, svāhā!"

Immediately thereafter, having made the formal resolve (*saṅkalpa*) saying, "I shall perform the rite of binding the protective thread (*rakṣābandhana*) for the sake of consecration (*pratiṣṭhā*)," and having caused the declaration of an auspicious day (*puṇyāha*) to be recited; having bound golden *pratisara* threads respectively upon the right and left hands of the God and the Goddess; and having prepared a pedestal of grain such as rice and other cereals before the image of the Child (Kumāra); and having placed upon that pedestal a great water-pot (*mahākumbha*) together with its small jars (*upakuṃbha*), along with iron, gems, *aśvattha* sprouts, and a bundle of grass (*kūrca*); and having invoked Indra and the other deities into the eight small jars.

Having worshipped—that is, having fully honored—the image of the Child (Bālabimba), one should invoke its Śakti into the great pitcher (mahākumbha) and Sudarśana into the water-vessel (karaka), and worship them. Thereafter, one should cause the priests (mūrtipās) to perform the final oblation (pūrṇāhuti) for each sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa). At that time, if the smoke of the oblation has the fragrance of a lotus or a blue water-lily (kuvalaya), if the fire is white like a jewel, and if it possesses flames curling to the right, then it portends extreme auspiciousness.

Then, making the formal resolve (*saṅkalpa*) with the sound of Vedic chants, "I shall sleep for the sake of the fulfillment of the good dream," one should spread *darbha* grass pointing eastward upon the ground. Upon these, the officiating priest (*ācārya*), the image of the deity (*mūrti*), and the sacrificer (*yajamāna*) should lie down for the sake of the dream. Thus ends the seventeenth chapter, titled "The Procedure for the Peace-Offering (*śāntihoma*)," in the *Kriyākairavacandrikā*. Chapter Eighteen:
The Installation of the Seat (*pīṭhasthāpana*).

Then, at dawn, having fulfilled his duties and having had auspicious dreams during the night, the preceptor (ācārya) should begin the installation of the deity without hesitation. If there were bad dreams, he should first perform a propitiatory fire-offering (śāntihoma) as previously described and then commence the work. In the case of a single image (ekabera), however, he should perform the Vāstuhoma as before on the southern side of the door. Thereafter, the preceptor, having entered the sanctum (garbhagṛha), should place within it a stone slab measuring one cubit in width and length, with four surrounding recesses, whether it be square or circular in shape.

Having offered one hundred oblations each with sacrificial fuel (samidh), clarified butter (ājya), and cooked rice (caru) into the Vāstu-homa fire while reciting the Viṣṇu-gāyatrī, one should place the seeds of eight grains—barley, rice, flat beans (niṣpāva), millet (priyaṅgu), sesame, black gram (māṣa), wild rice (nīvāra), and śāli rice—in the first enclosure within the pits for the stones, starting from the east. In the second enclosure, one should place the eight gems: diamond, pearl, lapis lazuli (vaiḍūrya), crystal (sphaṭika), topaz (puṣparāga), ruby (padmarāga), moonstone (candrakānta), and sapphire (nīla).

In the third enclosure, one should place eight substances: realgar, yellow orpiment, collyrium, black pigment, lead, saurāṣṭra clay, gorocana, and red ochre. In the fourth enclosure, one should place a tortoise, a conch, and a discus fashioned from gold, silver, copper, iron, tin, and brass; these, along with rice seeds, mercury, brahmarāga, and gold, are to be deposited in the pit for the liquor. Having covered it with a stone slab while reciting the Śrīsūkta, and having made it firm with lime, one should then cause the proclamation of an auspicious day and sprinkle the stone slab with water.

Having placed the Praṇava (Oṃ) upon the lotus of the woman-stone, and having assigned the sixteen letters beginning with *a* to the filaments and the letters from *ka* to *kṣa* to the petals starting from the east, one should worship those petals starting from the east as follows: Oṃ *vimalāyai namaḥ*, Oṃ *utkarṣiṇyai namaḥ*, Oṃ *jñāninyai namaḥ*, Oṃ *kriyāyai namaḥ*, Oṃ *yogātmikāyai namaḥ*, Oṃ *prahvyai namaḥ*, Oṃ *satyāyai namaḥ*, Oṃ *īśānyai namaḥ*.

Having invoked the nine powers with "Oṃ, obeisance to the power of grace (anugraha-śakti)" at the pericarp (karṇikā), and having worshipped them with perfumes and other offerings; having invoked [the goddess] with "Oṃ Śrīṃ, obeisance to Śrī" at the pedestal (piṇḍikā) and worshipped her; having covered [the deity] with a new cloth; having worshipped Sudarśana at the door as before; having displayed the discus-mudrā (cakramudrā); having gone outside; and having worshipped the Lord situated on the bed-altar according to the rules; one should then dismiss the deities residing in the door-arches (dvāratoraṇa) and the water-pots (kuṃbha).

Having first performed the ritual according to the Tantra, he should deposit even those [deities] residing in the sacrificial pits (kuṇḍas) into the heart of the deity. Then, having lifted the great pitcher (mahākumbha), the subsidiary pitchers (upakumbhas), and the eight vessels (maṇḍalas), the Preceptor himself, taking a water-pot (karaka) along with the image-bearers (mūrtipās) who carry them, sprinkles the path ahead with an unbroken, continuous stream of flowing water. Having circumambulated the house and entered the inner sanctum (garbhamandira), he should place the pitchers in order upon the grain-seat (dhānyapīṭha).

Again, having approached the deity near the bed-altar, and having raised the deity with both hands while reciting "uttiṣṭha brahmaṇaspate" following the permission of the Brāhmaṇas, the Ācārya—accompanied by umbrellas, banners, flags, and the like; by the sounds of all musical instruments; by the chanting of the Vedas (brahmaghoṣa); by learned Brāhmaṇas, Vaiṣṇavas, and students; and by the image-keepers (mūrtipāḥ)—having performed the six-fold placement (ṣaḍaṅganyāsa) and other rites, and having circumambulated the house, enters the primary temple.

There, having worshipped the deity at the door of the sanctum with water for the guest-offering (*arghya*) and other rites, and having led him inside, he should circumambulate the pedestal (*piṇḍikā*). At an auspicious moment, by the command of the preceptor (*guru*), while the image-makers recite the *Sāman* hymns "O thou art established" (*apratiṣṭhāsi*), "I have brought thee hither" (*ā tvāhārṣam*), and the mantra "Firm is the sky" (*dhruvā dyauḥ*), the Preceptor stands before the deity and, with the mantra "Oṃ lāṃ, salutation to the Supreme, salutation to the Self of All," installs the deity upon the pedestal.

Having determined the equidistance of the deity by means of a cord suspended from above, and having secured the cavity of the pedestal's shaft with a firm eight-fold binding produced by the intense grinding of lac, resin, kuruvinda, guggulu, red ochre, molasses, and oil; then, having caused the proclamation of an auspicious day and having sprinkled [the deity], one should thereafter invoke the deity: "I invoke that deity, who is beyond darkness, imperishable, blissful, all-pervading, eternal, transcending space, and higher than the highest."

Having meditated thus: "Vāsudeva, the unborn and all-pervading Lord, situated in the center of the circle of rays," and having invoked the God with the twelve-syllable mantra; having visualized Him as having entered the image through the aperture of Brahmā (brahmarandhra); having united the God residing in the water-jar with the image by means of the root-mantra; having performed the ritual placement (nyāsa) of the God upon that very [image]; having prayed for His presence (sānnidhya); and having arranged the retinue according to the previously mentioned procedure; one should worship the God with water for honor (arghya) and other offerings, and present milk-rice (pāyasa) as the food offering.

Having wrapped [the image] with fresh garments or woolen blankets while reciting the mantra “*yuvā suvāsāḥ*,” one should keep the door of the inner sanctum closed with a panel for three days. At that time, one should also satisfy the Brāhmaṇas with wealth, cows, food, and other offerings. When the fourth day arrives, having opened the panel early in the morning and performed the ritual bathing (*snapana*) of the deity according to the rules, one should perform the hoisting of the flag (*dhvajārohaṇa*) on that day. This procedure is to be carried out only for a single image (*ekabera*).

However, when many types of shrines are established, if the image is made of painting or similar materials, the placement of jewels (*ratnanyāsa*) should be performed at the very time of installing the central shaft (*śūlasthāpana*). At the time of consecration (*pratiṣṭhā*), having entered the inner sanctum (*garbhagṛha*), one should purify it by sweeping, smearing, and other means. Therein, having laid down eight cords each oriented toward the east and the north made from sandalwood, among those forty-nine squares, the central portion is the Brahma-square; the second is the Daiva-square; the third is the Mānuṣa-square; and the fourth is the Paiśāca-square.

In the Brahma-square is the seat of worship (*arcanā-pīṭha*); in the Daiva-square is the standing posture; in the Mānuṣa-square is the retinue; and in the Paiśāca-square are the weapons. Alternatively, having cast ten lines facing north and ten facing east: relying slightly on the Mānuṣa-square, the seat is in the Daiva-square; the bed belongs to both the Divya and Mānuṣa squares; the vehicle is in the Paiśāca-square; and the goddesses are in the Daiva-square. When the deity is seated, the goddesses are seated; when he stands, they stand by his side; and when he lies down or is mounted on a vehicle, the goddesses should be arranged as desired. Or else, having laid down ten lines facing north and ten facing east:

Having divided those eighty-one chambers into sections—namely, the central section as Brāhma, the second as Daiva, the third as Paitṛka, the fourth as Mānuṣa, and the fifth as Paiśāca—one should assign them accordingly. Alternatively, for a single image (ekabera), one may designate the Brāhma section; for multiple images (bahuberasya), the Daiva section; the seat (āsana) for both Daiva and Mānuṣa; the bed (śayana) for Daiva, Mānuṣa, and Paitṛka; and the vehicle (yāna) for Mānuṣa and Paiśāca. If these prescribed locations are reversed, the kingdom and its king will perish.

Therefore, one should perform the rite according to the scriptures. On the *napuṃsaka* stone, the placement of jewels (*ratnanyāsa*) is as before. Having first consecrated the jewels in a vessel for the other items such as the footstool (*pādamūla*) and the seat (*āsana*), one should perform the placement of jewels directly behind them. As for the worship of the ritual implements and so forth, the preceptor himself, having taken up the water-pot (*karaka*), should lift them up together with the great jar (*mahākumbha*), the secondary jars (*upakumbha*), and the small vessels (*karakas*), along with the image-makers (*mūrtipas*).

Accompanied by the sound of musical instruments, he sprinkles the path with an unbroken stream of water flowing from a water-dripper (*galantika*) placed before the deity, so that no one may pass between his own form and the image. Having thus entered the temple by circumambulation, he worships the deity at the entrance with *arghya* and other offerings. Entering within, he places the ritual image (*karmārcā*) upon the altar of worship (*arcanāpīṭha*) while reciting the *Nṛsūkta*, and places the images for festivals and other purposes on either side of it.

Having poured the water remaining from the stream into a small vessel (galantikā) and placed it in a shallow bowl (śarāva), and having performed the ritual sprinkling (pariṣecana) of the images with a stream [of water] measured by a small stick while reciting the root mantra, one should place the jars upon heaps of grain in front of the deity. Then, according to the procedure to be described, one should perform the invocation (āvāhana). At an auspicious moment, the Preceptor (ācārya), standing before the primary image (mūlabera), assuming the lotus posture (padmāsana), and having restrained his breath (prāṇāyāma), should meditate upon the eternal Brahman: Vāsudeva, the unborn, peaceful, radiant, and eternally manifest.

Without beginning, middle, or end, one, all-pervading, immovable, and stable; the mass of consciousness, supreme bliss, beyond darkness, and imperishable; endowed with knowledge, power, strength, sovereignty, valor, and splendor; without feet or hands, untouchable, and devoid of eyes, ears, and other senses; yet having hands, feet, and speech everywhere, with eyes, heads, and faces in every direction; eternally free from motion, possessing a radiance equal to ten million suns; consciousness, omnipresent, eternal, beyond the sky—that is the wondrous One.

The universal consciousness (*citsāmānya*) in this world is the supreme essence of the root mantra; it is Viṣṇu, who is eternally blissful and whose nature is the *praṇava*. Having meditated thus correctly, one should unite the eternal Viṣṇu with Mahāviṣṇu, and having united Mahāviṣṇu with Viṣṇu, one should invoke Viṣṇu into the lotus of one’s own heart with the mantra: “*Oṃ yāṃ namaḥ parāya puruṣātmane namaḥ*. Then, having formed the *añjali* gesture and visualized a lotus seat within the *añjali*, one should contemplate that auspicious throne (*bhadrāsana*).

Having invoked Viṣṇu residing in the lotus of one's own heart with the mantra: “Oṃ rāṃ, salutation to the Supreme, the Soul of the Universe,” and having meditated upon Him as held in the hollow of the joined palms, entering the image through the aperture of Brahmā (brahmarandhra) with the mantra: “Oṃ yāṃ, salutation to the Supreme, the Soul of Nivṛtti,” and remembering Him as remaining pervading the entire icon from all sides with the mantra: “Oṃ lāṃ, salutation to the Supreme, the Universal Soul.”

Having united the power (śakti) residing in the great pitcher, the power of the auspicious thread (kautuka) placed upon the pitcher, and the powers residing in the image-pitchers with the deity by means of the mantras and the tufts of grass (kūrca) placed in the water within those respective pitchers; having covered the aperture of the Brahma (the fontanelle) of the image with the syllable Om (praṇava); having displayed the mudrās of invocation and installation; having praised [the deity] with the hymn "Victory to You" (jitaṃ te); having displayed the mudrā of the image; having meditated upon the deity as facing oneself; and having prostrated and risen—

Having displayed the mudrās of presence (*sannidhāna*), cessation (*sannirodhana*), facing (*sāmmukhya*), and prayer (*prārthanā*), and having said, "Welcome to the Blessed One," while displaying the mudrā of welcome (*svāgata*), one should perform the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) upon the deity according to the rule by means of the root mantra (*mūlamantra*). When [the deity] is standing, there is the placement of stability (*sthitinyāsa*); on the seat, the placement of emanation (*sṛṣṭinyāsa*); for sleeping in dissolution (*saṃhāra*), the placement of withdrawal (*saṃhṛtinyāsa*); for sleeping in emanation (*sṛṣṭi*), the placement of emanation (*sṛṣṭinyāsa*); and for sleeping for enjoyment (*bhoga*), sleeping for yoga (*yoga*), and the universal form (*viśvarūpa*), there is the placement of stability (*sthitinyāsa*). When mounted on a vehicle (*yāna*), all three placements are performed.

Alternatively, the *sthitinyāsa* alone should be performed everywhere, including on the seats and other items. Having sprinkled the goddesses beginning with Śrī and the deities beginning with Brahmā with water from the great pitcher (*mahākumbha*) while reciting their respective name-mantras, one should perform the *ṣaḍaṅganyāsa* for the bed and other items, the *sṛṣṭinyāsa* for Brahmā, and the *saṃhāranyāsa* for Rudra. Having established Caṇḍa, Pracaṇḍa, Garuḍa, Viṣvaksena, and all the other members of the retinue in their respective places, the Preceptor himself should take hold of the great pitcher.

Having performed the sprinkling (prokṣaṇa) of Caṇḍa and the other members of the retinue at that very moment with the water from that [vessel] and a bunch of kuśa grass, using their respective mantras beginning with *oṃ* and ending with *namaḥ*; having poured the remaining water from the great pitcher (*mahākumbha*) upon the sacrificial altar (*balipīṭha*); and having established the Gārhapatya fire upon the hearth-fire pit (*kuṇḍa*) for the purpose of cooking; the Preceptor, together with the patron (*yajamāna*), having approached the side of the Deity, bowed down, stood up, and joined his palms in reverence (*añjali*), should utter this verse:

"O you who are affectionate toward devotees, O fulfiller of the desires of your devotees! O Lord, I entreat you with the wish for your grace: remain for a long time in this place prepared by me with faith. Be gracious, O God, O Lord of Gods, and accept my worship. O Consort of Indirā, bestow nourishment, contentment, and likewise the supreme goal upon the village, the king, the kingdom, and the subjects. Having thus informed the God, one should offer the *madhuparka*.

At that very moment, with the permission of the preceptor (ācārya), the patron (yajamāna), with his head bowed in devotion, should bring before the Lord’s right hand—preceded by water—cows, land, gold, and other articles of worship according to his means, as well as himself, his sons, grandsons, wife, and others, vehicles such as elephants, female and male servants, and his entire property, and offer them at the side of the Lord. In this same manner, he should also honor the preceptor. Then, the preceptor shall wash a vessel made of gold or other materials with the Viṣṇu-gāyatrī mantra.

Having placed that [image] upon a heap of grain before the Deity with the mantra, "Salutation to our thighs," and having filled it with scented water, one should invoke the Supreme Self (*paramātman*) therein. Having worshipped Him with the Vedic hymns and other offerings such as perfumes, one should summon the patron (*yajamāna*), have him stand facing the Deity, fill his joined palms (*añjali*) with the *arghya* water containing flowers, and cause him to recite this verse: "Without You, there is nothing for me; likewise, without me, there is nothing belonging to You."

"Therefore, O Supreme Lord, be gracious so that you may make me your own. For those whose feet have stumbled upon the earth, the earth alone is their support; for those who have turned away from you, O All-pervading One, you alone are the refuge. Having thus informed the God, the Preceptor should offer himself at the lotus-feet of the Deity of the sacrificer, along with the water from the flower-offering held in his joined palms, using the twelve-syllable mantra and saying: "Salutation to our broad thighs."

At the conclusion of the consecration (pratiṣṭhā), having gratified the Deity with offerings such as the sounds of dance, song, and instrumental music, and various kinds of hymns; having offered the fourfold food according to the rules; having established the perpetual fire (nityāgni) in a square sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) between the hearth (agni) and the image (yama); having consecrated it; and having performed oblations (homa) with fuel-sticks, clarified butter, and sacrificial porridge (caru) using the root mantra according to the ritual until the final full oblation (pūrṇāhuti); and having consecrated the offering pedestals (balipīṭhas) and installed them within their respective enclosures (āvaraṇas), one should daily offer the bali-oblation upon them according to the prescribed rules.

However, during the consecration of Bahubera, one should not perform the fastening of the door-panels. When the fourth day arrives, having bathed the deity according to the rules with ritual jars, preceded by worship in the four stations—using either the triad of superior or the triad of middling [mantras]—one should then conduct the festival, beginning with the hoisting of the banner.

Thereafter, at that time, the sacrificer, having gratified the Ācārya with gold flowers, garments, rings, earrings, fields, groves, houses, female and male slaves, palanquins, elephants, horses, and other such wealth consisting of both living and non-living things, and having offered himself to him along with his children, wife, and so forth, regarding the Guru as both mother and father.

Having prostrated before him, one should give a thousand cows, or else an excellent sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) of parched grain, or half of that, or even a quarter of that. In this context, one should not perform the marriage rite for the goddesses Śrī and the others together with the Lord; however, if it is performed separately, one should duly perform the marriage rite preceded by the *aṅkura* ceremony. Whatever has been prescribed as an ancillary part, from the plowing to the final consecration (*pratiṣṭhā*), all of that—whether performed or remaining—is the property of the Guru alone.

According to this statement, having given everything to the preceptor, and having bestowed sacrificial fees (*dakṣiṇā*) upon the image-protectors, the attendants, others devoted to dance and movement, and the members of the assembly, each according to their means; and thereafter, having praised the Deity and bowed down; the patron, graced by the Deity, together with the preceptor, having given gifts such as maidens, cows, land, gold, and so forth to the twice-born in the presence of the Deity; and having gone outside, feeling his purpose accomplished, he pays homage to the Deity and the teacher.

Having placed the Guru upon a palanquin or similar vehicle, and preceded by the sound of musical instruments, one should circumambulate the village and lead him into that house. The Sthāpaka (the consecrator) should perform the worship in the same manner as the former supreme preceptor of the God of Gods; even his descendants, though lacking in qualities, must perform it. O Lotus-seated One, that very worship is what pleases the God. Whatever extent of ritual elaboration was originally envisioned, one should carry it out with such wealth and resources, without any reduction.

One should compose [the rites] for those who subsist upon the deity in accordance with the prosperity of the deity; likewise, one should not cause distress to the devotees (bhāgavatas) or the attendants. Thus ends the eighteenth chapter, titled "The Procedure for Consecration," in the *Kriyākairavacandrikā* composed by the venerable Guru Varāha.
The nineteenth chapter: The Procedure for the Consecration of the Matsya and Other Forms.
Now, the procedure for the installation of the Vibhava forms is described.

For the Matsya and other forms, one should perform everything, such as the preliminary consecration (*adhivāsa*), just as in the case of the Great Installation (*mahāpratiṣṭhā*). However, the specific details here are stated: having consecrated the great pitcher (*mahākumbha*) with the *Vāruṇa Sāman* and the *Nṛsūkta*, the Preceptor (*ācārya*) should invoke [the deity] into it either with the mantra “Oṃ, obeisance to the Blessed One, Myūṃ, to the one in the form of the Fish” or with the root-mantra (*mūlamantra*). Having sprinkled [the image] with the water from the pitcher, [he should recite]: “Obeisance to You, the Fish-Self, the ordainer of the protection of the Vedas.”

One should worship with the mantra: “To him who sports in the irresistible flood of waters of the ocean of dissolution. Having consecrated the great pitcher for the Tortoise with the Vāruṇa-sūkta and having invoked [the deity] with the eight-syllable Vidyā, at the conclusion of the rite, one should worship with: “We offer salutation to you, the Creator in the form of the Tortoise, the sustainer of Mount Mandara, the bestower of joy upon the gods.”

For Varāha: having invoked the one in the form of Varāha into the great pitcher with the *Puruṣasūkta*, at the conclusion of the rite, he should worship him with the mantra: "Salutations to you, the soul of the boar, the creator whose body is sacrifice, O supporter of the earth who held the entire world upon the tip of your tusk! For Nṛsiṃha: having invoked the one in the form of Nṛsiṃha into the great pitcher with the hymn beginning "They yoke [the mind]," at the conclusion of the rite, he should worship him with the mantra: "Salutations to the one in the form of Nṛsiṃha, who has displayed affection for his devotees, and whose claws and thunderbolt-like fangs have shattered the chest of the Asura."

One should worship thus: having invoked Vāmana into the great jar with the hymn beginning “They yoke” (*yuñjate*), at the conclusion of the rite, one should worship with the verse: “Obeisance to you, the enemy of Bala; protector of the enemy of Bala; O Vāmana of great body, by whom all men have been deceived. Having invoked Paraśurāma, the son of Jamadagni, into the great jar with the *Puruṣasūkta*, at the conclusion of the rite, [one should worship him] who is the slayer of the Kṣatriyas twenty-one times over and who possesses fierce splendor.

One should worship with the mantra: “Salutations to you, the Blessed One, the wielder of the axe. If the installation of Rāghava is separate from that of his retinue, one should invoke Rāma, together with Sītā, Lakṣmaṇa, and the others, into a large water-pot (mahākumbha) using the Puruṣasūkta. At the conclusion of the ritual, one should worship with the mantra: “Salutations to you, the Blessed One, the high-souled Rāghava, who possesses great power in destroying Rāvaṇa and other enemies of the world. Furthermore, if the installation of Rāma is performed separately, one should also install the members of his retinue, headed by Hanumān.

In the first enclosure, having installed Bharata in the east, Jānakī in the south, Jāmbavanta in the west, and Lakṣmaṇa in the north; and in the intermediate directions starting from the southeast, Sugrīva, Vibhīṣaṇa, Nala, and Śatrughna. In the second enclosure, in the directions starting from the east, [one installs] Vasiṣṭha, Vāmadeva, Jābāli, Gautama, Bharadvāja, Kauśika, Vālmīki, and Nārada. In the third enclosure, [one installs] the world-protectors beginning with Indra, and Hanumān in the place of Garuḍa, and Nīla or Guha in the place of Viṣvaksena.

One should install [the deity]. During the festival, however, having painted either Garuḍa or Hanumān on a banner-cloth (*dhvajapaṭa*), one should perform the hoisting of the banner. For Balarāma, having invoked Balarāma into the water-pot (*kumbha*) as before, at the conclusion of the rite, one should worship with the mantra: "Obeisance to the mighty Balabhadra, to Śeṣa, the great serpent, by whom the earth was borne upon his head like a great garland. Thus one should offer salutation.

Having installed the image of Kṛṣṇa as that of the Blessed Lord, at the conclusion of the rite, one should worship with the words: "Obeisance to you, Kṛṣṇa, the best of the Vṛṣṇis, the enemy of Madhu, the destroyer of the great demons such as Kaṃsa who were a burden to the earth. Thus one should offer salutation. One should perform the marriage rites for Rukmiṇī, Satyabhāmā, and the others, just as those for Śrī and the other goddesses. Having performed the rites for Kalki-Viṣṇu as before, at the end of the ceremony, one should say: "Obeisance to you, the Blessed Lord, born into the lineage of the gods on earth (Bhūsurānvaya), the annihilator of the Mlecchas and the cause of stability for the virtuous."

Thus one should perform the ritual attendance (*upasthāna*). For the ten forms beginning with Matsya, the sixteen-fold placement (*ṣoḍaśanyāsa*) is not required, nor for those made of metal. If they are made of stone and are to be painted, one should first perform the preliminary rites such as the consecration (*adhivāsa*), and afterwards apply the paint; immediately thereafter, one should perform the invocation (*āvāhana*) and other rites. If the installation of the image for worship is to take place at a time different from that of the permanent installation (*dhruvabimba*), one should perform the rites of reclining (*śayana*) and so forth for them separately.

One should install the Brahma-karma image in the east, the festive kautuka image in the south, the bathing image for the pilgrimage site (tīrtha) in the north, and the sleeping and waking images in the south; furthermore, one should place the offering (bali) image and other worldly metal images in their desired locations. Alternatively, the images intended for festivals may be placed on either side of the door or facing south within the consecration pavilion (abhiṣeka-maṇḍapa).

For those [deities] suitable for water-consecration (*jalādhivāsa*), one should perform shadow-consecration (*chāyādhivāsana*), the ritual with the *kūrca* grass-bundle and the mirror-mandala, the bathing, and the bed-consecration via the *kūrca*; then, one should perform all remaining rites as before, excluding the sixteen-fold placement (*ṣoḍaśanyāsa*) and the fourth bathing. However, for the Lord who reclines on a banyan leaf (*vaṭapatraśāyin*), one should draw an ocean within the interior of the womb-chamber; then, having visualized by means of a painted image the dark-hued, tender-formed, infant-bodied Lord lying upon its petals, one should proceed.

Having depicted Mārkaṇḍeya and Mahī on both sides of the door according to the procedure described for the appearance of the paintings, one should perform the rite of installation (*pratiṣṭhā*). Now, the procedure for the installation of Lakṣmī and the others is stated: if the installation of the deity and the goddesses occurs at the same time, then the goddesses should be laid down together with the deity; however, if there is a difference in time, one should do so separately.
