Having prepared the pavilion (*maṇḍapa*) with a central altar (*vedikā*) as before, one should cause [the images] to lie upon that altar.

On the archways (toraṇas) starting from the east, one should worship Balākinī, Vanamālinī, Vibhīṣikā, and Śārī. On the water-pots at the doors (dvārakumbhas), one should worship in pairs: Jyeṣṭhā, Vidyā, Śraddhā, Kānti, Śrī, Tuṣṭi, Kṣamā, and Vṛddhi. On the banners (dhvajās) starting from the east, one should worship in pairs: Dhṛti, Lajjā, Jayā, Māyā, Sāvitrī, Kṣamā, Śuddhi, and Śraddhā. Having worshipped these, one should invoke Lakṣmī, Sarasvatī, Puṣṭi, and Tuṣṭi into the sacrificial pits (homakuṇḍas) starting from the east, and perform the fire-offering (homa) with their respective mantras.

The deities of the *kalaśas* are Vāgīśvarī, Kriyā, Kīrti, Lakṣmī, Sṛṣṭi, Prahvī, Satyā, and Brāhmī; in the great jar (*mahākumbha*) is Śrīdevī. Having worshipped them in this manner according to the rules, one should perform the remaining rites as before, excluding the sixteen-fold ritual placement (*ṣoḍaśanyāsa*). This is the procedure when [the deity] is not independent. However, when independent, the installation of Śrī in a village, city, town, or temple should be arranged facing toward the village.

On the upper part of the celestial chariot (vimāna), one should arrange Tuṣṭi, Puṣṭi, Sāvitrī, and Vāgdevī in the four cardinal directions, and Siṃha or Vainateya in the corners; then, having installed a representation made of stone or other materials in the Brahmā-position there.

One should station the attendants in their respective places: Caṇḍī and Pracaṇḍī at the two sides of the entrance; at the door of the half-pavilion, Balākinī on the south and Vanyamālinī on the north; at the first gateway, Vibhīṣikā and Śāṅkarī; at the second gateway, Śaṅkha and Padmanidhi; at the third gateway, Nalakūbara and Jṛmbhala; at the fourth gateway, Śibi and Kuṇḍala, and Maṇibhadra; and at the fifth gateway, Jayā and Vijayā; and at the station of Viṣvaksena, the four-armed goddess.

Having established her of yellow complexion and beautiful countenance, holding a staff in her left hand and making a threatening gesture with the other, while holding two lotuses with the remaining two hands; having likewise arranged for Vainateya in the pavilion at the front of the palace, and having conceived the retinue as belonging to the Primordial Form itself—having thus performed the installation independently—on the fourth day, after performing the ceremonial bath, one should raise the banner on that day and conduct a great festival.
Thus ends the nineteenth chapter, titled "The Ritual for the Installation of the Goddess Vibhavamūrti," in the *Kriyākairavacandrikā* composed by the venerable Varāhaguru.
The Twentieth Chapter: The Ritual for Taking the Hand (Marriage).
Now, the ritual for taking the hands of the goddesses, Śrī and the others, is described.

On the day as previously specified, having performed the rite of sowing the sprouts (aṅkurārpaṇa), on the auspicious moment of the wedding day, the Preceptor (ācārya), preceded by the formal resolve (saṃkalpa), shall separately tie the marriage-thread (udvāhakautuka) upon the God and the Goddess according to the rules. Having adorned the God with silken upper garments, crowns, necklaces, earrings, and other ornaments, and with perfumes, flowers, and so forth, he shall lead Him into the wedding chamber. There, having worshipped the God with the water-offering (arghya) and other rites, and having prepared a sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila), having drawn the lines upon it, and having established the sacred fire (agni).

The preceptor, having entered the inner sanctum with the deity, seated the deity upon a throne, and having clothed the Goddess in a new garment while circumambulating her clockwise with the mantra "yuvā suvāsāḥ," and having caused her to perform the ritual sipping of water (ācamana) and adorned her with ornaments, flowers, and other offerings, the preceptor himself united the Goddess with the Deity through the Vedas and other sacred texts. Thereafter, the patron, having restrained his vital breaths (prāṇas), made the formal declaration of intent (saṃkalpa).

"I offer my maiden, born of my own lineage, to the God who is the cause of the universe, for the purpose of performing duties together with her offspring. Having said this, he should present the Goddess to the God along with all her ornaments, gold, cows, land, and water accompanied by gold. Then, having led the God—whose hand has been taken—and the Goddess from the temple to the auspicious pavilion (*kalyāṇamaṇḍapa*), the Preceptor (*ācārya*) should seat the God and the Goddess upon their thrones. He himself, facing the northern direction, should perform breath-control (*prāṇāyāma*), make the formal resolve (*saṃkalpa*), and proceed.

Having strewn grass around the fire as previously described and having performed the preliminary ritual (tantra), one should offer the Āghāra oblations according to the sequence prescribed by the rules; then, with fuel-sticks while reciting the *Nṛsūkta*, one should offer sixteen oblations, and with the sacrificial porridge (*caru*) while reciting the *Viṣṇugāyatrī*, twenty-four oblations, and with clarified butter while reciting the *Śrīsūkta*, fifty oblations.

If the marriage ceremony for Śrī and Bhūmi is performed simultaneously, one should perform all the rites, beginning with the *aṅkura* (germinating of seeds), separately for both. Even when the performance is a single act occurring at the same time, all the rites for Śrī and Bhūmi must be separate. If they are performed sequentially at the same time, one should still carry them out as distinct acts. Alternatively, if the auspicious moments (*muhūrta*) are different, the marriage rites themselves must be separate. If the two auspicious moments coincide, one should perform the ritual actions in their respective order.

If Śrī and Bhūmi have different officiants, even though their marriage takes place simultaneously, the *pratisara* for Śrī and Bhūmi is distinct, while that of the Deity is only one. For those two as well, having performed the preliminary rites such as the marking (*ullekhana*) according to preference—either with a single fire or separate fires—one should perform all the ritual actions individually for each person; first for Śrī and subsequently for Bhūmi, in alternation.

At the taking of the bride's hand, having offered sixteen oblations of fuel sticks with the Earth-mantra, twenty-four oblations of cooked rice (caru) with the Viṣṇu-gāyatrī, and sixteen oblations of clarified butter with the Puruṣasūkta; then, having performed the offering of parched grains (lājahoma) with the Viṣṇu-sūkta and circumambulated the fire, the preceptor (ācārya), having made a single offering of the remaining parched grains with the syllable Om (praṇava);

Having offered oblations of clarified butter with the five verses addressed to Varuṇa—namely, “imaṃ me varuṇa,” “tat tvā yāmi,” “tvaṃ no agne,” “sa tvaṃ no agne,” and “tvaṃ agne ayāsi”—and having offered the expiatory oblations (*prāyaścittāhutīḥ*) with the five Upaniṣad mantras and the final full oblation (*pūrṇāhuti*) with the twelve-syllable mantra, one should satisfy the Brāhmaṇas, worship the Deity with the *arghya* offering and other rites, and perform the rite of placing the clarified butter (*ghṛtāropaṇa*).

Regarding the *ghṛtāropaṇa* (the offering of ghee): having placed ghee, *dūrvā* sprouts, sandalwood, and *śāli* rice grains into a vessel and taking them with both hands, the preceptor (*ācārya*) applies them to the limbs of the deity and the goddess—placing *dūrvā* on the limbs with the mantra “*sumaṅgalam*,” ghee on the feet with “*suśobhanam*,” sandalwood on the waist with “*subhadram*,” and *śāli* rice grains on the head with “*sumaṅgalam*” — and likewise causes all the members of the assembly to do so.

Having offered the *madhuparka* with the words, "I am [filled] with essence," and having adorned the Lord of Lakṣmī with ornaments and other decorations, the sacrificer should further embellish Him with appropriate garlands, unguents, and so forth. Having prostrated before the Deity, the sacrificer should give a cow as a sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) to the preceptor (*guru*), according to his means. Then, the preceptor, having performed the lustration (*nīrājana*) of Hari and having cast the pedestal (*piṇḍikā*) in the various directions, should perform all other remaining rites according to the worldly path.

Having caused the Lord, together with Śrībhūmi, to circumambulate the village abode, and having installed the Lord and the two Goddesses in the pavilion, one should worship them with royal services and offer the great oblation (*mahāhavis*). At the conclusion, one should feed the Brāhmaṇas. In this manner, performing the bathing ceremony day after day, as well as the fire-oblations (*homa*) and festivals day and night as previously described, one should offer one hundred and eight oblations separately with fuel-sticks, clarified butter, sacrificial porridge (*caru*), and parched grain (*lāja*) using the two root-mantras during the latter part of the night on the fourth lunar day and subsequent days.

Then, having also offered oblations with the five Upaniṣads, on the fifth day, having worshipped the God and the two Goddesses with oil, having bathed them according to the rules, and having presented the great sacrificial offering (mahāhavis), one should hold a great festival in the village. From that time forward, one should worship the God together with Śrī and Bhūmi in the temple. For the other goddesses as well, the procedure is exactly the same. One should perform the marriage of the goddesses such as Jāmadagnyā and others according to the Smārta tradition.
Thus ends the twentieth chapter, titled "The Procedure for the Taking of the Hand of the Goddesses beginning with Śrī.
Chapter Twenty-one.
The Ritual for the Consecration of a Vimāna.
Now, the ritual for the consecration of a vimāna is described:

as in a great consecration, one should prepare a pavilion in front of the vimāna, in its center, measuring four cubits in length and one cubit in height, provided with a central altar and equipped with either four or eight sacrificial pits (kuṇḍas).

There, having procured the items required for the installation—namely, small bowls (*pālikā*), jars (*ghaṭikā*), shallow dishes (*śarāva*), eight types of grain-vessels (*aṣṭadhānyakumbha*), pitchers (*kalaśa*), water-pots (*karaka*), rice, sesame seeds, new cloth, the nine gems, an archway (*toraṇa*), banners (*dhvaja*), fragrant substances for the bath (*mala-snāpana-dravya*), the *sruk* and *sruva* ladles, fuel-sticks (*samit*), *darbha* grass, flowers, ghee, lamp-stands, seats, and other such materials—the Preceptor (*ācārya*), with the permission of the patron (*yajamāna*) and together with the image-guardians (*mūrtipa*), [should act] twelve days, nine days, seven days, on the fifth day, or on the third day prior to the day of commencing the rite.

Having summoned the Brahmins, caused them to recite benedictions, and bestowed sacrificial fees upon them, he obtained their permission and proceeded toward the eastern or northern direction to collect the clay. There, having planted sprouts as desired in vessels such as small pots according to the previous procedure, and once the artisan had opened the eyes of the deities of the directions of the temple, he gratified him with garments, ornaments, and other gifts.

When he has departed, having purified the dwelling by means of sweeping, smearing, circumambulation with fire, sprinkling with the five products of the cow (pañcagavya), and so forth; having caused the proclamation of an auspicious day (puṇyāha); having sprinkled the inner and outer sanctum with mantras associated with water; and having adorned the entire dwelling on all sides with cow-ghee lamps, incense such as aloeswood, fragrant substances, incense smoke, lime powder, dūrvā grass, and unbroken rice grains.

Then, at the time of afternoon, having performed a peace-offering (*śāntihoma*) according to the rules on the roof of the temple to pacify the defects of deficiency or excess in the [proportions of] pride and so forth; having worshipped with the verse “*namastubhyaṃ bhagavate*”; having covered the images inside the temple with fresh cloths and *darbha* grass while reciting the root mantra; and having offered upper garments, he should worship them with the *Viṣṇugāyatrī* and with offerings such as the respectful water (*arghya*).

Having performed the binding of protective cords for the purpose of consecrating the shadow of the *vimāna*, for the deities residing therein, and for oneself; having worshipped the *vimāna* with the twelve-syllable mantra; and having prepared a sacrificial mound (*sthaṇḍila*) with rice, husked grain, and sesame seeds for the consecration of the shadow in front of it; having placed upon that mound a vessel made of gold or other metals, or a similar water-jar (*droṇī*); having filled it with scented water; having caused the proclamation of an auspicious day (*puṇyāha-vācana*); having established the door-arches and the ritual jars; and having performed the drying of the water and other preliminary rites.

Having meditated upon the Ocean of Milk, and having fashioned a pedestal within it—beginning with the support (*ādhāra*) and ending with the lotus (*padma*)—the preceptor, having invoked the celestial chariot (*vimāna*) with the root-mantra using a tuft of twenty-eight *darbha* grasses and having worshipped it, should, while recollecting the process of reabsorption (*saṃhārakrama*), lay it down there with its head facing east. Having displayed the wheel-gesture (*cakramudrā*), he should likewise perform the preliminary consecration of the shadows (*chāyādhivāsa*) for the deities residing in the chariot, individually before each of them in their respective vessels, using a tuft of twenty-two *darbha* grasses according to the prescribed rite.

To the south of the water-vat (jaladroṇī) previously established, having placed upon a sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila) made of grain as prescribed an altar-marked with signs and eight jars along with their lids, and having strewn [the ground] around it; having caused the declaration of an auspicious day (puṇyāha) to be recited and having sprinkled [the area]; having invoked Brahmā into the central jar, Sudarśana into the lid-jar (karaka), and Indra and the other deities into the eight subsidiary jars, and having worshipped them; and having covered the celestial chariot (vimāna) and the images situated therein, each with new garments that cover all its limbs.

Having scattered white mustard seeds (*siddhārtha*) in all directions with the mantra "rakṣohaṇa," having performed the binding of the quarters (*digbandhana*), and having lit the lamps; having proclaimed the Vedas in the four directions, having invoked and worshipped Sudarśana at the door, and having displayed the Cakra-mudrā; the Preceptor (*ācārya*), adorned with all ornaments, having exited the hall by way of circumambulation, together with the image-keepers (*mūrtipāḥ*), Veda-knowing Brahmins, and others, shall perform the Vāstu-homa in the previously mentioned pavilion according to the rules as before.

Then, having purified the pavilion by sweeping, smearing, and so forth; having adorned it with canopies, pillar-wrappings, strings of pearls, garlands, wreaths of *darbha* grass, arches, fruits, flowers, many lamps, *agaru* incense, banners, coconuts, and plantains; having established the door-arches, flags, and water-pots; and having prepared them according to the rules with cloths and other materials; then the Guru, having entered within, should perform the ritual dismissal (*udvāsa*) of the deities who have been consecrated in their shadows and of the celestial chariot (*vimāna*), and remove the cloths and other items situated upon the chariot.

Having opened their eyes upon those [images] according to the rules by the previously mentioned method, and then, having performed the entire sequence of bathing—including the preliminary smearing with clay—for both the vimāna and the deities of the directions individually, using seventeen jars filled with substances such as ghee and turmeric powder, and having reflected them in a mirror together with a *kūrca* grass-bundle; and having again invoked [the deities], covered the vimāna and so forth with new garments, and prepared a bed upon the central altar according to the ritual for installation (*pratiṣṭhā*).

Having invoked the deities of the celestial chariot (vimāna-devatās) through the *kūrca* at its door and having laid them down, one should place there upon a sacrificial mound (*sthaṇḍila*) fashioned from rice and other grains a great jar (*mahākumbha*) made of gold or other metal, or even of clay, wrapped with thread and accompanied by eight smaller jars (*karakopakuṃbha*). Having filled it with scented water and provided it with a lid made of jewels, metal, cloth, a *kūrca*, and *pippala* leaves, one should cause the proclamation of the auspicious day (*puṇyāha-vācana*) to be recited. Then, one should invoke the respective deities into the door-arches (*toraṇa*), the banners (*dhvaja*), and the jars in their proper order.

Having performed worship, the Guru should conceive of the pedestal (*pīṭha*) within the great jar (*mahākumbha*), beginning with the support (*ādhāra*) and ending with the lotus (*padma*). Within that, he should meditate upon the Lord in the form of a temple and then invoke Him, having visualized Him as follows: "The Puruṣa with a thousand heads, a thousand eyes, and a thousand feet; endowed with a thousand locks of hair and adorned with a thousand crowns; resembling a thousand suns and possessing a face like a thousand moons; joined by a thousand vehicles and possessing a nose in every direction; holding a conch, discus, and mace in His hands, and equipped with all weapons. Having thus meditated, the Guru should perform the invocation.

Having invoked and worshipped [the deity] with the mantra: “Oṃ, obeisance to the Blessed One, Nārāyaṇa, the presiding deity of the celestial chariot; come, come!”, and having likewise invoked and worshipped the Sudarśana discus, the eight deities of the subsidiary jars, and the forms of Viṣṇu and the others, and having meditated upon the celestial chariot and worshipped it, and having offered the four kinds of food, fed the Brāhmaṇas, caused them to pronounce blessings, and bestowed sacrificial fees upon them, he should enkindle the fire in the sacrificial pits according to the prescribed rite.

Having first performed the preliminary rites of the Tantra, such as the *mūrtihoma* (oblation to the deity’s form), and having meditated upon the *dhāman* (the abode) fashioned from gold and other materials and inlaid with jewels; one should also meditate upon the *jīva* (individual soul) therein as all-pervading, along with its substrates: the intellect (*buddhi*) as the pedestal (*piṇḍikā*), the ego (*ahaṅkāra*) as the feet, the two *pāda-śilās* (foundation stones) as the two feet, the womb-chamber (*garbhagṛha*) as the shanks, the interior as the belly, the pillars as the arms, the waist as the hips, the girdle as the hip-belt, the phonemes as the tongue, the eyes as the eyes, and the *pratīka-dvāra* (symbolic door) as the organ of generation.

Having meditated upon the air-exit as the anus, the nostrils as the nose, the windows as the eyes, the neck as the neck, the shoulders as the shoulders, the cheeks as the cheeks, the head as the pitcher, the flesh as the plaster, the sense of touch as the whitewash, the bones as the stones, the sinews as the wooden beams and flagstaffs, and the hair of the head and body as the beard—having thus meditated upon the abode in its primordial form, one should meditate upon the celestial chariot (vimāna) in the shape of a person.

Thereafter, having offered oblations of clarified butter (ājya) one hundred and eight times, twenty-eight times, or eight times for each separately, beginning with the Praṇava (Oṃ) and ending with Svāhā, for the Jīva-tattva; and having collected the residual drops of the offering, he should touch the respective limbs of the temple with those very mantras: "Oṃ Maṃ, salutation to the Supreme, who has the luster of crystal, the self of the Jīva-tattva, Svāhā"—[he should touch] the Dhāman. "Oṃ Bhaṃ, salutation to the Supreme, who is white in color, the self of Prakṛti, Svāhā"—[he should touch] the Dhāman.

‘Oṃ baṃ, salutation to the Supreme One who has the luster of crystal, the self of the principle of intellect (buddhitattva); svāhā!’—in the *dhāman*. ‘Oṃ phaṃ, salutation to the Supreme One who is pale-red in color, the self of the ego (ahaṃkāra); svāhā!’—on the pedestal (*piṇḍikā*). ‘Oṃ paṃ, salutation to the Supreme One who is white in color, the self of the principle of mind (manastattva); svāhā!’—on the pedestal. ‘Oṃ naṃ, salutation to the Supreme One who is white in color, the self of the subtle element of sound (śabdatanmātra); svāhā!’—in the small nose.

"Oṃ dhaṃ, obeisance to the Supreme, who is red-colored and whose self is the subtle element of touch; svāhā!"—on the plastering with lime. "Oṃ daṃ, obeisance to the Supreme, who is light-colored and whose self is the subtle element of form; svāhā!"—on the window. "Oṃ thaṃ, obeisance to the Supreme, who is pale-colored and whose self is the subtle element of taste; svāhā!"—on the paint. "Oṃ taṃ, obeisance to the Supreme, who is white-colored and whose self is the subtle element of smell; svāhā!"—on the large nostrils.

‘Oṃ ṇaṃ, obeisance to the Supreme One of pale-red color, the self of the sense of hearing, svāhā!’—on the nostrils. ‘Oṃ ḍhaṃ, obeisance to the Supreme One of golden color, the self of the sense of touch, svāhā!’—on the plastering of lime. ‘Oṃ ḍaṃ, obeisance to the Supreme One of black color, the self of the sense of sight, svāhā!’—on the window. ‘Oṃ ṭhaṃ, obeisance to the Supreme One of fair-white color, the self of the sense of taste, svāhā!’—on the color.

‘Oṃ ṭaṃ, obeisance to the Supreme One of white color, whose self is the sense of smell, svāhā!’—on the great nostrils. ‘Oṃ ñaṃ, obeisance to the Supreme One of white color, whose self is the organ of speech, svāhā!’—on the lips. ‘Oṃ jhaṃ, obeisance to the Supreme One of red color, whose self is the organ of the hands, svāhā!’—on the feet. ‘Oṃ jaṃ, obeisance to the Supreme One of red color, whose self is the organ of the feet, svāhā!’—on the footstone. ‘Oṃ chaṃ, obeisance to the Supreme One of red color, whose self is the organ of excretion, svāhā!’—at the water outlet.

"Oṃ Caṃ, salutation to the Supreme One of golden color, whose self is the organ of procreation; Svāhā!"—on the organ of procreation. "Oṃ Kaṃ, salutation to the Supreme One of the color of a water-cloud, who is formless, whose self is the principle of space (ākāśa-tattva); Svāhā!"—from the nose up to the top-knot (śikhā) and the pitcher (kumbha). "Oṃ Khaṃ, salutation to the Supreme One of smoky color, whose form is that of a pedestal, whose self is the principle of air (vāyu-tattva); Svāhā!"—from the inner sanctum (garbhagṛha) up to the nose. "Oṃ Gaṃ, salutation to the Supreme One of red color, whose form is triangular, whose self is the principle of fire (agni-tattva); Svāhā!"—in the inner sanctum.

"Oṃ ghaṃ, salutation to the Supreme One, who is crystal-colored, whose form is that of a half-moon, and whose self is the element of water; svāhā! [This is for] from the secondary pedestal (upapīṭha) up to the exit of the water. "Oṃ ṅaṃ, salutation to the Supreme One, who is yellow-colored, whose shape is square, and whose self is the element of earth; svāhā! [This is for] the feet of the secondary pedestal. Having thus performed the ritual placement (nyāsa) of the elements, one should then perform the ritual placement and the fire-oblation (homa) of the powers (śakti).

‘Oṃ, svāhā to Prakṛti, in the apāna; oṃ, svāhā to Śānti, in the jagatī; oṃ, svāhā to Pṛthivī, in the kumuda; oṃ, svāhā to Vāgīśvarī, in the throat; oṃ, svāhā to Rati, on the fillet. Thus in the five-joined vimāna.

In the twelve-fold arrangement: *Oṃ kītryai svāhā* on the great band (*mahāpaṭṭikā*); *Oṃ puṣṭyai svāhā* on the neck; *Oṃ māhīśaktyai svāhā* on the crossbar (*vājana*); *Oṃ tuṣṭyai svāhā* on the pedestal (*paṭṭī*); *Oṃ sṛṣṭyai svāhā* on the feet; *Oṃ māyāyai svāhā* on the pigeon-holes (*kapota*); *Oṃ mohinyai svāhā* on the garlands of spirits (*bhūtamālā*). In the eighteen-fold arrangement: *Oṃ mahālakṣmyai svāhā* on the peaks (*kūṭa*); *Oṃ vasudhāyai svāhā* on the cages (*pañjara*); *Oṃ atimohinyai svāhā* on the ledges (*prastara*); *Oṃ svāhāśaktyai*.

" Svāhā! On the altar: Oṃ, to Śrī, svāhā! In the abode! Thus one should perform the *śaktihoma* and the ritual placement (*nyāsa*). Thereafter, as before, one should perform the *śāntihoma* and the *sparśahoma*. Following that, having separately performed the *tattvahoma* and the ritual placement for the deities of the directions (*diṅmūrti*), one should feed a thousand or a hundred Brahmins and give them sacrificial fees (*dakṣiṇā*).

For the purpose of consecrating the celestial chariot (*vimāna*), one should duly perform the binding of protection (*rakṣābandhana*) with twenty-five threads upon the frame for the deities of the directions using gold. Following that, having prepared an offering (*bali*) consisting of a mixture of meat, turmeric powder, parched grain, curd, and barley meal, [one should recite]: "May those beings who dwell in the eastern direction—both those primordial and those born of karma—who desire the offering, receive it with joy and complete satisfaction. May those who reside in trees, on mountain peaks, and in the intermediate directions likewise accept it."

"May those who dwell on earth and in the sky also accept this offering. May the Vināyakas, the Kṣetrapālas, and others who desire offerings, as well as Pūṣan and the other attendants, accept this offering today. Having thus performed the offering of the *bali* in all directions with these mantras, thereafter, at an auspicious hour in the morning, the Guru, adorned with all ornaments, takes the great pitcher (*mahākumbha*) and the image-pitchers (*mūrtikumbha*).

Sprinkling with a stream of water flowing from a water-pot held before him, and having performed the circumambulation of the temple, the preceptor places those [deities] upon a sacrificial mound made of grain at the front of the vimāna. Facing north, he installs the power (*śakti*) of the great pot (*mahākumbha*) into the vimāna with the root mantra, and installs the powers residing in the image-pots (*mūrtikumbha*) into the images (*mūrti*). Then, meditating on the vimāna as the thousand-headed Puruṣa, he takes up the great pot.

Having sprinkled the deities of the directions with their respective mantras, and likewise having sprinkled the other deities residing in the temple-car (vimāna), one should then worship the temple-car and the deities within it with water for the guest-offering (arghya) and other offerings, and present the great oblation (mahāhavis). Thereafter, the patron (yajamāna), having prostrated before the preceptor (guru), should satisfy the image-protectors (mūrtipās) and the others with wealth consisting of both animate and inanimate objects, according to his means. Thus ends the twenty-first chapter, titled "The Ritual for the Consecration of the Temple-Car.
The Twenty-second Chapter:
The Ritual for the Consecration of the Pavilion (maṇḍapa).
Now, the procedure for the consecration of the pavilion (maṇḍapa) is described.

Having constructed the altar as before, and having performed the entire sequence of rites—from the purification of the temple up to the visualization—according to the rules prescribed for the consecration of a celestial chariot (vimāna), the Preceptor (ācārya) himself should meditate upon the pavilion as the work of Viśvakarman, adorned with all kinds of jewels, supported by many golden pillars resplendent with the nine gems, and consisting of all powers. Having thus meditated, he should duly consecrate the fire in front according to the ritual manual (tantra).

Then, having performed the *śānti-homa* (peace-offering), one should deposit the residual clarified butter (*sampātājya*) at the respective locations of the pavilion (*maṇḍapa*), reciting: “Oṃ *prakṛtyai* svāhā” at the base; “Oṃ *apāne* svāhā”; “Oṃ *vasudhāyai* svāhā” on the ground; “Oṃ *kriyāyai* svāhā” in the trench (*vapra*); “Oṃ *mohinyai* svāhā” at the shaking (*kaṃpa*); “Oṃ *ratyai* svāhā” at the pedestal (*vājana*); “Oṃ *māyāyai* svāhā” at the neck (*grīvā*); “Oṃ *vāgīśvaryai* svāhā” at the upper shaking (*prātakaṃpa*); “Oṃ *iṣṭāśaktyai* svāhā” at the lotus-base (*kumuda*); “Oṃ *kṣamāyai* svāhā” on the fillet (*paṭṭikā*). “Oṃ... [The text continues].

"Oṃ brāhmyai svāhā" [is offered] upon the pillar-base stone; "Oṃ vaiṣṇavyai svāhā" upon the pillar; "Oṃ kamalāyai svāhā" upon the pigeon-hole (kapota); "Oṃ śāntyai svāhā" in the north; "Oṃ padmāyai svāhā" upon the scale-beam (tulā); "Oṃ aiśānyai svāhā" upon the rows of steps; "Oṃ śāntyai svāhā" beneath the four archways at the gates of the pavilion; "Oṃ vāgdevyai svāhā" above the southern archway; "Oṃ śriyai svāhā" upon the northern archway; and "Oṃ ratyai svāhā. Thus [it is said].

Having performed the placement [of mantras] by means of the *saṃpāta* [offering], and having completed all the rites concluding the peace-offerings (*śāntihoma*) as before, then at an auspicious hour in the morning, the Guru himself should take the great jar (*mahākumbha*). Having placed the previously mentioned Śaktis in their respective locations within the pavilion according to the previously described positions—using their own mantras ending in *namaḥ* and joined with the word *āgaccha* (come)—and having meditated upon them in their pervasive form, he should sprinkle the various paintings and painted images located there with the water from the jar using the *kūrca* [grass-bundle], according to their respective mantras and as previously prescribed.

Thereafter, the patron (yajamāna) should give the sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) to the preceptor (guru) as before. Regarding the consecration of the assembly pavilion (āsthānamaṇḍapa) and so forth: having performed the purification of the pavilion, the circumambulation with fire (paryagnikaraṇa), the sprinkling with the five products of the cow (pañcagavya), the Vāstuhoma, the recitation of the auspicious day (puṇyāhavācana), the offering of oblations (bali), the installation of the water-pot (balikumbha), and other rites; and having offered oblations into a single sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa); the preceptor (ācārya) should sprinkle [the site] with the water from the great pot (mahākumbha) at an auspicious moment (sumuhūrta) as previously described. One may perform all these rituals either immediately or [at a later time].

The sacrificial fee for the preceptor is as before. The consecration of the gopura (city gate) should be performed in the same manner as the consecration of the vimāna (temple). Regarding the consecration of the enclosure wall (*prākāra*), however, having first performed everything beginning with the rite of sowing seeds (*aṅkurārpaṇa*) as previously prescribed, the preceptor should sprinkle the wall with water while reciting the *varma-mantra*. The sacrificial fee is as before. As for the consecration of the door-posts and the door-panels, these have already been mentioned; one should perform them here in exactly the same way.

Thus ends the twenty-second chapter, titled "The Ritual for the Consecration of the Pavilion, the Assembly Hall Pavilion, the Gateway, the Enclosure Wall, the Door Panels, and the Door Leaves," in the *Kriyākairavacandrikā* composed by the venerable Varāhaguru.
The Twenty-third Chapter: The Construction and Consecration of the Balipīṭha (Sacrificial Altar).

Now, the procedure for the construction of the *balipīṭha* (offering pedestal) is described: the *balipīṭhikā* should have a length and width equal to that of the inner sanctum (*garbhamandira*), or half of it, or a quarter of it; or alternatively, having divided the inner sanctum into five parts [one part may be used].

Having constructed it—whether consisting of two parts, one part, or equal to one part among nine; or, according to the requirements of the cubit, at least one cubit and at most five cubits in width—with a height double, triple, half, or half again that of the width; endowed with the arrangement of five components; and adorned with rows of pigeons, bhūtas, swans, and so forth—and having divided the width of its front into three parts, fashioning a lotus with two of those parts;

In the corners of the pedestal (pīṭhikā), one should fashion Garuḍas or lions; in the east and other directions, Vighnarāja, Īśa, Pakṣīśa, and Durgā; and on the sides according to the height, one should arrange rows of steps. Thus, having fashioned the pedestal between the gateway (gopura) and the pavilion (maṇḍapa), the ritual for the consecration of the sacrificial altar (balipīṭha) is now described.

In the eight directions as appropriate, one should construct offering-altars (*balipīṭha*) measuring two *tāla*s in length and width, each three finger-breadths (*catur-aṅgula*) high and provided with three tiers (*mekhalā*). In their center, one should fashion a pericarp (*karṇikā*) four finger-breadths in length and width, either circular or square in shape. These should be established all around the house, starting from the east. To the west of the great altar (*māhāpīṭha*), one should construct the pedestal for the flagstaff (*dhvajastaṃbha*); the staff should be positioned facing the temple.

Just as when the deity faces east the [practitioner] faces west, and when the deity faces west the [practitioner] faces east, having arranged everything accordingly; the preceptor, having performed the entire cycle of rites for the temple—including the Vāstuhoma, the sowing of sprouts (aṅkurārpaṇa), and so forth, concluding with the Śāntihoma—then, at an auspicious moment in the morning, sprinkles the pedestal with water from the great pitcher using the root-mantra and a tuft of grass (kūrca).

Having sprinkled water while reciting: "In that [lotus], to the east, obeisance to Vighnarāja; to the south, *oṃ* obeisance to Īśāna; to the west, *oṃ* obeisance to Pakṣirāja; to the north, *oṃ* obeisance to Durgā; and in the central pericarp, *oṃ* obeisance to all the attendants of Viṣṇu (*sarvebhyo viṣṇupārṣadebhyaḥ*)," one should invoke the Gaṇeśas beginning with Kumuda in all eight directions, together with their respective followers, using their individual mantras, and pray for their presence. One should offer a daily oblation (*bali*) to them.

The patron, having fed the Brahmins according to his capacity and having bestowed sacrificial fees upon them, should give a fee of one hundred niṣkas to the preceptor. Then follows the procedure for the installation of the kitchen: the preceptor, having performed there all the rites beginning with the Vāstuhoma, places a single jar marked with the auspicious signs upon a heap of grain; having invoked the deity into it with the root mantra and worshipped it, he prepares the fire and offers one hundred and eight oblations of fuel sticks, clarified butter, cooked rice, and milk-rice, using the root mantra for each substance.

Having performed the rites for those deities residing there—Caṇḍa, Pracaṇḍa, Kṣetrapāla, Rudra, Gaṇeśa, Jṛmbhala, Maṇibhadra, Śibi, Kuṇḍala, Dharma, Adharma, Dhātṛ, Vidhātṛ, Lakṣmī, and others—preceded by *homa* offerings and including the placement of the *tattvas* (*tattvanyāsa*) and so forth; one should place the fire upon the hearths with the mantra “*agnim īḷe*. There, the attendants should perform the cooking of the sacrificial oblations, such as milk-rice (*pāyasa*) and the like. For the purpose of the daily *homa*, having established the fire in the sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*) to the east according to the rules and preceded by the ritual procedure (*tantra*).

Thereafter, one should perform the installation of Caṇḍa and the others with water from the great pitcher (*mahākumbha*). At the kitchen door: *oṃ caṇḍāya namaḥ*, *oṃ pracaṇḍāya namaḥ*; on the right side: *oṃ kṣetrapālāya namaḥ*, *oṃ īśvarāya namaḥ*; in the north: *oṃ gaṇapataye namaḥ*, *oṃ jṛmbhalāya namaḥ*; in the west: *oṃ maṇibhadrāya namaḥ*, *oṃ śibikuṇḍalāya namaḥ*. If there are other doors, one should perform the visualization of Lakṣmī and the others according to the pattern of the temple doors (*prāsādadvāra*).

To the left of the hearth (culyā), [one should offer] "Oṃ, salutation to Dharma; Oṃ, salutation to Adharma. Behind it, "Oṃ, salutation to Dhātṛ"; in front, "Oṃ, salutation to Vidhātṛ. Right there, facing the hearth, [one offers] "Salutation to Mahālakṣmī. On both sides of a long hearth, one should arrange Dharma and Adharma. Having worshipped all of them, one should sprinkle all the vessels placed there with water from the *kumbha* while reciting the *Śrīsūkta*. And the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) for the preceptor is as before.

The preceptor shall perform for all the edifices constructed by artisans—such as granaries, treasuries, Sarasvatī-halls, bathing-sheds, flower-garden houses, betel-preparation rooms, oil-stores, and so forth—the entire ritual sequence beginning with the Vāstu-homa and ending with the sprinkling (prokṣaṇa), according to the procedure prescribed in the Śāstras, just as he would for the sacrificial pavilion (maṇḍapa). Sacrificial fees (dakṣiṇā) should also be given according to one's wealth.

Alternatively, for the consecration of a large pond, a well, or a tank, one should construct an altar measuring four cubits in length and one cubit in height on their western side. Having fashioned a small image of the presiding deity of water out of gold, and having placed nine jars—made of gold or other metals, or even earthen—filled with gems and covered with metal brushes upon a heap of fresh grain; one should then invoke and worship [the deities] according to the rules, and bathe the presiding deity of water with those jars in accordance with the prescribed rite.

Thereafter, having laid [the image] upon an altar possessing the required characteristics, and having placed a great water-pot (mahākumbha) there; having invoked and worshipped the presiding deity of the water therein; and having kindled the fire in four sacrificial pits (kuṇḍas) or in one; having invoked that deity there and offered one hundred and eight oblations separately with fuel-sticks, clarified butter, and sacrificial porridge (caru), using the mantras dedicated to those deities; and having caused the Brahmins to recite the Vāruṇa hymns; then, at dawn during an auspicious moment, having had the declaration of a "holy day" (puṇyāha) recited and having sprinkled the tank and other sites; [one should proceed].

The preceptor, having visualized [the vessels] as filled with the waters of immortality, then casts into the ponds and other bodies of water images of aquatic deities such as fish and tortoises made of gold or other metals, as well as the great pitcher (*mahākumbha*). Therein, he should invoke all the rivers, beginning with the Gaṅgā, using their respective mantras. The patron, having given the preceptor a sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) according to his means, and having fed the Brāhmaṇas there, should also give them a sacrificial fee according to his ability.

Thus ends the twenty-third chapter, titled "The Ritual for the Construction and Consecration of the Balipīṭha, the Kitchen, the Granary, and the Consecration of Ponds, Wells, and Tanks," in the *Kriyākairavacandrikā* composed by the venerable Varāhaguru.
Chapter Twenty-four: The Consecration of Prabhā.

Now, the ritual procedure for the consecration of the *prabhā* (halo) and other [emblems] is described. If the consecration of the *prabhā* and others takes place at a later time, the teacher, having performed all the rites such as the preliminary immersion in water (*jalādhivāsa*) exactly as before, should meditate upon the *prabhā* as being endowed with thousands of garlands of flames and resembling a mass of lightning. Having touched it, he should offer one hundred and eight oblations (*āhuti*) each with fuel-sticks (*samidh*), clarified butter (*ājya*), and sacrificial porridge (*caru*) into the fire using the root mantra (*mūlamantra*). Then, having performed the propitiatory oblation (*śāntihoma*) with clarified butter, he should touch the *prabhā* with the residual drops (*saṃpāta*).

At dawn, having sprinkled [the deity] with water from a jar while reciting the *mūla-mantra*, and having united the Deity with the *prabhā* (radiance) during an auspicious moment (*sumuhūrta*), one should perform a great festival. The sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) for the Guru is as before. Regarding the installation of the pedestal (*pīṭha-sthāpana*): Having established the pedestal there, the Guru, having offered oblations into the fire with the *yogāsana-mantras* beginning with the *ādhāra* and ending with the *padma*, and having touched the pedestal with the residual drops (*saṃpāta*), should unite the lotus-pedestal with the Deity during an auspicious moment. The sacrificial fee is as before.

Now, the consecration of the bell is described: having bathed the bell with the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*) using the five *vāruṇika* mantras; having wrapped it in a new cloth; having prepared a sacrificial mound (*sthaṇḍila*) with rice grains and sesame seeds; having spread a new cloth together with *darbha* grass upon that; having laid the bell there upon its own mantra; having covered it with a new cloth; and having placed a single jar (*kumbha*) endowed with the proper characteristics there.

Having invoked and worshipped [the bell] with the mantra, "Oṃ, salutation to the Bell, whose nature is the Sound-Brahman (Śabdabrahman)," one should offer one hundred and eight oblations separately with fuel-sticks and other materials using that mantra upon either the sacrificial pit or the sacrificial mound; then, having offered sixteen oblations of sacrificial porridge (caru) with the Nṛsūkta, and having meditated upon her as consisting of the Sound-Brahman, one should perform the propitiatory fire-oblation (śāntihoma). Having touched the bell with the residual drops (saṃpāta), one should sprinkle it in the morning with water from the ritual pitcher (kumbha).

Then, one should ring the bell of the deity during all ritual acts. The sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) for the preceptor is as before. Having performed all the rites for the installation of the incense and the lamp as previously described for those two, one should offer incense with the mantra: “Oṃ, salutation to Pāvaka, the presiding deity of the incense vessel,” and the lamp with the mantra: “Oṃ, salutation to Bhāskara, the presiding deity of the lamp vessel. Following the fire oblation (homa), one should sprinkle water from the great jar (mahākumbha). The sacrificial fee is also as before.

For the consecration (*pratiṣṭhā*) of drums and similar instruments, one should perform purification (*śuddhi*) for the drums and so forth using the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*). For chariots and the like, as well as for parasols and the like, the consecration is performed after first performing purification for the chariots and other vehicles as previously described; one should then perform the sprinkling (*prokṣaṇa*) with water from the great jar (*mahākumbha*) while reciting the mantra of their respective deities. For parasols and the like as well, having fed the Brahmins everywhere as before, one should perform all the rites according to the rules, preceded by the declaration of an auspicious day (*puṇyāha*). And the patron (*yajamāna*) should give a sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) to the preceptor (*guru*) according to his means.

The Ritual for the Consecration of the Rosary (Akṣamalā-pratiṣṭhā-vidhi). Now, the ritual for the consecration of the rosary is described: one should take beads made of gold, silver, copper, tin, lead, bell-metal, iron, crystal, sunstone, moonstone, *putrajīvī*, *indrākṣī*, *vibhītaka*, *nimba*, lotus, white lotus, *kamalākṣa*, *rudrākṣa*, conch, water-born [lotus seeds], *kuśa* grass, *granthi* wood, and so forth—beads that correspond to the desired rite of the reciter—and number them at one hundred and eight, fifty-four, twenty-seven, or an equal number to the bones of the *akṣa* tree.

Having procured [seeds] resembling the stones of the *dhātrī* fruit or similar to the stones of the *badara* fruit, and having inspected them to ensure they are free from defects, one should wash them with the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*) while reciting the five *vāruṇika* mantras and the five *upaniṣad* mantras. Then, having threaded them—back to back and face to face so that they do not touch one another—upon a triple-stranded thread made of gold or silver, or upon a cotton thread free from hair and other impurities, one should fix them in place with intervals between them secured by knots of gold or thread.

Having formed that garland into the shape of a bracelet and having placed another, larger gem within that garland, one should thus fashion the rosary (*akṣamālikā*). Having sprinkled it with *puṇyāha* water, placed it upon a lotus petal, and anointed it with saffron and other substances, one should prepare a sacrificial mound (*sthaṇḍila*) with rice grains measuring a *bhāra* or more. Having drawn a wheel and a lotus there, covered it with *kuśa* grass and new cloth, and placed a large jar (*mahākumbha*) filled with gold and cloth upon a pedestal of grain.

Having invoked and worshipped [the deity] with the mantra, "Oṃ, salutation to the presiding deity of the rosary, salutation to the Mantra-puruṣa," and having kindled the fire in either a sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) or on a leveled altar (sthaṇḍila), one should offer one hundred and eight oblations of fuel-sticks, sacrificial porridge, and clarified butter separately with that mantra. Then, having performed the drying and other rites upon it, and having meditated upon it as being composed of an egg, one should meditate upon the Puruṣa situated within its center with joined palms, four-armed, resembling a white lotus, and with hands in the gestures of granting boons and fearlessness.

Having meditated thus: "Holding a rosary that has the form of a bracelet at the tip of his crest," and thereafter, following the peace-offering (śāntihoma), having touched her with the residual drops (saṃpāta), and having deposited the principles (tattvas) upon her in the order of emanation during an auspicious moment, the preceptor (ācārya)—having meditated on the Vaiṣṇavī Śakti, who is non-different from himself and whose form is the mantra, resembling the sun in brilliance within the lotus of his own heart—invokes her from the aperture of Brahmā (brahmarandhra) into the rosary with its respective mantra; then, having sprinkled it with water from the great pitcher (mahākumbha).

"O Lord Janārdana, whose form is the mantra, please remain present here upon this rosary of prayer beads out of a desire to bestow grace upon your devotees. Having uttered this verse, and having meditated there upon the Lord—who possesses a mantra-body, who bears a rosary, who has four arms, and who has the luster of a dark cloud—the preceptor, after performing worship, should give it to the patron. The patron should then count that very mantra which the preceptor had previously established upon the rosary. A sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) should be given to the preceptor according to one's wealth.

Thus ends the twenty-fourth chapter, titled "The Ritual for the Consecration of the Prabhā-pīṭha, Bell, Incense, Lamp, Bherī-drum and other musical instruments, vehicles such as chariots, the parasol and other regalia, and the rosary," in the *Kriyākairavacandrikā* composed by the venerable Varāhaguru.
The Twenty-fifth Chapter: The Consecration of the Domestic Image (*Gṛhārcā-pratiṣṭhā*).

Now, the procedure for the consecration of the household image (gṛhārcā) is described: it should be made of gold or other metals, or else from trees such as sandalwood, agallochum, deodar, bilva, sarala, tamāla, mango, banyan, jackfruit, milky trees, saptalā, jāti, spandana, timiśa, kadamba, kuravaka, tilaka, madhūka, āsana, jambū, punnāga, kanaka, khadira, nimba, vibhītaka, or śālmali; it should be proportionate to the desired ritual of the patron, measuring one cubit for a Brāhmaṇa, or twenty-one finger-breadths for a Kṣatriya.

If it is for a Vaiśya, [the image] should be nineteen finger-breadths; for a Śūdra, twenty-seven finger-breadths. If it is made of metal, it should be made by an artisan according to the prescribed rite—measuring twelve finger-breadths for a Brāhmaṇa, nine for a Kṣatriya, seven for a Vaiśya, and five for a Śūdra—as an image of Śrī or Bhūmi, or of Śrī alone, joined with jewels or gems, or even without them, provided with a halo, a pedestal, and so forth, possessing all the auspicious marks, and excluding only the posture of reclining on the serpent Śeṣa.

One should establish [the deity] in the north-eastern direction of the house. Having gathered all the necessary materials for its installation, the patron (yajamāna) himself should perform the selection of the preceptor (ācārya). Then, having constructed a water-shed (prapā) with a central altar and four side-altars—or with a single altar—in either a courtyard, on a riverbank, or in a well-honored sacred field, he should have the installation performed by the preceptor. The preceptor, having first offered the ritual sprouts (aṅkura), [should proceed].

Thereafter, having performed the rites of the preliminary consecration in water (*jalādhivāsa*), the opening of the eyes (*nayanonmīlana*), the bathing with the jar of ritual substances such as the water for the feet (*pādyādi-dravyakalaśasnāpana*), the preliminary consecration of the bed (*śayanādhivāsa*), the invocation into the jar (*kumbhāvāhana*), and so forth, exactly as previously described in the *Pratiṣṭhā* [ritual]; and having kindled the fire in the sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*) and offered oblations beginning with the *tattvahoma* according to the primary procedure (*purastāttantra*) and ending with the *śāntihoma*; and having touched [the image] with the residual drops (*saṃpāta*) as before; and having performed the deposition of jewels (*ratnanyāsa*) at the site for the installation of the image during an auspicious moment (*sumuhūrta*); and having installed it there according to the prescribed rule.

One should perform the rites beginning with invocation (*āvāhana*). If the invocation and subsequent rites are intended for Jaṅghama, one should perform them upon the altar (*vedikā*) and thereafter install him in his place. At the door, one should invoke and worship Caṇḍa, Pracaṇḍa, Kṣetrapāla, Vighneśa, Vāstunātha, Durgā, Guha, Viṣvaksena, Śaṅkha, and Padmanidhi. Thereafter, the patron (*yajamāna*), prompted by the preceptor (*ācārya*), should prostrate himself on the ground like a staff and recite this verse: "O Lord of Gods, I am your servant, together with my sons, attendants, and kinsmen."

"O Acyuta, remain in my house for as long as there is progeny; accept, O Blessed One, even this incomplete worship offered by me according to my ability, out of a desire to show favor to your devotees. Having thus entreated the Blessed One in the presence of the preceptor, and having bestowed sacrificial fees (*dakṣiṇā*) upon the preceptor and the image-makers according to one's means, one should feed the Brahmins and give them sacrificial fees as well.

The Installation of Śrīvatsa: Now the procedure for the installation of Śrīvatsa is described. Having first placed the Śrīvatsa at the front upon a heap of rice with its cloth-covering, and having performed all the rites beginning with the declaration of the auspicious day (*puṇyāha*), one should perform the ritual placement of the principles (*tattva-vinyāsa*). Having invoked and worshipped [the deity] in the water-pot (*kumbha*), and having kindled the fire in the lotus-shaped sacrificial pit (*padmakuṇḍa*), one should offer one hundred and eight oblations each of fuel-sticks (*samidh*), clarified butter (*ājya*), and sacrificial porridge (*caru*) with the Śrīvatsa mantra. Having performed the oblation of the principles (*tattva-homa*) and the oblation for peace (*śānti-homa*), one should touch [the image] with the residual drops of the offering.

Having sprinkled [the image] with water from the *kumbha* vessel, one should place it upon the chest of Viṣṇu at an auspicious moment (*sumuhūrta*). The sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) for the preceptor (*guru*) is as before. Regarding the installation of the Kaustubha gem: having established the Kaustubha on the sacrificial mound (*sthaṇḍila*) with its own mantra as previously described, and having had a golden image fashioned in the form of the Kaustubha, one should place it within the great *kumbha* vessel and perform all the rites as before.

Regarding the consecration of the forest garland (*vanamālā*): having consecrated a golden forest garland, adorned with various jewels, according to the previously mentioned procedure and with its own mantra, one should suspend it around the neck of Viṣṇu at an auspicious moment. Next, regarding the consecration of the crown (*kirīṭa*): having fashioned a crown suitable for the Blessed One, made of pure gold or set with gems; having bathed it with seventeen jars containing water for the feet (*pādya*) up to clarified butter (*ghṛta*), using the *kirīṭa-mantra*; and having placed it upon a sacrificial mound (*sthaṇḍila*) prepared with cloth and grain.

Having invoked [the deity] into the pitcher with its respective mantra and worshipped it; having offered one hundred and eight oblations separately with sacrificial wood, clarified butter, and sacrificial porridge (caru) using that same mantra in either four fire-pits or a single fire-pit; having performed the propitiatory homa (śāntihoma); having touched the crown with the residual drops (saṃpāta); and having sprinkled [the deity] with the water from the pitcher at an auspicious moment while reciting its own vidyā; thereafter, having attended upon the God seated on the auspicious throne like a king, having bathed Him, adorned Him, and worshipped Him.

Accompanied by the sounds of the Vedas, the sounds of musical instruments, and all ritual offerings, the preceptor, together with the image-keepers, having placed the crown upon the head of the deity with the five Upaniṣadic mantras and having mounted the deity upon the vehicle, should circumambulate the village preceded by the sounds of trumpets, showers of flowers, and other offerings; then, having settled [the deity] in the temple, he should worship. A sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) should be given to the preceptor. As for the consecration of ornaments and so forth—the entire collection of ornaments from necklaces down to anklets—one should cleanse them with scented water while reciting the twelve-syllable mantra.

Having placed [the image] upon a heap of grain, having offered oblations into the fire with one's own vidyā, and having meditated upon each respective ornament, one should adorn [the deity] with those various ornaments using their respective mantras while reciting the twelve-syllable mantra. Now, the ritual procedure for the consecration of the weapons, such as the discus (cakra), is described. The discus should be one cubit in measure, or seventeen finger-breadths, or eighteen finger-breadths, or twenty finger-breadths, or even fourteen or sixteen finger-breadths.

Or, measuring twelve finger-breadths, it should be clearly defined by its own characteristics; equal in size to the face of the primary image, it should be a thousand-spoked wheel, brilliantly radiant. Alternatively, it may have a hundred spokes, or be endowed with twenty-four spokes, or sixteen, or eight, or the excellent six spokes. It may have a thousand flames or six flames, adorned with a hub. Having fashioned a discus made of three metals, complete with a stalk and a pedestal, one should visualize Sudarśana bearing a crown and a casket.

One should visualize the Discus (Cakra) endowed with such a form: possessing four arms, wrathful, with a face whose brows are knitted; or else, as a two-armed being, threatening with the right hand while touching the hip with the other, and with the remaining two hands joined in *añjali*; well-established upon a lotus seat with its two principal hands. Having thus fashioned the Discus in this form:

As before, having performed the rites of depositing the sprouts (*aṅkurārpaṇa*), water-consecration (*jalādhivāsa*), opening the eyes (*nayanonmīlana*), bathing (*snapana*), consecrating the bed (*śayanādhivāsa*), and the worship of the door-arches and the jars (*dvāratoraṇakumbhapūjā*), one should subsequently invoke Sudarśana into the great jar (*mahākumbha*) with his mantra and worship him. Then, one should meditate upon the exceedingly fierce Person (*atyugra-puruṣa*) as two-armed, clad in red garments, with a face of red fangs, the Lord of the Wheel (*cakranāyaka*) firmly established in the navel. Having thus meditated: "iti dhyātvā" (having thus meditated).

Having offered one hundred and eight oblations separately with fuel sticks (*samid*), clarified butter (*ājya*), and cooked rice (*caru*) using their respective mantras at each of the four *puṇḍa* sections—or at a single section—then, having dried the *cakra* by means of desiccation and other methods; and having touched the parts such as the nave (*nābhi*) with the remnants of the *śānti-homa* at its conclusion; and having sprinkled it with his own *vidyā* during an auspicious moment, he should worship it. Regarding the installation of the conch and the others: the preceptor, having performed the installation of the four items beginning with the conch according to the previous procedure with their respective mantras, should worship them according to the rules.

And the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) for the preceptor (*guru*) is as before. Regarding the consecration (*pratiṣṭhā*) of the gatekeepers such as Caṇḍa and others: having performed the rites of water-consecration (*jalādhivāsana*), opening of the eyes (*nayonmīlana*), bathing (*snapana*), bed-consecration (*śayanādhivāsa*), worship of the single pitcher (*ekakumbhapūjana*), the fire-oblation of reality (*tattvahoma*), ritual placement (*nyāsa*), the peace-offering (*śāntihoma*), the touching (*sparśana*), and so forth, the Preceptor shall sprinkle [the deities] with the water from the pitcher while reciting their respective mantras joined with the seed-syllables (*bīja*). The sacrificial fee for the preceptor is as before.

The Installation of Garuḍa: Now the procedure for the installation of Vainateya is described. Having performed the rites beginning with the sowing of sprouts according to the rules as previously stated, the preceptor shall, in order, invoke Satya, Suparṇa, Garuḍa, and Tārkṣya in the four corners starting from the east. Having offered one hundred and eight oblations for each substance respectively with the *Bṛhatsāman*, the *Suparṇamanu*, the *Rathantara*, and the *Garuḍagāyatrī* mantras;

Thereafter, one should perform the remaining rites as before. A sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) should be given to the preceptor. Regarding the installation of the Sun: in the installation of the Sun, there is the propitiation with the *Sāvitrī* verse; likewise, the fire-oblation (*homa*). One should perform the installation with the *anuvāka* beginning with "bibhrāṭ" and the *Sāvitrī*, and the sprinkling of the water-pot (*kumbha*) with the *Sūryavidyā*. For all the deities, including Brahmā and the others, it should be done as previously described. Whether in an independent (*svatantra*) or dependent (*paratantra*) ritual, the installation shall be performed with their respective mantras.

For Durgā, the Seven Mothers, and whatever female deities there may be, their installation—like that of Lakṣmī—is distinguished by their respective mantras. Having performed all the ritual acts for the installation of Viṣvaksena, one should perform the consecration of the image of the Blessed One (Viṣvaksena) with his own mantra. In all cases, the sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) is as previously described.

The ritual for the installation of devotees (*bhakta-pratiṣṭhā-vidhi*): For each individual devotee, having fashioned an image—either independent or following the tradition of the Lord—out of stone or other materials as available, with palms joined in reverence, gentle in appearance, standing or seated, possessing a form according to their caste, their stage of life (*āśrama-dharma*), and bearing the features appropriate to their age, and having had it installed upon a lotus pedestal by an artisan in accordance with the prescribed rites; then, on an auspicious day, the preceptor (*guru*) should first sow the sprouts (*aṅkura*) in pairs of small pots (*pālikā*).

The entire ritual procedure (*karmajāla*), with the exception of the consecration of the altar (*vedikādhivāsana*) and the eight jars (*kumbhāṣṭaka*), is to be performed as before. Having performed the worship of the door-arches (*dvāratoraṇa*) first, according to the rules, using the *praṇava* and other mantras; one should perform the sprinkling of the jars (*kumbhaprokṣaṇa*) with those very same mantras. If these [jars] are used independently, one should construct a temple excluding the forms [of the deities] belonging to the directions beginning with the East (such as Siṃha). For the sake of the success of the mantra, the preceptor (*ācārya*) should fashion an image of the initiation-guru (*dīkṣāguru*) for the purposes of initiation and installation (*pratiṣṭhā*).

Having performed the entire web of rituals for the devotees beginning with the *puṇyāha* ceremony, having fed the Brahmins, and having bestowed sacrificial fees (*dakṣiṇā*) upon them; and having had the Brahmins perform there the study of the Vedas (*svādhyāya*) and so forth, he himself should also do so. If they are independent, he should perform the festival without the hoisting of the flag, the fire-oblation (*homa*), the offering (*bali*), or the pilgrimage (*tīrthayātrā*). If they are dependent, he should perform it together with the Lord for the pleasure of the Lord. And the sacrificial fee for the preceptor (*guru*) is as before.

Thus ends the twenty-fifth chapter, titled "The Installation Ritual for the House-Worship, Śrīvatsa, Kaustubha, Vanamālā, Kirīṭa, Ornaments, Discus and Other Weapons, Caṇḍa and Other Gatekeepers, Garuḍa, Āditya, and the Devotees," in the *Kriyākairavacandrikā* composed by the venerable Varāhaguru.
The Twenty-sixth Chapter: The Ritual of Initiation (*Dīkṣā-vidhi*).
Now, the procedure for initiation (dīkṣā) is described.

Having constructed the initiation pavilion with a central altar similar to the installation pavilion, one should prepare the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa): to the west of the altar, at a distance of three tālas, a square pit measuring two tālas for a Brāhmaṇa; if for a Kṣatriya, a circular pit measuring a pair of gokarṇas; if for a Vaiśya, a quadrangular shape measuring two vitastis; and for a Śūdra, a triangular pit measuring two prādeśas. Thus, having prepared the pit, [the rite proceeds].

Having likewise prepared the *sruva* and *sruc* ladles according to the sequence of colors, as well as other vessels and sacrificial materials such as fuel-sticks (*samidh*) on the tenth day; thereafter, on the evening of the eleventh day, the initiation preceptor (*dīkṣācārya*), having arranged the door-arches, water-pots (*kumbha*), and so forth in the pavilion adorned with all ornaments as before, and having performed the sowing of sprouts (*aṅkurārpaṇa*) as before, sprinkles the central altar with the "Auspicious Day" (*puṇyāha*) water.

Preceded by breath control (*prāṇāyāma*), one should lay down seventeen threads extending eastward and an equal number extending northward upon that [surface] moistened with sandalwood paste. Then, having cleared away thirty-six squares from among the two hundred and fifty-six resulting squares, and having fixed a gnomon (*śaṅku*) in their center, one should rotate [the cord] so that five equal circles are formed. Among these, the first circle is the field for the pericarp (*karṇikā*); the second is divided into three parts.

When this has been done, one should first delineate the circle at the end of the filaments (*kesarāntavalaya*), secondly the circle at the end of the petals (*dalāntavalaya*), and thirdly the central hub (*nābhimaṇḍala*). Having divided that central hub into three parts, one should arrange the field of the spokes (*arakṣetra*) with two parts in the remaining sectors outside of it, and the rim-circle (*nemimaṇḍala*) with one part outside of that. Outside of that, one should fashion a pedestal (*pīṭhikā*) with twenty-eight squares, and outside of that, a walkway (*vīthikā*) with eighty squares in two rows.

Outside of that, having formed a square with one hundred and twelve squares by means of two rows, one should likewise create four doors from east to north using four squares each in the middle of those [squares], and also in the corners starting from Agni (southeast). One should then clear away two squares on each side of the doors in the outer path, and one square each in the intermediate paths; in this way, the half-ornaments (*ardhaśobhā*) are formed.

Between the two half-śobhās, there is one [square] in the outer row and three in the inner row; thus, the śobhās are formed by four squares. In this manner, having established eight śobhās and sixteen half-śobhās in the four directions, one should then perform the filling of the collection of colors (varṇakalāpa).

One should complete the positions of the mandala with the five jewels, or with the five elements, or with their powders, or with flowers of five colors. For white, there is the flour of rice and other grains; for black, charcoal burnt in a closed vessel (puṭadagdha); for dark green, the powder of crushed and dried leaves; for red, safflower; for yellow, turmeric powder. The term "of the colors" applies to all these materials. With yellow [powder], one makes the pericarp (karṇikā); with white, the dots; with pale-red (pāṭala), the lines of the pericarp; and having divided [the center] in two, the rows of filaments (kesara) with yellow.

The eastern portion [of the lotus] with white, the northern with yellow, the filaments with white, the dots with red, and the eight petals with white; the edges of the petals with red, and the rim of the petal-edges with either red or white; the three navel-circles with dark blue, yellow, and red respectively; the rim between the spokes with black; the twelve spokes with red; and having divided the circumference into two parts, the earth [the outer rim] with white and the felly with white.

The eastern portion is black, the northern white, and the intermediate spaces dark blue; or else, the eastern portion is black, the northern white, the intermediate spaces dark blue, and the pedestal outside of that yellow, pale red, or white. Outside of that, the pathway (vīthikā) is white and adorned with creepers and canopies; the eight beauties (śobhā) are red, and the sixteen half-beauties (ardhaśobhā) are yellow. The four doors, starting from the north, are respectively white, red, yellow, and black, and the corners are colored black throughout.

Having filled the intermediate spaces with a black or dark-blue color, and having fashioned white lotuses in the four corners, one should then perform the worship of the maṇḍala. One should worship the path of mantra (mantrādhvan) within the pericarp. Having uttered and worshipped its corresponding forms—the twelve-syllable mantra, the eight-syllable power-mantra (balamantra), the Viṣṇu-gāyatrī, the Sudarśana-mantra, the Pavitra-mantra, the Caturmūrti-mantra, the Nṛsiṃha-mantra, the Rāma-mantra, the Kṛṣṇa-mantra, and the Varāha-mantra—one should perform the worship.

On the filaments (kesara) is the path of the principles (tattvādhvan). The worship consists of the principles of the individual soul (jīva-tattvas) in the form of: life-force (prāṇa), mind (manas), intellect (buddhi), ego (ahaṅkāra), sound, touch, form, taste, smell, hearing, skin, eye, tongue, nose, speech, hands, feet, anus, genitals, earth, water, fire, air, and ether; as well as the principles of the deities such as Dhātṛ, Vidhātṛ, Mitra, Varuṇa, Bhaga, Vivasvat, Pūṣan, Savitṛ, Ravi, Tvaṣṭṛ, Viṣṇu, Vīrabhadra, Śambhu, Girīśa, Śarva, Māpatī, Īśāna, Hara, Sthāṇu, Bhava, Śiva, Śūlin, and others, beginning with the Praṇava.

One should worship those [syllables] ending in the dative case. On the petals is the worship of the path of phonemes (varṇādhvā), beginning with "Oṃ Kaṃ Namaḥ Parāya" and ending with "Kṣaṃ Namaḥ Parāya. In the region of the navel is the worship of the path of words (padādhvā).

Therein [he worships] Keśava and the others, as well as the Seven Sages; in the eastern and other directions, Ādivarāha, Nārasiṃha, Śrīdhara, Hayavaktra, Bhārgavarāma, Rāghava, Vāmana, and Vāsudeva; and those beginning with Kumuda and ending with Supratiṣṭha; and Jaya, Vijaya, Caṇḍa, Pracaṇḍa, Bhadra, Subhadra, Dhātṛ, Vidhātṛ, Sūrya, Candra, Kāma, Brahmā, Vināyaka, Ṣaṇmukha, Durgā, Kubera, and Śaṅkara; and the powers of grace (anugraha-śakti): Vimalā, Utkarṣaṇī, Jñānā, Kriyā, Yogī, Prahvī, Satyā, and Īśānā.

One should worship the deities beginning with Āditya and ending with Ketu, as well as Lakṣmī, Sarasvatī, Rati, Śānti, Tuṣṭi, Puṣṭi, Kriyā, Kīrti, and Vārāhī, using their names preceded by the *praṇava* (Oṃ) and ending in the dative case. On the spokes, one should perform the worship of the path of the *kalās*, wherein one should worship the vowels beginning with *a*. In the portion of the rim, one performs the worship of the path of the worlds (*bhuvanādhvan*).

Its varieties are as follows: Atala, Vitala, Sutala, Nitala, Mahātala, Rasātala, Talātala, Pātāla; Bhūrloka, Bhuvarloka, Svarloka, Maharloka, Janarloka, Tapoloka, Satyaloka; Gandharvaloka, Yakṣaloka, Apsaraloka, Kinnaraloka, Yamaloka, Nirṛtiloka, Varuṇaloka, Rudraloka, Devaloka, Brahmaloka, Śivaloka, Viṣṇuloka, Sadāviṣṇuloka; and [the hells]: Kumbhīpāka, Mahāraurava, Kṣurāla, Sannimāla, Śītala, Uṣṇajala, and Santapana.

One should worship the pure hells—pierced by the heated iron, the *śālmalī* tree, the *dhīyantra*, and the bow—as well as the *praṇava* and the others ending in the dative case. One should worship the twelve syllables in the dots (*bindu*s), the Supreme Self (*paramātman*) in the pericarp (*karṇikā*), Śrī, Sarasvatī, Rati, Śānti, Prīti, Kīrti, Puṣṭi, and Tuṣṭi in the filaments (*kesara*s), and the twelve powers (*śakti*s) beginning with Śrīvatsā in the regions of the petals. Around the petals, one should worship Vyāpti and the others. In the first nave (*nābhi*), one should worship Viṣṇu; in the second, Brahmā; in the third, Rudra; and in the twelve spokes, the twelve [deities] beginning with Viṣṇu.

One should worship the ten forms beginning with Matsya on the rim of the spokes; Śaṅkha and the others on the first rim of the felly; Ananta, Varāha, Nārasiṃha, and Hayagrīva in the four corners of the pedestal starting from the southeast (āgneya); the world-protectors (lokapālas) such as Indra on the creeper-path (latāvīthikā); the pairs beginning with Caṇḍa at the four doors; and Viṣvaksena in the northeast (īśāna) on the path, Vainateya outside the eastern door, Padma in the south, Gadā in the west, and Śaṅkha in the north—worshipping them with their respective mantras preceded by the Praṇava and ending in the dative case.

Thereafter, having filled a golden pitcher and a similar earthen water-vessel (karaka) with filtered water—both wrapped with thread, containing deposited gems and gold, sprinkled with flowing sandalwood water, and encircled by a pair of new, unwashed cloths—and having consecrated the water-vessel one hundred times with the Astra-mantra; then, carrying the water-vessel around the altar in a clockwise direction with an unbroken stream, followed by the pitcher behind it.

In the northeast corner of the lotus-cakra, having placed a water-pot (kalaśa) to the right and a small vessel (karaka) to the left upon a heap of grain, one should invoke Hari into the pot with the root mantra after performing the ritual preparation of the seat (pīṭhakalpana), and worship Him. Having worshipped the Supreme Self together with His limbs and retinue in the maṇḍala according to the prescribed rite, one should thereafter churn fire using the eight-syllable mantra and place it in the center of the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa). There, having divided the cooked sacrificial porridge (caru) into four parts:

Having offered one portion to Hari residing in the mandala and one portion to [Hari] residing in the pitcher, and having offered one portion into the fire, the Guru himself should consume one portion. Therein, having offered one hundred and eight fuel sticks and likewise oblations of clarified butter into the fire with the root mantra, and having offered the sacrificial porridge (caru) with the Puruṣasūkta, he should perform the final oblation (pūrṇāhuti).

Thereafter, the preceptor, having summoned the disciple—who has bathed, conquered anger, is free from pride and other defects, is pure, wears unwashed linen garments with an upper cloth, and is adorned—shall bind his eyes with a new cloth using his own mantra. Having seated him on his right side facing the east, and being touched by the disciple with *darbha* grass, he shall offer twelve oblations of clarified butter, sacrificial porridge (*caru*), fuel-sticks, flowers, and sesame seeds, while reciting the twelve-syllable mantra.

Then the Guru, touching the head of the disciple three times while moving clockwise with the *prasṛti* mudrā and the eight-syllable mantra, and having touched the head with white sacred ash (*bhasman*) while reciting the root mantra, he should apply the vertical sectarian mark (*ūrdhvapuṇḍra*) upon the disciple. Having bound a protective amulet (*pratisara*) with the weapon-mantra (*astramantra*), and having caused the disciple to consume the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*) and the sacrificial porridge (*caru*) while reciting the *praṇava*, he should have him brush his teeth. Having cast the tooth-stick (*dantakāṣṭha*) upon the ground, he should examine it.

If the first [digit] in the directions of Nairṛta, Varuṇa, or Yama is inauspicious, then one should offer one hundred and eight oblations of sesame seeds with the Nṛsiṃha mantra. Then, having caused the disciple to perform the ritual sipping of water (ācamana) and having taken him by the hand while bowing to the Lord of Gods, [the Guru should pray]: "O God, you alone are the refuge for the liberation from the bonds of worldly existence for those bound souls; no other goal is known. By this worship of You, which is the cause for the release from bonds, [I seek liberation] for these beings born as animals who are fettered by the bond of birth."

"O Lord of Gods, I shall untie [the bonds]; you should grant permission for that. Having uttered this verse, he takes a thread of white, black, and red colors, folds it three times, and then, with that triple-folded *māyāsūtra*, he approaches the disciple's topknot and winds it around from foot to head twenty-five times while reciting the root mantra.

Having offered one hundred and eight oblations of clarified butter with that very mantra, and having presented an offering (*bali*) of black gram and boiled rice to the spirits (*bhūta*), he should release the disciple’s eye-bandage and the binding of his body. Having placed the *māyāsūtra* in another bowl and covered it with another, he should set it aside at the side of the water-pot (*kumbha*). Then, having strewn *darbha* grass upon the ground, he should have the disciple lie down there. At that time, he should not dismiss the deities residing in the mandala and the fire of the sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*).

At dawn, if the disciple has seen auspicious dreams, he should be initiated immediately. However, if he has seen inauspicious dreams, the Guru should immediately bathe, enter the sacrificial pavilion (*yāgamaṇḍapa*), and make the formal resolve (*saṃkalpa*): "I shall perform a propitiatory fire-offering (*śāntihoma*) for the sake of pacifying the defects of the bad dreams. Having performed the *śāntihoma* as before, and having performed the worship of the arches (*toraṇa*), the banner (*dhvaja*), and the water-pot (*kumbha*) as before, he should worship the Deity residing in the mandala and the Deity residing in the pot, offer the four kinds of food (*caturvidham annam*), bow down, and circumambulate.

Having bound the eyes of the disciple as before, and having led him to his own right side, he offers one hundred and eight oblations for each of the materials beginning with the fuel-sticks (*samid*) using the root mantra. Then, having cut the *māyāsūtra* into twenty-five pieces, he offers one hundred and eight oblations for each piece eight times. Having offered the oblations for *prakṛti* and the other principles, the Guru, meditating on the Supreme Person within the lotus of his own heart, withdraws the life-force (*jīva*) of the disciple into that [Supreme Person] by means of the process of dissolution (*saṃhārakrama*).

Having performed the drying and other [purificatory rites] for that [disciple], and thereafter having created the disciple’s gross body preceded by the *tattva-sṛṣṭi-homa*, having visualized [the deity] residing in his own heart within the mandala, having meditated upon [the deity] situated in the mandala as being within the disciple, and having meditated upon the disciple as being endowed with life, he should sprinkle him with water from the pitcher while reciting the root mantra (*mūlamantra*). Having removed the blindfold from the disciple's eyes and having caused him to put on another garment with the root mantra, he should cause him to perform the washing of his feet ending with the ritual sipping of water (*ācamana*).

Having bound the eyes of the disciple with another cloth, the Guru, having seated him nearby facing east, purifies the six paths (ṣaḍadhvan). Having offered one hundred and eight oblations of clarified butter with the Mahāvyāhṛti mantra, he offers as many oblations of sesame seeds with that same mantra upon the disciple's feet using the remnants of the offering. He offers as many oblations of lotus flowers (*kuśeśaya*) with the previously mentioned Vidyā-mantra upon the disciple's navel using the remnants of the offering. He offers as many oblations of sacrificial porridge (*caru*) with the previously mentioned Manu-mantra upon the disciple's heart using the remnants of the offering, according to the previously stated number.

Having touched the head of the disciple with the remnants of the oblation (*hutaśeṣa*), at the conclusion of the fire sacrifice (*homānta*), the Guru takes the disciple by his right hand, causes him to circumambulate the water-pot (*kumbha*) and the mandala, and then, standing at any one of the four doors of the mandala, the Guru fills the disciple’s joined palms (*añjali*) with jewels, pearls, coral, or flowers alone.

Thereafter, permitted by the Guru with the consent of the assembly members, the disciple should scatter flowers and other offerings, held in his cupped hands, upon that mandala.
