Having bathed [the deity] with each substance preceded by the offering of a jar for the secondary bath (*upasnāna*), a cloth, an upper garment, a turban, water for the guest-offering (*arghya*), water for the feet (*pādya*), water for sipping (*ācamana*), fragrance, flowers, incense, and a lamp—using the *Viṣṇugāyatrī* for the water for the feet, the *Dadhikrāvṇa* verse for curd, the *Payovrata Sāman* for milk, the *Na te viṣṇo* verse for water for sipping, the *Madhuvātā* verse for honey, the *Viṣṇoḥ karmāṇi* verse for the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*), the *Yāḥ phalinīḥ* verse for fruit-water, and the *Ghṛtasnātā* verse for clarified butter—one recites: *Oṃ hiraṇyavarṇāṃ hariṇīm*.

Having smeared [the image] with turmeric, having washed it with the four verses beginning with *oṃ hiraṇyavarṇāḥ śucayaḥ*, and having smeared it with saffron using the *viṣṇugāyatrī* and the verse *gandhadvārām*, one should consecrate it with the *pāvamānī* hymns, the verse *brahmajijñānam*, and the verse *kayā naścitra*. Then: *oṃ tatsaviturvareṇyaṃ bhargo devasya dhīmahi dhiyo yo naḥ pracodayāt*.

Having thus sprinkled the deity, and having worshipped with "Oṃ, obeisance to the Full Moon, the presiding deity of the thousand-fold stream," one should sprinkle [the deity] with a jar from which a thousand streams flow while reciting the *Nṛsūkta*. Then, having worshipped with "Oṃ, obeisance to the Lord of the Conch, the presiding deity of the [conch-]stream; Oṃ, obeisance to the Lord of Waters; Oṃ, obeisance to Puṣṭi, the presiding deity of the lotus-stream," and having sprinkled [him], one should remove the water from the limbs with a cloth using the hymn "Agnirmūrdhā."

Having offered a garment with the Viṣṇu-Gāyatrī and the sacred thread (*yajñopavīta*) and upper cloth (*uttarīya*) with "Oṃ," and having worshipped him with the *arghya*, water for the feet (*pādya*), and other offerings; having given sandals as before for the purpose of the seat for adornment; having meditated upon the seat for adornment; and having worshipped it as before with the *arghya* and other offerings; [he should then] dry the damp hair with agallochum incense while reciting "Oṃ mūrdhānaṃ divaḥ."

Having anointed [the deity] with sandalwood paste while reciting the mantra *gandhadhvāra*, I offer divine-scented flowers while reciting the mantra *om tad viṣṇoḥ*. I offer all ornaments while reciting the mantra *jitanta*. Having offered collyrium while reciting the Viṣṇu-Gāyatrī, I invoke the presiding deity of the mirror, *oṃ śrī mahālakṣmyai namaḥ*, and offer the mirror while reciting the Vyāhṛtis. I worship the presiding deity of the incense vessel, *oṃ pāvakāya namaḥ*.

Having displayed the incense mudrā, one offers incense at the nose of the deity with the mantra *jitanta*. Then, having displayed the lamp mudrā for the presiding deity of the lamp, Bhāskara, with the words "Obeisance to Bhāskara," and having displayed the lamp before the eyes of the deity with "Om, shine forth (*uddīpyasva*"), one should offer sesame, cloth, gold, betel leaf, rice, fruits, the cow-product oblation (*gavyāghāra*), cows, grain, and whatever wealth is available. Having thus performed the offering of the materials, one should give a mouthful of grass to the cow in the presence of the deity, as it is said: "One should give [these] to the preceptor in the presence of the deity."

Having removed the curtain, having sounded musical instruments, and having caused the recitation of Vedic hymns and praises to be performed, he should perform the *nīrājana* rite for the Deity. Having worshipped with the mantra: "Oṃ, obeisance to the presiding deity of the *nīrājana*, Oṃ Svadhā," and having offered [the oblation], he should offer the seat for the meal to the Deity's meal-seat as before, having placed the sandals there. Having visualized the Deity seated upon the meal-seat, he should worship Him as before with the *arghya* and other offerings, present the *madhuparka*, and offer betel-leaf with the syllable *praṇava*.

One should present the prepared sacrificial offering (*havis*), consisting of various foods to be eaten and chewed, endowed with sweet and other flavors, as prescribed by the rules and prepared with great concentration. It may be prepared with unrefined grains or combined with other items such as fruits; one should arrange these appropriately, including both undercooked and overcooked varieties. Thus, having sprinkled the materials for the offering (*naivedya*) with the *astra-mantra* and having consecrated them by sprinkling with the *sarva-mantra*, [one prepares] the water for honoring (*arhaṇāmbu*), which is filled with cool water, mixed with cardamom and camphor, or lukewarm and scented.

Having said this and responded with "Om," he should offer the respectful salutation (*argha*). Having performed the burning and nourishing of the food offering (*naivedya*), and having displayed the *surabhi* mudrā, he should take a flower from the *arghya* water and offer it into the hand of Viṣṇu. Then, placing his right knee on the ground and raising his left knee, while being supported by the left hand, he should—with his right hand displaying the *grāsa* (mouthful) mudrā—offer the food offering as prescribed into the right hand of the Deity, reciting the mantra "devasya tvā."

Then, having offered a refreshing drink (*pānaka*) and water for drinking (*pānīya*), and having given the water for sipping (*ācamana*), one should offer betel-leaf (*tāmbūla*). In the case of the ritual image (*karmārcā*), one should perform everything that has been prescribed for the *dhruvaberā* and so forth. However, in the case of the *bahuberā*, one should invoke Śrī and Bhūmi: "Oṃ, obeisance to Śrī" for Śrī, and "Bhūṃ, obeisance to Bhūmi" for Bhūmi. Having offered a lotus-seat (*padmāsana*) and performed the six-limbed ritual placement (*ṣaḍaṅganyāsa*) with their respective mantras, one should display the lotus-gesture (*kamalamudrā*).

One should offer everything else, from the *arghya* to the *naivedya*, with their respective mantras. Thereafter, having praised the deity and recited the twelve-syllable mantra or another mantra the prescribed number of times, one should worship the deity in the fire according to the procedure to be described. Having performed the offering of the *bali* to the spirits and the daily festival (*nityotsava*), and having informed the Lord of Devas and prostrated, the officiant himself should take up the remaining articles of worship.

For the sake of pleasing the deity, one should perform self-worship by means of those [offerings]. Thus ends the twenty-eighth chapter in the *Kriyākairavacandrikā* composed by the venerable Varāhaguru. Chapter Twenty-nine:
The Procedure for the Fire-Rite (*Agnikāryavidhi*).
Now the procedure for the fire-ritual (*agnikārya*) is described.

At the door of the fire-chamber, the preceptor (*ācārya*), having worshipped with "Oṃ Śrauṃ, obeisance to Caṇḍa" and "Priṃ, obeisance to Pracaṇḍa," and in the center with "Oṃ Kṣaṃ, obeisance to Garuḍa," enters within. Sitting on a seat facing east in the western part of the fire-pit (*agni-kuṇḍa*), he performs the sweeping and smearing of the pit with the mantra: "Oṃ, to the weapon that is the discus which ends the Asuras, svāhā; Phaṭ! It is declared that the head is in the east and the pair of arms is situated [there].

The two shanks are in the northeast and southeast corners; the belly is said to be the pit (*kuṇḍa*), and the womb (*yoni*) is prescribed as the [central] womb. Having thus meditated upon the pit, one should make the formal resolve (*saṅkalpa*): "I shall perform the fire-oblation (*homa*). Then, having caused the declaration of an auspicious day (*puṇyāha-vācana*) to be recited, and having performed the sprinkling (*prokṣaṇa*), the pouring down (*avokṣaṇa*), and the sprinkling around (*abhyukṣaṇa*) with that water while reciting "Oṃ bhūr bhuvaḥ svaḥ," one should place a vessel of flowers on one's right side and other items on the left. Then, having performed the ritual placement of mantras (*nyāsa*) for each respective deity with the mantra "Oṃ ācakrāya svāhā."

Having spread six blades of *darbha* grass with their tips pointing eastward, he should place upon them—tilt-wise as far as possible—the vessel for clarified butter (*ājyapātra*), the pot for the sacrificial rice (*carusthālī*), the *prokṣaṇī* water-vessel, the *praṇītā* water-vessel, fuel-sticks (*samit*), *kuśa* grass, rice grains, the enclosing sticks (*paridhi*), the large and small ladles (*sruk-sruva*), the wooden spoon (*darvī*), the fire-shifting fan (*agnerviharaṇavyajana*), the stirring-ladle (*mekṣaṇa*), a wooden pestle, a bell, unbroken rice (*akṣata*), and fragrant substances.

In the center of the pit (*kuṇḍa*), having drawn three lines starting from the south and ending at the north, extending eastward, and likewise three lines starting from the west and ending at the east, extending northward, with the mantra *oṃ namo nārāyaṇāya*, and having discarded those fragments; having performed the circumambulation of the fire (*paryagni-karaṇa*) around the pit with handfuls of *darbha* grass; and having prepared a "Bhadra-seat" (*bhadrāsana*) in the center of the pit, one should worship it with: *oṃ bhadrāsanāya namaḥ* and *oṃ vimalāsanāya namaḥ*.

In the center of that sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa), one should likewise meditate upon Lakṣmī, adorned with all ornaments, complete in every limb, and having bathed after her menses. Having visualized the Lord Nārāyaṇa, marked by all auspicious characteristics—four-armed, large-eyed, tender, clad in yellow garments, distinguished by the four symbols of the conch, discus, mace, and lotus; with hands and feet like lotuses, his chest marked with the Śrīvatsa, resembling a dark rain-cloud, peaceful, and with a face like the orb of the moon.

Having meditated thus—[on the deity] adorned with necklaces and armlets, and graced by a diadem—and having contemplated the union of those two, one should meditate on the fire produced therefrom. Having churned the fire from fire-sticks (*araṇi*) or from a sun-crystal (*sūryakānta*), or having brought it from the house of a Vedic scholar (*śrotriya*), one should sprinkle it with the words "Bhūr Bhuvaḥ Svaḥ. Then, having meditated on the divine fire with the following: "For the seed-syllable of Agni, Kāśyapa is the seer (*ṛṣi*), Triṣṭubh is the meter (*chandas*), Agni is the deity (*devatā*); its application (*viniyoga*) is for the purpose of the oblation (*homa*). Thus, one should meditate upon the divine fire.

Having performed the six-limbed assignment (*ṣaḍaṅganyāsa*) with *oṃ rāṃ* and so forth; having cast the fuel into the fire with *oṃ ram agnaye namaḥ* and *oṃ asurānta cakrāya svāhā*; [for the seed-syllable of Vāyu]: Kiṣkindha is the seer (*ṛṣi*), Jagatī is the meter (*chanda*), Vāyu is the deity (*devatā*); the application (*viniyoga*) is for the purpose of kindling the fire. Having kindled the fire with *oṃ yaṃ vāyave namaḥ*, and having swept around it with water using the weapon-mantra (*astramantra*), one performs the six-limbed assignment with *oṃ ācakrāya svāhā*.

Having strewn around [the fire] with twenty-five *darbha* blades ending in knots—three, five, seven, nine, or eleven—pointing eastward and northward, starting from the east and ending in the north, proceeding clockwise: "Oṃ, obeisance to Vāsudeva; Oṃ, obeisance to Saṅkarṣaṇa; Oṃ, obeisance to Pradyumna; Oṃ, obeisance to Aniruddha"; then, having spread *darbha* blades pointing eastward in the middle of the sacrificial materials and the fire, and having placed the *praṇītā* water-vessel upon them, filled it with water, and honored it with unbroken rice grains (*akṣata*).

Having placed upon it a *kūrca* made of a pair of *darbha* blades and measuring a span (*prādeśa*), and having covered it with three *darbha* purifiers (*pavitra*), one should place the *prokṣaṇī* vessel in front of oneself. Having poured the water from the *praṇītā* vessel into the *prokṣaṇī* along with the *kūrca*, one should again pour the *āghāra* libation three times over its root using that *kūrca* held between the thumbs and ring fingers of both hands. Having sprinkled the *prokṣaṇī*, all the sacrificial materials, and [the sacrificer's] name-designation as appropriate with that *kūrca*, one should sprinkle them.

Having turned those vessels face upwards and sprinkled them again, he should pour out the *prokṣaṇī* water around them clockwise with the mantra, "I sprinkle you with truth," and then refill the *praṇītā* vessel with water. Into that [vessel], he should invoke [the deity] with the mantra, "Oṃ, obeisance to Vāsudeva, the bearer of the Kaumodakī mace, the conch, the discus, and the lotus," and worship him with perfumes and other offerings.

Having placed her upon a seat of *darbha* grass to the northeast of the fire; and having arranged a bundle (*kūrca*) made of twelve *darbha* blades with their tips pointing eastward upon *darbha* grass to the south of the fire; one should meditate upon Brahmā therein as golden-hued, four-faced, possessing two arms, holding a rosary, a water-pot, and a spear. Having thus meditated: "Oṃ kaṃ, obeisance to Brahmā," one should invoke him onto the bundle, meditate upon him, and worship him. Then, having washed the cooking vessel (*sthālī*) with the Viṣṇu-Gāyatrī mantra.

Having placed one *āḍhaka* measure of rice grains into it with the mantra “Oṃ ācakrāya svāhā,” having rinsed it with pure water with “Oṃ vicakrāya svāhā,” having purified it with “Oṃ sucakrāya svāhā,” having placed it upon the fire with “Oṃ sūryacakrāya svāhā,” having kindled the fire with “Oṃ jvālācakrāya svāhā,” and having cooked it with “Oṃ mahāsudarśanacakrāya svāhā.”

In this manner, having cooked the four kinds of food—consisting of plain rice, mung-bean rice, milk-rice, jaggery-rice, and so forth—in the kitchen on the stove, and having set them down to the north of the fire; having placed a vessel for clarified butter (ājya) in front of oneself; having poured the melted and strained clarified butter into that butter-vessel while reciting the mantra: “Oṃ aṃ, obeisance to Viṣṇu; Oṃ, may you swell together, O Soma, with strength from every side; be present at the gathering of nourishment”; and having spread darbha grass with tips pointing eastward to the north of the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa);

Having removed the embers from them, having placed the vessel of clarified butter (*ājyapātra*) upon them, having kindled *darbha* grass and shown it, and then discarded it; having covered [the vessel] with three *darbha* blades and placed a *kūrca* (a bundle) made of a pair of *darbha* blades measuring a span (*prādeśa*); and having again kindled *darbha* grass and shown it, one says: "I take refuge in the feet of the glorious Nārāyaṇa; obeisance to the glorious Nārāyaṇa."

Having cast two tips of *darbha* grass there with either the [mantra] "iti" or the root mantra (*mūla*), having performed the threefold circumambulation with a flaming bundle of *darbha*, and having released [the fire], having performed the lustration (*nīrājana*) with the two stalks of *darbha*, having taken down the vessel of clarified butter (*ājyasthālī*) toward the north, and having united the embers with the fire, having placed the vessel of clarified butter in front, having purified it three times with the root mantra using two northward-pointed *pavitra* strainers held between the thumb and ring finger, having untied the knot of the *pavitra*, and having touched water—

Having offered fragrant clarified butter (*ājya*) into the fire, having rendered it nectar-like by means of the *amṛtī-karaṇa* mudrā, and having displayed the *cakra-mudrā*, one should cover [the offering] with *darbha* grass. Having invoked Indra and the other deities in the eight directions of the fire and worshipped them, one should wash the *sruk* and *sruva* ladles with warm water. Then, using a bundle of five *darbha* blades (*pañca-kṛta-kūrca*), one should cleanse the base of the *sruk* and *sruva* with the base, the middle with the middle, and the tip with the tip, while reciting the *astra-mantra*. Finally, one should heat them in the fire and sprinkle them with water.

Having placed the *sruk* and *sruva* ladles to the north of himself, having untied the knot of the *kūrca* grass mat and cast it into the fire, and having taken clarified butter with the *sruva* and sprinkled it over the sacrificial materials, he should then establish the three enclosing sticks (*paridhi*) in sequence with the mantras of Śrīdhara, Nṛsiṃha, and Hayagrīva: one in the west of the pit, equal in length to the width of the pit and tied at the thumb-width; one to the south, one finger shorter than that and tied at the middle finger-width; and one to the north, one finger shorter than that and tied at the little finger-width.

Having touched the middle enclosing-stick (*paridhi*) with the *praṇava* (Oṃ), and having placed the two *āghāra* fuel-sticks in the south-eastern and north-eastern corners with the two mantras addressed to Agni and Īśāna, he sprinkles water all around from the south to the north, ending with the words: "Oṃ, Aditi, give your consent! O Anumati, give your consent! O Sarasvatī, give your consent! O God Savitṛ, impel [the sacrifice]! (*oṃ aditenumanyasva | anumate numanyasva | oṃ sarasvatenumanyasva | devasavitaḥ prasuva*).

Having placed the *anuyāja* fuel-stick (*samidh*) and the *praṇītā* water-vessel at the mouth [of the fire], one should offer fifteen fuel-sticks smeared with cow’s ghee all at once from one side, using the *muṣṭi-mudrā*, while mentally meditating upon Prajāpati and reciting the root mantra once. Then, having placed the vessel of ghee upon the palm of the left hand which is encircled by a bundle of *kuśa* grass, one offers the first oblation from the southwest to the northeast with "Oṃ, to Prajāpati, this is not mine," and the second from the northwest to the southeast with "Oṃ, to Indra, this is not mine. Having thus performed the *āghāra* libations:

Then, in the fire, to the north: *oṃ agnaye svāhā*, "To Agni, this [is] not mine. To the south: *oṃ somāya svāhā*, "To Soma, this [is] not mine. Having offered oblations in the center with the *vyāhṛtis* beginning with *bhūḥ*, one should thereafter meditate upon Agni as having two heads, seven hands, three feet, and seven tongues; granting boons, holding a spear in his hand, and likewise bearing a *sruk* and *sruva* ladle; bestowing fearlessness and holding a shield, while in his left hand he holds clarified butter (*ājya*); and as being Kālī, Karālī, Sumanā, Lohitā, and Dhūmrā.

Sphuliṅginī, Viśvarūpā, and Saptajihvā are proclaimed [as the tongues of fire]. Kālī’s place is in the center; Karālī’s is in the eastern direction. Manojava’s is in the southeast (Āgneyī), while Lohitā’s is in the west (Vāruṇa). Sudhūmrā resides in the north (Soma), Sphuliṅginī has the northwest (Anila) as her abode, and Viśvarūpī is in the northeast (Aiśānī); thus one should remember their positions in sequence. On the tongue in the southern mouth, with Dhūmrā, rites such as killing (māraṇa) are performed; with Lohitā, subjugation (vaśīkāra); and with Kālī, the rite of pacification (śāntika).

All accomplishments (*sarvasiddhi*) reside in *Sphuliṅginī*, located in the left face; in *Viśvarūparasajñā* resides the great fruit of the powers such as *aṇimā*. *Karālikā* bestows victory, and *Manojavā* bestows nourishment. Their colors are blackness, redness, and dark green respectively. Then, the color resembling sparks is like crystal, and that resembling molten gold is declared to be the sequence of colors for the tongues. Having thus meditated upon the "Child-Fire" (*bālāgni*).

The Fire of the Festival (Utsavāgni) has three eyes, five faces, and is red in color; he has ten arms, three girdles, and three feet, and is endowed with seven tongues. He is invested with the sacred thread (upavīta) and adorned with a crown of matted hair. In his right hands, he holds a discus, an axe, a sword, a thunderbolt, and the gesture of granting fearlessness (abhaya); in his left hands, he holds a chisel, a noose, a lotus, a discus, and the gesture of granting boons (varada). On his right side is Svāhā, and likewise on his left is Svadhā. [His consorts] are Hiraṇyā, Kanakā, Ākārā, Kṛṣṇā, and Suprabhā.

The *atirikta*, *bahurūpa*, and *saptajihva* fires are thus proclaimed. For the rite of festival (*utsava*), one should meditate upon the Youthful Fire (*yauvanāgni*) as mounted upon a ram. Having thus meditated upon the Festival Fire, one should then begin with the Eternal Fire (*nityāgni*): four-armed, three-eyed, single-faced, and bearing matted locks; holding a trident and an axe in his hands, endowed with the gestures of granting fearlessness and boons; possessed of seven tongues, wearing a sacred thread and an upper garment, seated upon a ram, white in color—this is the Elder Fire (*vṛddhāgni*) for the eternal rite. The Fire of Initiation (*dīkṣā*), Peace (*śānti*), and Installation (*pratiṣṭhā*) is designated as the Child (*bāla*).

Having thus meditated upon the fire in accordance with each respective rite and having worshipped it in this manner, one should thereafter offer sesame seeds mixed with *āghāra* ghee one hundred and eight times with the twelve-syllable mantra, in order to pacify any defects that may have arisen in the fire. Among these [rites], regarding Kālī, one should form the resolve: "I shall consecrate the fire through the rites beginning with *garbhādhāna*," and then sprinkle water around it with the mantra beginning with "O Aditi, grant your permission."

Thus, having performed the rites of conception (*garbhādāna*), the male-ensuring rite (*pumsavana*), the parting of the hair (*sīmantonnayana*), the birth-rite (*jātakarma*), naming (*nāmakaraṇa*), the first feeding (*annaprāśana*), tonsure (*caula*), initiation (*upanayana*), and the offerings to Prajāpati, Soma, Viṣṇu, and Śukra; as well as the gift of the cow (*godāna*), the entering of the secret doctrine (*upaniṣatkramaṇa*), the return home (*samāvartana*), and marriage—each preceded by the formal resolve (*saṃkalpa*) and accompanied by the sprinkling of water (*pariṣecana*) and oblations (*huta*); one should offer fuel-sticks (*samidh*) at dawn with the root mantra, clarified butter (*ājya*) with the syllable *Oṃ* (*praṇava*) during the *manojavā* [offering], and food (*anna*) with the Vāsudeva mantra during the *sulohitā* [offering].

In the Sudhūmrā fire, one should offer parched rice (*lāja*) with the *Saṅkarṣaṇa* mantra; in the Sphuliṅginī fire, sesame seeds (*tila*) with the *Pradyumna* mantra; and in the Viśvarūpā fire, green gram (*mudga*) with the *Aniruddha* mantra. Having thus offered sixteen oblations for each, one should then mentally conceive a *yogapīṭha* (yoga-seat) in the center of the fire. Having offered oblations once with clarified butter (*ājya*) using the respective mantras from *Ādhāraśakti* to the lotus (*padma*), ending each with *svāhā*, one should invoke the Supreme Lord in the form of consciousness (*cidrūpa*) from the heart and meditate upon Him there.

Having offered oblations once each with clarified butter (*ājya*) using the respective mantras from the *arghya* up to the *naivedya*, and having offered once for the sake of the recitation (*japa*), one should offer with fuel-sticks (*samit*), leaves, flowers, seeds, and fruits, as well as with clarified butter, using the mantras of the retinue (*parivāra*). This is the worship in the fire (*agni*). If it is elsewhere, such as before an image (*pratimā*) and so forth, one should subsequently offer with fuel-sticks and clarified butter according to the method to be described hereafter. The sequence [of the fingers] is: the thumb (*āyāma*), ending with the fuel-stick, and the little finger (*kaniṣṭhā*) and the ring finger (*anāmikā*) in order.

If it lacks bark, there will be destruction; if it is split, the lineage will perish. Under the Ārdrā asterism, there is loss of kinsmen; under the Purātana (Purva-phalguni), loss of sons. Under the Kṣata (Uttara-phalguni) asterism, there is the death of a wife; under the Śākhi (Hasta), it leads to quarrels. A thick branch brings anxiety, while a short one causes drought. A long branch produces excessive rain; a fuel-stick possessed of such defects should be discarded.

With such [a mantra], one should offer oblations with a hundred fuel-sticks (*samidh*), half that number, a quarter, or eight or four fuel-sticks anointed with clarified butter (*ghṛta*), using the root-mantra (*mūlamantra*). One should offer sixteen oblations of the sacrificial porridge (*caru*) sprinkled with clarified butter, using either a *pālāśa* leaf or the hand, with the *nṛsūkta* and the "mouth-gesture" (*grāsamudrā*) for each portion. Furthermore, one should offer oblations of clarified butter with the *sruva* ladle according to the number of fuel-sticks. Peace and good fortune result from offerings made with flowers from sacrificial trees; constant health from incense substances; nourishment from curd; and purity from milk.

With rice, one should offer various desires; with clarified butter, long-lived progeny; and a man desiring the glory of Brahman should offer white lotuses. One desiring prosperity should offer *lakṣmī* flowers, or else those belonging to Varuṇa. One desiring knowledge should offer lotus and *bilva* fuel-sticks, or clarified butter. With parched grain, one should bewitch a maiden; with cow dung, one desiring cattle. One desiring long life should offer *dūrvā* grass; one desiring land, soil. One desiring sensory power should offer barley; one who desires to be beloved by all people, sesame seeds.

One who desires spiritual luster (brahmavarcasa) shall achieve it through offerings made with materials produced from the *brahma* tree, as well as with bamboo, barley, wild rice (*nīvāra*), and *śāli* rice; indeed, all desires are fulfilled for the sacrificer by means of these seeds as prescribed. All desires are accomplished without doubt by the oblation of parched grain (*lāja*). One desiring food obtains it through cooked rice; one desiring a son, through milk-rice (*pāyasa*); one seeking gold, through *nimba* flowers; and all desires are fulfilled through clarified butter (*sarpiṣ*). In the fire-oblation, there should be streams of clarified butter, honey, and milk, four finger-breadths in width.

An offering of oyster-shell is an oblation of curd; an oblation of a mouthful consists of milk-rice and clarified butter. An oblation of edible food should be half of that [in size], while an oblation of unbroken fruits and flowers should be the measure of a *niṣpāva* seed. An oblation of incense substances should be the measure of a sesame seed. Oblations of sesame, rice, barley, and so forth, should be offered in succession at the measure of half of half a handful (*muṣṭi*). A fuel-stick (*samidh*) or *dūrvā* grass should be eight finger-breadths long, or half of that; alternatively, it may be six finger-breadths long. An oblation of cow-dung is desired at the measure of a grape or an *akṣa* berry. O Four-faced One, a full oblation (*pūrṇāhuti*) of clarified butter should be one *kuḍupa*.

The Dānavas and Daityas consume the oblations for the gods (havya) and the ancestors (kavya) in sequence according to deficient or excessive measures; thus it becomes fruitless. Thereafter, having meditated upon the Supreme Person within the fire and worshipped Him with water for the hands (arghya) and other offerings, one should cast a ball of sacrificial porridge (caru-piṇḍa), the size of a hen’s egg and soaked in ghee, into the whorl of the large ladle (sruc). Having sprinkled it with the small ladle (sruva), and having drawn up fuel-sticks, darbha grass, and flowers as far as the nose, one should offer them into the fire while reciting the root mantra.

Having performed the peace-offering (*śāntihoma*) with clarified butter (*ājya*) according to one's capacity using the five *upaniṣan-mantras*: *Oṃ ṣauṃ namaḥ parāya parameṣṭhyātmane vāsudevāya svāhā.* *Oṃ yāṃ namaḥ parāya puruṣātmane saṅkarṣaṇāya svāhā.* *Oṃ rāṃ namaḥ parāya viśvātmane pradyumnāya svāhā.* *Oṃ vāṃ namaḥ parāya nivṛttyātmane aniruddhāya svāhā.* *Oṃ lāṃ namaḥ parāya sarvātmane śrīmate nārāyaṇāya svāhā.* [Then] fill the *sruva* ladle with clarified butter.

Having covered the sacrificial grass (*sadarbha*) along with the fuel-sticks (*samit*) and flowers with the *sruva* ladle, and having lifted them up as far as the tip of the nose, he should offer them into the fire while reciting the root mantra (*mūlamantra*). Thereafter, placing the *sruva* before himself, the vessel of clarified butter (*ājyasthālī*) to her [the consort’s] right, and the *sruc* ladle to the north of the *sruva*, he should take all the used *kuśa* grasses with both hands, holding them with their tips pointing northward. Having touched the roots to the clarified butter vessel, the middle parts to the middle of the *sruc*, and the tips to the cavity of the *sruc* in due order, he should do this three times. Then, he should cast the *darbha* grasses into the fire.

Having offered the after-offerings (*anūyāja*), the enclosing sticks (*paridhi*), and the fuel-sticks (*samidh*) in sequence, he sprinkles water around the fire with the mantra: *adite 'nvamam̐sthāḥ*. Having established the *praṇītā* vessel in front of himself, having poured the *prokṣaṇī* water into it, and having sprinkled water from the east to the end of the north (the Soma direction), he pours it out in the west. Having sprinkled himself, he dismisses the Brahman priest, sprinkles water around the fire once more, and consigns the deity residing in the middle of the fire into his own heart. He then fills the *sruva* ladle with water.

Having sprinkled [the water] outside the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) in a clockwise direction, having sprinkled oneself with the remainder, having made a tilaka mark on the head with ashes, and having worshipped the Deity in the shrine with offerings such as *arghya* and so forth, one should offer the oblation at the feet of the Deity with the mantra: "O Supreme Lord, accept this worship of Yours which has been performed with devotion in the fire according to my capacity and according to the rules. In the case of daily homas, one should not place the enclosing sticks (*paridhis*) in the outer directions. Having thus performed the oblation previously...

Thereafter, one should perform the daily festival (nityotsava). Thus ends the twenty-ninth chapter, titled "The Procedure for Fire-rites," in the *Kriyākairavacandrikā* composed by the venerable Varāhaguru. The Thirtieth Chapter: Now begins the procedure for the daily festival.
Now, the procedure for the daily festival (nityotsava) is described.

After the worship of the fire, one should fill a vessel made of gold, silver, or copper with pure rice grains. Having drawn a twelve-petaled lotus and placed it before the ritual image (karmārcā), one should invoke the Lord from the root-mantra into that [vessel] by means of the root-mantra. Then, having invoked the twelve Śaktis beginning with Śrīvatsā and the forms (mūrtis) beginning with Viṣṇu upon its petals in the order starting from the east, one should perform a circumambulation at length in the morning of the day. At midday, however, one should do so likewise with food offerings.

Having performed this with clusters of flowers in the evening, one should circumambulate with them. Likewise, at the three junctions of the day (*trisandhya*), having invoked the deity into rice-flour images, one should offer the sacrificial oblation (*bali*) with three [portions]. Alternatively, one should perform the daily festival (*nityotsava*) for Hari with food at the three junctions, or twice a day, or once a day, using an image. Or, having circumambulated for all purposes at midday, one should cast the oblation; or the oblation may be placed before the festival image.

At the three junctions of the day (trisandhya), having prepared as before either rice and other grains or food alone, accompanied by parasols, chowries, and so forth; and having offered the *bali* offering within the five enclosures—that is, in the fivefold sanctuary—together with that [food]; then, preceded by song and instrumental music, the procession constitutes the superior festival (*utkṛṣṭotsava*). That which lacks one time-period is middling (*madhyama*); that which lacks two time-periods is inferior (*adhama*); and that which lacks all three time-periods is trivial (*kṣudra*). Without the offering of the *bali*, the festival does not bring about prosperity.

In the event of disturbances such as great winds and the like, one should not perform the perpetual festival (*nityotsava*). Alternatively, having offered only the oblation (*bali*) to Caṇḍa and Pracaṇḍa, one should cast the offering right there, saying: "Salutation to all the attendants (*pārṣada*) of Śrī Viṣṇu. Then, having summoned an attendant who is pure, wearing white garments, adorned with all ornaments, and conceived as being of the nature of Garuḍa, and having placed upon his head the vessel carried according to the previously mentioned rite—equipped with hymns of praise, a banner, chowries, and the vehicle (*cakravāhana*)—one should proceed.

Preceded by all musical instruments, song, and dance, one should offer the *bali* according to the prescribed rite, preceded by song, rhythm, and dance for Caṇḍa and the others: “Oṃ croṃ, salutation to Caṇḍa; I give the *bali*. Oṃ pṛṃ, salutation to Pracaṇḍa; I give the *bali*.”

After offering perfumes, flowers, incense, lamps, and sacrificial oblations (bali) to all the gatekeepers stationed from Caṇḍa and Pracaṇḍa in the first enclosure up to the fifth enclosure, one should display the dances of Mallatāla, the Ṛṣabha scale, and the Vaijayantī. Then, having offered a bali to Sūrya and Candramas at the northern hall of the main gate (gopura):

With the *dhaivata* note and the *bhadratala* rhythm, after offering oblations (*bali*) to all those residing in the hall, one performs the *sarvamaṅgala-nṛtta* for Kāma among the deities of the first enclosure; then, in the southern direction, having offered [the oblation] with the words: "Oṃ, salutation to Brahmā, together with his goddess, vehicle, and retinue; I give this oblation."

In the northeast, for Brahmā: *brahmatāla*, middle note (*madhyama-svara*), *megharañjanī* rāga, and the *sarvamaṅgala* dance; in the southwest (*nairṛta*), for Gajānana: *bhadratāla*, fifth note (*pañcama-svara*), *varāṭī* rāga, and the elephant dance (*hastinṛtta*); in the west (*vāruṇī*), for Ṣaṇmukha: *bhadratāla*, sixth note (*dhaivata-svara*), and the *sarvamaṅgala* dance; in the northwest (*vāyu*) for Durgā, and likewise in the north (*saumya*) for Dhanādhipati: *bhadratāla*, seventh note (*niṣadha-svara*), *takkeśī* rāga, and the *pṛṣṭakuṭṭima* dance; and in the northeast (*aiśāna*), for Īśa: *oṃ īśāya*.

The *ḍhakkarī* rhythm with the *dhaivata* note and the *śālāpāṇi* melody; the dance performed with the left knee raised; the *madhyama* note for Garuḍa and the *garuḍagāndhāra* melody with the *garuḍa* rhythm; the *viṣṇukrānta* dance; the *balitāla* rhythm for Viṣvaksena, the *ṛṣabha* note, the *varāṭī* melody, and the *svastika* dance. This [sequence] pertains exclusively to the single enclosure (*ekāvaraṇa*).

In the inner chamber of the first enclosure named Antarmaṇḍala, within the northern hall of the gateway: *Oṃ* to Puruṣa; to the south, *Oṃ* to Acyuta. [The following] are as previously described, beginning with the *tāla* (rhythmic beat). In the southeast (*āgneya*), *Oṃ* to Hayagrīva: *baddhāvatāla*, the *ṛṣabha* note, the *kollira* melody, and the *sarvatobhadra* dance. To the south (*yāmyā*), *Oṃ* to Saṃkarṣaṇa: the *gāndhāra* note, the *kauśika* melody, the *bhṛṅgiṇī* *tāla*, and the *bheṭaka* dance.

In the southwest: Oṃ to Varāha; the middle note (madhyama-svara), Naṭṭa rāga, Jayatāla, and the Cakramaṇḍala dance. In the west: Oṃ to Pradyumna; the fifth note (pañcama-svara), Śrī rāga, Sama tāla, and the Kāntāra dance. In the northwest: Oṃ to Ananta; the sixth note (dhaivata-svara), Kāmada rāga, Jayatāla, and the Kuṭṭima dance. In the north: Oṃ to Aniruddha; the Niṣadha note, Takkeśi rāga, Bhadratāla, and the Pṛṣṭakuṭṭima dance.

In the northeast (Aiśāna): *Oṃ* to Nṛsiṃha; the Dhaivata note, Gāndhāra rāga, Ḍhakkarī tāla, and the Kaṭibandhana dance. In the courtyard, at the locations of the pedestals for Indra and the others: in the east, *Oṃ* to the Holder of the Discus (Cakrin); the Ṣaḍja note, Gāndhāra rāga, Sama tāla, and the Vilāsa dance. In the southeast (Āgneya): *Oṃ* to the Holder of the Mace (Musalin); the Ṛṣabha note, Kollarī rāga, Baddhāva tāla, and the Sarvatobhadra dance. In the south (Yāmyā): *Oṃ* to the Holder of the Conch (Śaṅkhin); the Gāndhāra note, Kauśika rāga, Bhṛṅgiṇī tāla, and the Kheṭaka dance.

In the southwest: *Oṃ* to Khaḍgin, with the middle note (*madhyama-svara*), the Naṭṭabhaṣa rāga, the Mallatāla rhythm, and the *cakramaṇḍala-nṛtta* dance. In the west: *Oṃ* to Gadin, with the fifth note (*pañcama-svara*), the Śrīkāma rāga, the Maṅgalatāla rhythm, and the *kāntāra-nṛtta* dance. In the northwest: *Oṃ* to Śārṅgin, with the *kuṭṭima-nṛtta* dance, the *dhaivata* note, the Takkeśi rāga, and the Jaya tāla. In the north: *Oṃ* to Padmin, with the *pṛṣṭakuṭṭima-nṛtta* dance, the *niṣāda* note, the Dakṣa rāga, and the Bhadratāla rhythm.

In the northeast: *Oṃ Vajrine*. The dance is performed with the left knee raised; the musical note is *dhaivata*; the melody is *Śālāpāṇi*; the rhythm is *Ḍhakkarīta*. In the second enclosure, named Antarhāra, the deities beginning with Sūrya have already been described previously. In the eastern courtyard: *Oṃ Indrāya surādhipataye sadevīvāhanaparivārāya namaḥ*.

I offer the *bali* with equal rhythm (*samatāla*), the *ṣaḍja* note, the *gāndhāra* melody, and the *vilāsa* dance, to Agni in the southeast: *oṃ agnaye namaḥ*. With the *baddhāva* rhythm, the *ṛṣabha* note, the *kollira* melody, and the *subhadra* dance, to Nairṛti in the southwest: *oṃ nairṛtaye namaḥ*. With the *malla* rhythm, the *madhyama* note, the *naṭṭabhāṣā* melody, and the *cakramaṇḍala* dance, to Varuṇa in the west: *oṃ varuṇāya namaḥ*. With the *maṅgala* rhythm, the *pañcama* note, the *kāmadara* melody, and the *kāntāra* dance, to Vāyu in the northwest: *oṃ vāyave namaḥ*. [And] the *kuṭṭima* dance, the *dhaivata* note...

In the north (Saumya), for Oṃ Kubera: Pṛṣṭakuṭṭima dance, Niṣadha note, Dakṣa rāga, and Bhadratāla. In the northeast (Aiśāna), for Oṃ Īśāna: Vāmajānūrdhva dance, Dhaivata note, Śālāpāṇi rāga, and Ḍhakkarī tāla. In the third enclosure, named the Inner Necklace, for the door-keepers beginning with Dhātṛ and the twelve Ādityas: Bhadratāla, Dhaivata note, and Sarvamaṅgala dance.

Between Agni and Yama dwell the Vasus; between Yama and Nirṛti, the hosts of Pitṛs; between Nirṛti and Varuṇa, the Viśvedevas; between Varuṇa and Vāyu, the seven Maruts; between Vāyu and Kubera, the seven Ṛṣis; and between Kubera and Īśāna, the eleven Rudras. There is the Bhadratala rhythm and the Dhaivata note, along with the Sarvamaṅgala dance; in that courtyard are Kumuda and the others, whose rhythmic patterns, melodies, and dances have been described.

At the boundary are the gatekeepers, beginning with Durjaya; the deities of the enclosures are as follows: in the east, the Sādhyas; in the southeast, the nine planets; in the south, the Aṅgirasas; in the southwest, the two Aśvins; in the west, Lakṣmī, Sarasvatī, and Vighneśa; in the northwest, Indra and the others ending with Īśāna; in the north, the groups of deities of the site (Vāstu) beginning with Brahmā; and in the northeast, the twenty-seven lunar mansions (nakṣatras).

For them, the rhythmic measures (*tāla*) are Bhadratala and Dhaivata-svara; their auspicious dances are all *sarvamaṅgala* dances; and in the courtyard are Upendra and others, whose *tāla* and other attributes are like those of Indra and the other deities. In the fifth enclosure named Mahāmaryādā, the gatekeepers are Kumuda and others, whose *tāla* and other attributes have been described.

As for the deities of the enclosure: in the east are the Siddhas, Ṛṣis, and Nāgas; in the southeast, the Asuras; in the south, the Rākṣasas; in the southwest, the Yakṣas and Vidyādharas; in the west, the Saurabheyīs, Guhyakas, and Gandharvas; in the northwest, the Apsarases; in the north, the Prājāpatyas and humans; and in the northeast, the Adhirohiṇīs. For these, the musical rhythm (*tāla*) is *dhaivata*, and there is a dance of all auspicious types (*sarvamaṅgalanṛtta*). In the courtyard, upon the pedestals starting with Indra, are Viśveśa and the others. Their rhythms, melodies, and dances are like those of Indra and the other guardians.

In this manner, having offered the oblation (bali) alone at all the enclosures starting from the first, one should circumambulate the altar for the sake of the oblation; then, having entered the temple and circumambulated it, one should enter within, offer the *arghya*, and present [the offering] to the principal image (*mūlabera*) with the root mantra. Having placed a small portion of the remaining oblation on the head of Viṣvaksena, one should deposit the rest of the unbroken rice (*akṣata*) and other materials upon the oblation altar (*balipīṭha*).

During the perpetual festival (*nityotsava*), one should carry that image upon a palanquin or similar vehicle, or upon the head of an attendant, and perform a circumambulation. At that time, one should conduct the festival there, joined with various dances such as the *vilāsa* and *kartarī*, and crowded with flowers, water-vessels, umbrellas, chowries, all musical instruments, all songs, the chanting of the Vedas (*brahmaghoṣa*), and many lamps. Having displayed the eight auspicious marks (*aṣṭamaṅgala*) such as the *śrīvatsa* on that image, and having offered oblations (*bali*) to all [the deities] in the very presence of the Lord;

One should offer betel leaves with *pṛthukā* (puffed rice) and other items as the food offering (*naivedya*) within the enclosures. Having emerged through the gate of the rampart accompanied only by the sound of a conch, one should place the deity facing the temple in front of the sacrificial pedestal (*balipīṭha*). While musical instruments resound in all directions around the pedestal, the preceptor, having washed the pedestal and worshipped the attendants (*pārṣada*) of Viṣṇu upon it, should present the sacrificial offering (*bali*) there in its entirety. Then, having circumambulated the pedestal and entered the interior of the temple, [he should proceed].

Having placed the sandals of the Lord in the portico, having caused [the deity] to descend from the vehicle and other conveyances, having seated the Lord facing east upon a seat, having worshipped Him with the *arghya* and other offerings, and having presented the offerings and other items appropriate for the occasion, one should enter the inner sanctum (*garbhagṛha*). Having displayed the pure *tāṇḍava* dance in order to rectify any deficiencies in the singing, instrumental music, and dancing on the grounds of the outer courtyard, one should offer the Lord back to His primary location with the root mantra. Then, having prostrated, praised, and circumambulated [Him].

Having entered one’s own residence, one should worship the deity for one’s own purpose. Some maintain that the worship for one’s own purpose must come first. Thus ends the thirtieth chapter, titled "The Procedure for the Daily Festival," in the *Kriyākairavacandrikā* composed by the venerable Varāhaguru. The Thirty-first Chapter: The Procedure for the Bathing Ceremony (*Snapanavidhi*).

Now, the procedure for the ritual bathing (snapana) is described. A ritual bath performed on the equinoxes, solstices, eclipses, the two solstices, the twelfth lunar day (dvādaśī), the Śravaṇa constellation, the three days of the performer’s birth, the three specific lunar days (tithis), the Vyatīpāta yoga, Rohiṇī, the new moon (darśa), the full moon (paurṇamāsī), Punarvasu, and on auspicious lunar days such as the fifth (pañcamī), as well as under favorable asterisms and weekdays, is considered a "pure" (kevala) bath. In rites such as consecration (pratiṣṭhā) or festivals (utsava), the bath is an ancillary part of the ritual (karmāṅga). For an ancillary rite, one should perform the sowing of seeds (aṅkurārpaṇa), the night-rite (niśā), the powder-bath (cūrṇa-snapana), and so forth. In the case of a pure (kevala) bath, one should perform everything together with the worship of the four stations (catusthānārcana).

On the day preceding that, the preceptor should perform the preliminary consecration (*adhivāsa*) for the deity, preceded by the ritual of the sprouts (*aṅkura*) and the protective thread (*pratisara*), either immediately or on the previous day. As for the preliminary consecration, it should be performed upon the bathing image (*snapanapratimā*) or a representation of a sacred ford (*tīrthapratikṛti*). In the absence of these, one should perform the preliminary consecration upon the festival image (*utsavabimba*), the offering image (*balibimba*), the ritual image (*karmārcā*), or the *kūrca* grass-bundle and so forth; or, in the case of images made of plaster, clay, or those situated on a wall or depicted on a cloth, one should perform the preliminary consecration upon a mirror accompanied by a *kūrca*.

For the purpose of the ceremonial bath, one should have a pavilion constructed in front of the temple on all the surrounding grounds and in every direction, as space permits, adorned with four gates, four archways, pillars, enclosures, canopies, strings of pearls, full water-jars, *darbha* grass garlands, and so forth; the pavilion should be ten cubits wide and twice that length. Then, having divided that pavilion—either the one previously prepared or this one—into three parts:

In the western third portion, having constructed a square altar (*vedikā*) four cubits in width, made of stone or other materials, and provided with a staircase and so forth; upon that, one should fashion a circular or square rim (*valaya*) measuring one span in width and raised by eight, four, or two finger-breadths, which should be equal in height to the base of the altar and extend from the trench to the earth. In the case of images made of clay and the like, this arrangement is made outside the altar; however, when there is only a single image (*ekabera*), the bathing and the construction of the altar are not performed externally.

Having prescribed that "one should not construct archways and the like for the bathing of the domestic image," one should smear [the area] with cow dung. Having adorned it with lime powder, unbroken rice, sprouts of *dūrvā* grass, lamps, and earthen vessels containing sprouts, one should place in its northeast corner water-vessels such as wooden troughs filled with strained substances and fragrant water. On the ground to the south of the altar, one should arrange a vessel for the preliminary bath (*upasnāna*) along with its lid, consecrated with the hymns beginning with *pavamāna*.

The ritual materials for worship, beginning with the *arghya* and ending with the lamp, as well as those required for the ablution, [are arranged]. Thereafter, at the front of the altar (*vedikā*), one performs the procedure for the low and high ablutions: having stretched fourteen threads moistened with sandalwood paste, extending both eastward and northward, one delineates within the resulting one hundred and sixty-nine squares—measuring sixteen finger-breadths in length and breadth according to the size of the grain-seat (*dhānyapīṭha*)—eighty-one locations for the pitchers, consisting of nine squares each, extending from Brahmā to Īśāna.

Having swept the remaining eighty-eight squares for the sake of the pathways, one should construct a pedestal using one *āḍhaka* of rice—or half of that—or half of that again in sesame seeds on each square; then, having placed two blades of *darbha* grass upon each of those.

Above that, one should place seventeen water-pots made of gold, silver, copper, or clay—resembling ripe bimba fruits, without cracks, resonant, free from dark spots, unbroken, free from stone-like hardness, and suitable for being filled with either a *droṇa* or half a *droṇa* of water; as well as sixty-four pots of pure water suitable for being filled with a *vāryāḍhaka*. Having wrapped them with thread while reciting "Indraṃ natvā," one should wash them with the *Viṣṇugāyatrī*.

Having prepared a seat of grain on the western portion of the ground where the water-pot (kalaśa) is to stand, the preceptor himself performs the purification of the elements (bhūtaśuddhi), causes the declaration of an auspicious day (puṇyāha-vācana) to be recited, and sprinkles [the area] with consecrated water. Having spread darbha grass upon that spot with the tips pointing either eastward or northward, he places these [deities], beginning with Brahmā and ending with Īśāna, face-downward, while uttering "Oṃ. Upon those [darbhas], he arranges three darbhas each, saying: "Oṃ ṣauṃ, obeisance to the Supreme Self, the Parameṣṭhin; obeisance."

Facing east, having sprinkled [the area] with water for the *arghya* offering while reciting: "Oṃ yāṃ, obeisance to the Supreme, obeisance to the Self of Puruṣa"; having scattered unbroken rice grains (*akṣata*) while reciting: "Oṃ rāṃ, obeisance to the Supreme, obeisance to the Universal Self (*viśvātman*"); and having turned [the vessel] face upward while reciting: "Oṃ vāṃ, obeisance to the Supreme, obeisance to the Self of Nivṛtti"; having duly prepared the fire; and having consecrated the substances for the ablution (*snāna*) with clarified butter (*ājya*) by means of the Viṣṇu-Gāyatrī.

One should fill the jars with substances for bathing, such as ghee, purified by cloths as appropriate, while reciting their respective mantras. Having lifted seventeen jars with the mantra: *oṃ lāṃ namaḥ parāya sarvātmane namaḥ*, one should fill the central jar among them—the ninth jar of the group—with a *droṇa* measure of ghee, reciting *oṃ vāsudevāya namaḥ*. Having placed it in the center and filled it with hot water of the same measure, [one proceeds].

Saying "Oṃ, obeisance to Puruṣa," [one places] a jar of ghee to the east of that [central jar]. To its southeast, one fills a jar with water containing gems by means of the nine jewels named māṇikya, padmarāga, nīla, vajra, puṣyarāga, pravāla, mauktika, marataka, and vaidūrya, saying "Oṃ, obeisance to Keśava. To its south, one fills a jar with water and various fruits named kadalī, dāḍima, cūta, āmalaka, bilva, nālikera, panasa, and mātulaṅga, saying "Oṃ, obeisance to Satya."

To the west [of that], one should place a pitcher for Nirṛti filled with ghee, along with seven types of metal—iron, gold, silver, copper, lead, tin, and bronze—each weighing one *niṣka*, while reciting: *Oṃ namo nārāyaṇāya*. To its west, one should place a pitcher containing water and cleansing substances consisting of turmeric, *sūryavartī*, *sahadevī*, *śirīṣa*, *sadābhadra*, and the tips of *kuśa* grass, each measuring one handful, while reciting: *Oṃ acyutāya namaḥ*.

For that [deity], the water-filled pitcher of the Maruts should be filled with fragrant substances—namely sandalwood, kuṣṭha, saffron, agaru, uśīra, hrībera, mountain-born [mustaka], māṃsī, and murā—each weighing one *pala*, while reciting: *oṃ mādhavāya namaḥ*. For that [deity], the water-filled pitcher of Kubera should be filled with *nīvāra*, bamboo grain, *śāli*, *priyaṅgu*, barley, *kaṅgu*, *ṣāṣṭika* rice, and wheat rice, each measuring one handful, while reciting: *oṃ anantāya namaḥ*.

Having filled the water-pitcher for the Īśāna direction with barley, bamboo, and rice—each measuring one *kuḍuba*—while reciting "Oṃ Govindāya namaḥ"; and having filled the central pitcher of the nine pitchers at the Brahma-sthāna with water, while designating it as the *pādya*, and filling it with *tulasī*, lotus, *dūrvā*, unbroken rice, *śyāmāka*, *viṣṇuparṇī*, and *bilva* leaves, along with a *pala* of sandalwood paste, while reciting "Oṃ Viṣṇave namaḥ."

Into the middle vessel of the southern group of nine, known as the *arghya*, which contains water, one should place a handful each of white mustard seeds (*siddhārtha*), unbroken rice (*akṣata*), tips of *kuśa* grass, the previously mentioned fruits, barley, sesame, sandalwood, and flowers; and with three *niṣka*s of sandalwood paste, [one should recite]: "Oṃ, obeisance to Madhusūdana.

Into the middle vessel of the western group of nine, known as the *upasparśana*, which contains water, one should place half a *pala* each of *takola*, campaka buds, camphor, nutmeg (*jātīphala*), cardamom (*elā*), cloves (*lavaṅga*), cinnamon bark (*tvak*), sandalwood, and flowers; and [one should recite]: "Oṃ, obeisance to Trivikrama."

In the center of the nine northern pitchers, one should place the pitcher known as *pañcagavya*. It should be prepared with curd doubled [in quantity] by the *āghāra* water; milk triple that amount; urine quadruple that amount; and cow-dung water quadruple that amount. One should combine the cow-products thus: cow-urine with the *Viṣṇugāyatrī*; cow-dung with the verse "gandhadvārām"; milk with "āpyāyasva"; and curd with "dadhikrāvṇo akāriṣam"; and ghee with "śukram asi. Thus one should mix the products of the cow.

Alternatively, one may use the Viṣṇu-Gāyatrī; or else: "The Parameṣṭhin is the mantra for cow dung, the Puruṣa for cow urine, the Viśva-mantra for curd, and Nivṛtti for clarified butter. For milk, the Sarva-mantra should be used, or else the eight-syllabled mantra (Aghora). Having thus combined them, and having unified all the substances with the mantra *devasya tvā*, one should prepare this Pañcagavya in the measure of one Droṇa."

Such is the proportion of the ingredients for the rite of bathing; however, in the rite of sprinkling (prokṣaṇa), all these five are equal. But in the rite of consuming (prāśana), the cow-urine is equal to the cow-dung, and the curd is twice that amount. Then the clarified butter (sarpiḥ) is four times that, and the milk is eight times the clarified butter. This is declared to be the measure for the consumption of the five products of the cow (pañcagavya). The measure of the pañcagavya is one droṇa, and the measure of the clarified butter is the same; likewise the curd, the milk, and the honey are each of that same measure.

If it should be less than half an *āḍhaka* or even one *āḍhaka*, it would be of the *āsura* type; for the bathing of the household deity, one should prepare it with at least one *prastha*. One should take the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*) in a new and auspicious earthen vessel. The *pañcagavya* of a tawny cow or an old cow is highly recommended; never that of a distressed cow, nor of one that is pregnant, nor of an aged one. One should not take the urine or the two types of dung (urine and dung) from a cow whose calf has died. Cow-dung should be taken from the ground while still warm, free from worms and other such impurities.

Having squeezed it thoroughly, one should again take the juice of the cow dung. One should take clarified butter that has been freshly heated and purified; curd that has stood for a day and night; and milk that has not been heated, from a cow ten days after giving birth. Having prepared these in this manner, [one should recite]: *oṃ vāmanāya namaḥ*.

With curd, [one should fill] the middle jar of the nine jars in the southeast with "Oṃ, obeisance to Śrīdhara"; with milk, the middle jar of the nine jars in the southwest with "Oṃ, obeisance to Hṛṣīkeśa"; with honey, the middle jar of the nine jars in the northwest with "Oṃ, obeisance to Padmanābha"; and in the northeast, the middle jar of the nine jars [should be filled] with the barks of *śamī*, *palāśa*, *khadira*, *bilva*, *aśvattha*, *vikaṅkata*, *audumbara*, and *nyagrodha*.

Having filled [the vessel] with a decoction prepared from [ingredients] measured at half a *palā*, and having consecrated it with "Oṃ, obeisance to Dāmodara," one should establish seventeen substance-pitchers (*dravya-kumbha*) with the Viṣṇu-Gāyatrī. Around the central group of nine, and around the first eight groups of nine starting from the east, one should place eight pitchers of pure water for each, consecrating them with the twelve-syllable mantra. However, if the previously mentioned substances are unavailable, or if other materials for the *pādya* are lacking, even the tips of *dūrvā* grass and mustard seeds may be used.

For the water for sipping (ācamanīya), *takola* is prescribed; for the water for sprinkling (*mārjana*), *sahadevī*; for the scented water, powdered sandalwood is desired; and for the decoction water, *aśvattha*. When there is cold water, it is used as is, but in the case of hot water, [the aforementioned herbs are added]. For jeweled water (*ratnodaka*), a single diamond (*vajra*) is used; for fruit water, a single plantain fruit; for iron-water, gold; and for unbroken rice-water, *śāli* rice grains are recommended, O Lotus-seated One. In a jar of barley-water, *vrīhi* rice is praised. If curd is unavailable, milk is used; if milk is unavailable, then curd. If honey is unavailable, clarified butter is used; if that is unavailable, honey may be used.

"In the absence of the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*), clarified butter alone is prescribed; whichever of the five products might be lacking, clarified butter should take its place. Having thus completed the filling of the substances according to these words of the Blessed One, he should strew [the ground] and place *kūrca* grass-mats—made with seven, five, or three *darbha* blades—with their tips pointing downward into the jars, and a *kūrca* made with twenty-four *darbha* blades, reaching to the ear, into the great jar (*mahākumbha*). Then, having covered it with earthen saucers while reciting the *cakramantra*:

With the mantra "yuvā suvāsāḥ," having wrapped each [image] individually with a cloth—or, if that is not possible, having wrapped all of them—around each structural division (vyūha), the preceptor, together with the image-guarding Brahmins, approaches the presence of the deity. Having raised the deity with the mantra "uttiṣṭha brahmaṇaspate," and having seated Him upon the bathing-seat altar with the mantra "bhadraṃ karṇebhiḥ," he causes an odd number of Veda-knowing Brahmins to proclaim the auspicious day (puṇyāha). After satisfying them according to his means, the Guru performs breath control (prāṇāyāma).

Having invoked and worshipped the respective deities in the erected arches, banners, and jars; having caused the triple symphony (tauryatrika) to be performed at the doors of the pavilion; having offered oblations of clarified butter into the fire previously prepared, using the root mantra as many times as there are jars; having collected the residual drops of the butter in another vessel; and having offered sixteen oblations of sacrificial porridge (caru) with the *Nṛsūkta*; one should worship the Deity with perfumes and other offerings, and perform the rite of pouring the residual drops into the jars.

Having mentally conceived the pedestal (pīṭha) beginning with the base (ādhāra) and ending with the lotus (padma) within the jars containing substances such as ghee, and having worshipped it; one should invoke [the deity] into the jar of ghee with the mantra: "Oṃ, obeisance to the Blessed One, the Supreme Self, Vāsudeva; come, come! Having worshipped and fully honored [Him] with offerings from the water for the guest (arghya) up to the betel leaf (tāmbūla); [one should proceed].

Having invoked and worshipped Puruṣottama, Acyuta, Ananta, Keśava, Nārāyaṇa, Mādhava, Govinda, Viṣṇu, Madhusūdana, Trivikrama, Vāmana, Śrīdhara, Hṛṣīkeśa, Padmanābha, and Dāmodara in sequence within jars containing warm water, fruit, cleansing materials, unbroken rice, jewels, metals, perfumes, barley, water for the feet, the *arghya* offering, water for sipping (*ācamana*), the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*), curd, milk, honey, and decoctions, and having fully honored them with offerings beginning with the *arghya* and ending with betel leaf;

Having invoked and worshipped [the deities] in all the water-pitchers with the eight-syllable mantra, one should thereafter invoke and worship them with: "Oṃ, obeisance to the Earth, the presiding deity of the grain; Oṃ, phaṭ to the Astra, the presiding deity of the *kūrca*; Oṃ, obeisance to Sudarśana, the presiding deity of the *cakrikā*; Oṃ, obeisance to Viṣṇu, the presiding deity of the garment. And for the other sacrificial materials, one should likewise invoke and worship with: "Oṃ, obeisance to Janārdana."

Having offered the *arghya* with the *Viṣṇu-gāyatrī*, the *pādya* with "trīṇi padā," the *ācamana* with "āpaḥ punantu," the tooth-cleansing stick (*dantadhāvana*) with "tad viṣṇoḥ," the tongue-scraping with the *Viṣṇu-gāyatrī*, the oil massage (*abhyaṅga*) with the *Vāmadevya*, the *āmalaka* water with "viṣṇornukaṃ," the ritual bath (*abhiṣeka*) with "nate viṣṇuḥ," and the drying cloth (*plotavastra*) with "agniḥ mūrdhā," and having given the garment and upper cloth (*uttarīya*) with the *Praṇava*; then, having worshipped again from the *arghya* up to the lamp.

Having lifted the water-pot for the feet (*pādyakumbha*), which has its cord of ritual curiosity (*kautukatantu*) severed, is adorned with flowers, and has been duly worshipped, the Preceptor (*ācārya*) takes it in his hand from the hands of the image-guardian (*mūrtipa*). Then, having sprinkled the head of the Deity with the *praṇava* using water drawn from the water-pot for the feet by means of the *kūrca* grass placed at the bottom with its tip pointing downward.

With the Viṣṇu-gāyatrī, [he offers] water for the feet (pādya); with "praviṣṇur astu," water for the guest-offering (arghya); with "na te viṣṇuḥ," water for sipping (ācamana); with "viṣṇoḥ karmāṇi," the five products of the cow (pañcagavya); with "dadhikrāvṇe," curd; with the *payovrata* Sāman, milk; with "madhu vātā," honey; with "oṣadhyaḥ," astringent decoction (kaṣāya); with "tvaṃ viṣṇuḥ," warm water; with "yāḥ phalinīḥ," water with fruit; and with the Sāvitrī, water with unbroken rice grains (akṣata).

One should perform the ritual bathing with each substance from a pitcher using its respective mantras: with the mantra *trātāram indram* using water containing gems; with the *mahāvyāhṛti* using iron-water; with *gandhadvārām* using scented water; with *śatadhāram* using barley-water; and with the *ghṛtasnāte* Sāman using clarified butter. Alternatively, one may bathe the deity with the sixteen verses of the *Puruṣasūkta*, or with the hymn *idaṃ viṣṇuḥ*, or with the twelve-syllable or six-syllable *Viṣṇugāyatrī*, or with the specific *mūrti-mantras* for each respective substance—from the water for the feet (*pādya*) up to the clarified butter—performing the bathing with each pitcher followed by the secondary bath (*upasnāna*), the upper garment (*uttarīya*), the water for honor (*arghya*), and the water for sipping (*ācamanīya*).

Having worshipped the deity with offerings ending in perfumes, flowers, incense, and lamps, and having performed the consecration; and having intermittently lifted the material jars and poured pure water from them while reciting the twelve-syllable mantra and performing the consecration; thereafter, one should fill nine, seven, five, three, or even a single jar with the powder of turmeric and rice, preceded by the rite for an auspicious day (*puṇyāha*). Having placed them upon a pedestal of grain, one should cover them with cloth, gems, metal, a tuft of *kūrca* grass, and sprouts.

There, having invoked Śrī and worshipped her, and having consecrated the deity with them using the Śrīsūkta; then, having circumambulated the Lord, bowed down, and bathed him with a thousand streams; having offered the seat for ornaments with the Praṇava; having performed worship beginning from the offering of Arghya up to the waving of lights (nīrājana); having offered rice measuring one khāri or half a droṇa; having presented the fourfold food (caturvidha-anna); and having performed the daily fire-oblation (nityahoma); then, having bowed to the comfortably seated Lord and praised him, one should pray for one's heart's desire.

The patron (*yajamāna*), having given to the preceptor (*guru*) a sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) measured at one hundred *niṣkas*, half of that to the officiating priests (*ṛtvij*), and a quarter to the attendants, Veda-reciters, and so forth, should give all the remaining wealth brought for the purpose of worship to the teacher (*ācārya*). Among these [grades], the lowest of the high (*adhamottama*) consists of these eighty-one jars, excluding the thirty-two pure water jars located in all the corners; the lowest-middle (*adhamamadhyama*) is that which is deficient by all sixty-four pure water jars.

The Ritual for the Middling-Superior Consecration (*madhyamottamasnapanavidhi*). Now, the ritual for the middling-superior consecration is described: having established the eighty-one jars as previously prescribed for the inferior-superior [consecration] in the center, one should likewise stretch out threads in the four directions outside of that; then, having cleared away the ground all around it for the sake of two rows of pathways on each side.

Among the remaining eighty-one squares, one should install nine jars; six in each of the directions starting from Indra (East) and ending with Soma (North), four in each of the corners starting from Agni (Southeast), and so on, thus having established forty-nine jars. Then, having cleared the remaining thirty-two squares for the purpose of the pathways, and having done so in the four directions, one should fill the central jar among the nine in the middle of the previously established forty-nine with molasses-water, reciting: *oṃ varāhāya namaḥ*.

In the south, for the middle one of the central nine among the forty-nine jars: "Oṃ, obeisance to Nārasiṃha," with sugarcane juice. In the west, for the middle one of the central nine among the forty-nine jars: "Oṃ, obeisance to Śrīdhara," with coconut water.

In the center of the nine-pitcher arrangement among the forty-nine pitchers, one should place the central *śānti*-pitcher. Into it, one should put one *kuḍuba* each of *tulasī*, bamboo, *nīvāra* grain, *śāli* rice, white mustard, and sesame; and one handful of *tulasī*. In the absence of these *śānti*-substances, one may use even a single *tulasī* leaf with the mantra: *oṃ hayagrīvāya namaḥ*. In the absence of jaggery (*guḍa*), one should use sugarcane juice; in its absence, jaggery-water. The measure of the jaggery should be eighty *palas*, or half, or even half of that again.

In the absence of coconut water, milk is desired in its place. Having filled [the vessels], one should invoke and worship them with: "Oṃ, obeisance to Varāha" for the molasses-water; "Oṃ, obeisance to Nṛsiṃha" for the sugarcane juice; "Oṃ, obeisance to Śrīdhara" for the coconut water; and "Oṃ, obeisance to Hayagrīva" for the peace-water (śāntivāri). Then, having bathed [the deity] with the molasses-water while reciting "madhu vātā," with the sugarcane juice while reciting "madhu naktaṃ," with the coconut water while reciting "madhu māmnā," with the peace-water while reciting "vedāham," and with the pure water-pitchers while reciting "jitaṃ te."

Thereafter, one should perform the bathing with the materials beginning with the water for the feet (*pādya*) and ending with clarified butter (*ghṛta*). At the conclusion of the bathing, one should perform a bath with nocturnal powders (*niśācūrṇa*). This is the procedure for the middling and superior bathing. Incorporating the sixty-four vessels of pure water located around the eighty-one vessels, as well as the ninety-two vessels of pure water placed in the four directions within the forty-nine vessels, [one performs the rite] using the one hundred and fifty-six vessels of pure water, excluding the half-vessel of pure water.

The middling-middling [rite] is performed with all [the vessels] except for the water-pitchers; the low-middling [rite] is without them. Now, the procedure for the supreme-supreme ablution is described; thus, the procedure for the supreme-supreme ablution is explained.

When the forty-nine jars have been placed in each of the four directions—east and so forth—of the previously mentioned site for the eighty-one jars, one should likewise stretch the lines in the four corners starting from the southeast (āgneya) as before, following the path of those respective lines, and install the forty-nine jars in that same manner.

In the center of the nine-pot group within the forty-nine pots of the Āgneya [section], the central jar named Maṅgala should be filled with: sprouts of *indravallī*, *aśvattha* leaves, *kuśeśaya*, single-petaled lotus, sandalwood, *kuṣṭha*, saffron (*kuṅkuma*), *rohiṇadruma*, *yūthikā*, *mallikā*, three types of *utpala*, *jāti*, *campaka*, and *ketakī*; specifically, two *indravallī* sprouts, a handful of *aśvattha* leaves, one single-petaled lotus, one *kuśeśaya*, eight flowers in the measure of a handful, and sandalwoods.

One *pala* each of the following—namely, *māṃsī*, *kuṣṭha*, the two types of *haridrā*, *murā*, *śaileya*, *campaka*, *mukula*, *mustā*, *vacā*, and camphor (*karpūra*)—measured individually, [is placed] in the central ninth jar among the forty-nine jars in the southwest (Nairṛta) direction, with the mantra: *oṃ namo bhagavate vāsudevāya*. This is known as the "All-Medicines" (*sarvauṣadha*) jar.

Having ground [the following ingredients]: *oṃ namo bhagavate saṃkarṣaṇāya namaḥ*; for the Vāyavya direction, the central jar among the nine jars situated in the middle of the forty-nine jars, known as "All-Scented" (*sarvagandha*): camphor, saffron, costus, spikenard, sandalwood, *murā*, *priyaṅgu*, saffron, nut-grass, *tamāla*, *nāgakesara*, the two roots, *kaccora*, *suraparṇī*, *kesara*, vetiver, silver, *lodhra*, yellow sandalwood, the two types of agallochum, white costus, *kāleya*, and the sprouts of *granthi*.

With the powders of *campaka* buds, each weighing one *pala*, [reciting] "Oṃ, obeisance to the Blessed One Pradyumna, obeisance. In the northeast, for the central nine among the forty-nine jars, one should fill the middle jar—known as the "root-herb" jar—with *vyāghrī*, *siṃhī*, *balā*, *śarapuṅkhā*, *śatāvarī*, root of *bilva*, *vacā*, *śuṇṭhī*, *goraṇḍī*, and *śatamūlī*, each powdered separately and weighing one *pala*, [reciting] "Oṃ, obeisance to the Blessed One Aniruddha. Having filled it...

Having invoked Vāsudeva into the vessel of auspicious water (*maṅgalodaka*), Saṃkarṣaṇa into the vessel of all medicinal herbs (*sarvauṣadhī*), Pradyumna into the vessel of all perfumes (*sarvagandha*), and Aniruddha into the vessel of all root-herbs (*sarvamūlauṣadhī*), and having worshipped them; one should bathe [the deity] with the auspicious water while reciting *viṣṇornukaṃ*, with the water of all medicinal herbs while reciting *oṣadhyaḥ*, with the water of all perfumes while reciting the *Nārāyaṇānuvāka*, with the water of all herbs while reciting *yā oṣadhīḥ*, and with pure water while reciting the eight-syllabled mantra. Thereafter, one should bathe [the deity] ending with clarified butter (*ghṛta*). This is the most excellent of the excellent rites.

In all cases, having included [the previous sets], that which is performed with four hundred and forty-eight pure water-pitchers minus half-pitchers of pure water is the superior-middle; that which is performed with only twenty-five substance-pitchers, excluding all four hundred and forty-eight pure water-pitchers, is the inferior-superior. Thus ends the ninefold ritual of bathing (*snapananavaka*).

Now, the procedure for the consecration with one hundred and eight jars (*kalaśa*) is described. When six lines are drawn facing east and likewise six lines are drawn facing north, twenty-five squares (*pada*) are formed. Among those, having set aside twelve squares for the human [deities], one should consolidate the nine squares in the center, which constitute the divine Brahmā-square.

Having arranged the squares according to the method of the Sūtra so that they total one hundred, one should leave two rows each in the east, south, west, and north, and clear away two rows on each side of those. Therein, in the directions from Brahma to Īśāna and in the intermediate directions, there are nine squares for the locations of the jars; in this manner, one should thus prepare the locations for one hundred and eight jars. Having thus established the jars:

One should fill the four Brahma-central jars and the jar at the southeast corner with ghee according to the previously mentioned proportions; the remaining three should be filled with pure water. Surrounding those, one should fill the eight jars located in the eight directions starting from the east to the northeast—namely the eight jars of the southeast group—with warm water, jewel-water, fruit-water, metal-water, cleansing-water, scented water, unbroken-grain water, and barley-water, using the aforementioned measurements.

In the human portion, from the east to the northeast, eight sets of nine jars each—making eight groups of nine—are situated. When this is done, there are seventeen substance jars (*dravyakalaśa*) and eighty-one pure water jars (*śuddhodakumbha*). Thus, including everything, there are one hundred and eight jars in total. The deity-mantra consecrations (*devamantrābhiṣeka*) are as before. Now, the procedure for the forty-nine-jar bath (*snapana*) is described: one should stretch out ten threads extending toward the east and likewise ten extending toward the north.

In this way, there would be eighty-one squares. Having omitted two rows in each of the four directions from the square of the jar (kalaśāspada), then, when one row at a time has been cleared away, there will be nine squares in the center, six squares in each cardinal direction, and four squares in each intermediate direction; thus, there will be forty-nine squares for the jar.

In the center there is one, in the cardinal directions four, and in the intermediate directions four; thus there are nine substance-pitchers (*dravyakumbha*). If this is the case, there are seventeen substance-pitchers, thirty-two pitchers of pure water (*śuddhodakumbha*), the mantra-deities, and the ritual bathing (*snapana*) as before. Now, the procedure for the bathing with twenty-five pitchers (*pañcaviṃśatikalaśasnapanavidhi*): having stretched out the lines so that there may be eighty-one squares (*pada*) in total, omitting one row in each of the four cardinal directions, and then clearing away two rows at a time.

Having arranged nine jars in the center, three in each cardinal direction, and one in each intermediate corner; thus, the four sets of three located in the center and the four located in the four corners—these seventeen jars, along with eight additional jars filled with pure water, constitute the material vessels.

The substances, mantras, deities, and the ritual bathing are as before. Alternatively, the nine central jars and the four in the cardinal directions and the four in the intermediate directions should be filled with fragrant substances such as sandalwood, agallochum, saffron, kuṣṭha, tagara, vīṇā, black agallochum, yellow sandalwood, and hrībera; or else with tāla, white kuṣṭha, suraparṇī, juice, camphor, nāgakeśara, mustā, campaka buds, priyaṅgu flowers, kāleya, granthi-pallava, bīja, māṃsī, dates, śaileya, hrībera, drumamūra, and so forth.

One should fill all the jars. Now, regarding the procedure for the ritual bath with sixteen jars (*ṣoḍaśakalaśasnapanavidhi*): one should lay down nine threads extending eastward and likewise nine extending northward; thus, having omitted one row from each of the four sides, when two rows have been cleared away, there will be four positions in the cardinal directions and two in each intermediate direction—one in each—making sixteen locations for the jars.

In the center of the four pitchers, one should fill the pitcher in the southeast with the nine gems mentioned previously; likewise, the pitcher in the southwest with the seven metals; the pitcher in the northwest with fragrant substances; and the pitcher in the northeast with clarified butter (*ājya*). Then, the twelve pitchers situated starting from the east should be filled in sequence with the previously specified measures: water for the feet (*pādya*), respectful offering (*arghya*), curd, water for sipping (*ācamana*), the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*), milk, unbroken rice (*akṣata*), water for sprinkling (*mārjana*), honey, decoction (*kaṣāya*), water with *kuśa* grass, and barley.

Having invoked [the deities] beginning with Puruṣa and ending with Dāmodara, one should perform the ceremonial bathing (snapana) with the sixteen verses of the Nṛ-sūkta. Now follows the procedure for the bathing with twelve jars (dvādaśakalaśa-snapana-vidhi): one should draw seven threads extending eastward and likewise seven extending northward; thus, having left a four-square space in the center and having cleared away one row in each of the four directions, when three squares in each of the four corners have been cleared, there remain two squares each outside the central four-square area in the east, south, west, and north.

This being the case, there would be twelve locations for the pitchers (*kalaśa*). One should fill the central four squares as follows: the pitcher in the southeast (*āgneya*) with the nine jewels previously mentioned; the one in the southwest (*nairṛta*) with metals; the one in the northwest (*vāyavya*) with fragrant substances; and the one in the northeast (*aiśāna*) with clarified butter (*sarpiḥ*). Then, one should fill the eight pitchers situated in the positions starting from the east and ending in the north, in sequence, with water for washing the feet (*pādya*), curd, the respectful offering (*arghya*), milk, water for sipping (*ācamana*), honey, the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*), and fruits, using the measurements previously stated. The mantras and deities are as before.

If these are not available, one should fill the four central squares—starting from the southeast (āgneya) and ending at the soma-pitcher located on the outside—with the following substances in clockwise order: *agaru*, *kālīya*, sprouts of *granthi*, seeds, *candana*, *kāśmīra*, *māṃsī*, *tamāla*, *mura*, mountain-born gold-dust particles, and the sap of *campaka* buds and *kharjūra*. Now, the procedure for the nine-vessel consecration (*navakalaśasnāpana*): Four threads should be stretched eastward and likewise four northward; by doing so, there will be nine squares.

Starting from the central jar and proceeding clockwise to the northeast, one should fill them in sequence with ghee, water for the feet (*pādya*), curd for the respectful offering (*arghya*), milk for rinsing the mouth (*ācamana*), honey, the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*), and fruits; or alternatively, with the nine gems. The mantras and deities are as before. Now follows the procedure for the ablution with five jars: one in the center and four in the four cardinal directions. Starting from the center and ending in the north, they should be filled with gems such as ruby, coral, pearl, diamond, and lapis lazuli, or with the five metals; or else, each may be filled individually with the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*).
