The mantra-deities of the five products of the cow (pañcagavya) are the five Upaniṣads. Now follows the procedure for the ablution with a single pitcher (ekakalaśasnāpana): having placed one pitcher in the center, one should fill it with the five nectars (pañcāmṛta) or the five products of the cow (pañcagavya). A fee (niṣka) should be given to the preceptor according to one's capacity. Thus ends the thirty-first chapter, titled "The Procedure for the Ablution of the Uttama and Other Grades," in the *Kriyakairavacandrikā* composed by the venerable Varāhaguru. Chapter Thirty-two: Now the procedure for the ablution with one thousand and one pitchers (ekottarasahasrakalaśasnāpana) is described.

On the preceding day, having performed, as before, the consecration of the sprouts and the *pratisarā* cord for the Blessed One, one should construct another large pavilion—twice as long as thirty-two cubits in width and proportionate to the extent of the ground where the jars are to be placed—and arrange its doors and other features as previously described. Then, one should divide the ground where the jars are to be placed into twenty-five parts.

Having divided the middle Brahma-pada into eighty-one sections, each serving as a locus for a jar; having set aside nine by nine squares from Brahmā to Īśāna, totaling eighty-one jar-locuses; and having swept away the remaining eighty-eight squares; one should prepare a pedestal (pīṭhikā) with one āḍhaka of rice grains per square, half that amount of husked rice, and half of that again of sesame seeds; then, having placed two darbha grass blades upon each of those.

Thereafter, one should fill the vessels made of gold and other metals, as well as those made of clay—which possess the previously mentioned characteristics—with either a *droṇa* measure of water or half of that; and the jars (*kalaśas*) should be filled with an *āḍhaka* measure of water. Having washed the [metal] jars with the Viṣṇu-Gāyatrī, one should place the clay ones upon the palm of the left hand, take a thread with the other hand, and wrap it around them so that the space between the wrapped threads is the size of a barley grain or half a finger-breadth.

Having encircled [the site] with the mantra "indram natvā," having prepared a pedestal of grain on the ground to the west of the spot where the water-jar (kalaśa) was placed, and having had the declaration of an auspicious day (puṇyāha) recited; having spread darbha grass upon that [pedestal], with the tips pointing either eastward or northward; having placed the jars face-down there, starting from the Brahma direction and ending at the Īśāna direction, while pronouncing "Oṃ"; having placed three darbha blades over each of those jars as before with the Parameṣṭhi mantra; and having sprinkled them facing eastward with arghya water while reciting the Puruṣa mantra.

Having scattered unbroken rice grains (*akṣata*) with the *viśvamantreṇa* mantra, and having turned [the vessel] face-upward with the *nivṛttimantreṇa* mantra; thereafter, having duly prepared the fire, and having offered one hundred and eight oblations of clarified butter (*sarpiṣā*) with the *Viṣṇugāyatrī*, he should sprinkle the bathing substances with the remnants of the offering (*saṃpāta*). Having filled the jars (*kalaśa*) with those bathing substances filtered through cloth while reciting the respective deity-mantras, and having lifted the substance-jars, he should install them in their proper places according to the procedure to be described, using the *Viṣṇugāyatrī*.

In the central Brahma-section, there are eighty-one jars. In the divine sections of the East, South, West, and North—namely, the divine Indra, Yama, Varuṇa, and Soma sectors—there are eighty-one jars in each direction. Furthermore, in the four corners beginning with the Āgneya corner of the divine section, there are forty-nine jars in each corner. Having stretched ten lines with their tips pointing east and north, and having set aside two rows in each of the directions starting from the East, one should clear away one row on all sides.

In the center, nine [kalaśas] are to be placed from the east to the north; six each from the southeast to the northeast; and sixteen kalaśas, five each at every station, are to be placed in the sixteen locations surrounding that in the human portion. For this, ten lines should be drawn with their tips pointing east and north, omitting one row in each of the four cardinal directions, then clearing away two rows each, leaving nine in the center, three each in the cardinal directions, and one each in the intermediate directions.

In this manner, one should arrange twenty-five jars. If there are to be one thousand and one jars, then in the central group of nine belonging to Brahmā—specifically in the middle of that group—one should place [jars] made of all metals: gold, silver, copper, lead, tin, bronze, and iron, in quantities according to their value; as well as rubies, sapphires, blue diamonds, topazes, corals, pearls, emeralds, and lapis lazuli.

One pala each of plantain, citron, mango, emblic myrobalan, wood-apple, coconut, jackfruit, pomegranate, māṃsī, kuṣṭha, the two types of turmeric, murā, śaileya, campaka buds, mustā, vacā, and camphor [should be taken].

Camphor, saffron, costus, spikenard, sandalwood, *mura*, *priyaṅgu*, saffron filaments, nut-grass, *tamāla*, the two types of *nāgakesara* roots, *kacchūra*, *suraparṇī*, *kesara*, *uśīra*, *tagara*, *lodhra*, yellow sandalwood, and the two types of *agaru*—each of these, along with white costus, *kāleya*, *granthiparṇa*, and *campaka* buds, measured at one *pala* each, are to be ground into a powder.

Having placed the Śrīvatsa, forest garland, conch, discus, mace, lotus, sword, and Śārṅga bow—each fashioned from gold and weighing one *niṣka*—into a water-filled pitcher while reciting "Oṃ namo bhagavate vāsudevāya," and having wrapped it with two garments with the mantra "taṃ yuvāsā," and having made a lid of a *pippala* leaf together with a tuft of hair (*kūrca*), one should there conceive of the Yoga-pīṭha. Having invoked Vāsudeva along with his limbs (*aṅga*) and retinue (*parivāra*) upon that [seat], one should worship Him with offerings beginning with *arghya* and ending with the lamp.

In the central jar of the nine-jar set of the Brāhma [direction], there are a sun-crystal (*sūryakānta*) and a ruby (*padmarāga*); its presiding deity is Puruṣa. In the central jar of the nine-jar set of the Āgneya [direction], there are a lapis lazuli (*vaiḍūrya*) and a moon-crystal (*candrakānta*); its presiding deity is Vāsudeva. In the central jar of the nine-jar set of the Yāmya [direction], there are a sapphire (*indranīla*) and an iron-crystal (*ayaskānta*); its presiding deity is Satya. In the central jar of the nine-jar set of the Nairṛta [direction], there are a coral (*pravāla*) and a garuḍa-crystal; its presiding deity is Saṅkarṣaṇa.

In the central jar of the nine-jar array of the Brāhma and Vāruṇa [sections], there is a *puṣya* crystal; its presiding deity is Acyuta. In the central jar of the nine-jar array of the Brāhma and Vāyavya [sections], there is a ruby (*padmarāga*) and an emerald (*marataka*); its presiding deity is Pradyumna. In the central jar of the nine-jar array of the Brāhma and Vāruṇa [sections], there is a diamond (*vajra*) and silver; its presiding deity is Ananta. In the central jar of the nine-jar array of the Brāhma and Raudra [sections], there is copper and gold (*auttika*); its presiding deity is Aniruddha.

In all the pure waters, their presiding deity is Nārāyaṇa. In that eastern divine section, at the site of the eighty-one jars, in the central group of nine, within the middle jar, there are the fruits of the plantain, jackfruit, mango, citron, *bhavya*, *jambūkesara*, and jujube. Its presiding deity is Tattvātmā. In its [the eastern section's] Indra-group of nine, within the middle jar, there are the fruits of the citron and pomegranate. Its presiding deity is Pṛthvī.

In the central jar of its southeastern group of nine, there are *jambū* and orange fruits; its presiding deity is Apām (the Lord of Waters). In the central jar of its southern group of nine, there are *takola* and cardamom fruits; its presiding deity is Tejasvīpuruṣa (the Radiant Being). In the central jar of its southwestern group of nine, there are *kṣīrikā* and myrobalan fruits; its presiding deity is Vāyu (the Wind). In the central jar of its western group of nine, there are grapes and dates; its presiding deity is Ākāśātmā (the Ether-Self).

In the middle jar of the group of nine in the northwest (vāyavya) direction, there is a mango fruit and a pārāvata fruit; its presiding deity is the mind (manas). In the middle jar of the group of nine in the north (saumya) direction, there is a small jackfruit; its presiding deity is the ego (ahaṃkāra). In the middle jar of the group of nine in the northeast (aiśānya) direction, there is a bilva fruit and a plantain fruit; its presiding deity is the intellect (buddhi). In all the jars of pure water, jujube fruits are placed as the presiding deities, as before. The consecration of the jars is performed with the eight-syllable mantra and the five Upaniṣadic mantras.

In the divine-yāmya [direction], at the site of the eighty-one jars, in the central jar of the middle nine, there are powdered *uśīra*, *kuṅkuma*, *kuṣṭha*, *māṃsī*, *malayaja*, *mura*, *hrībera*, and *agaru*, each weighing one *pala*. Its presiding deity is Trailokyamohana. In its [adjacent] Indra-navaka, in the middle jar, there is *jalada-vāreṇamūla*. Its presiding deity is Babhru. In its Āgneya-navaka, in the middle jar, there are *karpūra* and *kāśmīra*. Its presiding deity is Śauri.

In the central jar of its southern group of nine, there are *campaka* buds and powdered *māṃsī*; its presiding deity is Dāśārha. In the central jar of its south-western group of nine, there are sandalwood and red sandalwood powder; its presiding deity is Annādhipati. In the central jar of its western group of nine, there are *suraparṇī* and the pollen of *maura*; its presiding deity is Vaikuṇṭha. In the central jar of its north-western group of nine, there are the root-powder of *girija* and the root-pollen of *praiyaṅgu*.

Its deity is Puruṣottama. In the central jar of its northeastern group of nine, there is *kuṣṭha* and white *kuṣṭha* ground together; its deity is Mukunda. In the central jar of the [remaining] northeastern group of nine, there is black and white *agaru* powder; its deity is Vṛṣākapi. In the remaining jars of pure water, there are *tamāla* leaves; their deities are as before. The consecration of the jars is performed with the Puruṣasūkta or with the hymns beginning with the Pavamāna.

In the divine *vāruṇa* [section], which consists of eighty-one jars, there are nine waters—of a pond, a well, a lake, rain, snow, a river, the ocean, a tank, and water—in the central jar of the middle nine. In the central jar of its eastern (*aindra*) group of nine, there is pond-water. In the jar of the middle of its southeastern (*āgneya*) group of nine, there is river-water. In the jar of the middle of its southern (*yāmya*) group of nine, there is well-water. In the jar of the middle of its southwestern (*nairṛta*) group of nine jars, there is lake-water.

In the central jar of the Varuṇa group of nine, there is snow-water; in the central jar of the Vāyavya group of nine, rain-water; in the central jar of the Saumya group of nine, river-water; and in the central jar of the Īśāna group of nine, ocean-water. The presiding deities for these, in order, are Bhārgava, Rāma, Matsya, and the others [the Fish and so forth]. For the pure waters, it is as previously described.

In the divine and auspicious central group of nine jars located at the site of the eighty-one jars, within the middle jar, there are barley, wheat, rice, *śāli*, mung beans, *priyaṅgu*, black gram, *śyāmāka*, and *nīvāra*. Its presiding deity is Padmanābha mounted upon Garuḍa. In the middle jar of its eastern group of nine, there is barley; its presiding deity is Vanamālā. In the middle jar of its southeastern group of nine, there is wheat; its presiding deity is Śaṅkha. In the middle jar of its southern group of nine, there is rice.

Its deity is Cakra. In the central jar of the southern group of nine, there is *śāli* rice; its deity is Kaustubha. In the central jar of the western group of nine, there is *mudga* bean; its deity is Padma. In the central jar of the northwestern group of nine, there is *priyaṅgu*; its deity is Śārṅga. In the central jar of the northern group of nine, there is *māṣa* bean; its deity is Gadā. In the central jar of the northeastern group of nine, there is *śyāmāka* and *nīvāra* grain.

Its presiding deity is Khaḍga. The remaining [deities] have pure water as their substance and their deities are likewise. In the divine fiery [group], there is ghee in the forty-nine jars located at the central nine. In its Indra-group of six, there is cow urine; in its Yama-group of six, milk; in the Varuṇa-group of six, curd; in the Soma-group of six, the liquid of cow dung. In its four Agni-pitchers, there is warm water; in the four Nairṛta [pitchers], the five nectars (pañcāmṛta).

In its four northeastern jars are milk, curd, clarified butter, honey, and sugar; their deity is Nārāyaṇa. In the divine southeastern group of forty-nine jar-positions, in the central nine, is oil; its deity is the form of Matsya. In its six eastern [jars] is camphor; in its six southern [jars] is parched grain; and in its six western [jars] is cleansing water.

In the gentle group of six, the cleansing substances are *rajanī*, *sūryavartinī*, *sahadevī*, *śirīṣa*, *sadābhadra*, and tips of *kuśa* grass, each in the measure of a single handful. In its four jars located in the four corners starting from the southeast and ending at the northeast, there is molasses-water (*guḍavāri*). Their presiding deity is Vāsudeva. In the divine wind-group, in the central group of nine which serves as the site for forty-nine jars, there is mustard oil. In its eastern group of six, there are the aforementioned substances for the foot-washing (*pādya*).

In its southern hexagon are the previously mentioned materials for the *arghya* offering; in the western hexagon, the materials for the *ācamanīya*; and in the northern hexagon, auspicious water such as *indravallī* and other herbs. In the sixteen jars located in the four corners from the southeast to the northeast, there is sugarcane juice; their presiding deity is Aniruddha. In the central group of nine jars situated at the divine northeast position, there is honey. In its eastern hexagon, there is water with all fragrances, such as camphor and saffron.

In its southern hexagon are *śāntivāri*, *tulasī*, bamboo, wild rice (*nīvāra*), and so forth; likewise in its western, northern, southeastern (*āgneya*), southwestern (*naiṛta*), and northwestern (*vāyavya*) quadrangles is coconut water; and in its northeastern (*aiśāna*) quadrangle is milk. Their presiding deity is Hari.

In the human region, within twenty-five jars situated in the east, there are eight substances in the central ninth jar: earth from a sacred field (*kṣetra-tīrtha*), the ocean, a mountain, an elephant, a boar, the tip of a tusk, an anthill, and the tip of a bull’s horn. In the eight jars surrounding that group, starting from the east and ending in the northeast, each of the aforementioned substances is placed one by one in sequence. Keśava is the deity of this group of nine. Nārāyaṇa is the deity for the remaining sixteen pure jars.

Then, in the twenty-five [pots] situated between those of Indra and Agni, within the central group of nine, there are eight powdered roots: *sahadevī*, *vacā*, *śatamūlā*, *śatāvarī*, *kumārī*, *guḍūcī*, *siṃhī*, and *vyāghrī*. In the eight pots standing around that [central group], there is one root each, starting with *sahadevī* and so on, in sequence. The deity of this group of nine is Nārāyaṇa. And likewise for the remaining sixteen pots of pure water.

In that regard, within the central jar of the fifty-agnis, there are the barks and their juices of eight [trees]: nyagrodha, audumbara, aśvattha, jambu, bilva, palāśa, madhuka, and śirīṣa. In the eight jars situated around it, the barks and juices of the nyagrodha and the others are placed in sequence. The deity of the group of nine is Mādhava; for the remaining pure water-jars, the deity is Nārāyaṇa.

In the space between the southeast and the south, there is a group of nine jars. In the central jar, there are eight sprouts from the *pālāśa*, *bilva*, *vakula*, *kadaṃba*, *āmra*, *śirīṣa*, *nyagrodha*, and *aśvattha* trees. In each of the eight jars situated around it, one sprout from each of these—beginning with the *pālāśa*—is placed in sequence. Govinda is the presiding deity of this group of nine. For the remaining sixteen pure jars, Nārāyaṇa is the deity.

In the southern row of twenty-five jars, within the ninth jar, there are eight flowers: *jāti*, *mallikā*, *priyaṅgu*, *padma*, *vakula*, *nandyāvartaka*, *campaka*, and *kundaja*. Around that, in each of the eight surrounding jars, one flower from the *jāti* group and so forth is placed in sequence. The deity of that group of nine is Viṣṇu; for the remaining [groups], it is as before.

In the intermediate space between the southern and southwestern [directions], among the twenty-five jars, there are eight items—white mustard seeds (*siddhārtha*), royal white mustard seeds (*rājasiddhārtha*), bamboo, yellow orpiment (*gorocana*), indra-veṇu, *ṣāṣṭha*, barley (*yava*), and *śamī*—placed in the central jar. In the eight jars situated around it, one of each [item] beginning with white mustard seeds is placed in sequence. The deity of that group of nine is Madhusūdana; for the remaining [deities], it is as before.

There, in the southwest among the twenty-five jars, within the central jar of the group of nine, there are eight substances: cultivated sesame, wild sesame, cumin, black cumin, linseed, *chinnaruhā*, *śatapuṣpā*, and the fruit of the *kuṭhārarṣi*. In the eight jars situated around it, there is one substance each, following the sequence beginning with sesame. The deity of that group of nine is Trivikrama; for the remaining [jars], the deity is Nārāyaṇa.

In the space between the Nairṛta and Vāruṇa [directions], among twenty-five jars, within the central jar of the group of nine, there are eight substances: *śyāmāka*, *ṣāṣṭika*, *śāli*, *nīvāra*, rice, sprouts of *dūrvā* grass, sprouts of *kuśa* grass, sprouts of *indravallī*, and sprouts of the *aśvattha* tree. In the eight jars situated around that [central one], there is one of these [substances] beginning with *śyāmāka* in successive order. The deity of that group of nine is Vāmana. For the pure waters, it is as before.

There, in the western [Vāruṇa] group of twenty-five jars, within the central jar of the nine, there are eight divine *kuśa* materials: *kāśa*, *uśīra*, *śarapuṃkhā*, *tagara*, and the roots of *apāmārga*. In the eight jars situated around that [central one], there is one root substance each, starting with *kuśa*, in successive order. The deity of that group of nine is Śrīdhara. For the pure [vessels], it is as before.

In the space between the Vāruṇa and Vāyavya [corners], among the twenty-five jars, there are nine in the central jar: *tulasī*, black *tulasī*, bamboo, *kesara*, *ketaka*, *bilva*, *śamī*, and eight *jātī* leaves. In the eight jars situated around that [central one], there is one of each starting with *tulasī* in sequence. The deity of that group of nine is Hṛṣīkeśa; for the remaining [deities], it is as before.

There, in the northwest, among twenty-five jars, in the central jar of the group of nine, there are two *mustā*, *vacā*, *kaccora*, *kumuda*, *utpala*, *kalhāra*, *śītalīyaka*, *kuvalaya*, and eight tubers. In each of the eight jars situated around that, one of these substances beginning with *mustā* is placed in sequence. The deity of that group of nine is Padmanābha; for the remaining [deities], it is as before.

In the space between Vāyu and Soma, among twenty-five jars, there are eight *āḍhakas* of mudga, māṣa, yava, niṣpāva, tuvarī, vrīhi, and kuluttha in the central jar of the group of nine. In the eight jars situated around that [central one], each of the substances beginning with mudga is placed in sequence. The deity of that group of nine is Dāmodara; for the remaining [groups], it is as before.

There, in the northern [section], among twenty-five jars, there are eight [herbs] in the middle jar of the nine: *śaṅkhapuṣpī*, *balā*, *viṣṇukrāntā*, *sadābhadra*, *ekapatrāmbuja*, *varasahā*, and the two types of *sahadevī*. In the eight jars situated around that [central group], one of these starting with *śaṅkhapuṣpī* is placed in each in sequence. The deity of that group of nine is Yajñanārāyaṇa; for the remaining [deities], it is as before.

There, in the space between Soma and Īśāna, within the twenty-five jars, in the central jar of the group of nine, [one should place] śvetārka, agnibhadrā, brahmasuvarcalā, sarasā, saraktā, and pṛśniparṇī; with these stable [plants], eight eggs [are prepared]. In each of the eight jars situated around that, one of the [plants] beginning with śvetārka is placed in sequence. The deity of that group of nine is Hari. For the remaining [jars], it is as before.

In the space between the directions of Īśāna and Indra, among the twenty-five jars, there are eight substances—scented water (*surabhi*), lotus (*padma*), filament (*kesara*), leaf (*patra*), cardamom (*elā*), clove (*lavaṅga*), cinnamon bark (*tvak*), *nāgakesara*, and jasmine vine fruit (*latājātīphala*)—placed in the middle jar of the group of nine. In each of the eight jars situated around that [central jar], one of these [substances] beginning with *surabhi* is placed in sequence. The deity of that group of nine is Kṛṣṇa; for the remaining [jars], it is as previously stated.

In the space between the northeast (Aiśāna) and the east (Indra), among the twenty-five jars, within the central jar of the group of nine, there are eight items in the form of individual replicas: gold, silver, and copper—each weighing five *niṣkas* and shaped like lotuses; a bell-metal mirror; cups shaped like iron ladles and so forth; and tin, lead, and brass. Around those, in the eight jars situated from the eastern direction up to the northeast, there is one of each [of the aforementioned materials] in sequence. Of that...

Hayagrīva is the presiding deity of the *navaka* [the nine-pitcher set]; Nārāyaṇa is the presiding deity of the remaining sixteen pure water-pitchers (*śuddhodakumbha*). Having thus arranged the materials and invoked the respective deities, one should worship them. In this ritual of bathing with one thousand and one pitchers, there shall be eight or four preceptors (*ācāryas*) and sixteen image-protectors (*mūrtipās*). Having worshipped the deities in this manner according to the rules, preceded by the declaration of an auspicious day (*puṇyāha*), one should make the formal resolve (*saṃkalpa*): “I shall perform the fire-oblation (*homa*) for the sake of pacifying all calamities.”

Having offered a thousand oblations of clarified butter with the five Upaniṣad mantras and with the root-vidyā, as well as oblations of sacrificial fuel sticks (samidh) and sixteen oblations of caru-oblation with the Nṛsūkta.

In the human station, within the twenty-five [squares], beginning with nine jars filled with earth and continuing through eighty-one jars ending with the "Brahma-place" (the central one), one should bathe [the deity] sequentially with one thousand and eight jars—starting from the middle group of nine and ending with the jar containing all jewels—using the mantras to be described hereafter for each substance, accompanied by bathing water, a cloth for wiping, an upper garment, water for the *arghya*, *pādya*, and *ācamana* offerings, as well as perfumes, flowers, incense, lamps, and worship.

In the *mānuṣa* and *aindra* [sections], for the nine jars filled with clay and containing pure water placed in the center, the mantra is “*viṣṇornukam*. For the jars containing pure water and root-water situated near them, the mantra is “*tad viṣṇoḥ*. In the *mānuṣa* and *āgneya* [sections], for the twenty-five jars, the mantra is “*pratad viṣṇuḥ*. For the jars containing pure water and root-water situated near them, the mantra is “*tāvā*.”

For the twenty-five jars of the *mānuṣa-nairṛta* [direction], the mantra is “*dhruvaḥ pātu*. For those situated near them, the mantra is “*bhadraṃ karṇebhiḥ*. For the twenty-five jars of the *mānuṣa-vāruṇa* [direction], the mantra is “*na te viṣṇo*. For those situated near them, the mantra is “*irāvati*. For those situated in the *mānuṣa-vāyavya* [direction], the mantra is “*ato devāḥ*. For those situated near them, the mantra is “*idaṃ viṣṇuḥ*.”

For those situated in the *mānuṣasaumya* [region], the mantra is “trīṇi padā. For those situated near that, the mantra is “viṣṇoḥ karmāṇi. For those situated in the *manuṣaiśāna* [region], the mantra is “tadviṣṇoḥ paramaṃ padam. For those situated near that, the mantra is “tadviprāsaḥ. In the divine *aindra* [region], at the site of the eighty-one jars, for the central one among the nine filled with fruit-water, the mantra is “yajñāyajñiya.”

In their vicinity, from Indra in the east to Īśāna in the northeast, the mantras are used in sequence: “*indrāviṣṇū pade*,” “*manīṣā*,” “*vaṣaṭ te viṣṇo*,” “*tisro vācaḥ*,” “*iṣe tvorje tvā*,” “*starīr u tvad bhavati*,” and “*yasmin viśvāni*,” as well as “*parjanyāya*. In the divine [quarter] and the southern [quarter], within the group of eighty-one vessels, one should begin with the *Nārāyaṇānuvāka* and, starting from the beginning, offer water scented with perfumes using eight verses—one verse at a time—in sequence from Indra to Īśāna.

In the divine western [direction], which is the site of eighty-one jars, and in the center of the group of nine, there are the mantras for the water and other substances in the jars: “*yā āpaḥ*,” “*sindhudvīpaḥ*,” “*eṣa te deva*,” “*imaṃ me varuṇa*,” and “*śannodevīḥ*”; [and those beginning with] “*yāsāṃ rājā*,” “*samudrajyeṣṭha*,” and “*yāsāṃ devāḥ*,” along with the *Vāruṇa-sūkta*, from Indra up to Brahmā.

In the divine and auspicious [mandala] containing eighty-one pitchers, in the center of the nine pitchers, the mantras for the nine pitchers of grain and other substances, starting from the eastern direction (Aindra) and ending with the Brahma direction, are, in order: *trātāram*, *ā tvā vahantu*, *jitaṃ te*, *āpo hi ṣṭhā*, *tāvati*, *sa tvaṃ no agne*, *tvaṃ no agne*, the Mahāvyāhṛtis, and *aṇor aṇīyān*.

In the divine southeast corner, at the site of the forty-nine jars, for the central group of nine jars starting from the eastern direction (Indra) and ending with Brahmā, one should [worship] using the following mantras: *gāyatrī*, *payovrata-sāman*, *dadhi-krāvṇaḥ*, *gandhadvārām*, *viṣṇorarāṭam asi*, *mūrdhānaṃ divaḥ*, *hiraṇyagarbhaḥ*, *āpyāyasva*, and *ghṛtasnātā*.

In the divine [direction], at the location of the forty-nine jars in the south-west (Nairṛta) corner, for the central group of nine, starting from Indra and ending with Brahmā, the sequence is: the Rakṣoghna Sāman, the first Sāman, "pavitraṃ te," the Lord Vāsudeva, the Vedavrata Sāman, the Vairāja Sāman, and the Aparājita [Sāmans]. In the divine [direction], at the location of the forty-nine jars in the north-west (Vāyu) corner, for the central group of nine, starting from Indra and ending with Brahmā, [the sequence is]: the twelve-syllable [mantra], "drupadādiva," the eight-syllable [mantra], "śanno devīḥ," "hiraṇyapāṇi," and the four [verses] beginning with "vedāham."

The *ṛcas* are in order: in the divine [quarter] of Īśāna, at the site of the forty-nine jars, for the nine [jars] in the center, starting from Indra and ending with Brahmā, one uses the mantra "ā no bhadrāḥ," the *Śrīsūkta*, "madhumānno vanaspatiḥ," "madhu naktam," and "madhu vātā. In the Brahmā-square, for the nine [groups] starting from Indra and ending with Īśāna, two *ṛcas* each from the beginning of the *Puruṣasūkta* are used in sequence for the eight central substance-jars.

For the remaining sixty-four water-pots filled with pure water, [one should worship] with the root mantra; for the central group of nine, specifically the middle pot, with the *Puruṣasūkta*; and for the remaining pots of pure water, with the root mantra. At the conclusion of that, with twenty-five, seventeen, sixteen, or twelve pots filled with turmeric powder, provided with gems, metal, brushes (*kūrca*), and *aśvattha* sprouts, covered with cloths, and worshipped as the deities of prosperity (*Śrī-devatā*) while placed upon heaps of grain, one should worship with the *Śrīsūkta*.

Having performed the consecration (*abhiṣeka*), having worshipped the Deity with water for the guest-offering (*arghya*) and other rites, and having presented the great oblation (*mahāhavis*), one should offer one thousand and eight oblations of clarified butter and fuel-sticks (*samidh*) while reciting the Root-Mantra (*mūlavidyā*). Then, one should offer sixteen oblations of each of the four kinds of food while reciting the *Puruṣasūkta*. As for the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*), it should be given to the preceptors (*deśika*) in an amount equal to the number of ritual jars; half of that to the officiating priests (*ṛtvij*); half of that to the attendants; and the same should be given to others as well.
Thus ends the thirty-second chapter, titled "The Procedure for the Thousand-Pitcher Consecration," in the *Kriyākairavacandrikā* composed by the venerable Varāhaguru.
The Thirty-third Chapter: The Procedure for the Festival (*Utsavavidhi*).
Now, the procedure for the festival is described.

First, the rite of sowing the germinating seeds (*aṅkurārpaṇa*) must be performed for the purpose of the consecration of Garuḍa. A preceptor distinguished by his specific qualifications, having worshipped Viṣvaksena or Garuḍa at an auspicious moment seven days, five days, or three days prior to the rite of Garuḍa’s consecration, and having gone with him toward the eastern or northern direction, should make this formal resolve (*saṃkalpa*): "In the rite of the nine-day great festival of this God of Gods, I shall perform the rite of collecting earth, which is a constituent part of the rite of sowing the germinating seeds. Having thus resolved, he should perform the rite of declaring an auspicious day (*puṇyāha*).

Having collected earth according to the prescribed rules as before, and having entered the pavilion for the offering of sprouts (*aṅkurārpaṇa-maṇṭapa*), one should perform the offering of sprouts there according to the previously mentioned procedure; thereafter, one should perform the consecration (*pratiṣṭhā*) of Garuḍa.

Now, the procedure for hoisting the banner (dhvajārohaṇa) is described: First, for the sake of the banner, one should take a flawless, fine cloth made of linen or cotton, ten cubits in length and half that in width; or else, equal in length to the base-drum (mūlabherī), the door, or the height of the temple, and half that in width; with a crest (śekhara) made of a quarter of that [width], provided with a symmetrical tail (puccha), and a tail-ear (pucchaka) of half that size; thus washed, treated with oil (khali), and dried.

Taking a banner-cloth distinguished by its true characteristics, one should depict upon it, in the center of the cloth, the Lord Garuḍa, possessing the luster of gold, measuring nine *tālas*, with two arms, wearing a tunic, holding his hands joined in a gesture of offering flowers (*puṣpāñjali*), clad in white garments, with a face formidable with fangs, eyes curved with a frown, a blue tip to his nose, his left foot drawn up, his right foot set behind, and adorned by the spreading of his wings.

He was beginning his journey through the sky, moving with perfect grace yet appearing terrible; he wore a crown of baskets and had locks of hair arranged upon his forehead. He shone with ornaments of necklaces, armlets, bracelets, and anklets. Ananta was his left bracelet, while Vāsuki served as his sacred thread. Kārkoṭa was placed upon his chest, and Takṣaka formed his waist-band. On his right ear he bore the serpent named Padma, and likewise Mahāpadma on the other, while Śaṅkha adorned his head.

The *gulika* (the central bead) and the serpent on the armlet, as well as their colors, are now described: they are like crystal, like blood, like yellow, and smoke-colored; like a red lotus, tawny, and with the luster of snow; and like a bee. These should be depicted in sequence, surrounded by an umbrella and a string of pearls. Above, a [parasol] should be made, and two chowries on the two sides. Below, a lotus, a full water-pot, and clay offering-bowls (*pālikā*) with sprouts should be drawn. Two lamps should be placed on both sides.

"One should paint the deity with five colors, the interior being dark blue; the best of painters should not decorate the intermediate space with black. Having thus painted Garuḍa, on the day of the preliminary consecration (adhivāsa), during the darkness of night, the preceptor, together with the image-makers, enters the workshop. After having the artisan perform the opening of the eyes for the deity residing on the cloth, and once that artisan has been satisfied with desired wealth and dismissed, the preceptor then takes the cloth, saying "Oṃ," and places it upon a golden vessel.

Having placed it upon the head of the presiding image of that deity, and having performed a circumambulation of the temple along with the sounding of musical instruments, one should lead it into the inner sanctum. Having worshipped the Blessed One with offerings such as *arghya* and the like, one should sprinkle the cloth painting (*paṭa*) with water from the *puṇyāha* rite while reciting the *astra-mantra*. Then, having struck it with white mustard seeds and flowers consecrated by the *astra-mantra*, and having performed the rites of burning and nourishing, one should bow to the God and recite this verse: "O Blessed One, lotus-eyed one, Lord of all, who pervades the universe!"

"However, it is not possible for you to act exactly as you have instructed, due to lack of independence, lack of capacity, and the absence of faith and other qualities. Therefore, for the sake of pacifying all excesses and deficiencies in pride and the rest, please be gracious to Vainateya, who removes all defects. Having thus petitioned the Blessed One, and having entered the sacrificial pavilion by way of circumambulation preceded by the sound of musical instruments, he placed the cloth-painting upon a seat of rice and spread it out.

Having made the formal resolve (*saṃkalpa*): "For the sake of accomplishing the rites ending with the consecration and dwelling in the shadow, I shall perform the rite of binding the protective thread (*rakṣābandhana*)," and having caused the declaration of an auspicious day (*puṇyāha*) to be recited and having sprinkled water for purification (*prokṣya*), one should bind the protective amulet (*pratisara*) onto the cloth image according to the prescribed rule. Then, sitting to its south, and having performed the purification of the elements (*bhūtaśuddhi*) and the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) of the eight-syllable mantra preceded by breath control (*prāṇāyāma*), one should thereafter [recite] this five-syllable mantra of the venerable Garuḍa: Kāśyapa is the seer (*ṛṣi*), the Paṅkti is the meter (*chandaḥ*), and the venerable Garuḍa is the deity (*devatā*).

*Kṣīṃ* is the seed-syllable (*bīja*). *Svāhā* is the power (*śakti*). Śrī Garuḍa is the deity (*devatā*). This is the application (*viniyoga*) for the sake of attaining the grace of Śrī Garuḍa. *Oṃ kṣīṃ* to the two thumbs, *namaḥ*. *Oṃ paṃ* to the two index fingers, *svāhā*. *Oṃ oṃ* to the two middle fingers, *vaṣaṭ*. *Oṃ svāṃ* to the two ring fingers, *huṃ*. *Oṃ hāṃ* to the two little fingers, *phaṭ*. *Oṃ kṣipa oṃ svāhā* to the nails, *vauṣaṭ*. *Oṃ jvala jvala mahāmate svāhā oṃ kṣāṃ* to the heart, *namaḥ*.

Oṃ garuḍa cūḍānane svāhā; oṃ kṣīṃ śirase svāhā. Oṃ garuḍa prabhañjaya prabhañjaya, prabhedaya prabhedaya, vitrāsaya vitrāsaya, vimardaya vimardaya svāhā; oṃ kṣaiṃ kavacāya huṃ. Oṃ ugrarūpadhara, O you who assume a fierce form, O terrifying of all serpents, rend, rend all poison! Terrify, terrify! Burn, burn! Reduce to ashes! Svāhā; oṃ kṣauṃ netrābhyāṃ vauṣaṭ.

Oṃ, to the one of unimpeded command; Oṃ, homage to Sudarśana, hūṃ phaṭ svāhā! Oṃ kṣaḥ, to the weapon, phaṭ! The visualization: The wise practitioner should meditate upon the self as having a golden luster from the knees to the navel, a snowy radiance from the navel to the neck, and a saffron-red hue from the neck to the tips of the hair, while the rest [of the body] is white. The right foot is in the *svastika* posture, while the left foot is drawn up. He has long arms, broad shoulders, and is adorned with serpent ornaments. One should contemplate him as having a dark blue tip to his nose and great wings.

One should meditate upon oneself in the form of Garuḍa during the three junctions of the day: with a face formidable with fangs, blazing with a crown and diadem, adorned with all ornaments, and beautiful in every limb; with Ananta as the bracelet on the left arm and Vāsuki as the sacred thread; Takṣaka as the waist-band and Kārkoṭaka as the necklace; Padma on the right ear and Mahāpadma on the left; Śaṅkha on the region of the head and Gulika between the arms. Thus one should meditate upon oneself as having the form of Garuḍa at the three periods of worship.

It quickly destroys poison, like fire cast into water. "Oṃ, salutation to the King of Birds, O Lord of the pair of wings of the Vedas! O Vainateya, salutations to you; salutations again and again to Śrī Garuḍa. Having thus meditated upon oneself as Garuḍa, and having meditated upon Garuḍa within the unmanifest lotus of the heart-lotus, one should worship him with mental offerings.

Thereafter, for the purpose of performing the preliminary consecration (*adhivāsa*) of the shadow-image (*chāyā*) before him, one should place upon a heap of grain a water-vat (*droṇī*) made of gold or other metals, or one made of clay, or likewise a large vessel (*kaṭāha*). Having filled it with scented water, having caused the declaration of an auspicious day (*puṇyāha*) to be recited, and having sprinkled [the area], one should perform the rites of drying, burning, and flooding. Then, having performed the worship of the archway (*toraṇa*), the banner (*dhvaja*), and the ritual pitcher (*kumbha*), one should invoke the cloth-painting (*paṭa*) onto a grass mat (*kūrca*) and lay it down there with its head toward the east, following the sequence of reabsorption (*saṃhārakrama*).

Having displayed the *cakramudrā* with the *sudarśana* mantra, one should place the protective jar (*rakṣākumbha*) together with the water-pot (*karaka*) right there upon a heap of grain in the direction of Yama. Within that [jar], having displayed the *cakramudrā* with the *sudarśana* mantra over Brahmā in the water-pot, one should perform the preliminary consecration (*adhivāsa*) for a watch (*yāma*), or half a watch, or immediately. Thereafter, having lifted the *kūrca* from the net and having invoked [the deity] onto the cloth painting (*paṭa*).

Having taken two such gold and silver rods (*śalākikā*) capable of filling an *āḍhaka* each for the purpose of opening the eyes, and having placed the gold vessel with its rod in front on the eastern side of the grain-platform and the silver vessel with its rod on the western side; and having placed the eight grains—wild rice, *śāli* rice, mung beans, millet, *priyaṅgu*, barley, sesame, and wheat—separately in vessels around those two; and having filled the first vessel with honey and the second with clarified butter.

Having made the formal resolve (saṃkalpa), “I shall perform the act of opening the eyes,” and having caused the declaration of an auspicious day (puṇyāha) to be recited; having sprinkled those [eyes] with water and strewn [the ground] around them; having invoked and worshipped the Sun in the honey and the Moon in the clarified butter; and with the sounding of Vedic chants and musical instruments, having opened the right eye with a golden probe smeared with honey using the mantra “citraṃ devānām” and the left eye with a silver probe smeared with ghee using the mantra “taccakṣuḥ. Then, having removed the covering cloth.

Having displayed honey and clarified butter, as well as the eight grains, and having performed the same for the eight *nāgas*, one should make the formal resolve (*saṃkalpa*): "I shall perform the rite of the shadow-bath. Then, having placed sixteen jars endowed with the proper characteristics upon a pedestal of grain in front [of the image], and having filled them with the respective substances according to the previously mentioned procedure, and having strewn [the ground with grass], one should perform the invocation of the deities preceded by the recitation of the *puṇyāha* formula. Finally, one should invoke Garuḍa from the cloth-painting into a mirror provided with a tuft of grass.

Having performed worship preceded by the offering of *arghya* and other honors, and having bathed [the image] with sixteen jars containing ghee while reciting the sixteen verses of the *Puruṣasūkta*, and having worshipped it with the *Garuḍagāyatrī*, one should again invoke [the deity] onto the cloth. Then, having prepared a pedestal of grain consisting of two *bhāras* of *śāli* rice, half that amount of *taṇḍula* rice, and half that amount of sesame seeds, and having covered it with new garments and spread *darbha* grass over it;

Having consecrated with fragrant substances a new cloth, a tiger skin, a cotton mattress, a jeweled woolen blanket, linen, and variegated garments; having strewn them around with *darbha* grass; having sprinkled them with water from the *puṇyāha* rite; and having laid [the image] upon that bed; and having performed the worship of the door and the archway; then, having laid it down, one should place on a heap of grain to the right side of the cloth-painting a great jar together with a small water-vessel, and eight subsidiary jars possessing the proper characteristics, and fill them with scented water.

Having prepared all those [images]—consisting of cloth with a beard (*sakūrca*), jewels, and idols of various deities covered with *aśvattha* sprouts—and having strewn [the sacrificial grass] around them (*paristīrya*) and sprinkled them (*prokṣya*), one should worship in the great jar (*mahākumbha*) from the base (*ādhāra*) up to the lotus (*padma*). Then, having invoked Garuḍa with the mantra: "Come, O Lord of the Sky, O mighty-armed Vainateya, Lord of Birds! O King of Birds, grant your presence; be gracious here; salutations to you! *Kṣipa oṃ svāhā āgacchāgaccha*," one should worship him with his *gāyatrī*.

Having performed [the rite] with *sahasrāra huṃ phaṭ*, having invoked [the deity] with "Come, come" (*āgacchāgaccha*), and having worshipped [him], one should likewise invoke Indra and the other deities in the pitchers located in the east and the other directions. Having purified the Garuḍa on the cloth-painting through the rites of drying (*śoṣaṇa*) and so forth, and having dissolved the principles (*tattvas*) in sequence and then re-generated them, one should perform the *adhivāsa-homa* (consecration oblation) either in the four sacrificial pits (*kuṇḍa*) or on the four altars (*sthaṇḍila*), or else in a single pit, in the kitchen, or in the perpetual fire-pit. Among the four pits, one should invoke Satya in the eastern pit.

Having invoked Suparṇa in the southern pit with the *Bṛhatsāman* mantra, and having invoked Garuḍa in the western pit with the *Gāruḍa* mantra; having invoked Tārkṣya in the northern pit with the *Rathantara Sāman* and the *Garuḍa* mantra; or else, having invoked [the deity] in all the pits with the respective mantras of those deities, or with sacrificial fuel (*samidh*), clarified butter (*ājya*), and *caru* oblation, using the *Puruṣasūkta*; or, in one single pit, having invoked [him] with the mantra: "Oṃ, obeisance to the Blessed Vainateya, obeisance."

Having offered oblations with the Garuḍa mantra, one should offer oblations in the four pits starting from the east, respectively with the mantras "Oṃ bhūḥ svāhā," "Oṃ bhuvaḥ svāhā," "Oṃ suvaḥ svāhā," and "Oṃ bhūrbhuvassuvaḥ svāhā," using honey, milk, curd, and clarified butter, each one hundred times. Then, having separately collected the remnants of the offerings (saṃpāta) into another vessel.

Having touched the feet, belly, and head of the image situated on the cloth, respectively, with the mantras accompanied by *svāhā* but devoid of *namaḥ*, and having likewise touched all the limbs with the *kūrca* grass-bundle; and having offered oblations of jaggery, clarified butter, and honey into the northern fire-pit (*auttarakuṇḍa*) with the Viṣṇu-Gāyatrī mantra; and having touched the face with the residual drops (*saṃpāta*); and having thus completed the fire-sacrifice (*homa*).

Having sprinkled [the deity] on the cloth with water from the four jars located in the cardinal directions—using respectively branches of the *pālāśa*, *khadira*, *aśvattha*, and *bilva* trees while reciting the *abliṅga* mantras—or alternatively with water from the jars situated in the corners, using the branch of this [tree] and the Viṣṇu-Gāyatrī; having spread the cloth facing the temple; having mentally conceived the Yoga-pīṭha upon it; having worshipped it with perfumes and other offerings; having meditated on the Yoga-pīṭha within one's own joined palms; and having brought down Garuḍa, who resides in the lotus of the heart, onto that [Yoga-pīṭha] by means of the *recaka* breath, one should meditate upon him.

Having meditated that [the deity] has entered through the *brahmarandhra* of the cloth [image] which was recited with the *gāyatrī*, having closed the *brahmarandhra* with the *praṇava*, and having restrained it with the *mudrā*, one should meditate and pray for its presence: "O Mahābala, O Mahābāhu, O Vainateya, O Lord of Birds! Be present upon this cloth; salutations to You, whose form is the *praṇava*. O Lord of Birds, being invoked, bring about the success of the rites. The three worlds are to be invoked for the prosperity of the festival of the God. Thus, having prayed to Garuḍa.

Having worshipped with the *arghya* and other ritual offerings using its *gāyatrī*, and having offered the four kinds of food, and having done likewise for the Great Jar (*mahākumbha*), one should thereafter recite: "Oṃ! Salutations to you, Garuḍa, the vehicle of Mahāviṣṇu, of immeasurable splendor, the lord of all serpents, and the death of [all] snakes. Salutations, salutations to you, O Lord of Birds, whose body is sacred study; salutations to you, O King of Birds, who uprooted the Kalpa tree. Salutations to the one who brought down the jar of nectar and who liberated those bound by birth."

Salutations to You, the conqueror of the lords of gods and asuras, who are adorned by the king of serpents; salutations to You, the support of all this universe which is Your own support. Whose two wings are the *Bṛhat* and *Rathaṃtara* chants, whose two eyes are the *Gāyatrī* and the *Trivṛt Sāman*, and whose head is known as the *Stoma*—salutations to Him, the perfection of whose limbs is the *Vāmadevya*. Salutations to the Lord of the vital breaths and the winds, the one with the form of Garuḍa. Drive away all defects, bring forth virtues from every side, destroy all obstacles, and make me Your very self.

Having praised [the deity] in this manner and recited the Gāruḍa-mantra according to his capacity, and having passed the night in vigil with the chanting of the Vedas and the sounding of musical instruments, the preceptor then, at dawn, having completed his daily rites, enters the inner sanctum (garbhagṛha). Having worshipped the primary image (mūlabera) with water for honor (arghya) and other offerings, he invokes [the deity] from that into the festival image (utsavabimba) and propitiates it with the sixteen modes of service (ṣoḍaśopacāra), excluding the ritual dismissal (udvāsana).

Having adorned that Garuḍa depicted on the cloth with garlands and other offerings, and having separately mounted the image for the procession upon the back of an elephant, a chariot, a palanquin, or some other vehicle, one should lead it—accompanied by the sounds of kettledrums, clay drums, tabors, conchs, and trumpets, as well as dance and song—around the village and the temple in a clockwise direction by Brāhmaṇas who carry on their heads a hundred pots containing sprouts, until reaching the vicinity of the flagstaff.

The flagstaff (dhvajastaṃbha) is of three kinds of wood: having pith within, having pith without, or being without pith. Campaka, devadāru, candana, khadira, sāla, bilva, kakubha, āmalaka, and others have pith within. Kramuka, nālikera, tāla, hintāla, veṇu, and others have pith without. Excluding that which is without pith, one should take wood with pith either within or without, auspiciously measuring one hundred cubits in length.

Having brought pillars equal in height to eighty *tāla*s, or the height of a palace, or the height of a gate-tower (*gopura*), and having divided them into four parts: one part at the top is for the capital (*namaskara*); the bases supporting it are two *tāla*s long, half that wide, and half that thick; they are thick at the base and taper toward the top, being perforated at the bottom from the three tiers of the pedestal (*pīṭha*). Having fixed those [ornaments] upon the tops of the pillars:

Having fixed the flagstaff (dhvajayaṣṭi) into the two perforated top-seats (agrapiṭha), and having likewise placed it upon the pillar; and having attached one bamboo pole to the flagstaff, or nine, seven, or five bamboo poles; having thus positioned the flagstaff-pillar on the northern side of the seat; the Preceptor (ācārya), together with Brahmins learned in the Vedas, washes it with mantras containing the word "water" (abliṅga), covers it with kuśa grass blades pointing upwards, and winds it around with garlands of darbha grass.

Once the pillar-base has been cleared, having placed iron seeds and other materials therein, one should firmly fix the flagstaff (dhvajastaṃbha) in that base with the *Viṣṇusūkta* so that it stands facing the temple. Then, at the location of the pillar's base, one should have a square altar constructed—measuring seven, five, or three cubits in length and the same in width, and rising one cubit in height. Having divided that altar into three parts:

In the middle of one side, there should be a pedestal (*pīṭha*) four finger-breadths in height, provided with three tiers (*mekhalā*). Upon its third part, having fashioned a lotus in the center of the pericarp (*karṇikā*) so that it may be properly positioned according to the commencement [of the rite], one should cause a water-shed (*prapā*) to be constructed around the pedestal. This shed should be equipped with sixteen pillars, adorned with curtains, variegated *darbha* garlands, flower garlands, canopies, and so forth, and provided with four doors. Having caused the proclamation of an auspicious day (*puṇyāha*) and having sprinkled [the site] with consecrated water, one should prepare a grain-platform (*dhānyapīṭha*) to the south of the pillars.

Having arranged a set of nine pitchers (kumbha) along with their characteristic marks upon that [pedestal], and having invoked and worshipped Garuḍa in the center and Indra and the others in the eight directions, one should sprinkle the pillar in due order with their respective mantras. Then, having fastened the banner-cloth to the opening at the top of the bamboo pole with a cord made of triple-stranded threads and having a thickness equal to the thumb, using the Puruṣa-mantra, one should hoist the flag according to the procedure to be described hereafter; or alternatively, one may install the pillar already fixed with the flag at its peak.

Thereafter, at an auspicious moment, the preceptor, having established Garuḍa depicted on the cloth facing the temple while the sounds of Vedic chants and musical instruments resound in all directions, himself reciting the *Garuḍamālā-mantra* and other mantras, worships Garuḍa with *arghya* and other offerings; sprinkles him with the water from the great pitcher using a *kūrca* while reciting the *Garuḍagāyatrī*; contemplates the pitchers as being Garuḍa by means of the *Gāruḍa-mantra*; performs the *prāṇapratiṣṭhā* (consecration of the vital breaths) according to the rules; and installs the root mantra upon him.

Having shown that mudrā with the Gāyatrī mantra, having worshipped with arghya and other offerings, and having invoked Indra and the other deities in the eight directions and worshipped them with perfumes, flowers, and so forth; having offered flattened rice, coconut, cakes, mung-bean rice, and other items to the one situated upon the cloth; and having hoisted the flag with the chanting of the Vedas while reciting the mantra "Suparṇo 'si," one should pray for the presence of Garuḍa within the interior of the flag until the concluding bath (avabhṛtha), using the verse that will be mentioned hereafter.

"O destroyer of enemies in battle, who dispelled the armor of the asuras with the wealth of the wind from the waves produced by the flapping of the wings of the Lord of Birds—be present upon this cloth until the moment of the concluding bath of the festival. Having thus prayed, he brings the festival image near the flagstaff, shows it the bird (Garuḍa), and appoints Garuḍa for the purpose of summoning all the deities. Then, taking a handful of flowers right in the presence of the festival image, [he recites]: "From this day forth, until the final day of the pilgrimage site..."

"O Lord of Birds, establish your presence for the king, the kingdom, the village, and especially for the sacrificer and the Vaiṣṇavas—for their satisfaction, nourishment, the destruction of all enemies, and for the sake of conquering untimely death. O Vainateya, be gracious! Om. Reciting this verse and offering a handful of flowers upon Garuḍa, one should thereafter petition the Blessed One: "Whether through ignorance or lack of knowledge, that which was prescribed has not been performed by me."

"May all that be fulfilled; may you always be well-satisfied. Having thus informed [the Lord]: "Oṃ Acyuta, O Lord of the World, O Janārdana whose form is mantra! Protect me, O Lotus-eyed One! Forgive me, O Ājya! Be gracious, Oṃ!"—and having led the Blessed One into the interior of the pavilion, one should worship Him according to the prescribed rites. Having established a lamp near the banner that remains unextinguished day and night, one should worship Garuḍa every day until the time of the banner's hoisting and lowering. Now follows the beating of the drum (bherī).

Now, the procedure for beating the drum is described. On that night, the preceptor, having worshipped the deity preceded by breath control (prāṇāyāma) and internal sacrifice (antaryāga), having presented the offering (naivedya), and having performed the fire oblation (homa), should smear the ground in front of the flag-pedestal with cow-dung water into a square shape. Having adorned it with lime powder and having prepared a square pedestal out of five *droṇas* of rice grain, he should draw the Wheel of Time (*kālacakra*) there.

In the midst of that, having installed the *balibimba*—the image of the deity into which the power (*śakti*) has been invoked from the *mūlabera*—facing the flagpole, and having worshipped it; and having placed a large drum (*mahābherī*) covered with a new cloth upon a pedestal of grain on a smeared ground in front of it, and having set down its southern corner.

In the eastern part of the drum, a collection of conchs; in the southeast, a heap of *kāhala* trumpets; in the south, *maddala* drums; in the southwest, *mukhatantī*, flutes, and lutes; in the west, *uḍuka*, *mṛdaṅga*, and small cymbals (*hrasvasaṃmardani*); in the northwest, *karaṭī* and bronze cymbals (*kāṃsyatāla*); in the north, *paṭaha* and small *paṭaha* drums; and in the northeast, *ḍuḍḍuka* drums, lutes (*vallī*), and hand-bells (*hastaghaṇṭā*). In the absence of these, one should arrange whatever is available according to the circumstances.

Outside of them, having stationed the courtesans on the south, the singers in front, the dancers on the north, the groups of panegyrists, and the other instrumentalists each in their respective places; and having placed a jar endowed with auspicious marks upon a heap of grain in the region to the west of the drums; and having caused the proclamation of an auspicious day; and having sprinkled the drums and other instruments, as well as a Pāraśava son who has bathed, is pure, adorned, holds *darbha* grass in his hand, and wears the sacred thread and an upper garment.

In the center of the drum: *Oṃ*, salutation to Prakṛti, whose nature consists of the three guṇas. On the right: *Oṃ*, salutation to Viṣṇu; *Oṃ Śrīṃ*, salutation to Śrī. In the center: *Oṃ*, salutation to Brahmā. On the right: *Oṃ*, salutation to Viṣṇu; on the left: *Oṃ*, salutation to Rudra. On the right face: *Oṃ*, salutation to Sūrya. On the left face: *Oṃ*, salutation to Candra.

In the leather cord: *Oṃ vāsukaye namaḥ*. On the right side, in the nine apertures: *Oṃ vāgīśvaryai namaḥ*, *Oṃ kriyāyai namaḥ*, *Oṃ kīrtyai namaḥ*, *Oṃ lakṣmyai namaḥ*, *Oṃ sṛṣṭyai namaḥ*, *Oṃ vidyāyai namaḥ*, *Oṃ kāntyai namaḥ*, *Oṃ durgāyai namaḥ*, *Oṃ gaṇapataye namaḥ*. In the apertures on the left side: *Oṃ atraye namaḥ*, *Oṃ bhṛgave namaḥ*, *Oṃ vasiṣṭhāya namaḥ*, *Oṃ bhārgavāya namaḥ*, *Oṃ nāradāya namaḥ*, *Oṃ*...

Salutation to Gautama; Oṃ, salutation to Bharadvāja; Oṃ, salutation to Viśvāmitra; Oṃ, salutation to Marīci—thus in the eight directions. Oṃ, salutation to Rambhā; Oṃ, salutation to Menakā; Oṃ, salutation to Urvaśī; Oṃ, salutation to Tilottamā; Oṃ, salutation to Sumukhī; Oṃ, salutation to Sundarī; Oṃ, salutation to Ramaṇī; Oṃ, salutation to Yāmavardhinī—thus. To the presiding deity of the corners: Oṃ, salutation to Vāyu. To the presiding deity of the conch: Oṃ, salutation to Viṣṇu. To the presiding deity of the trumpet...

To the presiding deity of speech, Oṃ, obeisance to Vāgīśvarī; to the presiding deities of the maddala drum, the three forms (Trimūrtis), obeisance; Oṃ, to the presiding deity of the mouth, Brahmā, obeisance; Oṃ, to the presiding deity of the mṛdaṅga drum, Rudra, obeisance; Oṃ, to the presiding deity of the jhallarī cymbal, Viṣṇu, obeisance; Oṃ, to the presiding deity of the paṭaha drum, Śrī, obeisance; Oṃ, to the presiding deity of the ḍamaruka drum, Īśāna, obeisance.

Oṃ, salutation to the presiding deity of Uḍukkā, the six-faced one (Ṣaṇmukha). Oṃ, salutation to the presiding deity of Karaṭī, Dharmarāja. Oṃ, salutation to the presiding deity of Timilā, Vāyu. Oṃ, salutation to the presiding deity of Ḍakkarī, Candraśekhara. Oṃ, salutation to the presiding deity of Tālā, Brahmā. Oṃ, salutation to the presiding deity of the fragment of the left hand, Śrī. Oṃ, salutation to the presiding deity of the fragment of the right hand, Pārvatī. Having thus worshipped with perfumes and other offerings.

Having invoked [the deities] into the water-pot with the mantra "And the sacrifices," and having worshipped them; and having invoked and worshipped Indra and the others in the directions starting from the east, and having offered the oblation; at an auspicious moment, having uttered the mantra "Oṃ naṃ, obeisance to the Supreme, obeisance to the one whose self is the subtle element of sound" and having recited "And the sacrifices," one should strike the drum with the corner [of the hand]. Thereafter, a man of low caste (pāraśava), taking hold of that drum, should cause it to be sounded by the Guru while Indra and the host of Maruts are being invoked.

The divine weapons, as well as the inhabitants of Vaikuṇṭha—all the attendants of Viṣṇu protected by Viṣvaksena—along with Kumuda and the others together with their leaders, are to be invoked in that sacrifice. Also, the invocation of Brahmā (Viriñci) should be performed by the sages headed by Marīci who dwell in the world of Brahmā, and likewise by those who dwell in the world of Rudra, together with the first assemblies and Rudra himself, whose vehicle is the bull; and similarly, the other inhabitants of those respective worlds are to be invoked.

In that great festival, together with their vehicles and retinues, the Vidyās personified and the Trayī (the three Vedas) along with the Aṅgas which bestow nourishment must be invited; they are to be summoned by the calling out of all their respective names. Having thus performed the invocation for all the gods, one should then, for the sake of the offerings to the deities of the quarters, lead the Sudarśana image—either from the Nityotsava shrine or from the Annamūrdhan—to each direction around the enclosures, preceded by the beating of drums, and having circumambulated it.

Having reached the center of the village, having invoked Brahmā there and worshipped him, and having invoked Indra and the other deities in each direction for the sake of the bali offering and worshipped them, and having prayed for their presence—having performed this together with their respective *tālas* and so forth—and having caused the *gāruḍa-tāla* to be sounded in the intervals elsewhere, he should enter the temple and install [the deity] as before; or else, taking either the festival image, or the Sudarśana alone in the form of food (*annamūrti*), or even the drum (*bherī*) alone.

One should perform the invocation of the deities in the various streets there according to the prescribed rule. Those people who hear the drum at the time of the invocation of the deities must not cross a river, nor travel more than a *yojana* by vehicle. If a person, disregarding the festival out of delusion, should go far away, he goes to hell and experiences suffering both after death and even here. Therefore, until the final purificatory bath (*avabhṛtha*), one should remain right there and not depart. If the one by whom the sprouts were sown for the sake of the banner, for whatever reason...

If the preceptor is somehow incapacitated or has passed away, another person—be it a son, a disciple, a brother, or a more qualified officiating priest (ṛtvij)—should complete the remainder of the rite with his permission. Thus ends the thirty-third chapter, titled "The Procedure for Hoisting the Banner," in the *Kriyākairavacandrikā* composed by the venerable Varāhaguru. Chapter Thirty-four:
Now, the procedure for the festival (utsava) is described.

Before the day of the festival’s commencement—on the seventh or the fifth day—the preceptor, in rites of initiation, in ceremonial bathing, in all expiatory rituals, at the beginning of the four Vedic vows, in sacrificial ceremonies, at the time of collecting the earth, in the rite of gathering the stone, at the time of installing the ritual pegs, in the rite of hoisting the banner, in various consecrations, in external and internal rites, and when the office of *ācārya* has been assumed, the performer should perform the shaving of the head and the ritual bath.

According to the statement, "If the ritual action were performed without sowing, it would be fruitless," one should first act accordingly; thereafter, during an auspicious moment (muhūrta), following the preliminary consecration (adhivāsa), one should cause the ritual offering of sprouts (utsavāṅkurārpaṇa) to be performed according to the rules for three sets of one hundred and eight vessels such as *pālikā*s, or for thirty-six vessels of the three types.

Having adorned the house, pavilion, palace, gate-towers, and walkways with arches, banners, canopies, plantain trees, betel-nut trees, full water-jars, rows of sprouting shoots, a hundred lamps, agallochum incense, and other such ornaments; and having constructed a sacrificial pavilion (yāgamaṇḍapa) in the first enclosure or the second enclosure—in the intermediate directions and all the quarters—according to the available space, measuring seven cubits or five cubits in length, with its width and length being proportionate, and provided with four doors; and having constructed a water-shed (prapā) surrounding it.

In the middle third of that [area], having caused an altar (*vedi*) to be constructed, one cubit in height and two or three cubits in width; to its east, a square pit for the *Āhavanīya* fire; to the south, a bow-shaped pit for the *Dakṣiṇāgni*; to the west, a circular pit for the *Gārhapatya*; to the north, a triangular pit for the *Sabhya*, a square pit for the *Āvasathya*, or else omitting the *Āvasathya*, or even a single pit for the *Āhavanīya*.

Having fashioned [the sacrificial implements] as before—having had the archways, the *sruk* and *sruva* ladles, the eight auspicious symbols, various vessels for the fire-oblation (*homapātra*), seats, and other requisites for the sacrifice prepared—and having adorned the sacrificial pavilion with such embellishments as canopies, garlands of *darbha* grass, archways, flower garlands, incense, lamps, unbroken grains (*akṣata*), and plantain pillars.

First, having performed the selection of the four *ācāryas*, then the sixteen *ṛtviks*, and subsequently their attendants, the patron (*yajamāna*) shall adorn them with ornaments such as bracelets, earrings, rings, linen garments, upper cloths, turbans, perfumes, and ointments. At the commencement and at the conclusion of the festival, one should perform the bath (*snapana*) prescribed for those two [the image and the deity]. On the day prior to the festival, the preceptor (*guru*), together with the guardians of the images (*mūrtipas*), shall enter the inner sanctum (*garbhamandira*) for the purpose of the preliminary consecration (*adhivāsa*) of the festival.

Having worshipped the primary image (mūlabera) with water for honor (arghya) and other offerings; having invoked [the deity] from the root-mantra into the festival image (utsavabimba) and worshipped it; having made the formal resolve (saṃkalpa) for the purpose of the preliminary consecration (adhivāsa), saying, "I shall perform the rite of binding the protective thread"; having performed the binding of the protective thread for the God and the Goddess according to the rules, preceded by the declaration of an auspicious day (puṇyāha); having worshipped them again with water for honor and other offerings; having presented large cakes (mahāpūpa) and other foods; having had them placed in another location by three devotees of the Lord (bhāgavatas); and having performed the ritual bathing (snāna) according to the rules, one should adorn them with garments of linen and other ornaments.

Having offered *paramānna* (sweet rice), having prepared a bed according to the prescribed rules as in a formal consecration (*pratiṣṭhā*), having laid the Lord upon it together with the two Goddesses, having placed lamps in the corners along with vessels containing sprouts, and having consecrated the fire, he should perform the *adhivāsa-homa* according to the rules with fuel-sticks (*samidh*), clarified butter (*ājya*), and sacrificial porridge (*caru*), using the root mantra and the *Puruṣasūkta*. Then, having praised the Lord with hymns accompanied by the sounds of musical instruments and the chanting of the Vedas, the Guru, with a concentrated mind, should pass the night in vigilance.

Then at dawn, during an auspicious moment, the preceptor shall raise the deity with the mantra "Arise," worship Him, and address Him with this verse: "Be gracious, O Lord of the gods! A festival is being performed by me, from this time until the day of the Flower Sacrifice. O Lord of the World, whatever action I perform for Your pleasure, having taken all of that unto Yourself, be gracious to me through Your mercy. Om. Having thus addressed Him, [he should proceed].

While the Brahmins in the various directions recite the Śākuna Sūkta, having placed the Lord upon a palanquin or other vehicle with the mantra "idaṃ viṣṇuḥ," and having invoked Garuḍa while the Brahmins carry the vehicle, one should lead the Lord—adorned with all ornaments and accompanied by all ritual offerings—clockwise around the entire series of enclosures. Then, having descended from the vehicle and seated Him upon a golden auspicious throne (bhadrāsana) within the pavilion;

Having displayed all the materials for the festival that had been gathered in the assembly of people, saying, "This has come from here; all this has come from there," and having performed the ritual of bathing according to the previously stated sequence, preceded by the placement of the mantra-seat, the preceptor and the patron—having considered the extent of their wealth—having offered the great oblation (mahāhavis) and having sacrificed according to the rules, lead the deity into the interior of the temple. Then, when the afternoon has arrived, they go outside together with Garuḍa or Viṣvaksena.

Having collected the clay according to the prescribed rules as before, and having entered the sacrificial pavilion (yāgamaṇḍapa), one should perform the rite of offering the festival sprouts (utsavāṅkura) into vessels such as the *trivarga* and *upālika*. Then, having set aside the rites of the binding of the auspicious thread (*kautuka-bandhana*) and the preliminary consecration (*adhivāsa*) for the Sudarśana, the bathing image (*snapana*), the daily festival image (*nityotsava*), and the offering image (*balibimba*)—just as was done for the auspicious thread of the primary deity—one should enter the sacrificial pavilion and seat them upon their respective seats. Thereafter, the preceptor (guru), having entered the hall together with the patron (yajamāna), should prostrate himself like a staff before the Deity.

"O Blessed One, O Lotus-eyed Lord of Gods, I shall perform the rite of festivity for the sake of the great festival; therefore, be gracious unto me. Having thus made this request, and having tied the *pratisara* (protective cord) for the festival to the root-image, the bathing image, the offering image, and the discus according to the rules, he should then prepare a pedestal of grain on the altar using five *bhāras* of rice and half that amount of sesame.

Having covered them at intervals with cloths, one should place there nine new jars—each washed, containing thread, scented water, the nine gems, the pollen of fragrant flowers, and a piece of coral, each filled with a *niṣka* of gold, and each having its opening covered with a bunch of *aśvattha* sprouts; the central jar should be covered with a pair of cloths, while the remaining ones are covered with a single cloth seven, six, or five cubits long and half that in width.

Having placed [the images] upon heaps of grain on the ground of the altar, having had the *puṇyāha* (day of merit) proclaimed together with the Vaiṣṇavas, and having sprinkled [them with water], one should worship the door-arches, the banners, and the jars. Having invoked Vāsudeva and the others into the jars situated in the directions starting from the east, and Puruṣa and the others as before into those in the corners starting from the southeast, and having worshipped them, one should wrap the Sudarśana and the *balibimba* separately with cloths for the eight auspicious signs. Then, having placed them upon heaps of grain beneath the altar and having worshipped them.

Having drawn the lotus-wheel (*cakrābja*) on the altar according to the rules and the previously mentioned method, and having worshipped Vāsudeva along with his limbs (*sāṅga*) and retinue (*saparivāra*) there according to the rules as before; and having performed the full worship while the chanting of the Vedas proceeds in the four directions, the Guru shall invoke Vāsudeva into the *āhavanīya* fire, Saṃkarṣaṇa into the *dakṣiṇāgni*, Pradyumna into the *gārhapatya*, Aniruddha into the *sabhyāgni*, and the Root-Mantra (*mūla-mantra*) together with its head (*mūrdhan*) into the *āvasathyāgni*; and having invoked them into the lotuses upon the auspicious seats (*bhadrāsana*) situated in the midst of the fires of their respective sacrificial pits (*kuṇḍa*), and having worshipped them, he shall pray for their presence at the conclusion of the ritual bath (*tīrthāvasānika*).

In the sacrificial pits (kuṇḍas), having offered one hundred and eight or twenty-eight oblations for each with their respective deity-mantras using clarified butter, flowers, incense materials, fuel-sticks, milk, curd, sesame seeds, rice, and barley; and having offered, in the sequence of the Āhavanīya and other fires, offerings of milk-rice (pāyasa), kṛsara, jaggery, turmeric-rice, and mung-bean rice, with each verse of the sixteen verses of the Puruṣasūkta.

In the fifth fire, one should offer milk-rice (pāyasa) dedicated to the gods beginning with Brahmā, uttering their respective names in the dative case followed by "svāhā" and accompanied by their retinues, according to the procedure to be described: Oṃ brahmaṇe saparivārāya svāhā | Oṃ prajāpataye saparivārāya svāhā | Oṃ rudrāya saparivārāya svāhā | Oṃ sarvebhyo devebhyaḥ saparivārebhyaḥ svāhā | Oṃ chandobhyaḥ saparivārebhyaḥ svāhā |

Oṃ, svāhā to the Vedas together with their retinues! Oṃ, svāhā to the Ṛṣis together with their retinues! Oṃ, svāhā to the Gandharvas together with their retinues! Oṃ, svāhā to the reptiles together with their retinues! Oṃ, svāhā to the Yakṣas together with their retinues! Oṃ, svāhā to the Apsarases together with their retinues! Oṃ, svāhā to the months and so forth together with their retinues! Oṃ, svāhā to the seasons together with their retinues! Oṃ, svāhā to the solstices together with their retinues!

Oṃ, to the years together with their retinues, svāhā! Oṃ, to all the goddesses together with their retinues, svāhā! Oṃ, to the continents together with their retinues, svāhā! Oṃ, to the oceans together with their retinues, svāhā! Oṃ, to the mountains together with their retinues, svāhā! Oṃ, to the rivers together with their retinues, svāhā! Oṃ, to the spirits together with their retinues, svāhā! Oṃ, to the animals together with their retinues, svāhā! Oṃ, to the trees together with their retinues, svāhā!

Oṃ, svāhā to the medicinal herbs together with their retinues! Oṃ, svāhā to the lords of the forest together with their retinues! Oṃ, svāhā to those born from sprouts together with their retinues! Oṃ, svāhā to those born from sweat together with their retinues! Oṃ, svāhā to those born from eggs together with their retinues! Oṃ, svāhā to those born from a womb together with their retinues! Oṃ, svāhā to the seven worlds beginning with Bhūr together with their retinues!

"Oṃ, svāhā to the seven netherworlds beginning with Atala, together with their retinues! Oṃ, svāhā to the gatekeepers beginning with Caṇḍa, together with their retinues! Having thus offered oblations, one should offer the final oblation (*pūrṇāhuti*) with the five Upaniṣadic mantras, the *vyāhṛtis*, and the verse "idaṃ viṣṇuḥ. In this manner, one should daily offer oblations in the evening and morning until the day of the pilgrimage, using the materials prescribed for the *bali* offerings on that specific day, omitting the ritual dismissal (*udvāsana*) of the respective deities at each stage.

One should offer the oblation substance into either a single fire, or into three, or into four fires; by that means, one should properly protect the fire. As for the offering of the *bali*, it should first be performed in the sacrificial pavilion (*yāgamaṇḍapa*). The procedure for this is as follows: having brought forth the image of the *cakra* along with the food-form (*annamūrti*) from the sacrificial pavilion, one should invoke and worship Kumuda and the other deities before the doors on pure ground, and then present the *bali*.

While the vessels for the *bali* offerings, the bell, the flower-vessel, the water-pitcher (*karaka*), the incense burner, the lamp-stand, and the torch-bearers proceed in front, the image of the food (*annamūrti*) follows behind them, then the discus (*cakra*), and after that the daily festival icon (*nityotsavārcā*). Having done this, and having offered the *bali* preceded by water at the doors and in the enclosures (*āvaraṇa*) to Caṇḍa and the other deities, and having displayed the *balimudrā* and the eight auspicious signs (*maṅgalāṣṭaka*).

Beginning from the center of the village and proceeding in order up to the northeast (Brahma) direction, one should worship the respective deities in those various locations together with the threefold music (tauryatrika), and offer the bali-oblation. Then, at the great bali-pedestal, one should offer the remaining sacrificial materials as a bali-oblation intended for all the attendants (pārṣadas). Having circumambulated the bali, one should enter the temple. In this manner, one should offer the bali in the evening and in the morning, starting from the hoisting of the flag until the conclusion of the pilgrimage (tīrtha).

On the night of the commencement day and on the day of completion, one should offer a single *bali* offering; during the intermediate days, one should offer two *balis*, both by day and by night. On the occasion of a sacred pilgrimage site (*tīrtha*), or when an eclipse, solstice (*ayana*), equinox (*viṣuva*), and so forth occur, one should offer two *balis*. In a place devoid of villages and the like, in the center of the site, one should present the *bali* to Brahmā in front of the Great Seat (*mahāpīṭha*). As for the materials for the *bali*: on the first day, one should combine fruits, flowers, powdered rice, *karaṃbha*, parched grain (*lājā*), and sacrificial porridge (*caru*).

On the second day, one should offer the oblation by mixing *caru* with sesame and rice. On the third day, however, one should mix parched grain (*lāja*) and flour cakes (*dhānyāpūpikā*) with *caru*. On the fourth day, one should mix groats (*saktu*), rice flour, and coconut water with *caru*. On the fifth day, one should mix lotus seeds, milk-rice (*pāyasa*), and rice grains with *caru*. On the sixth day, one should mix flour cakes (*apūpa*) with *caru*. For the three days beginning with the seventh, one should mix the four kinds of food with flour cakes and groats. One should offer the oblation (*bali*) in this sequence.

Then, when an auspicious moment (sumuhūrta) has arrived, the preceptor, having raised the Lord—who is seated upon His couch and adorned with the festive thread (utsavakautuka)—with the mantra “Arise,” and having exited that temple together with seven Brahmins while they recite the Svasti-sūkta; and having chanted the Rathantara Sāman; and having conveyed Him to another pavilion by means of a chariot, an elephant, or some other vehicle; and having placed Him upon the vehicle prescribed for that day with the mantra “Bhadraṃ karṇebhiḥ”; and having worshipped the Lord there preceded by the ritual of Nyāsa.

Having offered pṛthuka and other foods, having adorned [the deity] with silken garments, ornaments, garlands, and so forth, having sprinkled powdered camphor at the feet of the Lord, and having decorated the pathways on all sides with lamps well-sprinkled with ghee and other substances;
