He was preceded by well-adorned Brahmins carrying yak-tail fans, palm-leaf fans, peacock feathers, pearl umbrellas, swords, incense, and lamps; behind him, mounted upon Garuḍa—who stood with palms joined and a banner raised—was Viṣvaksena, who, having placed the two sandals in a golden vessel, held a staff in his hand and cleared the way for Viriñci and the other gods while bowing down. As he proceeded, he had ascended a golden palanquin.

Surrounded by Brahmins bearing royal insignia before him, by others learned in all the Vedas, Shastras, and Agamas, by Brahmins skilled in debate who were eager to defeat one another and chanting hymns composed of prose and verse, by bards dancing and singing, by musicians, and by others proficient in various branches of knowledge, he proceeded amidst the sounds of the four kinds of musical instruments—the stringed, the percussion, the wind, and the solid—while the entire retinue circumambulated him.

Likewise, having circumambulated the outer walkways clockwise, and at the time of entry, having also gone clockwise around the circular enclosure wall, one should lead the deity into the inner pavilion; there, having helped the deity descend from the vehicle onto the seat.

Having placed the mobile image (balibera) upon the offering pedestal outside the temple, and the fixed image (dhruvabera) within the sacrificial hall, one should worship them daily with the usual materials doubled in quantity. Following the deity’s circumambulation of the processional path, one should perform the ritual bathing according to the prescribed rules. In the case of a single image, the bathing should be performed upon the primary image (mūlabimba). In the case of multiple images, one should bathe either the festive image (utsavakautuka) or the bathing image (snapanakautuka), according to one's capacity and available materials.

Having seated the Lord upon the lion-throne in the pavilion, having performed the purification of the body and offered worship, having completed the rite of bathing and presented the great oblation (*mahāhavis*), and having reached the chamber of adornment, the preceptor (*deśika*)—having decorated the Lord with ornaments and the like while the image remains there—enters the sacrificial pavilion. Having performed the worship of the door-arches, the *kumbha*, the *mahākumbha*, the *upakumbha*, and the mandala, and having presented the offerings as prescribed, he performs the fire-oblation (*homa*) as before.

Having performed the offering of oblations (*balikarma*) along with the worship of the image (*bimba*) according to the previously prescribed rules, one should then adorn the festival image (*utsavārcā*), mount it upon the vehicle (*yāna*), and—accompanied by all ornaments as before—lead it clockwise around the village, the temple, and other sites. At various points along the way, having sprinkled with water all the offerings (*naivedya*) according to the rules—including betel leaves, rolls of betel (*vīṭikā*), flattened rice (*pṛthuka*), and other edible foods, coconut fruits, and water for drinking and sipping—using the *astra-mantra*, one should present them.

One should silently show a ripe fruit; having sprinkled all flowers, ornaments, and other items encountered on the way with the mantra, one should attach them to the limbs of the deity. Having thus led [the deity] clockwise around the village and the temple, and having entered the temple, one should place the deity from the carriage onto a palanquin, enter the pavilion, and worship there as before with all the ritual services (upacāras).

In this manner, until the day of the festival at the sacred site (tīrtha), one should daily please the Lord with unprecedented ornaments, garlands, garments, vehicles, gardens, and so forth, according to one's inclination. In villages and other such places, one should always perform a great festival for the Lord, either together with Śrī and Bhūmi or without them. On the sixth day, having placed the bathing image along with the festival procession and the auspicious throne (bhadrāsana) upon it, and having installed and worshipped water-pots upon a heap of grain in front of it.

Having worshipped the deity with services beginning from the seat for the mantra and ending with the seat for the bath; having bathed [the deity] with water-pots; and having fully honored [the deity] with services beginning from the garments and ending with the lamps—having performed all this in the same manner for the primary image (*mūlabera*) in the case of a single image; thereafter, having adorned the washed mortar with garments and other ornaments, having placed it upon a pedestal of rice, and having consecrated and honored it while meditating on Lakṣmī with the *Śrīsūkta*; and having washed and empowered the pestle with the root mantra.

The Guru, together with the image-worshippers (mūrtipas), having placed the night-powder (niśācūrṇa) in a mortar and taking up a pestle, grinds the night-powder with the pestle so that it becomes as fine as possible while the temple-maidens recite auspicious hymns. Having taken that powder, he places it in a jar wrapped in cloth. Having set down the jar—along with its brush (kūrca), small vessel (mallaka), and cloth—upon a pedestal on the sacrificial ground (sthaṇḍila), he worships it with the root mantra (mūlamantra) and offerings such as scents (gandha). Then, lifting the jar, he consecrates the Deity with those powders while reciting the Śrīsūkta.

The Guru, together with the image-worshippers (mūrtipās), having circumambulated the deity, prostrated with the eight-limbed salutation (aṣṭāṅga-praṇipāta), scattered handfuls of flowers (puṣpāñjali), and praised him with hymns, should conduct the festival adorned with all ornaments. On the seventh day, he should sprinkle the chariot with water from the "auspicious day" (puṇyāha) ceremony.

Having invoked and worshipped Brahmā on the pinnacle, Haṃsa at the solstice-mark, Ananta on the second floor, Vāsudeva in the vicinity of the neck, Takṣaka on the first floor, Garuḍa on the great pedestal, Indra and the other gods on the central pedestal, Vāyu in the wheels, and Vainateya in the chariot; having offered the oblation and presented the *bali* offering to Indra and the others, as well as to Kumuda and the rest; and having mounted the deity upon the chariot, one should perform the festival as before. Thereafter, having performed the morning festival for the deity...

In the afternoon, one should perform the immersion of the deity in a water-vat (*jaladroṇī*). Having placed a water-vat or a large cauldron on a heap of grain at the edge of a pond near a flight of stairs, having filled it with scented water, having scattered unbroken rice grains (*akṣata*) all around, and having had the declaration of an auspicious day (*puṇyāha*) recited; then, having strewn grass around [the vessel], having performed the rites of drying that water and so forth, and having invoked and worshipped the rivers such as the Gaṅgā and others therein; and having consecrated the water with mantras containing the word "water" (*abliṅga*), one should pray to the Deity.

"O Blessed One, lotus-eyed one, compassionate toward those who have sought refuge! O Lord, on this day you must perform a water-sport for the purification of all the worlds and for the delight of the gods, O All-pervading One. For that purpose, out of a desire to show me favor, you should undertake this procession. Having thus petitioned the God, having prostrated before Him, and having worshipped Him with the ritual services beginning from the seat of counsel and ending with the bath, while the sounds of musical instruments resounded, he entered the water there with the God, using mantras such as the Vāruṇa Sūkta and other hymns containing the syllable 'ap'.

Thereafter, having mounted [the deity] upon a vehicle and brought him to another pavilion, one should worship the Lord there as well until the conclusion of the oblation. Alternatively, on the eighth day, having performed the morning festival, one should then engage in the activity of hunting or enter a wooden water-vat. On that day, having mounted the Lord upon an elephant or a mechanical horse, equipped with weapons, ornaments, and armor appropriate for the hunt—

Having led [the deity] clockwise around the village boundaries and other sites, either together with or without the two goddesses and the troops of elephants and so forth; having brought the deity to the garden pavilion; having seated him there in the center upon a golden throne; having performed worship preceded by bathing; having seated him on another seat; having offered the great oblation (mahāhavis); having mounted him onto the vehicle; and having led him into the interior of the temple that night—thereafter, one should perform the daily festival (nityotsava).

Having made the formal resolve (*saṅkalpa*) at the latter part of the night, "I shall perform the ritual sowing of sprouts (*aṅkurārpaṇa*) for the sake of the pilgrimage site," and having performed the invocation (*āvāhana*) according to the rules and worshipped the deity, one should recite this verse: "O God, Lord of the Suras, you must undertake the journey to the pilgrimage site tomorrow; you ought to grant permission for the commencement of the *pratisarā* there. Having thus informed [the deity], one should invoke [the deity] from the root-mantra into the image of the pilgrimage site.

Having bound [the thread] to a sacred image at a pilgrimage site (*tīrtha*), or in its absence to a permanently installed festival image (*nityotsavabimba*), or in its absence to the bathing image (*snānārcā*), or in its absence to the festival image (*utsavabimba*); having performed the preliminary consecration (*adhivāsa*) over a heap of grain according to the rules as before; then, having performed the festival (*utsava*) in the morning; thereafter, having raised the image that was lying down and placed it upon the bathing throne (*snānapīṭhikā*) in the bathing pavilion (*snānamaṇḍapa*); and having taken the jars (*kumbha*) placed on the grounds of the sacrificial pavilion (*yāgamaṇḍapa*), one should carry them around the temple (*dhāma*) clockwise accompanied by the chanting of the Vedas.

Having placed the deity upon a heap of grain in the vicinity of the image at the sacred ford (tīrtha), and having first bathed the deity with the preliminary rites of the mantra-seat (mantrāsana); thereafter, at an auspicious moment (sumuhūrta), the preceptor (guru) shall bathe [the deity] with the established pitchers—starting from the eastern one and ending with the central one—while reciting the root-mantra (mūlamantra) and while the chanting of the Vedas proceeds; and having honored [the deity] with the services beginning with garments and ending with lamps; if, however, the rite of the single image (ekaberavidhāna) is performed, all of this should be done to the primary image (mūlabimba). Thereafter, as before, one should perform the powder-bath (cūrṇasnāna) for the deity according to the prescribed rule.

Having praised the deity, circumambulated him, prostrated with the eight-limbed salutation (*aṣṭāṅga-praṇipāta*), and scattered a handful of flowers; thereafter, having placed the image upon a vehicle adorned with auspicious ornaments, and having brought it—preceded by the sacred image and accompanied by the ritual wheel, along with parasols, banners, yak-tail whisks, lamps, and the sound of musical instruments—to the ocean, a river, or a lake; and having settled it upon a seat at a water-stall on that shore.

Having first established twenty-five, seventeen, or nine jars according to the prescribed rule, filled with their respective substances; having worshipped them; having performed the drying out of the waters of rivers and other sources; having caused the proclamation of an auspicious day (*puṇyāha*); having sprinkled [the site]; having invoked and worshipped the rivers such as the Gaṅgā and others there, and having offered oblations; having fully worshipped the image of the sacred ford (*tīrtha-bimba*) preceded by the ritual of the mantra-seat (*mantrāsana*); and having bathed the jar according to the prescribed rule.

Having sprinkled the Cakra with the remaining water, and having sprinkled the Tīrtha image—which has been brought forth as an auspicious token—with water from a river or other source using the *kūrca* grass-bundle; the Guru, placing that image upon his head in the presence of the auspicious token—or in its absence, placing either the Cakra or the *kūrca* there—should immerse himself in the water while reciting the Cakra-mantra. Then, at that very moment, the Guru should remove the protective threads from the images and from himself, casting them into the water.

Thereafter, having brought the Deity into the pavilion and worshipped Him as before, one should place Him upon the vehicle and lead Him into the interior of the temple. That night, having led the Deity into the pavilion and worshipped Him according to the rules, one should offer abundant food. "O Lord, O Lotus-eyed One, who art affectionate toward those who have sought refuge! From the commencement of the sprout for the flagstaff until the final concluding bath of the festival—whatever rite has been performed by me for Your great pleasure, O All-pervading Lord, as well as that which has been performed by other preceptors authorized by me; [may all this be accepted]."

"O Lord, for the sake of fulfilling those various requirements and for the pacification of deficiencies or excesses, we—along with practitioners and other diverse attendants—are prepared today to worship You who abide in the four stations. Grant us permission to proceed, desiring Your grace. Having thus informed the Lord of Gods and obtained His permission, they then, at dawn, in the pavilion frequented by devotees and followers of the Bhagavata tradition, mentally conceived upon the ground a lotus-diagram (cakrābja) complete with its enclosures according to the prescribed method.

Having decorated [the area] according to the rules with various colored flowers such as *tulasī* and others, and having placed the radiant [image] there upon an auspicious seat (*bhadrapīṭha*), and having fastened the auspicious marriage-thread (*kalyāṇakautuka*) upon it, one should worship the Blessed One with the twelve-syllable mantra after honoring Him with the water-offering (*arghya*) and other rites, while the chanting of the Vedas and the sounding of musical instruments proceed in all directions. [The mantra is: *Oṃ*, the twelve-syllable mantra.

The sages are Parameṣṭhin, Sananta, Sanaka, Prajāpati, Bhṛgu, Sanatkumāra, Pulastya, Pulaha, Kratu, Marīci, Atri, and Āṅgīrasa. The meters are Gāyatrī, Bṛhatkṣetra, Prajāpati, Triṣṭubh, Paṅkti, Bṛhatī, Virāj, Vaṣṭha, Trivatsaka, Uṣṇik, and Śrī. The twelve deities begin with Viṣṇu and end with Govinda.

The principles (tattvas) are consciousness, the individual soul, primordial nature, intellect, mind, and the qualities of sattva, rajas, and tamas, along with ether, fire, air, and water. The sacred fields (kṣetras) are the Supreme Ether, Vāyu, Agni, Jala, Satya, Tapa, Jana, Maha, Svarga, Bhuvar, Bhūr, and Pātāla. Their colors are white, black, smoky, dark, coppery, crystal-like, conch-white, red, pale, crimson, dark, and yellow. Having meditated upon Hari in each of these twelve syllables respectively.

Having worshipped the auspicious *kautuka* with the nine services beginning with *arghya* and ending with *bhūṣā*, and having also addressed the limbs beginning with the heart (*hṛdaya*) with flowers, one should conclude with the mantra: "By these flowers may there be fruit for me; obeisance to the flowers. Then, addressing the ornaments such as the *śrīvatsa* and *kaustubha*, the divine weapons such as the discus (*cakra*) and others in their proper order, the deities stationed in the enclosures (*āvaraṇa*), the ten forms beginning with Viṣṇu, and the forms beginning with Keśava, one should worship them with their respective mantras.

Having offered flowers at the feet with the *Puruṣasūkta*, the *Nārāyaṇānuvāka*, the *Viṣṇusūktas*, and the mantras of the five Upaniṣads; having thus gratified the God with white and other flowers; and having presented the four kinds of food; one should kindle the fire in the southeast corner of that pavilion and offer oblations one hundred and eight times for each of the following—fuel sticks, clarified butter, sacrificial porridge (*caru*), and the four kinds of food such as milk-rice—with the root mantra. Then, one should circumambulate the God.

Having offered praise, prostrated on the ground like a staff, placed the deity upon the auspicious palanquin, and brought it to the first enclosure (prathamāvaraṇa), he remained there. Having dismissed Brahmā and the other deities, the devotees, the Bhāgavatas, and other Vaiṣṇavas who had come for service to return to their respective abodes, he circumambulated that enclosure. Leading the deity back inside the temple, he seated the Lord upon the bathing throne in the pavilion during the first watch of the night of that day.

Having performed the ritual bathing appropriate for the conclusion of the festival according to the rules, and having led [the deity] into the interior of the pavilion, the Guru reaches the sacrificial hall (*yāgamaṇḍapa*). Having performed the fire-oblation (*homa*) there according to the rules, and having offered a thousand or a hundred oblations of clarified butter with the five *upaniṣad* mantras for the sake of expiation (*prāyaścitta*)—in accordance with the previously mentioned procedure—and having then offered the final oblation (*pūrṇāhuti*) and dismissed the fire; and having bid farewell to the deities in the archways (*toraṇa*) and other locations as well as the one situated within the mandala; he approaches the flagstaff (*dhvajastambha*).

Having worshipped the Lord of Birds (Garuḍa) and performed a circumambulation, he should, by means of the process of reabsorption (*saṃhārakrama*), cause [the deity] to descend into the water-pot (*kumbha*) and fix it within the primary vessel (*mūlabherī*). Then, at the very presence of the auspicious festive banner, having lowered the flagstaff in the dead of night, the Guru himself should take hold of both the pillar and the banner. Thereafter, in each respective place, he should offer oblations (*bali*) to the deities who have been invoked, accompanied by the sounds of musical instruments and silent attendants, doing so once for each location.

Having performed the ritual dismissal (*udvāsya*) with the respective mantras of their own names, the preceptor (*guru*), while muttering the eight-syllabled mantra (*aṣṭākṣara*), enters the abode of the deity. Having informed the deity [of his intention], he places the deity upon a vehicle such as a cart. Having brought the festive icon (*makhakautuka*) into the abode, having worshipped it, and having joined its power (*tacchakti*) with the primary image (*mūlabimba*), he worships the primary image. Having offered praise, prostrated, made a request, and performed circumambulation (*pradakṣiṇa*), he should enter his own home. The patron (*yajamāna*) also, having satisfied the preceptor with wealth consisting of living beings and life-essences (*jīvajīvātma*) according to what satisfies his mind, [should likewise enter].

In the same manner, having prostrated before the other image-protectors (*mūrtipā*) and attendants, and having placed [the deity] upon that vehicle together with all ornaments, one should perform a circumambulation of the village and bring [the deity] to that house. Thus ends the thirty-fourth chapter, titled "The Procedure for the Great Festival," in the *Kriyākairavacandrikā* composed by the venerable Guru Varāha.
The Thirty-fifth Chapter:
The Procedure for Renovation (*jīrṇoddhāra*).

Now, the procedure for the restoration of a dilapidated image (*jīrṇoddhāra*) is described. In the case of images made of the four materials—self-manifested (*svāyaṃbhū*), divine (*ārṣa*), celestial (*divya*), and human (*mānuṣa*)—or those made of precious gems (*ratnaja*), if there is a deficiency in any limb, that specific limb must be restored using refined gold (*tapanīya*); its removal is not appropriate. The same applies to images made of stone (*śailaja*). In the case of the five types of images made of wood and so forth, if they have deficient limbs, one should discard those parts and create them anew. Whether creating the entire image or merely restoring a missing limb, one should invoke its power (*tacchakti*) into the ritual pitcher (*kumbha*).

Having fashioned [the image] as before, one should perform all the rites such as the water-consecration (*jalādhivāsa*) and so forth, just as in the case of a formal installation (*pratiṣṭhā*). If the meditative absorption (*samādhi*) can be maintained while the images are in the states of standing, sitting, reclining, or mounted [on a vehicle], then their abandonment is not appropriate. A metal image that has been abandoned should be melted down and fashioned again. If the goddesses remain in their proper positions during a re-creation after the [original] goddesses have decayed, the deity should be joined with those very same [images]; one should not fashion others. When worship toward them is continuous, a remarriage (*udvāha*) should not be performed.

In the event of a deficiency or displacement of the radiance (*prabhā*), the lotus-seat (*padmāsana*), the weapons (*āyudha*), and so forth, or if the image becomes unsettled, one should withdraw (*udvāsya*) that power (*śakti*) from the primary image (*mūlabimba*) or the vessel. Having restored those items to their original positions and consecrated them according to the ritual rules (*yathāvidhi*), one should again invoke (*samāvāhya*) that power into the image and worship it. Having constructed a house for the child (*bālageha*), one should invoke the power from worn-out stones and other materials therein and worship it. After the restoration, one should then again invoke [the original power] and worship it.

In that case as well, one should join together those suitable for joining; however, those unsuitable should be cast either into the earth or into water. When the temple is dilapidated and accompanied by its own attendants, one should worship the deity in the childhood chamber (bālaveśmana) just as before. When the permanent image (dhruvabimba) has become worn out while the temple remains intact, one should install the deities and their attendants residing therein into the primary image (mūlabimba). When the temple is worn out but the permanent image remains intact, the removal (udvāsa) of the deities residing there must not be performed elsewhere.

If the temple or other structure is not yet completed and is free from defects such as structural weakness (aṅgabhaṅga), no further construction should be undertaken. If one were to rebuild it, self-destruction would result. Previously, if a temple or similar structure was built without the correct proportions, one should construct it again in accordance with the prescribed characteristics when rebuilding. In the case of multiple images or a single image, one should build exactly as before; if one acts contrary to this, a great fault ensues. If the previous multi-image shrine was without the two goddesses, at the time of subsequent construction, one may include them or exclude them.

In the case of non-human [icons], if the image and so forth were previously devoid of the [thirty-two] marks, then even in a renovation, it must be exactly the same and not otherwise. Furthermore, regarding the seats, beds, and vehicles of non-human images, they should remain exactly as they were before during a renovation. In the case of human [images], however, there is no fault in creating them anew according to one's desire. A divine chariot, whatever its former substance, measurement, or appearance may have been, must be exactly like that upon reconstruction and not otherwise.

Whether the dwelling is of the sages (*ārṣa*), of humans (*mānuṣa*), made of bricks (*aiṣṭaka*), or made of clay (*mṛṇmaya*), if it is dilapidated and is to be reconstructed, it should be done with stone or brick. There is no fault in adding [materials] on the exterior for the protection of the already constructed bases (*upapīṭha*) and other parts. If the *sāla*, gate-towers (*gopura*), bases, and so forth have shifted or become worn out, one should make them firm and spacious with stones, or otherwise as required. If a temple or similar structure is damaged by the force of river water and the like, one should reconstruct it again in another location where it is free from such affliction.

In the first conception, those authorized for the installation of the embodied mantra are of such a kind, and likewise in the second conception; it is not otherwise. Regarding the sanctuaries and so forth, the fruit is exactly the same in the initial construction as well as in the restoration of what is dilapidated (*jīrṇoddhāra*). In that case, one should not effect a change in the form of the image. However, when restoring only parts of the many-limbed [image] that have become worn, one should—just as in the case of consecration (*pratiṣṭhā*)—place the ritual image (*karmārcā*) upon the altar (*vedī*), lay it upon the bed, and then proceed.

One should perform all rites except for the preliminary consecration in water (*jalādhivāsa*), the opening of the eyes (*nayanonmīlana*), and the dissolution and generation of the principles (*tattvasaṃhāra-utpādana*). Now, the procedure for the installation of a small shrine (*bālālaya-pratiṣṭhā*) is described: the preceptor (*ācārya*), together with the patron (*yajamāna*), having personally invited Vaiṣṇavas who are learned in all the Śāstras, Vedas, Āgamas, and Purāṇas, as well as Brāhmaṇas; having prostrated before them and requested their presence; having fed them; having honored them with gold ornaments, garments, perfumes, betel, and other offerings; and having circumambulated them— [The text continues with the ritual sequence.]

Having prostrated and meditated upon Vāsudeva with palms joined in reverence, one should petition him thus: "This image of Viṣṇu was formerly installed by the wise; yet, while it is being worshipped, O Lord, a defect of physical impairment has arisen here. We now resolve to undertake the effort to restore this worn-out image, acting in accordance with the sacred scriptures, so that it may be employed in the worship of the God without reproach."

Just as incense, flowers, and so forth are later disparaged as *nirmālya* (remnants), so too a worn-out image is employed for worship and subsequently that worn-out image is disparaged as *nirmālya*. "I now desire to perform the removal (*uddhāra*) of this image; may you grant us your permission, for I shall act according to your command. Having thus made his request.

Having been authorized by them, one should offer a hundred thousand, a thousand, or one hundred and eight oblations of *dūrvā* grass mixed with honey at the top of the palace while reciting the *vyāhṛtis*. Having performed the *śānti-homa* with the five *upaniṣad* mantras, and having had the *puṇyāha* and *śānti* proclaimed by the Brahmins, one should pay obeisance to the Guru preceded by the surrender of oneself (*ātmasamarpaṇa*). Then, having given the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*), one should prepare an image made of metal or wood, endowed with the previously mentioned characteristics.

Having performed the rites such as the consecration in water (*jalādhivāsa*) within the pavilion, one should prepare an altar (*vedikā*) in the previously mentioned location—made of brick, wood, or clay according to the dimensions of the temple (*vimāna*), one cubit in height, and provided with a pericarp and petals. Having placed the preliminary image (*bālabimba*) upon it and having performed the formal installation (*pratiṣṭhā*) on the following day, one should enter the main temple at night on the day after that, worship [the deity] in due order with ablutions and other rites, and perform the binding of the protective thread (*rakṣābandhana*).

Having performed the *śāntihoma* as before in the four directions of the temple, one should prepare a sacrificial mound (*sthaṇḍila*) in front of the ritual image (*karmārcā*). Having placed a great jar (*mahākumbha*) made of either metal or clay, along with eight smaller jars (*kalaśa*) arranged around it; and having fashioned for them golden lotuses provided with eight petals of the prescribed size, together with threads, cloth covers, and tufts of grass (*kūrca*), as well as unhusked rice; one should then invoke the deities beginning with Indra into the great jar and the other jars using the root mantra from head to base, and worship them.

The preceptor should lie down to the north of the water-pot. Then, having bathed at dawn, the Ācārya, having approached the child’s house and performed worship, having purified [the site] by way of the dissolution and emergence [of the cosmic cycles], and having mentally conceived the Yoga-pīṭha, should utter this verse: "O Janārdana, for how long a time shall you remain in this temporary abode? O Lord of Gods, dwell in this constructed temple of the child. From this day forward, O Lord of Gods, until the end of twelve years, O Master, Vāsudeva permits no others—such as Keśava and the rest—to reside here."

Thus, with a joyful mind, having bowed to the Lord and joined his palms in reverence, he should utter this: "O Blessed One, Lord of the gods of gods, wielder of the conch, discus, and mace! O Lord of gods, I desire to construct a temple for the lowly and a beautiful image; therefore, you should deign to grant me permission. Having thus requested in his mind, the preceptor, acting as the patron, should slowly inform [the deity] at the proper time, invoke [the deity] into the great pitcher (mahākumbha) with the five mantras, and cause [the deity] to emerge with the syllable Om (praṇava).

Having circumambulated the temple and the house of the child, and having placed a large water-pot (mahākumbha) before it; having requested the Brahmins for permission and informed them of the time; having sprinkled the image with the water from the large pot while reciting the five Upanishadic mantras; then, having prostrated to and worshipped the Deity; having offered the sacrificial oblation (bali) at the corners of the temple; having adorned the image and caused the declaration of an auspicious day (puṇyāha) to be recited; and having performed the ritual placement (nyāsa) of emanation and reabsorption, he should worship [the deity] with perfumes, flowers, and other offerings.

While the Brahmins were chanting Vedic and Tantric mantras, the Guru—wearing a turban and adorned with ornaments—took a golden plow. Having released the binding of the pedestal with the root mantra, and having meditated upon Viṣvaksena while regarding the image or the temple as being like discarded floral offerings (nirmālya), he covered it with cloths, bound it with a rope accompanied by the *vyāhṛtis*, and lifted it up. Together with the sounds of musical instruments, the Ācārya placed it either on the ground or in water. Then, having bathed according to the rules, he entered the temple.

Having had the declaration of an auspicious day (*puṇyāha*) recited; having offered oblations (*bali*) on all sides; having dismissed the deities residing in the house; having caused cows to stay there; having dug [the ground], filled it with sand after removing [the earth]; and having performed a protective fire-sacrifice (*rakṣā-homa*) at the top of the palace—having thus caused the Brahmins to recite the *Ṛgveda* in the west, the *Sāmaveda* in the north, the *Yajurveda* in the east, and the *Atharvaveda* in the southern direction—and having thus performed the peace-offering (*śānti-homa*).

On the fourth day, having performed the ceremonial bathing (*snapana*) of the image or the temple and so forth, one should hold a festival at its conclusion, ending with a flower sacrifice (*puṣpayāga*). The patron (*yajamāna*), having given the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) to the preceptor (*guru*) according to the rules, and having completed the original shrine or the image according to the rules, should perform the consecration (*pratiṣṭhā*) according to the rules. Thus ends the thirty-fifth chapter, titled "The Procedure for Restoration" (*jīrṇoddhāravidhi*), in the *Kriyākairavacandrikā* composed by the venerable Varāhaguru.
The Thirty-sixth Chapter: The Procedure for Consecration by Sprinkling (*saṃprokṣaṇavidhi*).

The procedure for ritual sprinkling (saṃprokṣaṇa) is now described: [it is required] for a temple, when there is a fracture of its limbs or other parts, or upon its reconstruction; for a new and auspicious [structure]; for an image, its pedestal, its halo, and its weapons; when worship has been interrupted; O Lotus-seated One, when the site is concealed; and in cases of weeping, sweating, trembling, or even falling [of the image]; upon the emergence of anthills and the like; when defiled by rain, wind, and so forth; upon contact with those born of illicit unions (kuṇḍa-golaka); by those who sell the Vedas; upon being touched by those of inverse castes (pratiloma) and others condemned for their perpetual impurity.

In a house defiled by contact with those born of inverse or natural unions, such as Sūtas and Rathakāras; by Vaikhānasas who worship the scriptures of Bhārgava; by Śaivas and other heretics (pāṣaṇḍas) tainted by the murder of a Brahmin and similar sins; by those afflicted with consumption, epilepsy, leprosy, and the like, or those undergoing penance for such; by women in their courses and others, including artisans, when touched; or in a dwelling defiled by contact with feces, urine, blood, or corpses; and likewise during birth or death, or when dogs, jackals, donkeys, and the like [enter].

When an image has been touched, when a confusion of tantras has occurred, and in other such circumstances, the rite of consecration by sprinkling (saṃprokṣaṇa) should be performed. If the temple and so forth, as well as the images and so forth, are not thus consecrated, then during worship, the kingdom, the sovereign, the subjects, and the abode of Hari shall become desolate, barren, and overwhelmed by calamities; furthermore, the conditions of life will consist mostly of famine, disease, strife, and death. Therefore, the consecration of the temple and other structures must be performed according to the prescribed rule.

The preceptor, having first collected the clay for that purpose and performed the rite of sowing seeds (*aṅkurārpaṇa*), shall on the following day cleanse the image, the temple, and the pedestal with pure water. Having caused the proclamation of an auspicious day (*puṇyāha*) to be made, he shall wash [the image] with the two water-related mantras, "Viṣṇornukam" and "Idaṃ viṣṇuḥ. Then, having adorned the sacrificial pavilion, he shall bathe [the deity] according to the prescribed rules using one of the superior methods of bathing, preceded by the proclamation of an auspicious day.

Having caused the proclamation of an auspicious day (*puṇyāha*) and having worshipped the door-arches, the water-pots (*kumbha*), and so forth; having prepared an altar (*vedikā*) in the center of the pavilion; having constructed a pedestal (*pīṭha*) covered with cloth at intervals, using twenty *bhāra* of rice, half as much of husked grain (*taṇḍula*), and half as much of sesame seeds; and having drawn a lotus in its center; having again caused the proclamation of an auspicious day; and having placed the great water-pot (*mahākumbha*) there, provided with thread, cloth, and other requisites.

Having fashioned a single image out of gold of the prescribed measure and having embedded the nine gems within it, one should cover it with the Astra-mantra. Having likewise placed a water-pot (karaka) to its south, and having arranged eight jars around it, one should construct a mandala to its north according to the rules. In that mandala, having prepared a bed as before with tiger-skin and other necessary materials, and having adorned it with canopies and the like, one should have the proclamation of an auspicious day (puṇyāha-vācana) performed.

There, having caused the Lord of Gods to lie down, having invoked the Supreme Self into the primary pitcher (*kumbha*), Sudarśana into the small vessel (*karaka*), and Viṣṇu and the others into the eight secondary pitchers (*upakumbha*), and having worshipped them—having performed the full worship up to the offering of food (*naivedya*)—and having kindled the fire in either a sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*) or on a sacrificial mound (*sthaṇḍila*), and having performed the *mūrtihoma* with fuel-sticks, clarified butter, and sacrificial porridge (*caru*) according to the rules using the root mantra and their respective mantras, and having performed the binding of the protective thread (*rakṣābandhana*) preceded by the declaration of an auspicious day (*puṇyāha*); then, at dawn, one should raise the image that was laid to rest.

Taking the established water-pots together with the image-makers (mūrtipās), and circumambulating the temple while accompanied by the sound of Vedic instruments, one should place them upon a heap of grain in front of the deity. Having caused the proclamation of a "day of merit" (puṇyāha) to be recited, and having taken water from the pots with a blade of *kūrca* grass, one should sprinkle the deity with the root mantra (*mūlamantra*), the five Upaniṣads, mantras containing the syllable *ap*, and other peace-mantras (*śāntimantras*). Then, one should worship according to the prescribed ritual, beginning with the offering of water for honor (*arghya*) and ending with the great oblation of food (*mahāhavir-naivedya*).

The patron, having given appropriate sacrificial fees (*dakṣiṇā*) to the preceptor, the image-makers, and the attendants, and having fed the Brahmins, should also give them sacrificial fees. Thus ends the thirty-sixth chapter, titled "The Ritual of Sprinkling" (*saṃprokṣaṇa-vidhi*), in the *Kriyākairavacandrikā* composed by the venerable Varāhaguru.
The thirty-seventh chapter:
The Ritual of the Offering of the Sacred Thread (*pavitrārohaṇa-vidhi*).
Now, the procedure for the *pavitrārohaṇa* (the offering of the sacred grass ring) is described.

To pacify the defects of deficiency or excess in all obligatory (*nitya*), occasional (*naimittika*), and optional (*kāmya*) rites, the *pavitrotsava* should be performed like the *pūrṇāhuti*. One should perform the *pavitrotsava* during the bright fortnights of the months of Śrāvaṇa, Āṣāḍha, Bhādrapada, and Āśvayuja, on the lunar days (*tithis*) of the twelfth, eighth, first, full moon, fifth, eleventh, thirteenth, or second; and under the asterisms (*ṛkṣas*) of Puṣya, Rohiṇī, Revatī, Bharaṇī, Svātī, Hasta, Punarvasu, and so forth.

Having brought together threads made by Brahmin maidens, or faultless cotton or silk threads, or even purchased ones; having washed them with pure water mixed with the powder of mudga beans and other grains; having dried them in the sun; having tripled them; and having done the same again with such [threads]; or having quadrupled them—whether from that [triple] amount or making them threefold; and having tripled those [quadruple] ones; and having done the same again with such [threads].

Having multiplied those [threads] by four, or else by three—having brought them to a state of fourfoldness—or having tripled them by three, or alternatively, having brought them to unity; having smeared the ground with cow dung; having fixed two stakes made from sacrificial wood there according to the prescribed measurements; and having, with the permission of the preceptor, had devotees of the Lord who are purified by bathing and skilled in that craft lay the threads there facing eastward—they should fashion the *pavitra* [sacred grass rings] so that they are worthy of being ornaments.

Having fashioned the first sacred thread (*pavitra*) for the primary image (*mūlabera*) and other images for the purpose of consecration (*adhivāsa*), measuring up to the navel, provided with one hundred and eight threads and thirty-two knots; and having likewise fashioned the measurements for the lotus-neck and the girdle of the mandala, the water-pot (*kumbha*), and the sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*); [one should fashion] the sacred threads for the wheel-lotus (*cakrābja*)—the outer rim, the spokes, the hub, and the pericarp—respectively with three hundred and four, two hundred, one hundred, and four hundred threads, and with twenty-seven, double that (fifty-four), quadruple that (one hundred and eight), and quintuple that (two hundred and seventy) knots.

Having fashioned the *pavitra* for the Mahākumbha with one hundred and eight threads and twenty-seven knots, and for the *karaka* with eighty-one threads and twenty knots; and for the images (*beras*), the *pavitras* known as Śrīvatsa, Kaustubha, Vanamālā, and Kirīṭa—measured respectively by the navel, the heart, the shanks, and the crown—with one hundred and eight, eighty, one hundred and eight, and four hundred threads, and with thirty-two, twenty-five, and the same number [of knots] respectively.

The *pavitra* (sacred threads) of the highest class and so forth have their limits at the knees, thighs, and navel, respectively, and are made with four hundred, three hundred, and two hundred threads; they possess one hundred and eight, eighty, and sixty knots, respectively. For the purpose of a necklace (*hāra*), there is one with three hundred threads and twenty-seven knots, and another with two hundred threads and thirty-two knots, having its limit at the navel. Furthermore, there is a *pavitra* with one thousand and eight threads and many knots, having its limit at the feet, which serves as the limit for the innate pedestal (*sahajapīṭha*).

The *prabhā-pavitra* (light-purifier) is provided with one hundred and eight threads and twenty-five knots, while the *pavitra* (purifier) itself has a length equal to those threads and is provided with numerous knots. Thus it is for all independent (*svatantra*) images; however, in the case of images belonging to other systems (*paratantra*), there are only the three superior types [of knots]. For the goddesses such as Śrī and others, it is exactly the same: they are provided with one hundred and eight threads and many knots. For the sacrificial fire-pit (*agnikuṇḍa*), there is a purifier for each girdle (*mekhalā*) made of twenty-seven, twenty-five, or twenty-two threads.

The girdles, boundary-markers, and purifiers should have knots according to their respective measurements; the vessels such as the *sruk* and *sruva* ladles should have many knots and boundary-lines made with twenty-five threads; and for all items such as the vessels for *arghya* and *pādya*, incense burners, bells, and rosaries, they should be provided with one hundred and eight strands and knots as desired, measuring twelve finger-breadths (*aṅgula*) each. Furthermore, for the retinues of Sena-īśa, Garuḍa, the deities of the directions, Brahmā (Druhiṇa), Durgā, Vināyaka, Rudra, and others, [the number] is one hundred and eight.

They are made of threads, provided with thirty-two knots, and measure one cubit; for Caṇḍa and the others, they consist of twenty-seven threads, with an equal number of knots, and of that same measurement.

Likewise, for the pitchers, archways, and so forth, the measurement of the pericarp of the *balipīṭha* (offering pedestal) should be similar. For the preceptors (*ācāryas*) and ascetics (*yatīs*), one should fashion the sacred threads (*pavitra*) with one hundred and eight strands, reaching as far as the navel; for the image-keepers (*mūrtipās*), worshippers, and Brahmins, with eighty-one strands; for the king, with one hundred and eight strands featuring many knots and according to his specific measurement; and for those who depend on him, as well as for Vaiśyas and others, with eighty-one and twenty-four strands respectively—having thus prepared the sacred threads like a sacred thread (*upavīta*).

Having filled [the interior] with gems such as jewels, pearls, and corals, and with metals such as gold; having tied knots shaped like conch shells, or resembling *dhātrī* fruits, or equal to pearls; having smeared the spaces between them with a paste of musk, saffron, camphor, sandalwood, and resin; or alternatively, having filled the knots with flowers such as *mallikā*.

Having delighted [the assembly] with night recitations and having thus prepared the purificatory substances (pavitrāṇi), he should arrange the pavilion as before, complete with a central altar and sacrificial pits (kuṇḍa). Having adorned it with arches, canopies, garlands of *darbha* grass, and other ornaments, and having procured all the implements for the sacrifice therein, he should perform the ritual sowing of sprouts (*aṅkurārpaṇa*) according to the rules on the third day of that seven-day or five-day period, or immediately, preceded by the formal declaration of intent (*saṅkalpa*).

Thereafter, the preceptor, having fulfilled his duties and observed a fast, shall enter the inner sanctum at the onset of night on the tenth day, accompanied by the image-keepers and the patron. Having worshipped the deity according to the prescribed rites with offerings such as *arghya*, and having prostrated before the deity along with them, he shall, with palms joined in reverence, recite this verse: "For the pacification of deficiencies and excesses, O Blessed One, this supreme investiture of the sacred thread (*pavitrāropaṇa*) is an act of worship capable of dispelling all evils and is the unsurpassed means for generating all forms of prosperity."

"I shall perform that which is enjoined by the ritual so that it may proceed without obstacle; therefore, I request your permission—grant me leave for that rite. Having thus informed the deity, he enters the pavilion from the temple. There, having spread *darbha* grass with the tips pointing eastward, he sits upon it facing east, fasting, with a concentrated mind, intent on recitation and meditation. Having passed the night in vigilance, on the following day at midnight, he should perform the rite of consecration (*adhivāsana*) according to the procedure to be described.

In the case of a single image (*ekabera*), however, after the ritual bathing (*snāna*), the protective thread (*kautuka*) is tied; in the case of multiple images (*bahubera*), the auspicious thread (*kalyāṇakautuka*) is tied. Then, having gone out to the pavilion (*maṇḍapa*), one performs the worship of the door-arches (*dvāratoraṇa*) preceded by the rite for an auspicious day (*puṇyāha*). Having stationed Brahmins learned in the four Vedas and others in the cardinal and intermediate directions, and while the sounds of musical instruments and auspicious chants proceed everywhere, the preceptor (*ācārya*) then takes the sacred vessels (*pavitrapātra*) and places them upon a heap of grain on the ground toward the northeast in the pavilion.

Having caused the proclamation of an auspicious day (*puṇyāha*), having purified the sacred threads (*pavitra*) by means of drying and other rites, having fumigated them with fragrant substances, having smeared them with a paste of musk and other ingredients, having scattered flowers over them, having wrapped those sacred threads in new cloth while holding them in one's hands, having displayed the discus-mudrā (*cakramudrā*), and having worshipped them with the weapon-mantra (*astramantra*); then, in the pavilion, having encircled the northeast direction with threads using the weapon-mantra, and having meditated upon a discus above the pavilion, a lotus on the ground, and maces at the doors.

There, having offered an oblation of black-gram rice (*māṣaudana*) in the cardinal and intermediate directions; and in the case of the *bahubera* [image], having placed the auspicious *kautuka* outside on the bathing seat; having bathed it according to the rules; having performed the services up to the end of the sacred thread (*upavīta*); having drawn the discus-lotus (*cakrābja*) on the altar; having worshipped it and established the auspicious *kautuka* upon the discus-lotus; and having presented the sacrificial food (*havis*); one should place the great jar (*mahākumbha*)—which possesses the proper characteristics—along with its water-pitcher (*karaka*) and eight subsidiary jars (*upakumbha*), upon a heap of grain within the pavilion.

In the midst of those [vessels], having consecrated the pedestal (pīṭha), one should invoke Vāsudeva and the others in the directions starting from the east, and Puruṣa and the others in those situated in the corners. Having invoked them, worshipped them, and fully honored them, one should kindle the fire in the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa). Having performed the preliminary consecration oblation (adhivāsa-homa) according to the rules with fuel-sticks, clarified butter, and sacrificial porridge (caru), and having collected the remnants (saṃpāta), one should sprinkle them into the vessels containing the sacred grass (pavitra) while reciting the *sparśa-mantra*.

In the case of a single image (*ekabera*), having performed the bathing and other rites upon the primary image (*mūlabimba*) without the auspicious thread-marking (*kalyāṇakautuka*), and having first applied the sacred threads (*pavitra*); in the case of multiple images (*bahubera*), having first performed the auspicious thread-marking and applied the sacred threads with the mantra "Idam Viṣṇuḥ" upon the pitchers, the potter’s wheel, the fire, and the lotus-mandalas; then, entering the main temple accompanied by all auspicious rites, having worshipped the primary image with water for the guest-offering (*arghya*) and so forth, and having applied the sacred threads with the previously mentioned mantra; and having done likewise for all the [subsidiary] icons.

Having surrounded the temple with the sounds of Vedic recitation and musical instruments, he spent that very night there in vigil. On the following day, having placed the deity situated within the mandala upon the bathing throne, and having bathed and adorned him, he drew the lotus-wheel (cakrābja) as before in the purified pavilion. Having performed the worship of the doors and other parts, and having worshipped the lotus-wheel, he established the auspicious image within it as before and honored it with the water for the guest (arghya) and other offerings.

Having worshipped the water-pot and other vessels, and having offered the four kinds of food, one should offer oblations into the fire with the four types of food beginning with milk-rice (pāyasa), reciting the Puruṣasūkta; and with rice, bamboo-shoots, sesame seeds, parched grain, flowers, agallochum, ghee, and sacrificial fuel-sticks, one should separately offer one hundred and eight oblations while reciting the root mantra.

At an auspicious moment, the preceptor takes the purificatory threads (*pavitra*) and, having separately adorned the discus-lotus (*cakrābja*) along with its limbs while reciting "This is Viṣṇu," he then fastens the purificatory threads upon the vessels—the water-pitcher (*kumbha*), the small jar (*karaka*), the sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*), the fire, the archway (*toraṇa*), the door-pitcher, and so forth. Thereafter, having circumambulated the deity situated within the mandala and entered the temple—which is encompassed by all auspicious things—he offers the oblation (*havis*) after the primary image has been worshipped with ritual bathing and other rites.

Having performed [the rite] likewise for the deities residing therein, such as Śrī and others, and having adorned the primary image (mūlabera) with the previously mentioned mantras and sacred threads (pavitra), and having done so for all images—both independent and dependent—thereafter, one should perform the investiture of the sacred thread (pavitrāropaṇa) for the deities beginning with Caṇḍa and ending with those on the offering pedestal (balipīṭha), as well as for Brahmā and the other deities, for Tārkṣya and Seneśa, and for other devotees of Viṣṇu, using either the Viṣṇu-gāyatrī, the mantra “idaṃ viṣṇuḥ,” or the eight-syllabled or twelve-syllabled mantras.

Thereafter, the preceptor, having entered the interior of the temple together with the image-keepers and the patron, fills his joined palms (*añjali*) with jewels, golden flowers, or simple blossoms; praises the deity with hymns; scatters the contents of his joined palms at the base of the deity’s feet; places the purificatory cloths (*pavitra*) made of linen and other materials—intended for human use—before the deity’s feet like flowers; and makes a formal request to the deity.

Having first taken for oneself the *pavitra* made of linen and other materials, and thereafter having distributed the *pavitra*s to the chief worshippers, the officiating priests (*ṛtvij*), the assistants, the other kings, their dependents, the Vaiśyas, and others; and having beheld the face of the God and touched His feet, one should recite this verse in private to pacify any deficiencies or excesses: "O Blessed One, Lord of the gods of gods, wielder of the conch, discus, and mace! This has been performed by me for the sake of fulfilling any transgressions committed during the year."

"Accept this worship from me out of a desire for the welfare of your devotees. I am not independent; I perform nothing except that which is ordained for my benefit. Rather, impelled by you, I do everything, being myself under no control. Therefore, may all omissions and other such lapses in my performance be forgiven. Having thus made his representation:

In the afternoon, having placed the deity upon a vehicle and the like, and having adorned it, one should perform a great festival with all ritual services while circumambulating the village. Every day, at the time of worship, one should sprinkle the sacred threads (*pavitra*) and offer them. Thus, for fourteen days, twenty-one, seven, three nights, or one night, one should constantly perform the great festival together with the door-worship and other rites. On the day of completion, one should perform the ritual dismissal (*udvāsana*) of those respective deities.

Having offered the purificatory materials with the *Pauruṣa Sūkta*, the *Rathantara*, the *Trisuparṇa*, or the root mantra; having performed the bathing ritual (*snapana*) for the deity and worshipped Him; and having first caused the teacher (*guru*) to receive the purificatory offerings, he should thereafter cause them to be given to the devotees. The patron (*yajamāna*), having satisfied the teacher with wealth consisting of both animate and inanimate objects, and having prostrated before him, should place him upon a vehicle and lead him to that temple accompanied by all auspicious rites.

Thus ends the thirty-seventh chapter, titled "The Ritual for the Great Festival of the Investiture of the Sacred Thread," in the *Kriyākairavacandrikā* composed by the venerable Varāhaguru; and with this, the *Kriyākairavacandrikā* is complete.
